# 1 Corinthians

## 1:1 Introduction
[Tilemann Heshusius, Explicatio Prioris Epistolae Pauli ad Corinthios (Jena, 1573). English: machine translation, The Faith Received (Mere Orthodoxy); the original follows each comment.]
ARGUMENT OF THE FIRST EPISTLE OF PAUL TO THE CORINTHIANS.

The Epistle of Paul written to the Corinthians does not contain any one single disputation, or the treatment of one argument, in the manner that the Epistle to the Romans and to the Galatians explain in order the article concerning the justification of man before God; and then concerning good works: But it treats various matters and questions. For here Paul reproves the various vices of the Corinthians: He responds to the various questions of the Corinthians: He corrects many abuses which had crept into the tender Church: He teaches how the gifts of the Holy Spirit are to be used in the Church: He exhorts the Corinthians to mutual and sincere love: He refutes the errors of false teachers by setting forth sound and salutary doctrine. Therefore, this Epistle can instruct us concerning very many controversies and articles.

The Apostle Paul had faithfully delivered the entire doctrine of Christ, the law and the Gospel, to the Corinthian Church: for he had remained at Corinth for a year and a half: Assiduously expounding the articles of faith, and the benefits of the mediator, as Luke testifies. Acts 18. Others also had taught in this Church, such as Sosthenes the ruler of the synagogue: Apollos the Alexandrian and Crispus. The ruler of the synagogue: Acts 18 & 19. So that the harvest of the Lord was plentiful in this city, and the Church frequent, just as the voice of Christ testifies to Paul: Do not fear, but speak, and do not be silent, Because I am with you, and no one will attack you to afflict you. Because I have many people in this city. But wherever the Son of God by the ministry of his Apostles and Pastors scatters the seed of his word, and gathers a holy Church for God, there Satan, the enemy of human salvation, with the greatest and tireless zeal sows his Tares: He stirs up the pursuits of contentions: He drives men to crimes: He deforms the Church with scandals: He scatters corruptions of doctrine: And in every way he tries to hinder the building up of the Church. The Church of the Corinthians has experienced these arts and assaults of Satan. For immediately after the departure of Paul, factions and schisms were born in it: So that they made some as authors of a sect, others as others. Many in the doctrine of the Gospel sought the display of wit, sharpness, wisdom, eloquence. But they judged the ministers ineptly and wrongly. For they did not consider the spiritual power and efficacy of the ministry; They did not weigh the Apostles sublime authority: They did not respect the faithfulness of the ministers and the diverse gifts of the Holy Spirit: But they only admired the external gifts of eloquence: And each one followed and extolled with praises him who had pleased his own ears the most. Some returned to the former vices of the Greeks, to pride, to φιλονειχείαν, to lusts, to drinking bouts, to confidence in their own intellect, to πλειονεξίαν. who while among the baptized had taken his stepmother as his wife. Others would openly commit fornication, as they had been accustomed to do before Baptism: Just as if religion were not hindered by this crime. Various disputes were also stirred up by the Corinthians concerning marriage, concerning Virginity, concerning things sacrificed to idols. Some thought it lawful for them to eat any food whatsoever: And with this opinion they approached the impious rites of the Heathens, and contaminated themselves with Idolatry: Others, more timid, not only avoided Heathen sacrifices and idols, but did not even dare to buy things sacrificed to idols in the meat market nor to attend the banquets of friends lest they be contaminated by things sacrificed to idols. There was also great ἀταξία in the administration of the Lord's supper, while the richer ones neglected the poor, and drank more liberally. In public assemblies they contended with the gifts of tongues. Finally, Satan had so deformed and troubled this Church established by the Apostle, that some teachers openly denied the resurrection of the dead.

Therefore, for these so great and so various wounds and diseases of the Church, the Apostle Paul attempts to heal in this Epistle. And just as there was not one kind of disease, so he does not apply remedies of one kind: But now he sharply rebukes them, now he faithfully instructs them: Now he uses the severity of discipline: Now he refutes and confutes corruptions. Moreover, the whole Epistle is full of reproofs, although here and there he intersperses the most wholesome doctrine of the Gospel concerning the benefits of the mediator.

The scope therefore of this whole Epistle is that the Apostle severely taxes the vices and errors of the Corinthians and exhorts them to concord, and the pursuit of peace, to the true fear of God, and mutual love, and that they may contribute all gifts and all labors to the glory of God and the edification of the Church, and that they may diligently protect the sound and incorrupt doctrine of the Gospel, and adorn it with every kind of piety and virtue.

1. In the individual chapters, however, he treats almost individual arguments. He begins the Epistle with a congratulation by which he commends the beneficence of God toward the Corinthian Church, which He adorned and instructed with most excellent gifts: And he not only congratulates the Corinthians on such illustrious gifts of wisdom, faith, eloquence, and knowledge of God: But he also consoles them, showing the constancy of the will of God toward them, who is to mercifully confirm them in this faith. With this intention, however, Paul prefaces this congratulation, so that he may demonstrate that he does not rebuke the Corinthians with the intention that he envies their gifts: But rather that he may instruct, excite, and warn them, so that they may use their gifts rightly and that they may be increased and confirmed in them. Then he exhorts the Corinthians to a sincere study of peace and concord, and that they should avoid dissensions and schisms. And because the fountain and root of all dissensions, schisms, and contentions in the Church is the pride of the human mind, and the admiration of one's own wisdom, eloquence, doctrine, and similar gifts: That he may pluck out this root, he condemns with a most grave sentence the darkness of the human mind, he shows how no true wisdom exists in man without the illumination of the Holy Spirit: That the human mind is so blind that it cannot know God by its own powers: And that God opposes the counsels of the wise: And he has revealed a doctrine altogether alien from the judgments of the wise, and has chosen for himself into the Church the weak, the foolish, and the abject, so that whatever is sublime in the world he might put to shame, so that no man might have any cause before God of boasting or exalting himself: But all boasting of wisdom, justice, and life might remain for our Lord Jesus Christ alone.

II. In his second Chapter he teaches by his own example that in the ministry of the Gospel human wisdom or eloquence is not to be displayed: Nor is one to serve the desires of men with plausible speech and

sweet: But the word of God must be preached in all humility: For the reason that human reason understands nothing of divine things: And the Gospel of Christ is the word of the cross, alien to carnal judgment and to all external splendor. And here he shows the distinction between the wisdom of the Spirit and the judgments or thoughts of the world: He teaches how horribly the whole nature of men is depraved: That it is occupied in the densest darkness of ignorance and the saddest gloom of folly and errors, so much so that it understands nothing of those things which are of the Spirit: That it cannot acknowledge God: But holds the entire word of God for folly. Those things, however, which the Holy Spirit has revealed in the word are heavenly wisdom.

III. In the third chapter he continues in the description of the weakness of the Corinthians: That they not only labor from nature with ignorance and errors; But also indulge in carnal affections: Wherefore they ought not to take up the crests of pride, but rather to think modestly and humbly of themselves, to acknowledge their weakness, and to invoke God assiduously for the increase of gifts. Then he teaches upon whom the efficacy of the word and the donation of salvation depends, namely not on the excellent gifts of the ministers, or eloquence, or sharpness, or dignity, or the position of the minister: But on the power of the omnipotent God: He warns that ministers are only instruments which God uses to gather the Church; God, however, of the ministers or by the voice of the Apostles, or of the Prophets, or of the Bishops, to kindle light and life in the heart and to work salvation. And therefore, one must look not to the ministers, but to God Himself. And lest anyone by his pride or obstinacy disturb the Church of Christ, he warns that the elect are the temple of the Holy Spirit.

IV. In the fourth chapter he teaches how miserable and wretched is the condition of the Apostles and of all pious pastors in the world: what dangers, calamities, exiles, and miseries accompany the ministry: for the Corinthians, boasting in the gift of eloquence, were hunting for worldly glory from the ministry, and one was preferring himself to another: just as if Christ had died and instituted the ministry of the Spirit for that reason, so that men might have an occasion for being proud and for petulantly exalting themselves above others. The Apostle therefore warns that the nature of the ministry is far different, namely, joined with the greatest miseries, wretchedness, poverty, contempt, and dangers: And the more sublime the office one performs in the Church, the more necessary it is for him to undergo heavier calamities, struggles, and dangers. Whence the Apostle: we were held in the world as καθαρματα καὶ περιψήματα. For by this condition and exercise Christ wished to fortify the Apostles and pastors, lest they should contend among themselves through ambition or pursue the pleasures of the world, or aspire to civil domination. V. In the fifth chapter he teaches that impure men and

those polluted by manifest crimes are to be separated from the society of the Church, lest the other members of the Church be infected by their contagion and the name of God be blasphemed by public scandal. Therefore, he delivers to Satan the incestuous man who, after his father had died, had taken his stepmother as a wife, and the Apostle commands that the Corinthians should so avoid the society and company of all fornicators, idolaters, and impure men, that they should not even take food with them, provided that they have given their name to Christ and yet pollute themselves with crimes devastating the Church.

VI. In the sixth chapter he reproves the lawsuits and quarrels of the Corinthians, because they contend in the forum before an ethnic judge, and do not rather settle their controversies peacefully among themselves. Then he reproves those who, under the pretext of liberty, were openly fornicating and polluting themselves with various crimes. And he hands down the rule that no one is an heir of eternal life who pollutes himself with external crimes, such as lusts, injustice, idolatry, theft, drunkenness, and the like.

VII. In the seventh chapter he explains the doctrine concerning marriage: and he responds to the various questions of the Corinthians. For the Corinthians were debating:

1. Whether it is permitted to be celibate; or whether it is indeed necessary to become married.

2. To what extent a spouse ought to provide due benevolence to a spouse.

3. Whether it is free to desert a spouse for the sake of religion.

4. Whether divorce is to be made on account of dissimilarity of religion: Whether a pious husband is contaminated by the association of an impious wife. Even if the impious party makes a divorce, what is permitted to the innocent party.

5. Whether second marriages are lawful.

6. Whether circumcision, or uncircumcision, whether servitude, or lordship hinders religion. Whether circumcision is necessary for him who was converted from the Gentiles: Whether uncircumcision is necessary for him who was converted from a Jew. Whether it is lawful to be a slave: Whether it is lawful to be a master: Whether it is lawful to strive and contend for liberty.

7. Whether it is advisable to remain a virgin, or to become married.

8. What duty is incumbent upon a parent in giving daughters in marriage: Whether a parent is necessarily compelled to give a daughter in marriage: Whether it is not lawful to nourish her at home. Paul answers these questions in order, and shows what the will of God is in these matters.

VIII. In the eighth chapter he censures the abuse of Christian liberty and commands that no one be a stumbling block to the weak by a rash use of liberty. The Corinthians had heard that Christians were called in liberty and that idols were nothing. Under this pretext, some were eating things sacrificed to idols even with the scandal of the weak: and they were approaching ethnic sacrifices: in which they were contaminated by idolatry. He teaches, therefore, that liberty must be used rightly: And first, one must beware that we do not violate our conscience by consent to Idolatry: Next, that regard must also be had for the weak conscience.

IX. In the ninth Chapter, by his own example, he teaches that liberty in the use of external things, which are not eternal justice, is not to be abused: but rather that all things are to be bestowed upon the Church, and all actions of life are to be directed toward the illustration of the divine name and the propagation of the Gospel. He also treats the topic of providing food for the ministers of the word; and he admonishes both: that the Church, under the pretext of liberty, ought not to deny ministers their just and necessary stipends: nor ought ministers to be a burden to the Churches, or to seek wealth from the Gospel.

X. In the tenth Chapter, by the examples of the Church of the old testament, he proves that not an external title, but true piety is the certain argument that we are citizens of God elected to the fellowship of eternal life. And so, after various rebukes of vices, he appends a general admonition concerning the avoidance of carnal security, from which crimes of every kind are accustomed to spring. He intermixes, however, a notable consolation. That God is faithful and will not allow us to be tempted beyond our strength. Finally, he most gravely exhorts the Church to separate itself from all worship of Idols and not to approach the Ethnic sacrifices of idols, but rather to declare by its confession that it condemns them: And in the whole of life and in the use of liberty let him diligently consider what he may do to illustrate the glory of God, and to edify the Church.

XI. In the eleventh chapter he reproves ἀταξίας, which had crept into the Church in public assemblies. Men were praying with covered heads: Women with uncovered: In the administration of the supper the richer were drinking: the poor were neglected: He censures this confusion gravely and corrects it: And that he may restore the true use of the holy supper, he delivers the whole institution of the Lord's supper to the Corinthians with a most grave exhortation.

XII. In the twelfth chapter he teaches that the gifts of the Holy Spirit in the Church of Christ are various and diverse: And that as they proceed from one Spirit of God: so they are to be referred to one end, namely to the glory of God, and the edification of the Church. And he declares this by a similitude taken from the consent, offices, and concord of the members in the human body: He adds also that there are degrees both of offices and of gifts in the Church; as it pleased the Lord to distribute his gifts to each one. Therefore, that everyone ought to apply himself to this, that in that place in which he has been placed by God, and with his gift which he has received from God, he may serve the Church faithfully and with fruit.

XIII. In the thirteenth chapter he reproves those who were abusing the knowledge of many languages for ostentation and pride. And he teaches that Love ought to shine forth in all gifts: Which if it is absent, all gifts, however excellent and splendid, are useless and pernicious to the Church.

XIV. In the fourteenth chapter: He shows in what order all things in the Church in public assemblies are to be administered: That one must not contend by the ostentation of gifts: That it is not to be permitted that many preach at the same time: That foreign languages are not to be used without interpretation: But that all things are to be performed decently and in order in the Church: That the holy scripture is to be interpreted in the popular language, with fruit for the Church: That the voice of the teacher is not to be disturbed by untimely interruptions: That those who have peculiar revelations of the Holy Spirit are to be heard.

XV. The whole fifteenth chapter is consumed in the treatment of the article concerning the resurrection of the dead, which he explains with an apostolic spirit, and demonstrates with most valid arguments: but he most gravely refutes the tricksters, who were attempting to overturn this goal of religion, and to lead it away from the eyes of the Church.

XVI. In the last chapter he exhorts the Church to the contribution of alms for the aid of the Jerusalem Church and commends Timothy to the Corinthians: He then concludes the Epistle with an admonition that they should watch and persist in the true faith and sincere love.

Latin:

ARGUMENTUM PRIMAE EPISTOLAE PAULI AD CORINTHIOS.

EPISTOLA Pauli ad Corinthios scripta non continet unam aliquam disputationem, aut unius argumenti tractationem, quemadmodum Epistola ad Rom: Et ad Galat: Articulam de iustificatione hominis coram Deo; Et deinde de bonis operibus ordine explicant: Sed materias & quaestiones varias tractat. Varia enim vicia Corinthiorum repraehendit hic Paulus: Ad varias quaestiones Corinth: respondet: Multos abusus qui in teneram Ecclesiam irrepserant corrigit: Quomodo donis Spiritus sancti in Ecclesia utendum sit docet: Ad mutuam & synceram dilectionem hortatur Corinthios: Errores falsorum doctorum refellit exposita sana & salutari doctrina. De plurimis igitur controversiis & articulis haec Epistola nos erudire potest.

Apostolus Paulus integram doctrinam Christi, legem & Evangelium fideliter tradiderat Ecclesiae Corinthiacae: sesquiannum enim haeserat Corinthi: Adsiduè exponens articulos fidei, & beneficia mediatoris, ut Lucas testatur. Act: 18. Docuerant & alii in hac Ecclesia, ut Sosthenes Archisynagogus: Apollo Alexandrinus & Crispus. Archisynagogus: Act: 18 & 19. Adeò ut copiosa fuerit messis domini in hac urbe, & frequens Ecclesia, quemadmodum vox Christi ad Paulum testatur: Ne metuas, sed loquaris, & ne sileas, Eò quod ego tecum sum, & nemo invadet te ut te adfligat. Quia populus multus est mihi in hac urbe. Ubicunque autem filius Dei ministerio suorum Apostolorum & Pastorum spargit semen sui verbi, & colligit Deo sanctam Ecclesiam, isthic summo & indefesso studio Satan salutis humanae hostis serit sua Zizania: Suscitat contentionum studia: Impellit homines ad scelera: Deformat Ecclesiam scandalis: Spargit doctrinae corruptelas: Et omnibus modis impedire conatur aedificationem Ecclesiae. Has Satanae artes & insultus, Corinthiorum Ecclesia est experta. Statim enim post Pauli discessum natae sunt in ea factiones & schismata: Ut alii alios facerent quasi sectae authores. Multi in doctrina Evangelii quaerebant ostentationem ingenii, acuminis, sapientiae, eloquentiae. De ministris verò ineptè & perperam iudicabant. Non enim considerabant vim et efficaciam ministerii spiritualem; Non expendebant Apostolorum sublimem authoritatem: Non respiciebant fidelitatem ministrorum & diversa Spiritus sancti dona: Sed tantum externa eloquentiae dona admirabantur: Et eum quisque maxime sequebatur, et laudibus efferebat, qui suis auribus plurimum Placuisset. Redierunt aliqui ad pristina graecorum vicia, ad superbiam, ad φιλονειχείαν, ad libidines, ad compotationes, ad confidentiam ingenii, ad πλειονεξίαν. Qui dum ex Baptizatis novercam suam duxerat in uxorem. Alii palam scortabuntur, ut ante Baptismum consueverant: Perinde ac si hoc scelere non impediretur religio. Variae etiam disputationes movebantur à Corinthiis de coniugio, de Virginitate, de Idolothytis. Alii existimabant licere sibi vesci quolibet cibo: Et hac opinione accedebant ad impia sacra Ethnicorum, & contaminabant sese Idolatria: Alii timidiores, non tantum sacrificia Ethnica et idola vitabant, sed ne in macello quidem Idolothyta emere nec ad amicorum convivia accedere audebant ne Idolothytis contaminarentur. Erat & magna ἀταξία in administratione coenae domini, dum ditiores negligerent pauperes, & largius potarent. In congressibus publicis donis linguarum certabant. Tandem adeo deformaverat ac turbanerat Satan hanc Ecclesiam ab Apostolo constitutam, ut aliqui doctores palàm negarent resurrectionem mortuorum.

His ergò tantis & tam variis vulneribus & morbis Ecclesiae mederi conatur Apostolus Paulus hac Epistola. Utque morborum non erat unum genus, ita nec unius generis remedia adhibet: Sed nunc acriter illos corripit, nunc fideliter eos erudit: Nunc severitate disciplinae utitur: Nunc corruptelas refellit atque refutat. Tota autem Epistola plena est oburgationibus, licet passim saluberrimam doctrinam Evangelii de beneficiis mediatoris interspergit.

Scopus ergò totius huius Epistolae est, quòd Apostolus severè taxat vicia & errores Corinthiorum & hortatur eos ad concordiam, & pacis studium, ad verum timorem Dei, & mutuam dilectionem, utque omnia dona & omnes labores ad gloriam Dei & aedificationem Ecclesiae conferant, utque sanam & incorruptam Evangelii doctrinam diligenter tueantur, eamque omni genere pietatis & virtutum ornent.

1. In singulis autem capitibus, fere singula tractat argumenta. Orditur Epistolam à gratulatione qua commendat Dei beneficentiam erga Corinthiam Ecclesiam, quam excellentissimis donis ornavit, & instruxit: Et non solum gratulatur Corinthiis de tàm illustribus donis sapientiae, fidei, eloquentiae & cognitionis Dei: Sed etiam consolatur eos, ostendens constantiam voluntatis Dei erga ipsos, qui eos clementer in hac fide sit confirmaturus. Hoc autem consilio praemittit Paulus hanc gratulationem, ut demonstret se non eo animo repraehendere Corinth: quod donis eorum invideat: Sed potius ut erudiat, excitet & moneat eos, ut donis suis rectè utantur eaque in ipsis augeantur & confirmentur. Deinde Corinthios hortatur ad syncerum pacis & concordiae studium, utque vitent dissidia & schismata. Ac quia scaturigo & radix omnium dissidiorum, schismatum & contentionum in Ecclesia est superbia humani ingenii, & admiratio propriae sapientiae, eloquentiae, doctrinae & similium donorum: Ut hanc radicem evellat, gravissima sententia condemnat tenebras humanae mentis, ostendit quàm nulla existat vera sapientia in homine absque illuminatione Spiritus sancti: Quòd adeò caeca sit mens humana ut propriis viribus Deum cognoscere non possit: Quodque Deus adversetur consiliis sapientum: Et patefecerit doctrinam prorsus alienam à iudiciis sapientum, & elegerit sibi in Ecclesiam infirmos, insipientes, et abiectos, ut quidquid in mundo sublime est pudefaceret ne ullus homo ullam haberet causam apud Deum gloriandi aut sese efferendi: Sed omnis gloriatio sapientiae, iustitiae & vitae soli Domino nostro Iesu Christo maneret.

II. In secundo Capite suo exemplo docet in ministerio Evangelii non esse ostentandam humanam sapientiam vel eloquentiam: Nec serviendum esse cupiditatibus hominum oratione plausibili &

suavi: Sed in omni humilitate praedicandum Dei verbum: Eo quod humana ratio de divinis rebus nihil intelligit: Et Evangelion Christi sit verbum crucis alienum à carnali iudicio & ab omni externo splendore. Atque hîc ostendit discrimen inter sapientiam Spiritus, & iudicia seu cogitationes mundi: Docet quàm horribiliter depravata sit tota hominum natura: Quòd in densissimis tenebris ignorantiae & tristissima caligine stultitiae atque errorum versetur, adeò ut nihil eorum intelligat quae sint Spiritus: Quòd non possit agnoscere Deum: Sed universum Dei verbum habeat pro stultitia. Ea verò quae Spiritus sanctus in verborevelaverit caelestis sit sapientia.

III. In tertio Capite pergit in descriptione infirmitatis Corinthiorum: Quòd non solum inscitia & erroribus laborent à natura; Verum etiam carnalibus adfectibus indulgeant: Quare non debeant cristas superbiae sumere, sed potius modeste & humiliter de se sentire, agnoscere suam infirmitatem & Deum pro incremento donorum adsiduè invocare. Deinde docet à quo pendeat efficacia verbi, & salutis donatio, nimirum non an excellentibus donis ministrorum, vel eloquentia, vel acumine, vel dignitate, vel loco ministri: Sed à virtute omnipotentis Dei: Monet ministros tansum esse organa quibus utatur Deus, ad colligendam Ecclesiam; Deum, autem ministrorum sive Apostolorum, sive Prophetarum, sive Episcoporum voce accendere lucem & vitam in corde & operari salutem. Ideoque non administros, sed ad ipsum Deum respiciendum esse. Ac ne quis sua superbia vel pertinacia turbet Ecclesiam Christi, monet electos esse templum spiritus sancti.

IIII. Quarto capite docet, quam sit misera & aerumnosa conditio Apostolorum & omnium piorum pastorum in mundo: quae pericula, calamitates, exilia, & aerumnae comitentur ministerium: Corinthii enim dono eloquentiae super bientes gloriam mundanam ex ministerio aucupabantur, & alius alii sese praeferebat: perinde ac si ideò mortuus esset Christus & ministerium spiritus instituisset ut haberent homines occasionem superbiendi, & sese supra alios petulanter efferendi. Monet igitur Apostolus longè diversam esse rationem ministerii, nimirum coniunctam cum summis aerumnis, miseriis, paupertate, contemptu & periculis: Et quò quis sublimiore munere fungitur in Ecclesia, hoc necesse est eum graviores calamitates, certamina & pericula subire. Unde Apost: in mundo tanquam καθαρματα καὶ περιψήματα habiti fuerunt. Hac enim conditione & exercitio Christus praemunire voluit Apostolos & pastores, ne ambitione inter se certarent aut voluptates mundi sectarentur, aut civilem dominationem adiectarent. V. Capite Quinto docet homines impuros &

manifestis sceleribus pollutos, à societate Ecclesiae esse separandos, ne ipsorum contagio alia Ecclesiae membra inficiantur & publico scandalo nomen Dei blasphemetur. Incestum igitur qui patre mortuo novercam suam duxerat in uxorem, Satana tradit, et iubet Apost: ut Corinthii omnium scortatorum, Idolatrarum, & impurorum hominum societatem & consuetudinem adeò vitent, ut ne cibum quidem cum eis capiant, nimirum si nomen dederunt Christo, & tamen polluunt se sceleribus vastantibus Ecclesiam.

VI. Sexto capite repraehendit lites & rixas Corinthiorum, quòd in foro coram iudice Ethnico contendant, et non potius inter se placide componant controversias. Deinde repraehendit eos qui praetextu libertatis palam scortabantur, & variis se polluebant sceleribus. Ac regulam tradit Neminem esse haeredem vitae aeternae, qui polluat se externis sceleribus, ut libidinibus, iniustitia, Idolatria, furto, ebrietate & similibus.

VII. Septimo capite exponit doctrinam de coniugio: & ad varias Corinthiorum quaestiones respondet. Disputabant enim Corinthii:

1. An liceret esse coelibem; an verò necesse esset fieri coniugem.

2. Quatenus coniunx coniugi debeat praestare debitam benevolentiam.

3. An liberum sit deserere coniugem causa religionis.

4. An propter dissimilitudinem religionis divortium sit faciendum: An pius maritus impiae uxoris consuetudine contaminetur. Etsi pars impia divortium faciat, quid liceat innocenti parti.

5. An secundae nuptiae sint licitae.

6. An Circumcisio, vel praeputium, An servitus, vel dominium impediat religionem. An ei qui ex gentibus esset conversus, necessaria sit circumcisio: An ei qui ex Iudaeo conversus praeputium sit necessarium. An liceat esse servum: An liceat esse dominum: An liceat niti & contendere ad libertatem.

7. An sit consultum manere virginem, an coniugatum fieri.

8. Quod officum incumbat parenti in elocandis filiabus: An necessariò cogatur parens elocare filiam: An non liceat domi alere. Ad has quaestiones Paulus ordine respondet, & ostendit quae sit Dei voluntas in hisce rebus.

VIII. Octavo capite taxat abusum libertatis Christianae & praecipit ne quis infirmis sit offendiculo temerario usu libertatis. Audiverant Corinthii Christianos in libertate vocatos esse & Idola nihil esse. Hoc praetextu vescebantur quidam Idolothytis etiam cum scandalo infirmorum: & accedebant ad sacrificia Ethnica: in quibus Idolatria contaminabantur. Docet igitur recte utendum esse libertate: Ac primùm cavendum esse ne nostram conscientiam Idolatriae consensu violemus: Deinde & infirmae conscientiae rationem habendam esse.

IX. Nono Capite suo exemplo docet non esse abutendum libertate in usu rerum externarum: quae non sunt iustitia aeterna: sed potius omnia largienda esse Ecclesiae, & omnes vitae actiones dirigendas esse ad illustrationem nominis divini & ad propagationem Evangelii. Tractat et locum de alimentis praebendis ministris verbi; Ac utrumque monet: Nec Ecclesiam praetextu libertatis debere denegare ministris iusta & necessaria stipendia: Nec ministros debere oneri esse Ecclesiis, aut ex Evangelio opes quaerere.

X. Decimo Capite Ecclesiae veteris testamenti exemplis, probat non externum titulum, sed veram pietatem certum esse argumentum quòd simus cives Dei electi ad societatem vitae aeternae. Itaque post varias repraehensiones viciorum subnectit generalem admonitionem de vitanda securitate carnali, ex qua omnis generis scelera scaturire solent. Admiscet autem insignem consolationem. Quòd fidelis sit Deus & non sinat nos tentari supra vires. Tandem gravissimè hortatur Ecclesiam, ut sese ab omni cultu Idolorum separet nec ad sacrificia Ethnica idolorum accedat, sed potius confessione sua declaret, se ea damnare: Et in tota vita & in usu libertatis diligenter cogitet quid faciat ad illustrandam dei gloriam, & aedificandam Ecclesiam.

XI. Undecimo Capite ἀταξίας repraehendit, quae in publicis congressibus irrepserant in Ecclesiam. Viri orabant tecto capite: Mulieres aperto: In administratione caenae ditiores potabant: pauperes negligebantur: Hanc confusionem taxat graviter eamque emendat: Et ut veram sacrae caenae usum restituat totam institutionem caenae dominicae cum gravissima adhortatione tradit Corinthiis.

XII. Duodecimo capite docet varia & diversa esse spiritus sancti dona in Ecclesia Christi: Atque illa ut ab uno spiritu Dei proficiscantur: ita ad unum finem nimirum ad gloriam Dei, & aedificationem Ecclesiae esse referenda. Idque declarat similitudine sumpta à consensu, officiis, & concordia membrorum in corpore humano: Addit & gradus esse cùm officiorum, tùm donorum in Ecclesia; prout domino placuit singulis sua dona distribuere. Unumquemque igitur in hoc incumbere debere ut eo loco, in quem à Deo collocatus est, & suo dono quod à Deo accepit fideliter & cum fructu Ecclesiae serviat.

XIII. Decimo tertio Capite repraehendit eos, qui cognitione multarum linguarum, ad ostentationem & superbiam abutebantur. Ac docet in omnibus donis elucere debere Dilectionem: Quae si absit, omnia dona quantumvis excellentia & splendida esse inutilia & perniciosa Ecclesiae.

XIIII. In decimo quarto Cap: Ostendit quo ordine omnia in Ecclesia in publicis congressibus sint administranda: Non ostentatione donorum certandum esse: Non permittendum esse ut plures simul concionentur: Non peregrinis linguis sive interpretatione esse utendum: Sed omnia decenter & ordine peragenda in Ecclesia: sacram scripturam lingua populari, cum fructu Ecclesiae interpretandam esse: Docentis vocem non esse turbandam intempestivis interpellationibus: Eos qui peculiares habent Spiritus sancti revelationes audiendos esse.

XV. Totum decimum quintum Caput consumitur in tractatione articuli de resurrectione mortuorum, quem apostolico spiritu exponit, & validissimis argumentis demonstrat: praestigiatores autem, qui hunc scopum religionis evertere, et ex oculis Ecclesiae abducere conabantur gravissimè refellit.

XVI. Ultimo Capite hortatur Ecclesiam ad contributionem Eleemosynae in subsidium Ecclesiae Hierosolymitanae & commendat Corinthiis Timotheum: Concludit deinde Epistolam admonitione ut vigilent & in vera fide & syncera dilectione persistant.

## 1:1 Argument
CHAPTER I.

Latin:

CAPUT I.

## 1:1-10
Paul, called an Apostle of Jesus Christ, through the will of God, and Sosthenes our brother, to the Church of God which is at Corinth, to those sanctified in Christ Jesus, called to be saints with all who in every place call upon the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, both theirs and ours.

Paul in all his Epistles ascribes his own name and makes mention of his Apostolic office: And he does this with this purpose, that it may be established in the Church of God, through which ministers and teachers this admirable doctrine, which he sets forth in his Epistles, was delivered and propagated: What kind of testimonies they had for their doctrine, by whom they were sent: Whence they proved that they were sent by God. For the Church does not embrace just any dogmas: Nor does it circulate uncertain fables: But it hears only those heralds whom it knows to have been sent by God: And to have indubitable testimonies that they profess saving truth. Therefore Paul testifies that he was called an Apostle through the will of God; As if he were to say: Not by my own rashness, or confidence of wit, did I break into this office or take upon myself the parts of teaching; But by the counsel and will of God I was sent to spread the light of the Gospel in the world, and call all men to repentance: He also confesses that he did not arrive at this sublime Apostolic office by his own merit, but by the divine will and clemency, since he was otherwise unworthy: As 1. Timoth: 1. he confesses that he was called to be an Apostle. He also signifies that he was not called by men in the common way: But immediately by Christ: So that we may know that his voice is to be received no differently than the voice of God himself sounding from heaven. For an Apostle is a Person immediately called by the son of God himself, our Lord Jesus Christ, to preach the Gospel of God in the world, and to be a witness of the doctrine, miracles, passion, death, and resurrection of Jesus Christ, not bound to a certain place: But sent into the whole world so that he may teach the Gospel everywhere, instructed with the gift of performing miracles, and of healing the sick, and adorned with the visible gift of the holy Spirit and the skill of various languages. Whence it is established that he does not err in doctrine, but brings the undoubted truth concerning the attainment of eternal salvation. Therefore, let us not read the Epistles of Paul as if they were those of some ancient writer, or of a famous Bishop: In which it is permitted to us to apply our own judgment and censure: And to examine individual points to see whether they agree with divine testimonies: But let us establish that these are mere heavenly oracles: Since the holy Spirit spoke through the mouth of Paul. Sosthenes, of whom he makes mention here Paul was the ruler of the Corinthian synagogue, concerning whom Luke Acto: 18. reports that he was almost oppressed by the Jews before the tribunal of Gallio, proconsul of Achaia, with Gallio caring nothing about it. Eusebius writes in book 1, chapter 12, that he was one of the 70 disciples of the Lord.

To the church of God which is at Corinth: Although the whole Epistle is full of rebukes in which he most severely censures the atrocious crimes of the Corinthians, the confusions, abuses, and errors: nevertheless, he does not detract the august name of Church from this assembly. For because he had preached the pure doctrine of the Gospel in that place, he does not doubt that God has His own there, who rightly call upon God, truly believe in the mediator, and are temples of the Holy Spirit: Neither the Epicureans who deform the Church with crimes, nor the hypocrites or heretics who mix themselves into the assembly of the pious, utterly cut off the Church: For the Church is forced to bear these as if they were cancers in the world. Therefore, the Anabaptists, Donatists, and Cathars err, who seek such a Church on earth in which there are no evil ones mixed with the good: And in which no schisms and scandals arise: For the evangelical net encloses good and bad fish, until the angels on the shore select the good from the bad. From this, therefore, let the definition of the Church be sought.

The Church is a visible assembly of those embracing the uncorrupted doctrine of the Gospel, and using the sacraments according to the institution of the Son of God, in which assembly the Holy Spirit is efficacious, and communicates righteousness, life, and salvation to believers: In which assembly there are many who are not holy, who nevertheless agree concerning the doctrine.

To them that are sanctified in Christ Jesus, called to be saints: By the term of sanctification he here embraces all the benefits of the mediator, as well justification as renovation. I write to you Corinthians, he says, who are sanctified through Jesus Christ, that is, who through Christ have received the remission of sins, are justified and reconciled with God, are adopted into the sons of God, and endowed with the Holy Spirit, who renews in you the image of God, kindles new light, righteousness, joy, and life: And these benefits you do not have from yourselves by free will or your own virtue, but through Jesus Christ the Mediator who by his blood obtained life for you, freely forgave sins, and poured the Holy Spirit into you: thus the word of sanctification is placed generally: 1. Corinth: 6: And such were some of you; But you are washed, but you are sanctified, but you are justified: Item, I sanctify myself for them that they also may be sanctified in the truth. Called to be saints: He wishes them to be always mindful, not only from whom they have been sanctified, namely by the gratuitous benefit of the Mediator Jesus Christ: But also through what medium they have arrived at this glory of sanctification, namely not by their own wisdom, talent, or virtue; But through the calling of the Apostles and ministers of Christ: Let not the Saints be understood as ἀναμάρτητοι who are without any stain of sin at all: But saints imputatively and inchoatively: For to those believing in Christ the entire righteousness and holiness of Christ is imputed: Then the Holy Spirit is communicated to them who begins true holiness in them: But the filth which remains in the saints is covered by the shade of Jesus Christ: But believers will be adorned with perfect holiness in the future life.

With all who call upon the name of our Lord Jesus Christ. And if Paul addresses the Corinthians especially in this Epistle, as those who on account of dissensions and other vices were in need of this grave castigation: Nevertheless, because he understands that the Churches in all times and places are in need of this admonition and instruction, he proposes and commends this Epistle to the universal Church. Moreover, by a notable mark he distinguishes the true Church from the impious assemblies of the nations and idolaters. The true Church, he says, is that in which the true knowledge of God shines, and which calls upon the name of our Lord Jesus Christ; therefore, the nations that call upon Jupiter, Mars, and other idols are not the Church. Nor are the Turks or Mahometans the Church of God: because they do not call upon the name of our Lord Jesus Christ. But because the Apostle testifies that the universal Church in all places calls upon the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, he confirms that Jesus Christ is eternal and all-powerful God. In every place of his and ours: The Church of Christ is not included or bound to one and some certain place; For the Father gave to the Son all the ends of the earth as a possession; therefore, in the whole world, in all nations, Jesus Christ gathers for himself a holy Church by the ministry of the word: Go, he says, into the whole world and preach the Gospel to every creature: The earth is the Lord's and all its fullness. Therefore, wherever two or three are gathered in the name of Jesus, there is the Church: in which dwells Christ the King and Priest. Therefore, the Roman Pontiff errs, who pretends that the Church is bound to the Chair of Peter which is at Rome, and condemns all Churches which do not acknowledge the Roman Pontiff as the visible head of the Church.

In this subscription and inscription these heads of doctrine are to be observed.

1. That one must not run without a calling with a rash daring: but that a certain calling must be awaited, by which God commands that we teach the Church.

2. Concerning the double calling, mediate and immediate, of the Apostles.

3. The third place is concerning the benefits of the mediator, which are comprehended by the word of sanctification.

4. The fourth: Concerning the Church, what and of what kind it is, by what mark it is recognized, namely by the acknowledgment and invocation of Jesus Christ, and that it is bound to no place: but that it is gathered in the whole world.

5. Fifth. Concerning the divinity of Jesus Christ, inasmuch as He is invoked by the universal Church dispersed throughout the whole world, at all times and in every necessity.

Grace to you and peace from God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ.

Grace signifies the gratuitous favor of God, the mercy and clemency by which He freely, without our compensation and merit, remits sins, accepts us into grace, and pronounces us righteous and heirs of eternal life.

Peace signifies spiritual and corporal benefits; namely, the gift of the Holy Spirit, the peace of conscience, new righteousness and life, joy in God, the inheritance of eternal life: furthermore, defense, nourishment, governance, consolation, and all the goods of which we are in need both in this life and in the future life. When Paul wishes all these things for the Church in the Spirit, he certainly also promises them: just as Christ also testifies: Whatever you ask the Father in my name, He will give to you. Moreover, it is certain that these goods, both spiritual and corporal, are not to be sought from pagan deities, from Jupiter, Mars, Pallas: nor from papistic idols, from Peter, Paul, Anne, Odile, Christopher: but from God the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, who alone and one is God: whom alone, and one, it behooves us to adore: who alone and one out of all evils can snatch us and bestow all good things. Moreover, he joins in the invocation with God the Father our Lord Jesus, that he may testify that Jesus Christ is of the same divine essence with the Father, and is almighty God; and that we, on account of Christ, are heard by the Father.

I give thanks to my God always for you, for the grace of God which is given to you in Christ Jesus: that in all things you are enriched by him, in every word, and in every knowledge, as the testimony of Christ is confirmed in you, so that no gift is lacking to you, who wait for the revelation of our Lord Jesus Christ: Who also shall confirm you unto the end, blameless in the day of our Lord Jesus Christ: faithful is God by whom you were called into the fellowship of his son, Jesus Christ our Lord.

In the beginning, the Apostle Paul congratulates the Corinthians, concerning the excellence of the gifts with which God adorned that Church, as much to celebrate the goodness and clemency of God, as to show his own benevolence toward this Church declares: And because the Corinthians had need of sharp castigation, lest the weak should suspect, or the malevolent should slander, that Paul envied the gifts and glory of the Corinthians, he prefaces this joyful congratulation and thanksgiving: To which he also attaches a notable consolation, that it will come to pass that God, who is faithful and most observant of His promise, will confirm the spiritual gifts to them, and guard their salvation until the day of the revelation of Christ. But because the Apostle gives thanks to God for the gifts of the Corinthians, he testifies and teaches that they by no means attained and possessed them by the power of free will, or by their own talent, virtue, or industry: Or even that they deserved them: But that they were bestowed upon them only by the singular mercy and beneficence of God: Wherefore, with Paul, they ought to celebrate the goodness of God, to give thanks to Him: But always to acknowledge their own unworthiness and infirmity: And they ought to use the gifts themselves for the illustration of divine glory and the edification of the Church.

Grace in this place does not signify only the gratuitous favor and mercy of God, by which God for Christ's sake remits sins to believers: But it also embraces the other benefits of Christ, and the gifts of the Holy Spirit: For thus Paul explains himself, since he names χαρίσματα, that is, gifts, namely speech and knowledge. For those whom God justifies freely through faith in Christ, to them He also bestows the Holy Spirit, who is not destitute nor an idle guest, but he brings manifold gifts with him, and contributes to his lodging, namely a new and admirable knowledge of God and of His will, an understanding of Holy Scripture, the ability to preach the Gospel, wisdom in the government of the Church, constancy in undergoing the dangers of confession, industry, sagacity in judging spirits, dexterity in refuting errors, and other gifts, by which the Church of Christ is both built up and adorned. What Paul here calls λόγον καί γνῶσιν, Christ Luc: 22. calls στόμα καὶ σοφίαν: a mouth and wisdom: For these two excellent gifts are required most of all in the teachers and governors of the Church: That they may be instructed with the faculty of speaking: so that they may be able to teach, admonish, rebuke others, and refute those who err: Then that they may be imbued with true wisdom, so that they may discern the true from the false: understand the mysteries of God: and be able to apply the prudence of the Spirit in the whole ministry. Athanasius, Augustine, Luther, were instructed at once in both speech and knowledge; which their writings show.

Even as the testimony of Jesus Christ was confirmed in you: that is: you did not hear the Gospel concerning the benefits of Jesus Christ incidentally and cursorily: but it was confirmed in you by the knowledge of Prophetic Scripture, by miracles, by the testimony of the Holy Spirit: by the peace of conscience, by the excellence of spiritual gifts, and in a manifold way; So that you may be certain in your conscience that the doctrine of Jesus Christ is not similar to the fables of the heathens, but is the eternal truth of God, which certainly shows us the way to eternal life. Paul warns at this point with what diligence and zeal the doctrine of the Gospel is to be learned, namely that it is not to be known only cursorily, just as we read the histories of empires and nations, just as we know the deeds of Cyrus, Sennacherib, Alexander the Great, Pyrrhus, and the like: but that the certain and immovable foundations of the individual articles of faith are to be inquired into: upon which we may firmly and without hesitation rely, and from which we may certainly hope for eternal salvation.

That no gift may be lacking to you: It is not a hyperbole. For it is most true that those sanctified through faith and gifted with the Holy Spirit are destitute of no spiritual gift which is required for their own salvation and the edification of the Church: Not indeed that the saints are perfect without sin, nor does the Holy Spirit confer all His gifts upon individual saints: But He distributes according to His counsel and will, just as He judges it expedient for the salvation of the Church: Yet He shares out individual things with such wisdom that the saints are destitute of no gift: For what is lacking to them in the holiness of life, that Jesus Christ the mediator provides and fills copiously: And whatever gifts of faith, or patience, or fortitude, or wisdom, or eloquence they need, He bestows and supplies them in His own time the Holy Spirit. We do not have such ample knowledge of the scriptures as the Apostle Paul had: And yet we are not destitute of any gift of the Spirit: Since all things that are necessary for our salvation are kindly conferred upon us by God: And we hold the foundations of our faith. To attain eternal salvation it is not necessary that individuals have equal gifts of the Holy Spirit: But the Holy Spirit bestows gifts upon each one according to the measure which God has established for him: And by this very diversity He both demonstrates His wisdom and adorns the Church.

Waiting for the revelation of our Lord Jesus Christ. He shows here what is the end of the entire Christian religion: And with what hope the Corinthians ought to sustain themselves. The Corinthians had been reconciled to God through faith in Jesus Christ, and had received the Holy Spirit who conferred upon them gifts of every kind: but nevertheless they carried about infirmities and sins, from which the saints desired to be freed: they desired also a greater knowledge of God, wisdom, fortitude, faith, and similar gifts. Therefore Paul teaches that these things are laid up for them against the day of the revelation of Jesus Christ, when, the dead having been raised, Jesus Christ is to appear in the clouds with all the Angels and the elect: and is to adorn his faithful ones with eternal glory.

Who shall confirm you unto the end blameless in the day of our Lord Jesus Christ: Pious Looking upon their own immense weakness, and the ceaseless snares and machinations of Satan: at the same time also considering the most sorrowful examples of great men, such as Aaron, Reuben, Judas, Gideon, Samson, Saul, David, Joab, and the like, they tremble vehemently, and fear lest they too, overtaken by some infirmity, might fall from the grace of God and lose the salvation they have once attained. Therefore, against this sharp temptation, he confirms the Corinthians with this notable consolation: That the Son of God, Jesus Christ, will be present to them and will confirm them with his Holy Spirit, so that they may be blameless in the day of judgment: that is, that they can be accused neither by the law, nor by Satan, nor by their own conscience: For when they persist in faith, all the righteousness of Christ is imputed to them: He who is clothed with this can be blamed by no creature: and before God he is fully righteous. He calls the final day the day of Jesus Christ: for then Christ will present himself to be seen by the whole world in the clouds.

God is faithful, by whom you were called into the fellowship of his Son Jesus Christ our Lord: He proves the certainty of his consolation from the truth of God: he is faithful and most observant of his promise. It is God who has called you: Moreover, he has promised that he will preserve us in faith: How much more will your Father give the Holy Spirit to those who ask him: Luke 11. Likewise, No one shall snatch my sheep out of my hands; John 10.

Therefore we ought to conceive a certain hope of salvation: And yet to beware of security, lest we fall away from God.

The communion of Jesus Christ: He calls it the participation of the kingdom of Christ, and of all his benefits: For Christ has transferred us from the kingdom of sin and death; And has co-opted us into the society of all heavenly goods; So that we are to reign with Christ: If, however, we also suffer with him in the world. The doctrines of the place in this thanksgiving are.

1. That the universal gifts of the Holy Spirit in the Church do not proceed from free will: But are given divinely, and indeed freely without our merit: On account of our Lord Jesus Christ.

2. Concerning the various gifts of the Holy Spirit, by which God both instructs and adorns the holy Church of Christ.

3. Concerning the infallible certainty of the doctrine of the Gospel, upon which the saints can certainly rely, so that they may hope for salvation without hesitation.

4. Concerning the last day of judgment, on which our Lord Jesus Christ will be revealed to the whole Church and will appear in the clouds with all the elect angels and men: and the judgment having been completed, he will adorn the Church with eternal blessedness.

5. Concerning perseverance in faith, which does not depend on the virtue of free will, but on the goodness and truth of God: Who promised that he would preserve us in faith.

I exhort you, brethren, by the name of our Lord Jesus Christ: That you all say the same thing. And that there be no schisms among you: But that you be joined together in the same mind and in the same judgment.

This is the principal proposition of the whole Epistle, in which Paul exhorts the Corinthian Church, divided by various sects and factions, to salutary concord and the pursuit of Christian unity. For God is not the God of ἀκαταστασίας or of dissensions, but of peace and concord. And Christ did not call us to contentions, but to mutual love and affection: And therefore one and the same Spirit is poured out upon the pious, so that He may glue them together with God the Father and the Son, and among themselves, that they may be one in God. Whence Christ says: By this shall all men know that you are my disciples, if you have love one to another: John 13. Item: John 17: The glory which you gave me, I have given to them, that they may be one, as we also are one: I in them, and you in me: That they may be made perfect in one. Therefore, all Christians must strive with the greatest zeal to avoid dissensions and contentions, and to foster concord and the unity of the Spirit. Basil gravely said: The right hand does not need the left so much: And the Church needs the concord of those who teach: And Augustine: The sacrilege of schism surpasses all crimes: For it inflicts most grievous wounds upon mother Church.

However, heresy and schism differ: Heresy is an error against an article of faith, which overturns the foundation of religion: And it is defended pertinaciously against scripture: The error of Samosatenus, Nestorius, and Pelagius was heresy.

Schism is a dissension which is excited by pertinacity or by a desire for contention, on account of ceremonies or certain dissimilar deeds, without the depravation of the articles of faith: As Donatus excited a schism, while he accused Cecilianus of the betrayal of the sacred books, and refused to acknowledge him as a true member of the Church. Victor excited a schism, who attempted to excommunicate the Asian Churches on account of the diverse celebration of the feast of Easter. Joined together: κατηρτισμένοι: A metaphor taken from physicians, by whom καταρτιζείν signifies to replace dislocated limbs into their joints. Moreover, Paul warns us that the faithful are members of the one body of Jesus Christ: And therefore that there ought to be the highest consent and concord among us: Therefore, those who excite dissensions are like dislocated limbs, which not only do not perform their duty, but also bring both pain and danger to the body by their dislocation.

In the same mind and in the same judgment: That is, let there be the same will in you, so that all thoughts, refer your counsels, studies, and actions to one end, namely to the illustration of divine glory and the edification of the Church: Let there also be the same sentiment, that is, let there be consensus in doctrine, the same confession concerning the articles of faith: Do not invent new and various opinions: Do not invent new dogmas: But persist constantly in the same and that sound doctrine. Paul clearly shows here to what concord he exhorts the Church: Not to a worldly one, but a spiritual and Christian one. The world so composes dissensions and enters into concord that it sets aside the controversies of religions: Or it dissimulates them, or holds them all in equal place: And through simulation it sanctions concord and friendship: Nor does it keep it longer than it seems convenient to itself: And under the pretext of concord it generally fosters the most bitter hatreds: Whence are those complaints:

It is a safe and frequent way to deceive through the name of a friend.

Paul does not speak of this kind of concord: But he demands a spiritual one, true, not feigned; but Christian: Which has consensus in the doctrine of Jesus Christ: For it is impossible for a firm concord to be established unless first, as a foundation, consensus in the doctrine of Christ is placed: For it is necessary that the most fragrant balsam flow from the head of the high priest Christ: And Christ says that they also may be one in us: Therefore not concord, but a conspiracy against God must be called, when men in the Church attempt reasons for concord, having disregarded the consensus in the doctrine of Christ: As the Poet piously sang:

Cursed be the love, peace, and sacred concord, Which violates the true dogmas of Christ God.

Latin:

Paulus vocatus Apostolus Iesu Christi, per voluntatem Dei, & Sosthenes frater, Ecclesiae Dei quae est Corinthi, sanctificatis in Christo Iesu, vocatis sanctis cum omnibus qui invocant nomen domini nostri Iesu Christi, in omni loco, ipsorum & nostro.

Paulus in omnibus Epistolis suis adscribit suum nomen & muneris sui Apostolici facit mentionem: Idque hoc consilio facit ut constet in Ecclesia Dei, per quos ministros & doctores haec admiranda doctrina, quam in Epistolis suis exponit sit tradita & propagata: Qualia habuerint testimonia suae doctrinae, à quo fuerint ablegati: Unde probaverint se divinitus missos esse. Non enim quaevis dogmata amplectitur Ecclesia: Nec circumfert incertas fabellas: Sed eos tantum praecones audit quos scit divinitus missos esse: Et indubia habere testimonia quòd salutarem veritatem profiteantur. Testatur ergò Paulus se vocatum esse Apostolum per voluntatem Dei; Quasi dicat: Non propria temeritate, aut confidentia ingenii irrupi in hoc munus aut sumo mihi docendi partes; Sed consilio & voluntate Dei sum ablegatus ut in mundo spargam lucem Evangelii, & omnes homines vocem ad paenitentiam: Fatetur etiam se non suo merito ad hoc sublime munus Apostolicum pervenisse, sed divina voluntate & clementia cum alioquin indignus esset: Ut 1. Timoth: 1. Fatetur vocatum esse in Apostolum. Significat etiam se non per homines communi modo: Sed immediate à Christo vocatum esse: Ut sciamus eius vocem non aliter accipiendam esse, atque ipsius Dei vocem de coelo sonantem. Apostolus enim est Persona immediatè vocata ab ipso filio Dei domino nostro Iesu Christo, ad praedicandum in orbe Evangelion Dei, & ut fit testis doctrinae, miraculorum, passionis, mortis, & resurrectionis Iesu Christi, non alligata certo loco: Sed missa in orbem terrarum ut passim doceat Evangelion, instructa dono edendi miracula, & sanandi aegrotos, & ornata visibili donatione Spiritus sancti & peritia variarum linguarum. Unde constat eam in doctrina non errare, sed indubiam veritatem de consequenda salute aeterna adferre. Non ergò legamus Epistolas Pauli tanquam antiqui cuiusdam scriptoris, vel clari Episcopi lib: In quo licet nobis & nostrum iudicium et censuram adhibere: Et singula examinare num congruant cum divinis testimoniis: Sed statuamus haec mera esse coelestia oracula: Siquidem Spiritus sanctus per os Pauli locutus est. Sosthenes cuius hic mentionem facit Paulus, fuit princeps synagogae Corinthiacae, de quo Lucas Acto: 18. refert, quòd ante tribunal Gallionis proconsulis Achaiae pene oppressus fuerit à Iudeis Gallione nihil curante. Euseb: scribt lib: 1. cap: 12: Fuisse unum ex 70. Discipulis domini.

Ecclesiae Dei quae est Corinthi: Etsi tota Epistola plena est obiurgationibus in quibus severissimè taxat atrocia scelera Corinthiorum, confusiones, abusus & errores: Tamen augustum nomen Ecclesiae non derogat huic caetui. Quia enim puram in isto loco praedicaverat Evangelii doctrinam, non dubitat quin Deus habeat ibi suos, qui rectè Deum invocent, verè credant in mediatorem, & sint templa Spiritus sancti: Nec Epicurei qui sceleribus deformant Ecclesiam, nec hypocritae aut haretici qui sese immiscent piorum caetui penitus excindunt Ecclesiam: Haec enim tanquam carcinomata ferre cogitur Ecclesia in orbe. Errant ergò Anabaptistae, Donatistae & Cathari qui talem Ecclesiam quaerunt in terris, in qua nulla sint mali admixti bonis: Et in qua nulla exoriantur schismata & scandala: Evangelica enim sagena concludit bonos & malos pisces, donec Angeli in littore seligant bonos àmalis. Hinc ergò definitio Ecclesiae petatur.

Ecclesia est coetus visibilis, amplectentium incorruptam Evangelii doctrinam, & utentium sacramentis iuxta institutionem filii Dei, in quo coetu Spiritus sanctus est efficax, & credentibus communicat iustitiam, vitam & salutem: In quo caetu multi sunt non sancti, qui tamen de doctrina consentiunt.

Sanctificatis in Christo Iesu, vocatis sanctis: Vocabulo sanctificationis complectitur hic omnia beneficia mediatoris, tàm iustificationem quàm renovationem. Vobis Corinthiis scribo inquit, qui estis sanctificati per Iesum Christum, hoc est, qui per Christum accepistis remissionem peccatorum, estis iustificati & reconciliati cum Deo, estis adoptati in filios Dei, et donati Spiritu sancto, qui renovat in vobis imaginem Dei, accendit novam lucem, iusticiam, laeticiam & vitam: Atque haec beneficia non ex vobis ipsis ex libero arbitrio aut virtute vestra habetis, sed per Iesum Christum Mediatorem qui suo sanguine vitam vobis impetravit, peccata gratis condonavit, & Spiritum sanctum in vos effudit: sic generaliter ponitur vox sanctificationis: 1. Corinth: 6: Atque tales quidam ex vobis fuistis; Sed abluti estis, sed sanctificati estis, sed iustificati estis: Item, Ego me sanctifico pro eis ut & ipsi sint sanctificati in veritate. Vocatis sanctis: Vult eos semper esse memores, non tantum à quo sanctificati sint, nimirum gratuito beneficio Mediatoris Iesu Christi: Sed etiam per quod medium ad hanc sanctificationis gloriam pervenerint, videlicet non propria sapientia, ingenio vel virtute; Sed per vocationem Apostolorum & ministrorum Christi: Sancti non intelligantur ἀναμάρτητοι qui sine omni prorsus labe peccati sint: Sed sancti imputativè & inchoativè: Credentibus enim in Christum universa iustitia & sanctitas Christi imputatur: Deinde communicatur ipsis Spiritus sanctus qui in ipsis veram sanctitatem inchoat: Sordes verò quae remanent in sanctis teguntur umbraculo Iesu Christo: Perfecta verò sanctitate ornabuntur credentes in futura vita.

Cum omnibus qui invocant nomen domini nostri Iesu Christi. Et si Corinthios praecipuè alloquitur in hac Epistola Paulus, ut qui propter dissensiones & alia vicia hac gravi castigatione indigebant: Tamen quia intelligit Ecclesias omnibus temporibus, & locis hac commonefactione & institutione indigere universae Ecclesiae Epistolam hac proponit atque commendat. Insigni autem nota veram Ecclesiam ab impiis caetibus gentium & Idolatrarum distinguit. Vera est Ecclesia inquit, in qua lucet vera Dei noticia, & quae invocat nomen domini nostri Iesu Christi; Ergò gentes quae Iovem, Martem, & alia idola invocant non sunt Ecclesia. Nec Turcae aut Mahometistae sunt Ecclesia Dei: Quia non invocant nomen domini nostri Iesu Christi. Quia autem testatur Apostolus universam Ecclesiam in omnibus locis invocare nomen domini nostri Iesu Christi, confirmat Iesum Christum esse aeternum et omni potentem Deum. In omni loco suo et nostro: Ecclesia Christi non est inclusa vel alligata uni & certo aliquo loco; Nam pater dedit filio in possessionem omnes fines terrae; in toto ergo orbe, in omnibus nationibus colligit sibi Iesus Christus ministerio verbi sanctam Eccle: Ite, inquit, in universum orbem et praedicate Evangelion universae creaturae: Domini est terra et omnis plenitudo eius. Ubicunque ergo sunt duo aut tres congregati in nomine Iesu, ibi est Ecclesia: in qua habitat Christus rex & sacerdos. Errat ergo pontifex Ro: qui fingit Ecclesiam alligatam esse ad Cathedram Petri quae sit Romae, & damnat omnes Ecclesias quae non agnoscunt Romanum pontificem caput visibile Ecclesiae.

In hac subscriptione & inscriptione haec doctrinae capita sunt observanda.

1. Non esse currendum sine vocatione temerario ausu: sed expectandam esse certam vocationem, qua mandet Deus ut doceamus Ecclesiam.

2. De duplici vocatione mediata & immediata Apostolorum.

3. Tertius locus est de beneficiis mediatoris, quae compraehenduntur vocabulo sanctificationis.

4. Quartus: De Ecclesia, quae & qualis sit, qua nota agnoscatur, nimirum agnitione & invocatione Iesu Christi, & quòd nulli loco sit alligata: sed quòd in toto orbe colligatur.

5. Quintus. De divinitate Iesu Christi, siquidem ab universa Ecclesia in toto orbe dispersa, omnibus temporibus & in omni necessitate invocatur.

Gratia vobis & pax à Deo patre nostro & domino Iesu Christo.

Gratia significat gratuitum Dei favorem, misericordiam & clementiam qua gratis absque nostra compensatione & merito remittit peccata, acceptat nos ingratiam, pronunciat nos iustos & haeredes vitae aeternae.

Pax significat beneficia spiritualia & corporalia; nimirum donationem spiritus sancti, pacem conscientiae, novam iustitiam & vitam, laeticiam in Deo, haereditatem vitae aeternae: deinde defensionem, nutricationem, gubernationem, consolationem, & omnia bona quibus cùm in hac tùm in futura vita indigemus. Haec omnia cum optat Paulus Ecclesiae in spiritu, certò etiam illa promittit: quemadmodum & Christus testatur: Quidquid petieritis patrem in nomine meo, dabit vobis. Nec esse est autem haec bona cum spiritualia tùm corporalia peti non à numinibus Ethnicis, à Iove, Marte, Pallade: Nec ab Idolis papisticis, à Petro, Paulo, Anna, Otilia, Christophoro: sed à Deo patre domini nostri Iesu Christi, qui solus & unus est Deus: quem solum, et unum adorare nos oportet: qui solus & unus ex omnibus malis eripere & omnia bona largiri potest. Coniungit autem in invocatione cum Deo patre dominum nostrum Iesum ut testetur Iesum Christum eiusdem esse divinae essentiae cum patre, et omnipotentem Deum; Et nos propter Christum à patre exaudiri.

Gratias ago Deo meo semper pro vobis, pro gratia Dei quae data est vobis in Christo Iesu: quòd in omnibus ditati estis per ipsum, in omni sermone, & in omni cognitione, sicuti testimonium Christi confirmatum est in vobis, ut nullum donum vobis desit, qui expectatis revelationem domini nostri Iesu Christi: Qui & confirmabit vos usque ad finem, inculpatos in die domini nostri Iesu Christi: fidelis Deus per quem vocati estis in consortium filii ipsius, Iesu Christi domini nostri.

Initiò gratulatur Apostolus Paulus Corinth:, de excellentia donorum, quibus Deus illam Ecclesiam exornavit, cum ut Dei bonitatem & clementiam celebret, tùm ut suam erga hanc Ecclesiam benevolentiam declaret: Et quia acri castigatione opus habebant Corinth: ne suspicarentur infirmi, aut calumniarentur malevoli Paulum invidere donis &gloriae Corinthiorum, praemittit hanc laetam gratulationem & gratiarum actionem: Cui etiam insignem attexit consolationem, fore ut Deus, qui fidelis est, & servantissimus promissionis, confirmet ipsis dona spiritualia, et custodiat ipsorum salutem usque ad diem revelationis Christi. Quia verò Apostolus gratias agit Deo pro donis Corinth: testatur & docet, eos nequaquam ea consecutos esse & possidere virtute liberi arbitrii, aut proprio ingenio, virtute, industria: Aut etiam meritos esse: Sed tantum singulari Dei misericordia, & beneficentia ipsis esse collata: Quare cum Paulo, Dei bonitatem celebrare, ipsi gratias agere: Propriam verò indignitatem & infirmitatem semper agnoscere: Ipsis quoque donis ad illustrationem gloriae divinae, & aedificationem Ecclesiae uti debent.

Gratia hoc loco non significat tantum gratuitum Dei favorem & misericordiam, qua Deus propter Christum remittit peccata credentibus: Sed complectitur etiam caetera Christi beneficia, & Spiritus sancti dona: Sic enim Paulus se ipsum ex ponit, si quidem nominat χαρίσματα, id est, dona, videlicet sermonem et cognitionem. Quos enim gratis iustificat Deus per fidem in Christum, illis Largitur, etiam Spiritum sanctum, qui non est inops nec ociosus hospes, sed multiplicia dona secum adfert, & hospicio suo confert, nimirum novam & admirandam cognitionem Dei & voluntatis ipsius, intellectum sacrae scripturae facultatem praedicandi Evangelion, sapientiam in gubernatione Ecclesiae, constantiam in subeundis periculis confessionis, industriam, sagacitatem in iudicando Spiritus, dexteritatem in refellendis erroribus, & alia dona, quibus & aedificatur & exornatur Ecclesia Christi. Quòd hic Paulus nominat λόγον καί γνῶσιν Christus Luc: 22. appellat στόμα καὶ σοφίαν: os & sapientiam: Haec enim duo excellentia dona requiruntur maximè in doctoribus & gubernatoribus Ecclesiae: Ut facultate dicendi sint instructi: ut alios docere, monere, corripere, & errantes refellere possint: Deinde ut sapientia vera imbuti sint, ut vera à falsis discernere: mysteria Dei intelligere: & in toto ministerio prudentiam Spiritus adhibere possint. Athanasius, Augustinus, Lutherus, simul & sermone, & cognitione fuerunt instructi; quod scripta ipsorum ostendunt.

Quemadmodum testimonium Iesu Christi in vobis confirmatum est: hoc est: non obiter & cursim audivistis Evangelium de beneficiis Iesu Christi: sed id in vobis confirmatum est cognitione Propheticae scripturae, miraculis, testimonio Spiritus sancti: pace conscientiae, excellentia spiritualium donorum, & multiplici ratione; Adeò ut certi sitis in conscientia vestra doctrinam Iesu Christi non esse similem fabulis ethnicorum, sed esse aeternam Dei veritatem, quae certò nobis monstret viam ad vitam aeternam. Monet hoc loco Paulus qua diligentia & studio addiscenda sit doctrina Evangelii, nimirum quod non obiter tantum cognoscenda sit, sicut legimus imperiorum & gentium historias, sicuti res gestas Cyri, Sennacharib, Alexandri magni, Pyrrhi & similium cognoscimus: sed singulorum articulorum fidei, certa atque immota inquirenda esse fundamenta: quibus firmiter & absque dubitatione inniti, & unde aeternam salutem certò sperare possimus.

Ut nullum vobis donum desit: Non est hyperbole. Verissimum est enim sanctificatos per fidem & donatos Spiritu sancto, nullo spirituali dono destitui quod ad salutem ipsorum, & Ecclesiae aedificationem requiratur: Non quidem perfecti sunt sancti absque peccato, nec singulis sanctis omnia sua dona confert Spiritus sanctus: Sed distribuit iuxta suum consilium & voluntatem, quemadmodum iudicat expedire Ecclesiae saluti: Ea tamen sapientia partitur singula, ut sancti nullo dono destituantur: Quod enim deest ipsis in vitae sanctimonia, id praestat & implet copiosè Iesus Christus mediator: Quibuscunque verò donis vel fidei, vel patientiae vel fortitudinis, vel sapientiae vel eloquentiae indigent ea suo tempore largitur & suppeditat Spiritus sanctus. Nos tàm amplam cognitionem scripturarum non habemus, atque habuit Apostolus Paulus: Et tamen non destuimur ullo dono Spiritus: Siquidem omnia nobis benignè conferuntur à Deo quae ad salutem nostram sunt necessaria: Et fundamenta fidei nostrae tenemus. Ad consequendam salutem aeternam non necesse est ut singuli paria habeant Spiritus sancti dona: Sed unicuique iuxta mensuram quam illi Deus constituit largitur Spiritus sanctus dona: Et ipsa diversitate & sapientiam suam demonstrat & exornat Ecclesiam.

Expectantes revelationem domini nostri Iesu Christi. Ostendit hic quis sit finis universae religionis Christianae: Et qua spe se Corinthii sustentare debeant. Erant Corint: reconciliati Deo per fidem Iesu Christi, & acceperant Spiritum sanctum qui omnis generis dona illis conferebat: sed tamen circumferebant infirmitates et peccata, quibus sancti liberari cupiebant: desiderabant & maiorem Dei cognitionem, sapientiam, fortitudinem, fidem, & similia dona. Docet ergò Paulus haec ipsis esse reposita in diem revelationis Iesu Christi, quando resuscitatis mortuis, Iesus Christus cum omnibus Angelis & electis appariturus est in nubibus: & suos fideles aeterna gloria ornaturus.

Qui confirmabit vos in finem irreprehensibiles in die domini nostri Iesu Christi: Pii intuentes suam ingentem imbecillitatem, & indesinentes insidias & machinationes Satanae: simul etiam considerantes, tristissima exempla magnorum virorum, ut Aaronis, Ruben, Iudae, Gedeonis, Samsonis, Saulis, Davidis, Ioab, & similium, vehementer trepidant, et metuunt ne & ipsi infirmitate aliqua praeventi, excidant Dei gratia & amutant rursus adeptam salutem. Adversus igitur hanc acrem tentationem confirmat Corinthios hac insigni consolatione: Quòd filius Dei Iesus Christus ipsis sit adfuturus & eos confirmaturus suo Spiritu sancto, ut sint irreprehensibiles in die iudicii: hoc est, neque à lege, neque à Satana, neque à propria conscientia accusari possint: Quum enim persistunt in fide imputatur ipsis omnis iustitia Christi: Qua qui vestitus est à nulla creatura culpari potest: & coram Deo plenè est iustus. Extremum diem nominat diem Iesu Christi: tum enim Christus in nubibus toti mundo se conspiciendum praebebit.

Fidelis est Deus, per quem vocati estis in communionem filii sui Iesu Christi domini nostri: Consolationis suae certitudinem probat à veritate Dei: fidelis est & servantissimus promissionis suae. Deus est qui vos vocavit: Promisit autem se nos servaturum esse in fide: Quantò magis pater vester dabit Spiritum sanctum petentibus: Luc: 11. Item, Nemo rapiet oves meas ex manibus meis; Ioan: 10.

Certam ergò spem salutis concipere debemus: Et tamen cavere securitatem ne à Deo deficiamus.

Communionem Iesu Christi: Vocat participationem regni Christi, & omnium beneficiorum eius: Christus enim transtulit nos ex regno peccati & mortis; Et cooptavit nos in societatem omnium coelestium bonoram; Ita ut cum Christo regnaturi simus: Si tamen & patiemur cum ipso in mundo. Loci doctrinae in hac gratulatione sunt.

1. Quod universa dona Spiritus sancti in Ecclesia, non proveniant à libero arbitrio: Sed donentur divinitus, & quidem gratis absque nostro merito: Propter dominum nostrum Iesum Christum.

2. De variis donis Spiritus sancti, quibus Deus & instruit & ornat sanctam Ecclesiam Christi.

3. De infallibili certitudine doctrinae Evangelii, cui sancti certò inniti possunt, ita ut sine haesitatione sperent salutem.

4. De extremo die iudicii, quo revelabitur Ecclesiae toti dominus noster Iesus Christus & apparebit in nubibus cum omnibus electis angelis & hominibus: & iudicio peracto Ecclesiam aeterna beatitudine ornabit.

5. De perseverantia in fide quae non pendet à virtute liberi arbitrii, sed à Dei bonitate & veritate: Qui promisit se conservaturum nos in fide.

Adhortor autem vos fratres, per nomen domini nostri Iesu Christi: Ut idem dicatis omnes. Et ne sint inter vos dissidia: Sitis autem inter vos coagmentati in eadem mente & in eadem sententia.

Haec est totius Epistolae principalis propositio, in qua Paulus Corinthiam Ecclesiam variis sectis, & factionibus divisam hortatur ad salutarem concordiam, & studium Christianae unitatis. Deus enim non est Deus ἀκαταστασίας aut dissidiorum, sed pacis & concordiae Et Christus non vocavit nos ad contentiones, sed ad mutuum amorem & dilectionem: Atque ideò effunditur in pios unus & idem Spiritus, ut eos cum Deo Patre & Filio, & inter sese conglutinet, ut unum sint in Deo. Unde Christus inquit: In hoc cognoscent quòd discipuli mei sitis: Si vos invicem dilexeritis: Ioan: 13. Item: Ioa: 17: Ego gloriam quam dedisti mihi, dedi ipsis ut sint unum quemadmodum & nos unum sumus: Ego in ipsis, & tu in me: Ut sint consummati in unum. Omnibus igitur Christianis summo studio annitendum est, ut caveant dissidia & contentiones, & iuvent concordiam & Spiritus unitatem. Basilius graviter dixit: Non tàm sinistrae opus est dextra: Atque Ecclesiae opus est concordia docentium: Et August: Sacrilegium scismatis omnia scelera superat: Gravissima enim vulnera infligit matri Ecclesiae.

Differunt autem haeresis & schisma: Haeresis est error contra articulum fidei, qui evertit fundamentum religionis: Et pertinaciter contra scripturam defenditur: Haeresis fuit error Samosateni, Nestorii, Pelagii.

Schisma est dissidium quod pertinacia vel contendendi studio excitatur, propter ceremonias vel facta quaedam dissimilia, sine depravatione articulorum fidei: Ut Donatus excitavit schisma, dum Cecilianum accusavit de traditione sacrorum librorum, & eum noluit agnoscere verum Ecclesiae membrum. Victor schisma excitavit, qui conatus est Asiaticas Ecclesias excommunicare propter diversam celebrationem festi Paschatos. Coagmentati: κατηρτισμένοι: Metaphora sumpta à medicis, quibus καταρτιζείν significat luxata membra in artus reponere. Monet autem Paulus nos fideles membra esse unius corporis Iesu Christi: Ideoque summum in nobis oportere esse consensum & concordiam: Qui ergò dissidia excitant, hi sunt veluti luxata membra, quae non solum non praestant officium suum, sed etiam luxatione sua & dolorem & periculum corpori adferunt.

In eadem mente & in eadem sententia: Id est, sit eadem in vobis voluntas, ut omnes cogitationes, consilia, studia, & actiones ad unum finem referatis, nimirum ad illustrationem gloriae divinae, & aedificationem Ecclesiae: Sit etiam eadem sententia, hoc est, sit consensus in doctrina, eadem confessio de articulis fidei: Non fingite novas & varias opiniones: Non fingite nova dogmata: Sed in eadem eaque sana doctrina constanter persistite. Disertè hic ostendit Paulus ad quam concordiam hortetur Ecclesiam: Non ad mundanam, sed spiritualem & Christianam. Mundus ita componit dissidia & init concordiam ut seponat controversias religionum: Vel eas dissimulet, vel omnes pari loco habeat: Et per simulationem sancit concordiam & amicitiam: Nec eam servat diutius, quàm ipsi commodum videtur: Ac sub praetextu concordiae plerumque acerbissima odia fovet: Unde sunt illae querelae:

Tuta frequensque via est per amici fallere nomen.

De huiusmodi concordia non loquitur Paulus: Sed postulat spiritualem, veram, non fictam; sed Christianam: Quae consensum habeat in doctrina Iesu Christi: Impossibile est enim firmam constitui concordiam nisi prius tanquam fundamentum collocetur consensus in doctrina Christi: Oportet enim fragrantissimum balsamum de vertice summi pontificis Christi manare: Et Christus inquit ut & ipsi in nobis unum sint: Non ergò concordia, sed conspiratio est contra Deum dicenda est, quando homines in Ecclesia tentant rationes concordiae, post habito consensu in doctrina Christi: Sicut piè cecinit Poeta:

Sit maledictus amor, pax & concordia sacra, Quae violat Christi dogmata vera Dei.

## 1:11-12
For it has been signified to me concerning you, by those who are of the household of Chloe, that there are contentions among you: Now I say this concerning the matter, that each of you says, I am of Paul, I am of Apollos, I am of Cephas: I am of Christ.

Paul explains the occasion and the cause why he exhorts the Church of the Corinthians to concord with such diligence: Because he understood that there were dissensions and factions in it: And lest they suspect that Paul has this from uncertain rumors, he writes from where he learned this, namely from the household of Chloe. For the household of Chloe performed a holy duty, in that it indicated this wound of the Church to the Apostle, so that a timely remedy might be applied.
