Nobili generè ortus fuit Iesaia, Daniel, Iosias, Hiskia, Zadock, Ioseph: Et tamen testimonium habent Spiritus sancti, quòd adscripti sint haeredes vitae aeternae. Non ergò abiecit Deus omnes sapientes, potentes, divites & nobiles, sed eos tantum qui sua sapientia, potentia & nobilitate confidunt, & Evangelio Iesu Christi contumaciter resistunt. Sapiens fuit Daniel, sed ille in timore Dei & vera humilitate omnia defert Deo, fatetur in se nihil esse consilii, nisi Deus spiritu suo illuminaverit ipsum. Qui ergò ingenii, sapientiae vel nobilitatis dono à Deo ornatus est, tantò magis se demittat & ne glorietur, ne iram Dei provocet & seipsum à societate Ecclesiae excludat. Monet nos haec Pauli sententia, ne offendamur abiecta specie Ecclesiae: Sic enim placuit Deo eligere quae in mundo abiecta & vilia sunt, ut ipsius virtus & gloria locum habeat. Consolatur etiam haec sententia homines miseros & calamitosos, & in infima sorte positos, ne suspicentur se propterea negligi vel minus curari, quia sint miseri, sed potius statuant quò quis fidelium sit calamitosior, & miserior in mundo, hoc eum Deo maiori curae esse. Tertiò docet Apostolus omnem gloriationem soli Deo sapienti & omnipotenti competere: Et universum genus humanum ab omni gloriatione se prorsus abstinere debere.

## 1:30-31
But of Him you are in Christ Jesus.

Because Paul had said that most of the wise, the powerful, and the noble were rejected and passed over in the calling, in order to console the Corinthians, he separates them from that multitude of the rejected: You, he says, are not in that number of the rejected wise and noble: But you are born of God, illuminated by the word and the Holy Spirit, gathered into the society of the Church, and co-opted into the heirs of eternal life. And therefore it befits you not to glory in your wisdom, nobility, or power: But with true humility and gratitude of mind to acknowledge and proclaim the benefits of God.

Who was made for us wisdom from God, righteousness, and sanctification, and redemption, that as it is written, He who glories let him glory in the Lord.

As Paul strips everything from human nature, and leaves absolutely nothing remaining to it: So again he attributes everything to Christ, and shows that the Church and individual believers possess all ornaments and gifts in Jesus Christ. From ourselves we have nothing: Nothing at all is ours. In us there exists no crumb of virtue, no spark of wisdom: But if we are grafted into Christ through faith, we possess all things in him. O immense consolation, O most ample riches which the Holy Spirit offers and gives to those who acknowledge their own nakedness and place all their confidence in our Lord Jesus Christ. O foolish, O insane men who proudly arrogate to themselves virtue and wisdom and by this reason hinder themselves, so that they can never arrive at true justice and virtue. Why therefore do we not cast away all pride and arrogance, and confess what the thing itself speaks, that in us there is nothing but sin and death. And we flee to our Lord Jesus Christ, who supplies all things to us.

Wisdom signifies the true and salutary knowledge of God and of His will: When a man understands who the true God is, how He has revealed Himself in His word, how He wishes to be worshipped, invoked, and celebrated, who is the Mediator and redeemer of the human race, what are His benefits, and what is the way of arriving at eternal blessedness. Moses, Samuel, David, Nathan, Jeduthun, Ethan, Jehoshaphat, Jehoiada, Isaiah, Paul, Polycarp were wise. But those who do not have the knowledge of these greatest and most necessary things cannot be held as wise. Simonides, Socrates, Plato, Themistocles, Laelius, Scaevola, Cato, Scipio, Agrippa, Maecenas, were not wise: because they did not know God. Nor was Ahithophel wise, because he lacked the true fear of God, which is the beginning of wisdom. But to us who are small and before the world foolish, Christ has been made wisdom by God, that is, the eternal Father has given us his only-begotten Son, in whom all the treasures of wisdom are hidden: he shows us who the true God is, what his will is, why he sent his Son, whence sin and death are, what kind of kingdom Christ's is, what his benefits are, why he exercises the Church with the cross, how he wishes to be worshipped and celebrated, and what the most certain way of arriving at eternal life is. The world indeed does not care for these such great goods, and by so much is it more furious and foolish.

Justification, is the gratuitous remission of sins, the imputation of the obedience of Jesus Christ, and the acceptance unto eternal life. The world proudly boasts of its own justice and preaches its own virtue: But the whole world lacks all justice and is full of sin. Christ says, John 8: Unless you believe in the Son of Man, you will die in your sins, and in John 16: The Holy Spirit will convict the world of sin, because they do not believe in me. But to us sinners, who acknowledge our uncleanness and sins, and by faith apprehend the promise of the Gospel: Christ is justice before God, that is, in him, through and on account of him we are just before God. For he who knew no sin was made sin for us, that we might become the justice of God in him. 2 Cor. 5 And as many as have been baptized into Christ, we have put on Christ with all his justice.

Sanctification, signifies in this place renewal, vivification, and the gift of the Holy Spirit. Those who are outside of Christ, these remain in death, they do not perceive consolation, they are not vivified, they are not transformed into the image of God, nor do they become dwellings of the Holy Spirit: But the god of this world works effectively in them, heaps sins upon sins, and subsequently increases the darkness of the mind and the malice of the heart. But Christ is sanctification to us who believe in him: That is, he pours into us the Holy Spirit, who reforms and renews our old nature, and imparts to us new righteousness, light, life, and joy.

Redemption signifies liberation from the wrath of God, from the curse of the law, from the burden of sin, from the empire of death, from the tyranny of Satan, and from the violence of all the enemies of the Church. All these things our Lord Jesus Christ provides for us, according to the promise: The discipline of our peace is upon him, and by his stripes we are healed Iesa: 53. Item, have confidence in me, I have overcome the world, Iohannis. 16. The world, however, which is alien to Christ, however much it may boast of its power, even if it joins all its forces, is nevertheless oppressed by these enemies.

By these most significant words, Paul has embraced the most ample, eternal, heavenly, spiritual, and corporal benefits of the whole kingdom of Christ. Therefore, Paul infers from the Prophet Jeremiah: as it is written, he who glories, let him glory in the Lord: Therefore he says, God gives and exhibits all things to us in our Lord Jesus Christ, lest anyone in his flesh, that is, in his wisdom, justice, virtue, power, merit, should glory, but that individuals should defer all things to God, and he alone should be glorified. Notable places of doctrine are to be observed in this Chapter.

1. First: By the example of the Corinthians we are admonished that such a Church is not to be imagined on earth, in which there are no dissensions, no struggles, no scandals: but that the mind must be fortified so that although struggles, dissensions, and scandals arise in the very bosom of the Church: nevertheless we do not depart from the Church, nor do we cast away the profession of the Gospel. For Satan does not cease to sow his tares while men are sleeping. Let us at least take pains that we may be the wheat of the Lord.

2. Second: Let the Apostolic explanation of the words of Baptism be diligently observed, I baptize you in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit, which words, as Paul testifies, have such force that it is not permitted for men to be baptized in the name of any Apostle. For in Baptism a man enters into a covenant with God himself. Therefore the words of Baptism are a most clear testimony concerning the divinity of Jesus Christ and the Holy Spirit.

3. Third. The Apostle hands down here the distinction between Christ the mediator and the remaining saints: For he confesses that neither he himself, Paul, nor any other Apostle was crucified for the Corinthians: Indicating that this glory is owed to Christ alone, as he who alone the winepress he trod, Isaiah 63 and with his own blood he redeemed the Church.

4. Fourthly, notable in this chapter is the passage concerning the distinction between the wisdom of the world and the wisdom of the Spirit. The world utterly abhors the cross of Jesus Christ, nor does it understand the counsel of God concerning the gathering of the Church: and in all spiritual matters it is opposed to divine wisdom. Therefore God detests the wisdom of this world, inasmuch as it is foolishness before God. The wisdom of the Spirit, however, has been revealed in the word of God.

5. Fifthly, most worthy of note is the passage concerning the efficacy of the cross of Jesus Christ: by which, although nothing in the world may appear weaker, yet nothing is more powerful. For by the cross and death of Jesus Christ the head of the serpent has been crushed, and the entire power of sin, death, and Satan has been destroyed.

6. Sixthly, it is most evidently clear from this chapter that all the powers of free will, as far as spiritual matters are concerned, have been utterly extinguished and lost through sin. For Paul testifies that the world could not know God by its own wisdom: and that it is averse to the divine wisdom which delights in the cross of Christ and the Church. Paul also testifies that God detests and will destroy the wisdom of the wise: and will bring to nothing those things that are, so that no man may have any cause for boasting.

7. Seventhly, when Paul censures the Jews, because they ask of God signs and miracles, he teaches that God is not to be tempted by the petitioning of signs and miracles: but that one must assent to the express word of God, already previously confirmed by miracles, and to the most evident truth in the fear of God.

8. Eighthly: How sad, abject, and squalid the appearance of the Church is, is painted before our eyes in this place. Not many wise, not many noble, not many powerful: but God has chosen the weak things of the world.

9. Ninthly. By what thing we are justified before God, Paul clearly teaches here, namely not by our virtue, justice, works, or motions: but only by the merit and obedience of Jesus Christ. For Paul confesses that there is nothing in us: that we can boast in nothing: but that Jesus Christ has been made unto us justice from God. Therefore His obedience toward the law is imputed to us.

10. The tenth place is concerning the various and innumerable benefits of the kingdom of Christ; that in Christ we possess all things.

Latin:

Ex ipso autem vos estis in Christo Iesu.

Quia dixerat Paulus plerosque sapientes, potentes, & nobiles reiectos & praeteritos esse in vocatione, ut consoletur Corinthios, separat eos ab illa multitudine reiectorum: Vos, inquit, non estis in illo numero sapientum & nobilium reiectorum: Sed vos estis ex Deo nati, per verbum & Spiritum sanctum illuminati, ad societatem Ecclesiae adgregati, & in haeredes vitae aeternae cooptati. Atque idcirco decet vos non in vestra sapientia, nobilitate, potentia gloriari: Sed vera humilitate, & animi gratitudine agnoscere & praedicare Dei beneficia.

Qui factus est nobis sapientia à Deo, iustitia, & sanctificatio, & redemptio, ut sicut scriptum est, Qui gloriatur in domino glorietur.

Ut omnia detrahit Paulus humanae naturae, ac planê nihil reliqui ei facit: Ita rursus omnia tribuit Christo, & ostendit Ecclesiam & singulos fideles omnia ornamenta & dona possidere in Iesu Christo. Ex nobis nihil habemus: Nihil plane est nostrum. In nobis nulla existit mica virtutis, nulla scintilla sapientiae: At si Christo per fidem inseramur, Omnia in ipso possidemus. O immensam consolationem, O amplissimas opes quas offert & donat Spiritus sanctus his, qui agnoscunt suam nuditatem, & omnem fiduciam in dominum nostrum Iesum Christum ponunt. O fatuos, O insanos homines qui superbè sibi arrogant virtutem & sapientiam & hac ratione sese impediunt, quò minus unquam ad veram iustitiam et virtutem pervenire possint. Quin igitur abiicimus omnem superbiam & arrogantiam, & fatemur quod res ipsa loquitur in nobis nihil esse nisi peccatum & mortem. Et confugimus ad dominum nostrum Iesum Christum, qui nobis omnia suppeditat.

Sapientia significat veram & salutarem Dei & voluntatis ipsius noticiam: Cum homo intelligit quis sit verus Deus, quomodo sese in verbo suo patefecerit, quomodo coli, invocari, & celebrari velit, quis sit Mediator, & redemptor generis humani, quae eius beneficia, & quae sit via perveniendi ad aeternam beatitudinem. Sapiens fuit Moises, Samuel, David, Nathan, Ieduthun, Ethan, Iosaphat, Ioiada, Iesaias, Paulus, Polycarpus. Qui verò harum maximarum & summ è necessariarum rerum noticiam non habent pro sapientibus haberi non possunt. Simonides, Socrates, Plato, Temistocles, Laelius, Scaevola, Cato, Scipio, Agrippa, Maecenas, non fuêre sapientes: quia Deum non noverunt. Nec Achitophel fuit sapiens, quia caruit vero Dei timore, qui est initium sapientiae. Nobis autem pusillis et coram mundo insipientibus Christus factus est sapientia à Deo, id est, aeternus pater dedit nobis unigenitum filium in quo omnes Thesauri sapientiae reconditi sunt: hic nobis ostendit quis sit verus Deus, quae eius sit voluntas, cur miserit filium, Unde sint peccatum & mors, quale sit regnum Christi, quae eius beneficia, cur exerceat Ecclesiam cruce, quomodo coli & celebrari velit, quae sit certissima via perveniendi ad vitam aeternam. Mundus quidem haec tanta bona non curat, atque tantò est furiosor & stolidior.

Iustitia, est gratuita remissio peccatorum, imputatio obedientiae Iesu Christi, & acceptatio ad vitam aeternam. Mundus superbè iactitat suam iustitiam & praedicat suam virtutem: Sed universus mundus caret omni iustitia & plenus est peccato. Christus inquit, Ioannis: 8. Nisi credideritis in filium hominis, moriemini in peccatis vestris, & in Ioan: 16. Spiritus sanctus arguet mundum de peccato, quia non credunt in me. Nobis autem peccatoribus, qui agnoscimus nostram immundiciem & peccata, & fide adpraehendimus Evangelii promissionem: Christus est iustitia coram Deo, id est, in ipso, per & propter ipsum coram Deo sumus iusti. Qui enim peccatum non novit pro nobis factus est peccatum, ut nos fieremus iustitia Dei in ipso. 2. Cor: 5. Et quotquot in Christum Baptizati sumus, Christum cum omni eius iustitia induimus.

Sanctificatio, significat hoc loco renovationem, vivificationem & donationem Spiritus sancti. Qui extra Christum sunt, hi manent in morte, non percipiunt consolationem, non vivificantur, non transformantur in Dei imaginem, nec fiunt domicilia Spiritus sancti: Sed Deus huius seculi efficaciter in ipsis operatur, cumulat peccata peccatis, & subinde auget tenebras mentis & maliciam cordis. At Christus nobis in ipsum credentibus est sanctificatio: Id est, effundit in nos Spiritum sanctum, qui nostram veterem naturam reformat & renovat, & impertit nobis novam iustitiam, lucem, vitam & laeticiam.

Redemptio significat liberationem ab ira Dei, à maledictione legis, ab onere peccati, ab imperio mortis, à tyrannide Satanae, & à violentia omnium hostium Ecclesiae. Haec omnia nobis praestat dominus noster Iesus Christus, iuxta promissionem: Disciplina pacis nostrae super eum, & livore eius sanatisumus Iesa: 53. Item, confidite in me, ego vici mundum, Iohannis. 16. Mundus autem qui à Christo alienus est quantumvis glorietur de sua potentia, etiamsi omnes vires coniungat, tamen ab his hostibus opprimitur.

His verò significantissimis vocabulis Paulus complexus est totius regni Christi amplissima, aeterna, coelestia, spiritualia & corporalia beneficia. Infert ergò Paulus ex Propheta Hîeremia: ut sicut scriptum est, qui gloriatur in domino glorietur: Idcirco inquit, Deus omnia nobis donat & exhibet in domino nostro Iesu Christo, ne quisquam in sua carne, hoc est, in sua sapientia, iustitia, virtute, potentia, merito glorietur, sed ut singuli omnia deferant Deo, & is solus glorificetur. Insignes doctrinae loci in hoc Capite observandi sunt.

1. Primùm: Exemplo Corinthiorum admonemur, non esse talem fingendam in terris Ecclesiam, in qua nulla sint dissidia, nulla certamina, nulla scandala: sed obfirmandum esse animum ut quanquàm certamina, dissidia & scandala in ipso Ecclesiae sinu exoriantur: tamen non discedamus ab Ecclesia, nec proiiciamus Evangelii professionem. Satan enim dormientibus hominibus non desinit serere sua zizania. Nos saltem operam demus, ut frumentum domini simus.

2. Secundo: Diligenter observetur Apostolica explicatio verborum Baptismi, Baptizo te in nomine patris, & filii & Spiritus sancti, quae verba teste Paulo eam habent vim, ut non liceat in ullius Apostoli nomine Baptizari homines. In Baptismo enim init homo faedus cum ipso Deo. Ergò verba Baptismi luculentissimum sunt testimonium de divinitate Iesu Christi & Spiritus sancti.

3. Tertiò. Tradit hîc Apostolus discrimen inter Christum mediatorem & reliquos sanctos: Fatetur enim nec se Paulum, nec alium quemvis Apostolum pro Corinth: crucifixum esse: Indicans hanc gloriam soli Christo deberi, ut qui solus torcular calcavit, Iesaia: 63 & sanguine suo redemit Ecclesiam.

4. Quartò, Insignis est in hoc Capite locus de discrimine inter sapientiam mundi, & sapientiam Spiritus. Mundus prorsus abhorret à cruce Iesu Christi, nec intelligit Dei consilium de colligenda Ecclesia: atque in omnibus spiritualibus adversatur sapientiae divinae. Itaque detestatur Deus sapientiam huius mundi, utpote quae coram Deo est stultitia. Sapientia autem Spiritus in verbo Dei patefacta est.

5. Quintò, Notatu dignissimus est locus de efficacia crucis Iesu Christi: qua cum nihil in mundo videatur infirmius: nihil tamen est potentius. Cruce enim & morte Iesu Christi contritum est caput serpentis, & destructa tota potentia peccati, mortis, & Satanae.

6. Sextò, evidentissimè patet ex hoc capite vires liberi arbitrii omnes, quòd ad spiritualia prorsus per peccatum extinctas & amissas esse. Paulus enim testatur mundum sua sapientia Deum non potuisse cognoscere: & aversari sapientiam divinam quae delectatur cruce Christi & Ecclesiae. Testatur etiam Paulus Deum detestari & perditurum esse sapientiam sapientum: & ea quae sunt redacturum in nihilum, ne ullus homo ullam habeat gloriandi causam.

7. Septimò, cum Paulus taxat Iudaeos, quòd petant à Deo signa & miracula, docet non esse tentandum Deum petitione signorum & miraculorum: sed expresso Dei verbo, iam antea confirmato miraculis, & evidentissimae veritati in timore Dei esse adsentiendum.

8. Octavò: Quàm tristis, abiecta & squalida sit species Ecclesiae, pingitur hoc loco ob oculos. Non multi sapientes, non multi nobiles, non multi potentes: sed infirma mundi elegit Deus.

9. Nonò. Qua re coram Deo iustificemur perspicuè hîc docet Paulus, videlicet non nostra virtute, iustitia, operibus aut motibus: sed tantum merito & obedientia Iesu Christi. Fatetur enim Paulus in nobis nihil esse: in nullo gloriari nos posse: sed Iesum Christum factum esse nobis iustitiam à Deo. Ipsius ergò obedientia ergà legem nobis imputatur.

10. Decimus locus est de variis & innumeris beneficiis regni Christi; quòd in Christo omnia possidemus.

## 2:1 Argument
CHAPTER II.

Latin:

CAPUT II.

## 2:1
And I brothers when I came to you, I came not with excellence of speech or wisdom, declaring unto you the testimony

Latin:

Et ego fratres cum ad vos venirem, non veni cum eminentia sermonis aut sapientia, annuncians vobis testimonium

## 2:2-5
of God: For I judged not myself to know anything among you, except Jesus Christ and him crucified. And I was with you in weakness, and in fear, and in much trembling. And my speech and my preaching was not in the persuasive words of human wisdom: But in demonstration of the Spirit and of power: That your faith might not be in the wisdom of men, but in the power of God.

That Paul may prove that it is in no way fitting that anyone in the ministry or in the Church should show off his own talent, or wisdom, or eloquence: But that the Gospel of the cross of Jesus Christ must be preached in all humility and modesty: And that only the glory of God and the salvation of the Church must be regarded, he proposes his own Example to the whole Church: With what modesty and humility he performed his ministry among the Corinthians: That he did not seek his own glory, and the praise of either wisdom or eloquence: But was entirely occupied in this, that he might reveal Jesus Christ crucified to the world. For the Apostles not only instructed the Church with doctrine, but also went before their hearers with examples of piety. Whence Paul says: Phil: 3. Be followers of me. Of speech or the eminence of wisdom, he names eloquence and human wisdom, which is in admiration and is looked up to, and he signifies that he did not display his own fluency and knowledge of many things, which those are accustomed to do who study their own glory and court popular favor. For our Lord Jesus Christ did not suffer for that reason, nor did he institute the ministry so that we might have a field for contending about the praise of wit: But to this end, that the glory of God alone might be made known, and that the salvation of the Church might be consulted. Therefore, those who seek their own glory in the ministry, these abuse the highest benefit of Christ and declare their own unfaithful spirit. He calls the preaching of the Gospel the testimony of God: For God himself has testified through the Prophets and Apostles, and even by his own voice from heaven, concerning his son appointed as mediator. Therefore, those who do not assent to the word of the Prophets and Apostles, these accuse God of false testimony.

Because Paul says that he knows nothing except Jesus and him crucified: He shows that there is no greater wisdom under the sun than to acknowledge Jesus Christ and his benefits. Paul certainly had knowledge of very many things: nor was he ignorant of Philosophy and the doctrine of the Greeks: but he sees that outside of Christ, philosophy is not only lame and mutilated, but also insulting to God, and all human wisdom outside of Christ is foolishness before God, and blindness which stumbles everywhere. Therefore, Paul arrogates to himself the glory of no erudition, but boasts only of the knowledge of Jesus Christ crucified, in whom he sees the most merciful will of God, and the wisdom concerning the gathering of the Church, concerning the true worship of God, and concerning the obtaining of eternal life. For the head of the whole Gospel of Jesus Christ, and the sum of our religion, is that Jesus Christ the Son of God was crucified for us. And in this Jesus Christ crucified, all the treasures of divine wisdom are hidden. Thither, therefore, the Apostle invites and calls the Corinthians, that they may learn to acknowledge Jesus Christ crucified, and not seek the praise of erudition or wisdom, which outside of Christ is absolutely nothing.

Paul is not ashamed to confess his own weakness, fear, and trembling, so that he may teach that the ministry is not concerned with our praise, but with the salvation of the Church. That the Apostles were often in great consternation of mind, and were gravely struck by terrors, they themselves sometimes confess: 2. Cor: 7. without, he says, were fightings, within were fears. And 2. Cor: 1. he writes that he was so consternated in mind that he despaired of life. By these terrors, however, God exercised even the Apostles and Prophets for many reasons.

1. That they might look more closely at the magnitude of the wrath of God against the atrocity of sin, and might perceive some taste of it.

2. Next, that they might value more highly the immense benefits of the Son of God, who redeemed us from such terrors of conscience by His own blood.

3. Thirdly, that they might not exalt themselves because of those highest gifts with which they were adorned by God, and that they might not have confidence in themselves.

4. Fourthly, that by this mortification of the old Adam, the desire for eternal life might be kindled more ardently within them.

4. Fifthly, that by their example they might be a consolation to other weaker members of the Church. For when many in the Church are overwhelmed by such dreads and trepidations, they can firmly conclude that these are not signs of an angry God, since they see that the Apostles, Prophets, and fathers also experienced similar terrors.

6. Sixthly, that the power of God may be the more conspicuous, and all the glory of the gathered Church and of the destroyed kingdom of Satan may return to God. Let the pious mind think on these things when it reads of the horrendous dreads of the greatest men, such as Abraham, Jacob, Moses, Joshua, David, Hezekiah, Paul: And let it observe that the strength and joy of the Spirit do not always shine with the same brightness in the saints.

He calls popular sermons persuasive speeches of human wisdom, which are entirely directed to the end that in whatever way they may affect and delight the listeners, and snatch them into admiration of the speaker. Samosatenus, Arius, Nestorius, Origen, and Pelagius bring forward persuasive discourses: For they say things which agree with reason and are pleasing to the flesh: Thus the Calvinists and forgers of the testament of Jesus Christ say plausible and persuasive things: For they remove every struggle of faith, and say those things which are pleasing to reason: And which can be adorned with oratory and figures. Paul, however, testifies that he did not study this art, or rather fraud, but taught the Evangelion in all simplicity and rectitude: And that he applied himself to this, that he might rather demonstrate the truth of his preaching by Spirit and power. This is, that he might confirm the faith of the listeners both by the miracles proper to the Church: And might prove his doctrine by experience itself in consolations. For then the faith of the listeners rests upon a solid and stable foundation: Namely, not human wisdom than which nothing is more uncertain, nothing more futile; But by the divine power of the omnipotent God.

Latin:

Dei: Non enim iudicavi me scire quidquam in vobis, nisi Iesum Christum & hunc crucifixum. Et ego in infirmitate, & timore, ac tremore multo fui apud vos. Et sermo meus & praedicatio mea non fuit in persuasoriis humanae sapientiae verbis: Sed in demonstratione Spiritus & virtutis: Ut fides vestra non sit in sapientia hominum, sed in virtute Dei.

Ut evincat Paulus nullo modo decere, ut quis in ministerio vel in Ecclesia ostentet suum ingenium, vel sapientiam, vel eloquentiam: Sed in omni humilitate & modestia praedicandum esse Evangelion de cruce Iesu Christi: Et tantum Dei gloriam, & Ecclesiae salutem respiciendam esse, proponit toti Ecclesiae suum Exemplum: Qua modestia & humilitate functus sit suo ministerio apud Corinthios: Quòd non quaesiverit suam gloriam, & laudem vel sapientiae vel eloquentiae: Sed totus in eo fuerit ut Iesum Christum crucifixum mundo patefaceret. Apostoli enim non solum doctrina erudiverunt Ecclesiam, sed etiam pietatis exemplis suis auditoribus praeiverunt. Unde inquit Paulus: Phil: 3. Imitatores mei estote. Sermonis vel sapientiae eminentiam, nominat eloquentiam & sapientiam humanam, quae in admiratione est & suspicitur, ac significat se non ostentasse suam facundiam, & multarum rerum cognitionem, quod illi facere solent qui suae student gloriae & captant Popularem auram. Non enim ideò passus est dominus noster Iesus Christus, nec instituit ministerium ut campum haberemus certandi de laude ingenii: Sed in hunc finem, ut solius Dei gloria innotesceret, & saluti Ecclesiae consuleretur. Qui ergò suam quaerunt gloriam in ministerio, hi abutuntur summo Christi beneficio & animum suum infidelem declarant. Testimonium Dei, adpellat Evangelii pradicationem: Ipse enim Deus per Prophetas & Apostolos, atque etiam propria voce de coelo de suo filio constituto mediatore testatus est. Qui ergò verbo Prophetarum & Apostolorum non adsentiuntur, hi accusant Deum falsi testimonii.

Quòd inquit Paulus se nihil scire nisi Iesum & hunc crucifixum: Ostendit non esse maiorem sub sole sapientiam, quàm agnoscere Iesum Christum & eius beneficia. Habuit sanè Paulus plurimarum rerum noticiam: neque ignarus fuit Philosophiae & doctrinae Graecorum: sed videt extra Christum Philosophiam non solum esse mancam & mutilam, sed etiam contumeliosam in Deum, & universam sapientiam humanam extra Christum esse stultitiam coram Deo, & caecitatem quae passim impingit. Nullius ergò eruditionis gloriam arrogat sibi Paulus, sed de sola noticia Iesu Christi crucifixi, in quo videt clementissimam Dei voluntatem, & sapientiam de colligenda Ecclesia, de vero cultu Dei, & de consequenda vita aeterna gloriatur. Caput enim totius Evangelii Iesu Christi, & summa nostrae religionis est, Quòd Iesus Christus filius Dei pro nobis est crucifixus. Atque in hoc Iesu Christo crucifixo, omnes Thesauri sapientiae divinae sunt reconditi. Huc ergò invitat & vocat Apostolus Corinthios, ut discant Iesum Christum crucifixum agnoscere, & ne captent laudem eruditionis vel sapientiae, quae extra Christum prorsus nulla est.

Non erubescit Paulus suam fateri imbecillitatem, timorem & tremorem, ut doceat non agi in ministerio de nostra laude: sed de salute Ecclesiae. Apostolos saepe in magna fuisse consternatione animi, & terroribus fuisse perculsos graviter, aliquoties ipsi fatentur: 2. Cor: 7. foris inquit pugnae, intus pavores. & 2. Cor: 1. scribit se adeò consternatum fuisse animo ut desperaverit de vita. His autem terroribus exercuit Deus etiam Apostolos, & Prophetas propter multas causas.

1. Ut propius aspicerent magnitudinem irae Dei adversus atrocitatem peccati, & eius aliquem perciperent gustum.

2. Deinde, ut pluris facerent beneficia immensa filii Dei, qui nos à talibus terroribus conscientiae suo sanguine redemit.

3. Tertiò, ne summis illis donis, quibus à Deo ornati fuerunt sese efferrent, ac ne fiduciam in seipsis haberent.

4. Quartò, ut hac mortificatione veteris Adami, desiderium vitae aeternae ardentius in ipsis accenderetur.

4. Quintò, ut exemplo suo aliis membris Ecclesiae imbecillioribus consolationi essent. Cum enim multi in Ecclesia eiusmodi pavoribus & trepidationibus obruuntur, certò statuere possunt non esse eas signa irati Dei, siquidem & Apostolos, Prophetas, & patres vident similes terrores expertos esse.

6. Sextò, ut eò conspectior sit virtus Dei & omnis gloria collectae Ecclesiae, et destructi regni Satanae ad Deum redeat. Haec cogitet pius animus, quando legit summorum hominum horrendos pavores, ut Abrahae, Iacobi, Moisis, Iosuae, Davidis, Hiskiae, Pauli: Et animadvertat non semper eodem fulgore robur & laeticiam Spiritus lucere in sanctis.

Persuasorios humanae sapientiae sermones vocat populares conciones, quae totae eò directae sunt, ut quoquo modo adficiant & delectent auditores, eosque in admirationem dicentis rapiant. Samosatenus, Arrius, Nestorius, Origenes, & Pelagius persuasorios adferunt sermones: Dicunt enim quae congruunt rationi & carni grata sunt: Sic Calvinistae & falsarii testamenti Iesu Christi dicunt plausibilia & persuasoria: Removent enim omnem luctam fidei, & ea dicunt quae grata sunt rationi: Et quae oratione & figuris ornari possunt. Paulus autem testatur, se huic arti vel fraudi potius non studuisse, sed in omni simplicitate & rectitudine docuisse Evangelion: Et in hoc incubuisse ut Spiritu & virtute potius demonstraret veritatem suae concionis. Hoc est, ut & miraculis propriis Ecclesiae confirmaret auditorum fidem: Et ipsa experientia in consolationibus comprobaret eius doctrinam. Tum enim fides auditorum nititur solido & stabili fundamento: Videlicet, non humana sapientia qua nihil est incertius, nihil futilius; Sed divina virtute omnipotentis Dei.

## 2:6-7
But we speak wisdom among the perfect: Yet not the wisdom of this world, nor of the princes of this world that come to nought: But we speak the wisdom of God in a mystery, a wisdom which is hidden, which God ordained before the world unto

Latin:

Sapientiam autem loquimur inter perfectos: Sapientiam non huius seculi, neque principum huius seculi qui abolentur: Sed loquimur sapientiam Dei in mysterio absconditam, quam praefinivit Deus antè secula in gloriam

## 2:8
our glory: Which none of the Princes of this world knew.

Because Paul most modestly submitted himself, and confessed his own ignorance and infirmity, lest he should seem to detract anything from the majesty of the doctrine of the Gospel, he excepts, that nevertheless an excellent wisdom is delivered in the Gospel, however great that simplicity of words may be, and in a humble appearance without all pomp and noise of the world it is proposed. And again he accurately distinguishes between the wisdom of the Spirit and of the world. We speak, he says, wisdom. For immense wisdom is revealed in the law, which cannot be exhausted in this life: In the first commandment there is more of true wisdom than in all the writings of all men in the whole world: And although the wisdom of all men were gathered into one man, he nevertheless could not express the entire wisdom of one commandment. Then how infinite wisdom shines in the mission of the son, in the assumption of human nature, in the passion and death of Christ, in the resurrection of the same, in the institution of the ministry, in the gathering of the Church, in the remission of sins, in the distribution of spiritual gifts, in the demonstration of eternal salvation. This wisdom in the Gospel not only men, but even angels admire when they hear it.

He calls the faithful perfect, who truly and without hypocrisy embrace the Gospel: In whom the Holy Spirit dwells through faith. These see and understand this admirable wisdom, which is contained in the Gospel of Jesus Christ. The world indeed condemns the pious to extreme madness, for the reason that they postpone fortunes, advantages, peace, home, spouses, children, and life itself to the glory of God and the edification of the Church, but the Holy Spirit himself provides a distinguished testimony to the pious: That they do not labor under madness, but rather that a divine and heavenly wisdom shines in them. He names the wisdom of this age and of the princes of this age the philosophy and prudence and counsels of politicians. Solon, Lycurgus, Themistocles, Laelius, Scaevola, Cato, Maecenas, Agrippa, and the like were considered wise. Paul affirms, however, that the wisdom which is revealed in the Apostolic writings is clearly different from the wisdom of those who govern the republics and kingdoms of the world. For these follow only the judgment of reason: And they are ignorant of the divine word. Because he says that the princes of this age are being abolished, he warns that neither does political wisdom bring eternal life, nor will these worldly kingdoms remain perpetually, but the kingdoms themselves will perish along with human counsels. We speak, he says, the wisdom of God in a mystery, hidden. He calls the law and the Gospel the wisdom of God: For in these chapters of doctrine the knowledge of the true God and of his will, which is the highest wisdom, is revealed, without which heavenly revelation, truly is and remains a hidden mystery. For man is so corrupted by sin, that by the powers of his intellect he cannot see who God is: and how He wishes to be worshipped: Nor does he understand what kind of obedience God demands of us in His law. But he is entirely ignorant of the secret counsel concerning the redeeming of the human race through the Son the mediator, and concerning the gratuitous remission of sins. John says: No one has ever seen God: the only-begotten Son who is in the bosom of the Father, He has made Him known to us. John 1. Nor indeed have we merited this grace and glory, that the eternal Father has revealed this heavenly wisdom to us: But before the ages He foreordained it for our glory: that is, out of His immense mercy and goodness He determined in the Son to gather an eternal Church, and to reveal His secret wisdom comprised in the Gospel to His elect through the ministry of the Spirit: so that we who are now the most abject in the world, by the benefit and kindness of God are made the most glorious and most happy of all. There is therefore no reason that we should boast of our own intellect as if we were sharper than other men: Nor can we allege any merits of our own: but the whole benefit of the revealed Gospel is to be ascribed to the immense mercy and divine goodness. Paul repeats: with a universal and exclusive particle, that no prince of this world has known the wisdom of the Gospel: namely, by the powers of nature or the faculty of free will. For he names the princes of this age who are not illuminated by the Holy Spirit: nor do they have a part in the kingdom of God. None of these understood the wisdom revealed in the Gospel. It is necessary, therefore, that the entire power of free will in spiritual matters be completely extinguished, since none of the worldly princes could understand or perceive the doctrine of the Gospel. But if the most ingenious, the most wise, the most learned, and the most excellent of all could not perceive the counsel of God contained in the Gospel: much less can the remaining crowd, in whom there is not equal wisdom, or sharpness, or diligence, or talent, arrive at this by the powers of free will. From this it also appears how gravely Zwingli, Andradius, and those like them err, who imagined that Theseus, Hercules, Themistocles, Scipio, Fabricius, Cato, and the like have arrived in heaven, and will be companions of eternal blessedness. For no one comes to the Father, except through Christ: but the entire wisdom of the Spirit and the Gospel concerning the spiritual kingdom and the benefits of our Lord Jesus Christ was unknown to the princes of this age. Therefore, the Gentiles and similar worldly princes ignorant of the Gospel do not have a part in the eternal kingdom of Christ.

For if they had known, they would not have crucified the Lord of glory.

By a most evident sign and by the very effect of ignorance he proves that the wisdom of the Gospel is unknown to the princes of this world: Because they crucified the Lord of glory, the only-begotten Son of God, the redeemer and savior of the human race. And this the common people did not do, nor Gentiles ignorant of God: But the highest princes and priests among the people of God: To whom before others the Messiah had been promised: Who assiduously heard the sermons of the Prophets concerning the advent and spiritual kingdom of the Messiah. Who were princes among the people of God, held the law and the promises concerning the Messiah, and ought to have instructed the whole world. These, although they heard the heavenly sermons of Christ, saw with their eyes his stupendous miracles: Nevertheless, driven by horrible madness and fury, together with Pilate the Roman prefect, they crucified the Lord of glory, and the prince of life, and the founder of the Church. By which act they most evidently testified that they had neither recognized the Messiah himself, nor understood the doctrine of the Gospel concerning the benefits of the mediator. But if the princes among the people of God could not understand this wisdom, much less could the princes and wise men of the Gentiles. The doctrine concerning the communication of idioms can in some way be sought from this saying; And how one must speak piously and circumspectly concerning our Lord Jesus Christ, God and man, so that the personal union is not dissolved, and the natures are not confounded. The divinity in Christ did not suffer, nor was it crucified, nor did it die: For it is immutable: And yet it is rightly said that God the Word, the Lord of glory, the Son of God, has suffered, was crucified, died, and was buried. For a property suitable to one nature is attributed to the whole person in the concrete on account of the hypostatic union. Each nature retains its essential properties and idioms, which are nevertheless communicated in the concrete, to signify the personal union: nor is this an empty contention about words or phrases: but a matter of the greatest moment is urged here, namely, that the hypostatic union of the two natures in Christ may be expressed: When Polycarp is placed on the pyre, God does not suffer: even though the Holy Spirit dwells in the heart of Polycarp: because God and Polycarp are not one person. But when the man Jesus Christ is crucified, the Lord of glory himself is crucified: for the reason that Jesus Christ, God and man, is one person.

Latin:

nostram: Quam nemo Principum huius seculi cognovit.

Quia Paulus modestissimè sese submisit, & suam inscitiam & infirmitatem fassus est, ne videatur derogare aliquid maiestati doctrinae Evangelii, excipit, eximiam tamen sapientiam in Evangelio tradi, quantavis illa simplicitate verborum, & humili specie sine omni pompa & strepitu mundi proponatur. Ac rursus accuratè distinguit inter sapientiam Spiritus & mundi. Loquimur inquit, sapientiam. Immensa enim sapientia in lege patefit, quae in hac vita exhauriri non potest: In primo praecepto plus est verae sapientiae, quàm in omnibus scriptis omnium hominum in toto orbe terrarum: Et licet omnium hominum sapientia collata esset in unum hominem, is tamen unius praecepti integram sapientiam exprimere non posset. Deinde quàm infinita sapientia lucet in missione filii, in adsumptione humanae naturae, in passione & morte Christi, in resurrectione eiusdem, in institutione ministerii, in collectione Ecclesiae, in remissione peccatorum, in distributione donorum spiritualium, in demonstratione aeternae salutis. Hanc sapientiam in Evangelio non solum homines, verum etiam angeli cum eam audiunt admirantur.

Perfectos vocat fideles, verè & sine Hypocrisi amplectentes Evangelion: In quibus per fidem habitat Spiritus sanctus. Hi vident & intelligunt hanc admirandam sapientiam, quae in Evangelio Iesu Christi continetur. Mundus quidem pios extremae condemnat dementiae, eò quòd fortunas, commoda, pacem, domum, coniuges, liberos, & vitam ipsam postponunt gloriae Dei & aedificationi Ecclesiae, sed ipse Spiritus sanctus praebet piis insigne testimonium: Quòd non laborent dementia, sed potius diviva & coelestis in ipsis luceat sapientia. Sapientiam huius seculi & principum huius seculi nominat Philosophiam & prudentiam ac consilia politicorum. Sapientes habiti fuerunt Solon, Lycurgus, Themistocles, Laelius, Scaevola, Cato, Maecenas, Agrippa & similes. Adfirmat autem Paulus sapientiam quae in scriptis Apostolicis patefit, planè diversam esse à sapientia eorum qui respublicas & regna mundi gubernant. Hi enim tantum iudicium rationis sequuntur: Et ignari sunt verbi divini. Quòd dicit principes huius seculi aboleri, monet nec politicam sapientiam adferre vitam aeternam, neque mundana haec regna perpetuò mansura esse, sed ipsa regna cum humanis consiliis peritura. Sapientiam, inquit, Dei loquimur in mysterio absconditam. Dei sapientiam adpellat legem & Evangelion: In his enim doctrinae capitibus noticia veri Dei & voluntatis ipsius, quae summa est sapientia, revelatur, sine qua revelatione coelesti, verè est & manet absconditum mysterium. Homo enim ita corruptus est per peccatum, ut viribus ingenii videre non possit quis sit Deus: & quomodo coli velit: Nec intelligit qualem obedientiam Deus in lege sua à nobis postulet. Arcanum verò consilium de redimendo genere humano per filium mediatorem, & de gratuita remissione peccatorum prorsus ignorat. Ioan: inquit: Deum nemo vidit unquam: Filius unigenitus qui est in sinu patris ipse enarravit nobis. Ioan: 1. Nec verò nos meriti sumus hanc gratiam & gloriam, quòd aeternus pater nobis hanc coelestem patefecit sapientiam: Sed antè secula eam persinivit in nostram gloriam: hoc est, ex immensa misericordia & bonitate sine omni merito nostro constituit in filio colligere aeternam Ecclesiam, & arcanam suam sapientiam in Evangelio compraehensam electis suis per ministerium Spiritus patefacere: ut nos qui nunc in mundo sumus abiectissimi, Dei beneficio & benignitate efficimur omnium gloriosissimi & foelicissimi. Non est igitur quòd gloriemur de nostro ingenio quasi caeteris hominibus acutiores simus: Nec ulla nostra merita allegare possumus: sed totum beneficium revelati Evangelii immensae misericordiae et bonitati divinae est adscribendum. Repetit Paul: cum particula universali & exclusiva, nullum principem huius seculi cognovisse sapientiam Evangelii: scilicet, viribus naturae vel liberi arbitrii facultate. Nominat enim huius seculi principes qui non sunt illuminati per Spiritum sanctum: nec habent partem in regno Dei. Horum nullus intellexit sapientiam in Evangelio patefactam. Necesse est igitur universam vim liberi arbitrii in rebus spiritualibus prorsus extinctam esse, siquidem nemo principum mundanorum potuit intelligere vel percipere doctrinam Evangelii. Quòd si omnium ingeniosissimi, sapientissimi, eruditissimi, & praestantissimi non potuerunt percipere Dei consilium in Evangelio compraehensum: Multò minus reliqua turba, in quibus non est par sapientia, vel acumen, vel diligentia vel ingenium huc pervenire viribus lib: arbit: potest. Hinc etiam patet quàm graviter errent Zwinglius, Andradius & horum similes, qui finxerunt Theseum, Herculem, Temistoclem, Scipionem, Fabricium, Catonem & similes in coelum pervenisse, & aeternae beatitudinis fore socios. Nemo enim venit ad patrem, nisi per Christum: tota autem Spiritus & Evangelii sapientia de spirituali regno & beneficiis domini nostri Iesu Christi ignota fuit principibus huius seculi. Non ergò Ethnici & similes mundani principes ignari Evangelii partem habent in regno aeterno Christi.

Si enim cognovissent, dominum gloriae: non crucifixissent.

Signo evidentissimo & ipso effectu inscitiae probat principibus huius mundi ignotam esse sapientiam Evangelii: Quia dominum gloriae unigenitum filium Dei, redemptorem & salvatorem generis humani crucifixerunt. Idque non fecerunt homines plebei, aut Ethnici ignari Dei: Sed summi principes et sacerdotes in populo Dei: Quibus antè alios promissus erat Messias: Qui adsiduè audiebant Prophetarum conciones de adventu & spirituali regno Messiae. Qui erant principes in populo Dei, tenebant legem & promissiones de Messia, & totum orbem erudire debebant. Hi etsi audiebant Christi coelestes conciones, videbant oculis stupenda eius miracula: Tamen horribili amentia & furore praeciti, unà cum Pilato praefecto Romano dominum gloriae, & principem vitae, & conditorem Ecclesiae crucifixerunt. Quo facto evidentissimè testati sunt se nec ipsum Messiam agnovisse, nec doctrinam Evangelii de beneficiis mediatoris intellexisse. Si autem principes in populo Dei hanc sapientiam intelligere non potuerunt, multò minus principes & sapientes Ethnici. Doctrina de communicatione idiomatum, aliquomodo ex hoc dicto peti potest; Et quomodo piè & circumspectè de domino nostro Iesu Christo Deo & homine sit loquendum, ita ut unio personalis non dissolvatur, & naturae non confundantur. Divinitas in Christo non est passa, nec crucifixa, nec mortua: Est enim immutabilis: Et tamen rectè dicitur Deus logos, dominus gloriae, filius Dei est passus, crucifixus, mortuus, sepultus. Proprietas enim uni naturae conveniens, tribuitur toti personae in concreto propter unionem hypostaticam. Retinet utraque natura essentiales suas proprietates & idiomata, quae tamen in concreto communicantur, ad significandam unionem personalem: neque haec est inanis contentio de verbis seu phrasibus: sed res maximi momenti hîc urgetur, nimirum ut exprimatur hypostatica unio duarum naturarum in Christo: Quandò Polycarpus imponitur rogo, non patitur Deus: etiamsi Spiritus sanctus habitat in corde Polycarpi: quia Deus & Polycarpus non sunt una persona. Sed quando homo Iesus Christus crucifigitur, ipse dominus gloriae crucifigitur: eò quòd Iesus Christus Deus & homo est una persona.

## 2:9
But as it is written: Things which eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor have they ascended into the heart of man, those things God has prepared for those who love him.

The second reason taken from the testimony of the Prophet Isaiah, by which he proves that the princes and wise men of this age cannot by the light of nature investigate or understand the wisdom of the Gospel concerning the benefits of the mediator. But although Isaiah speaks of the immense glory of the future life, which God prepared for his elect: nevertheless Paul rightly applied it to the whole doctrine of the Gospel: For the doctrine concerning the resurrection of the dead and concerning eternal life promised to the elect on account of Christ, is the scope of the whole Gospel. Moreover, this saying is a sharp thunderbolt against the patrons of free will. For Isaiah and Paul leave absolutely nothing to man regarding spiritual things: What the eye, he says, has not seen, nor the ear heard, nor have they ascended into the heart of man, those things God has prepared for those who love him. As often as the Prophets call it the heart, they understand the mind and the will of man: and the principal powers of the soul. Most shamefully, therefore, do they err who imagine that natural things have remained intact: The Erasmians and Synergists also err who attribute to unregenerate man a little bit, a small faculty, a meager power of assenting, or of applying himself to grace, or at least a nod. For here Paul testifies that the whole mystery concerning the gathering of the Church did not ascend into the Heart of any man: That is, no man ever saw, or heard, or understood, or thought, or willed anything concerning the wisdom of the Gospel. Therefore, it is the benefit of God alone: the knowledge of the mediator Jesus Christ, and of his benefits, who through the ministry of the word revealed from heaven, and through the Holy Spirit, both illuminates our blind minds, and bends our wills to assent. When also the Apostle says that God to us salvation and that He has prepared this glory, He warns that we have deserved nothing, but that all things proceed from the mere goodness and beneficence of God. This saying is rightly accommodated to the whole mystery concerning the spiritual kingdom of Christ: But especially it significantly expresses the doctrine concerning the resurrection of the dead, and concerning the immense glory with which the faithful will be adorned in the other life. In Isaiah it is not for those who love him, but for those who wait for you: But the meaning is the same: To wait for the Lord is to trust and hope in the Lord: Which trust begets the love of God: And without faith and hope love cannot exist: Nor does trust and expectation remain without the love of God: but it soon begets fruit of this kind. Therefore Isaiah and Paul signify that this heavenly glory is promised to those who are living members of the Church; In whom true faith and hope in God shine, and who demonstrate by true love, that their faith is without hypocrisy.

Latin:

Sed quemadmodum scriptum est: Quae oculus non vidit, nec auris audivit, nec in cor hominis adscenderunt, ea praeparavit Deus his qui diligunt eum.

Secunda ratio sumpta à testimonio Prophetae Iesaiae, qua probat, principes & sapientes huius seculi luce naturae non posse indagare aut intelligere sapientiam Evangelii de beneficiis mediatoris. Etsi autem Iesaias loquitur de futurae vitae immensa gloria, quam Deus electis suis praeparavit: tamen rectè accommodavit Paulus ad totam Evangelii doctrinam: Nam doctrina de resurrectione mortuorum & de vita aeterna promissa electis propter Christum, scopus est totius Evangelii. Est autem hoc dictum acre fulmen contra patronos liberi arbitrii. Prorsus enim nihil relinquunt Iesaias et Paulus homini quò ad spiritualia: Quae oculus inquit, non vidit, nec auris audivit, nec in cor hominis adscenderunt, ea praeparavit Deus his qui diligunt eum. Quoties cor appellant Prophetae intelligunt mentem & voluntatem hominis: & praecipuas animae vires. Turpissimè igitur errant qui fingunt naturalia mansisse integra: Errant etiam Erasmiani & Synergistae qui homini non renato tribuunt modiculum, parvam facultatulam, exiguam vim adsentiendi, vel adplicandi sese ad gratiam, vel nutum saltem. Hîc enim testatur Paulus totum mysterium de collectione Ecclesiae non ascendisse in ullius hominis Cor: Id est, nullus hominum unquam quidquam de Evangelii sapientia vel vidit, vel audivit, vel intellexit, vel cogitavit, vel voluit. Solius ergò Deî beneficium est: noticia mediatoris Iesu Christi, et beneficiorum eius, qui per ministerium verbi de coelo revelati, & per Spiritum sanctum & caecas nostras mentes illuminat, & flectit nostras voluntates ad ad sentiendum. Cum etiam Apostolus dicit Deum nobis salutem & gloriam hanc praeparasse, monet nihil nos esse meritos, sed omnia ex mera Dei bonitate et beneficentia proficisci. Rectè accommodatur hoc dictum ad totum mysterium de regno Christi spirituali: Inprimis verò significanter exprimit doctrinam de resurrectione mortuorum, & de immensa gloria qua fideles in altera vita ornabuntur. In Iesaia non est diligentibus eum, sed expectanti te: Verum eadem est sententia: Expectare dominum est fidere & sperare in dominum: Quae fiducia gignit dilectionem Dei: Abque fide & spe dilectio existere non potest: Neque manet fiducia & expectatio sine dilectione Dei: sed mox gignit huiusmodi fructum. Significant igitur Iesaias et Paulus iis promitti coelestem hanc gloriam, qui sunt viva Ecclesiae membra; In quibus vera in Deum fides & spes lucent, quique vera dilectione demonstrant, quòd fides ipsorum sit sine hypocrisi.

## 2:10-12
But to us God has revealed, through His Spirit.

Paul proved with firm arguments that the wise of this world understand nothing of the mysteries of God, concerning the spiritual kingdom of Christ. He attributes this glory, however, to Christians. He teaches, therefore, whence they have this light. The Holy Spirit, he says, has revealed this wisdom to us. As far as we are concerned we were not more acute or more talented than other men: Unless God had looked upon us, we would have had to perish in the same darkness as others. But the Holy Spirit, whom God the Father poured out on account of the mediator Son, illuminated our minds and through the word of God and the holy scripture revealed to us the true knowledge of God, and of His will. Therefore, we do not attribute it to our own free will, but to the Holy Spirit alone, that we understand the wisdom of the Gospel.

The Apostles indeed had peculiar gifts of the Holy Spirit, and singular revelations. But here the Apostle speaks of the revelation of the Gospel, which is made through the Holy Spirit in the ministry of the word: in which He instructs, illuminates, consoles, and governs the whole Church. For to individual pious persons the Spirit imparts the knowledge of the true God and the understanding of the benefits of Christ. And thus Paul leads us to the revelation of the word: That we may not wander with our own speculations, that we may not inquire into the will of God toward us according to our own senses, or external events, or the judgments of men: But from the word of God which the Holy Spirit has revealed in the holy scriptures, let us seek the true knowledge of God, and inquire into His counsel concerning the redemption of the human race, and His will toward us. To the law, he says, and to the testimony: if they do not speak according to this word, the morning light shall not rise for them. Iesaia: 8. And Christ says:

They have Moses and the Prophets: let them hear them Luke 16.

For the Spirit searches all things, even the deep things of God. For who among men knows the things that are of a man, save the spirit of man which is in him? So also the things that are of God no man knows, but the Spirit of God.

Lest any of the faithful should doubt concerning the most merciful will of God toward us, which the Holy Spirit has revealed to us in the Gospel, Paul demonstrates that the wisdom of the Holy Spirit is immense: And that there is nothing in God which escapes the Holy Spirit. The Spirit, he says, searches all things, even the most hidden things in Him whose Spirit it is. As in man no one knows more rightly or more fully what is in man than the Spirit, that is, the soul of man: Which searches the innermost recesses and hiding places of the heart, and understands and knows all the thoughts of man. So the Spirit of God, who is not only in God, but is God Himself, understands and knows the entire wisdom and all the most secret counsels of God. This immense and infinite wisdom of the Holy Spirit first most strongly proves that the Holy Spirit, the third person in the divinity, is an omnipotent and eternal God, of the same essence with the eternal Father and the only-begotten Son.

Furthermore, he not only renders us certain concerning the most merciful will of God toward us and his secret counsel, but he also most effectively consoles us: since that Spirit in whom the infinite wisdom of God shines, and who proceeds from the essence of the Father and the Son, has revealed to us the Gospel of Jesus Christ: And he bears witness in our heart that through Christ the mediator salvation has certainly been obtained for us. This passage also testifies that the papal dogma, which commands us to doubt the will of God toward us, is full of impiety and blasphemy. For it contradicts this passage of Paul, who affirms that the wisdom of that Spirit is infinite, who has made known to us the will of God concerning our salvation. But just as he makes the faithful, who are governed by the guidance of the Holy Spirit, most certain of the will of God toward them: so he withdraws all understanding and knowledge of the true God and his counsels from all who are alien to the Spirit of God. No one, he says, knows the things that are of God, that is, who and what the true God is, and what his will is toward the human race, except the Spirit of God. It is therefore impossible to arrive at the true knowledge of God and eternal life without the illumination of the Holy Spirit. There is therefore no power or faculty of free will in those things which are of the Spirit of God.

We, however, have received not the spirit of the world, but the Spirit which is from God.

After he demonstrated that the infinite wisdom of the Holy Spirit and the mysteries of God cannot be understood by anyone without the illumination of the Holy Spirit, he now adds that the faithful have been gifted the Holy Spirit by God: And he distinguishes them from the remaining multitude of the damned, who are alien to the Spirit of God; and for that reason are oppressed by blindness and darkness more than the Egyptians. The spirit of the world is the spirit of darkness which blinds the hearts of men and depresses them into the deep mire of ignorance. This spirit of the world, which the world follows, is effective in the impious, and rules them.

We, however, who believe in Jesus Christ, as Paul testifies, have received the Spirit which is from God, who is the Holy Spirit, the third person of the divinity, coeternal with the Father and the Son. Since we are the temple of this Spirit, it is certain that we hold the mind and will of the eternal God, what He has decreed concerning our redemption and eternal salvation.

Again, here we have a most evident argument that the Holy Spirit is eternal and omnipotent God of the same essence with God. For God is a spiritual essence: John 4. God is a Spirit. But the Holy Spirit is from God. Therefore the Holy Spirit is not any creature, but is eternal and omnipotent God, of the same essence with the eternal Father and Son. Therefore, the error of Macedonius and the Pneumatomachi is to be execrated, who contended with blasphemous mouth that the Holy Spirit is not eternal God, but a creature inferior to the Son.

That we may know the things that are given to us by God: which also we speak in words, not which human wisdom teaches, but which the Holy Spirit teaches, comparing spiritual things with spiritual.

He explains for what purpose the eternal God has communicated His Spirit to us, namely, that He might reveal to us that secret wisdom concerning the spiritual kingdom of Christ and the immense benefits of God, that He might illuminate our minds, and that He might most closely unite us, once sanctified, with God. Here Paul delivers the doctrine concerning the indwelling of the Holy Spirit: That through faith not only are all sins remitted to us, and the righteousness of Christ imputed: But also that the Holy Spirit is poured out into all believers, who renews their mind and will and kindles in their heart new light, life, and joy. He then distinguishes the form of speech which human wisdom hands down and admires, from the form of speech which the Holy Spirit teaches in the Church. Human wisdom teaches them speeches which smell of erudition, which are tinged with urbanity: which are painted with various colors of figures and the allurements of words: which in no way offend the minds of the listeners, but always delight them: which swell with bombastic words, so that they make an elephant out of a fly, and carry everyone away into admiration: Whence the speeches of human wisdom are for the most part full of vanities, flatteries, and lies. But the form of speech which the Holy Spirit teaches is entirely different: First of all, it strives for the most certain and infallible truth: Your word, says Christ in his prayer to the Father, is truth. The speech of the Spirit has nothing feigned, nothing simulated, nothing painted; let your speech, says Christ, be yes, yes, no, no, whatever is more than these is from the evil one. Next, the speech of the Spirit does not flatter the fickleness of men, but refers all things to the glory of God: And it does this one thing, that it celebrates in the world the truth, justice, goodness, clemency, and mercy of God. The speech of the Spirit is full of gravity, and everywhere carries with it heavenly majesty: Everywhere it serves the necessity and salvation of the Church: It does not dissimulate the sins of the powerful: It does not seek the benevolence of the mob: It does not fear the fury of men: It does not flatter the rich, but freely and constantly according to the law taxes sins; And according to the Gospel he consoles those terrified by doctrine. There is also nothing simpler than the speech of the Spirit, nothing clearer, nothing more covered. For the Holy Spirit speaks to all men, He wishes to be understood by all. Therefore, Paul says that he adapts to spiritual things a form of speech of this kind, in which human reason does not delight. Therefore, speech that smells of human wisdom ought always to be suspect to us: And the minister of the Church ought to strive with the greatest zeal, so that he may imitate the truth, simplicity, perspicuity, and gravity of the Apostolic speech, as much as it is possible.

Latin:

Nobis autem Deus revelavit, per Spiritum suum.

Firmis argumentis probavit Paulus sapientes huius mundi, nihil intelligere mysteriorum Dei, de spirituali regno Christi. Tribuit autem hanc gloriam Christianis. Unde ergo hanc lucem habeant docet. Spiritus sanctus, inquit, nobis revelavit hanc sapientiam. Quod ad nos attinet non eramus caeteris hominibus acutiores aut ingeniosiores: Nisi Deus nos respexisset, in eisdem tenebris nobis cum aliis pereundum fuisset. Sed Spiritus sanctus quem Deus pater propter filium mediatorem effudit, mentes nostras illuminavit & per verbum Dei & sacram scripturam patefecit nobis veram Dei noticiam, & voluntatis ipsius. Non igitur libero nostro arbitrio, sed soli Spiritui sancto acceptum ferimus, quòd sapientiam Evangelii intelligimus.

Habuerunt quidem Apostoli peculiaria dona Spiritus sancti, et singulares revelationes. Verum hic loquitur Apostolus de revelatione Evangelii, quae fit per Spiritum sanctum in ministerio verbi: in quo totam erudit, illuminat, consolatur & gubernat Ecclesiam. Singulis enim piis impertit Spiritus veri Dei notitiam & intellectum beneficiorum Christi. Atque ita deducit nos Paulus ad patefactionem verbi: Ut non vagemur nostris speculationibus, non inquiramus Dei voluntatem ergà nos, iuxta nostros sensus, vel eventus externos, vel iudicia hominum: Sed ex verbo Dei quod Spiritus sanctus in scripturis sacris revelavit & veram noticiam Dei petamus, & eius consilium de redemptione generis humani, & voluntatem erga nos inquiramus. Ad legem inquit & ad testimonium: nisi dixerint iuxta verbum hoc, non orietur illis matutina lux. Iesaia: 8. Et Christus inquit:

Habent Moisen & Prophetas: Eos audiant Lucae. 16.

Spiritus enim scrutatur omnia, etiam profunda Dei. Quis enim hominum novit ea, quae sunt in homine, nisi Spiritus hominis qui est in ipso? Sic & ea quae Dei sunt nemo novit nisi Spiritus Dei.

Ne quis fidelium dubitet de clementissima Dei erga nos voluntate, quam Spiritus sanctus in Evangelio nobis patefecit, demonstrat Paulus immensam esse Spiritus sancti sapientiam: Et nihil esse in Deo, quod Spiritum sanctum lateat. Spiritus, inquit, scrutatur omnia, etiam occultissima in eo cuius est Spiritus. Ut in homine nemo rectius aut plenius novit quid sit in homine, quàm Spiritus, id est, anima hominis: Quae intimos recessus & latebras cordis scrutatur, & omnes hominis cogitationes intelligit & novit. Sic Spiritus Dei qui non solum in Deo, sed ipse Deus est, totam sapientiam & omnia etiam arcanissima Dei consilia intelligit & novit. Haec immensa atque infinita Spiritus sancti sapientia primùm validissimè probat Spiritum sanctum tertiam personam in divinitate esse omnipotentem & aeternum Deum, eiusdem essentiae cum aeterno patre & filio unigenito.

Deinde non tantum nos certos reddit de clementissima Dei erga nos voluntate & arcano ipsius consilio, verum etiam efficacissimè nos consolatur: Siquidem ille Spiritus in quo infinita Dei sapientia lucet, & qui de essentia patris & Filii procedit & nobis revelavit Evangelion Iesu Christi: Et in corde nostro dicit testimonium quòd per Christum mediatorem salus nobis certò sit parta. Testatur etiam hic locus plenum impietatis & blasphemiae esse dogma pontificium, quod iubet nos dubitare de voluntate Dei erga nos. Contradicit enim huic loco Pauli, qui adfirmat eius Spiritus sapientiam infinitam esse, qui nobis voluntatem Dei, de nostra salute patefecit. Ut autem fideles qui Spiritus sancti ductu reguntur facit certissimos de Dei erga se voluntate: ita omnem intellectum & noticiam veri Dei & consiliorum ipsius detrahit omnibus qui à Spiritu Dei sunt alieni. Nemo, inquit, novit ea quae sunt Dei, Id est, quis & qualis sit verus Deus, & quae eius sit voluntas erga genus humanum nisi Spiritus Dei. Impossibile est igitur pervenire ad veram Dei & vitae aeternae cognitionem sine illuminatione Spiritus sancti. Nulla ergò vis aut facultas est liberi arbitrii in iis, quae sunt Spiritus Dei.

Nos autem accepimus non Spiritum mundi, sed Spiritum qui est ex Deo.

Postquam demonstravit Spiritus sancti infinitam sapientiam, & mysteria Dei non posse à quoquam sine Spiritus sancti illuminatione intelligi, addit nunc fideles Spiritu sancto à Deo donatos esse: Et distinguit eos à reliqua multitudine damnatorum, qui à Spiritu Dei alieni sunt; atque ideò caecitate & tenebris plus quàm Aegyptiis oppressi sunt. Spiritus mundi, est Spiritus tenebrarum qui excaecat hominum corda & ea in profundum coenum ignorantiae deprimit. Hic mundi Spiritus, quem mundus sequitur, in impiis est efficax, eosque regit.

Nos verò qui credimus in Iesum Christum teste Paulo accepimus Spiritum qui est ex Deo, qui est Spiritus sanctus tertia persona divinitatis, coaeternus patri & filio. Huius Spiritus templum cum simus, certum est nos tenere mentem & voluntatem aeterni Dei, quid de nostri redemptione & salute aeterna decreverit.

Rursus hîc evidentissimum argumentum habemus, quòd Spiritus sanctus sit aeternus & omnipotens Deus eiusdem essentiae cum Deo. Deus enim est essentia Spiritualis: Ioan: 4. Deus est Spiritus. At Spiritus sanctus est ex Deo. Ergò Spritus sanctus non est creatura aliqua, sed est aeternus & omnipotens Deus, eiusdem essentiae cum aeterno patre & filio. Execrandus igitur est error Macedonii & pneumatomachorum qui blasphemo ore contenderunt Spiritum sanctum non esse aeternum Deum, sed creaturam inferiorem filio.

Ut sciamus, quae à Deo donata sunt nobis: quae & loquimur sermonibus, non quos docet humana sapientia, sed quos docet Spiritus sanctus, spiritualibus spiritualia coaptantes.

Exponit quo fine aeternus Deus nobis communicaverit suum Spiritum, nimirum ut arcanam illam sapientiam de spirituali regno Christi, & de immensis beneficiis Dei nobis patefaceret, mentes nostras illuminaret, & nos sanctificatos cum Deo arctissimè copularet. Tradit hic Paulus doctrinam de inhabitatione Spiritus sancti: Quod per fidem non solum remittantur nobis omnia peccata, & imputetur iustitia Christi: Verùm etiam quòd effundatur in omnes credentes Spiritus sanctus, qui renovat illorum mentem & voluntatem & in corde ipsorum novam lucem, vitam & laeticiam accendit. Discernit deinde sermonis formam quam humana sapientia tradit & admiratur, à forma sermonis quam docet Spiritus sanctus in Ecclesia. Humana sapientia eos docet sermones qui redoleant eruditionem, qui tincti sint urbanitate: qui variis figurarum coloribus & verborum lenociniis sint fucati: qui auditorum animos minimè offendant, sed semper delectent: qui tumeant ampullis verborum, ita ut ex musca Elephantum faciant, & omnes in admirationem rapiant: Unde sermones humanae sapientiae plerumque pleni sunt vanitatibus, adsentationibus, & mendaciis. Sermonis autem forma quam Spiritus sanctus docet prorsus alia est: Inprimis studet certissimae & infallibili veritati: Sermo tuus, inquit Christus in precatione ad patrem, est veritas. Nihil ficti, nihil simulati, nihil fucati habet sermo Spiritus, sermo vester, inquit Christus, sit est, est, non non, quod ultra est à malo est. Deinde sermo Spiritus non adulatur hominum levitati, sed omnia refert ad gloriam Dei: Et hoc unum agit ut celebrat in mundo veritatem, iustitiam, bonitatem, clementiam & misericordiam Dei. Sermo Spiritus plenus est gravitatis, et passim coelestem maiestatem prae se fert: Ubique servit necessitati & saluti Ecclesiae: Non dissimulat potentum peccata: Non captat vulgi benevolentiam: Non metuit hominum furorem: Non blanditur divitibus, sed liberè & constanter iuxta legem taxat peccata; Et iuxta Evangelii doctrinam perterrefactos consolatur. Nihil etiam sermone Spiritus est simplicius, nihil planius, nihil opertius. Omnibus enim hominibus loquitur Spiritus sanctus, ab omnibus vult intelligi. Huiusmodi ergò sermonis formam, qua ratio humana non delectatur, Paulus, dicit se rebus spiritualibus adaptare. Semper igitur nobis suspectus esse debet sermo humanam redolens sapientiam: Et Ecclesiae minister summo studio anniti debet, ut veritatem, simplicitatem, perspicuitatem & gravitatem sermonis Apostolici, quantum fieri potest, imitetur.

## 2:14
But the natural man does not perceive the things that are of the Spirit: for they are foolishness to him: Neither can he understand them: Because they are spiritually discerned.

This is that most celebrated passage, which most evidently settles the whole controversy, which in all times has been agitated in the Church concerning the powers of free will. For the Apostle Paul, by the instinct of the Holy Spirit, most explicitly pronounces: That the natural man understands nothing of those things which are of the Spirit of God, and pertain to eternal salvation, to such a degree that he holds them all for foolishness. Now, patron of free will and defender of synergy, and against Paul, assert that there is something in the unregenerate man, either a little bit, or a tiny faculty, or a little spark, or at least a nod, by which man can apply himself to grace, or to assent to the offered truth of the Gospel. What could be said more clearly and even more gravely against synergism? But the weights of the words must be pondered by us.

Paul calls the natural man the whole man, soul and body, with all the powers of the mind, will, and heart, insofar as he is naturally begotten by parents: not yet reborn through the Holy Spirit. For he opposes the natural to the spiritual. He speaks, therefore, of him who has been left in pure naturals: such as are not only the Gentiles and all outside the Church, but also all within the Church who have not been converted through the Holy Spirit. However much, therefore, one may possess either wisdom, or erudition, or talent, or virtue, or skill in affairs: unless one is regenerated and illuminated through the Holy Spirit, he is natural and perceives nothing of those things which are of the Spirit. In the same sense, Holy Scripture elsewhere calls him flesh, whom Paul in this place calls the natural man, as John 3 Whatever is born of the flesh is flesh: And Matthew 16 Flesh and blood have not revealed these things to you. Isaiah 40 All flesh is grass. In these places, flesh signifies the whole man, soul and body with all powers and faculties, just as he is begotten by parents: but he has not been illuminated by the light of the Holy Spirit. Natural are the Gentiles, however much endowed with wisdom, Themistocles, Solon, Plato, Xenophon, Scipio, Laelius, Augustus: these are animal men, as are Gamaliel and Nicodemus before their conversion, the Pharisees, and all who are destitute of the light of the Holy Spirit. When Christ says: Unless one is born again of water and the Spirit, he shall not see the kingdom of God, he teaches exactly the same thing that Paul does here, namely, that the animal or carnal man, who has not been born again through the Holy Spirit, cannot see those things which pertain to the heavenly kingdom of God and are of the Holy Spirit.

For these are things of the Spirit, which cannot be understood without the illumination of the Holy Spirit, such as the doctrine concerning the true knowledge of God. No one can call Jesus Lord (says Paul) except in the Holy Spirit. And no one knows the Father except the Son. Furthermore, human reason does not understand how sublime the judgment of God is according to the law: The law, says Paul, is spiritual: but I am carnal, Rom: 7. Moreover, the entire doctrine of the Gospel concerning the mediator, God and man, concerning his death and resurrection, concerning his benefits, and concerning his spiritual kingdom, in which, sitting at the right hand of the eternal Father, he gathers and rules the Church by his word and Spirit, and distributes righteousness and eternal life, is of the Spirit. All these things which pertain to the kingdom of Christ and have been revealed from heaven, but have not ascended into the heart of man without the revelation of the Holy Spirit, are of the Spirit of God. Therefore, Paul now affirms that the animal man is able to perceive nothing of those things which are of the Spirit of God. It is necessary, therefore, that free will be extinguished, as far as spiritual things are concerned: It is necessary that the powers of man be dead in spiritual things: since the natural man perceives nothing of those things which are of the Spirit of God. What impudence, therefore, is that of the Pelagians and Synergists against so manifest a sentence of the Holy Spirit, that they dare to assert that in the natural man, not yet reborn, there remains some power of free will, by which he can apply himself to grace, or assent to the preaching of the Gospel, or of himself agree to the drawing of the Father.

I. Let students, therefore, observe this distinguished testimony of the Holy Spirit, which is clearer than the midday light, and can be broken by no sophistry: that it testifies that there is no free will in man in spiritual things: And let other similar testimonies be added here, such as John 3 Whatever is born of the flesh is flesh, Item. Rom. 8 The mind of the flesh is enmity against God. Item: John 6 No one comes to me unless my Father has drawn him. Therefore, the doctrine is false and impious that writers affirm that there are three causes concurring in conversion, the Holy Spirit, the word of God, and the mind and will. Since the Holy Spirit alone works conversion to God through the word in the very blind mind and perverse will.

II. Many other chapters of doctrine besides this can be sought from the statement, that all men by nature are sinners and children of wrath. For man was so created that he might acknowledge and celebrate the true God: But he is so corrupted, that he cannot see those things which are of the Spirit, namely who the true God is. And since the natural man does not understand the spiritual judgment of the law, it is manifest that he does not perform complete obedience.

III. Thirdly, it is evident from this statement that the Gentiles, however much they were endowed with virtue, wisdom, and learning, were nevertheless not members of the Church of God, nor did they have any hope of obtaining eternal life. For they were entirely ignorant of the doctrine of the Holy Spirit.

IIII. Fourthly, Paul teaches that without the ministry of the Spirit and the word, no one arrives at the knowledge of the Mediator Jesus Christ: For the natural man, although he may be endowed with the highest genius and may speculate for a thousand years, yet he does not perceive those things which are of the Spirit.

V. Fifthly, this statement warns that the Church is not to be governed by human counsels: But the express word of God is to be followed.

VI. Sixthly, Paul warns that here we should take captive reason and all thoughts concerning God and eternal life into the obedience of Jesus Christ: For reason perceives nothing of those things which are of the Spirit. Therefore, Philosophy is not to be mixed with Theology: Nor are the articles of faith to be explained or formed from Philosophy, but the true meaning of the articles of faith from revelation of the Holy Spirit, which is consigned to the Prophetic and Apostolic writings, must always be sought.

For they are foolishness to him: Namely, those things which are of the Spirit. It is a most sorrowful speech that Paul said, that the natural man does not perceive the things which are of the Spirit, but it is much more grievous that he said the natural man condemns the counsels and doctrine of God and the Holy Spirit as foolishness. He is therefore insulting toward God and an enemy of God. How, therefore, could it happen that such a blasphemous enemy of God, in his conversion to God, would cooperate with the Holy Spirit by assenting to the doctrine which he holds for foolishness? It is necessary, therefore, that human nature is horribly corrupted. It is also manifest that all are by nature children of wrath and liable to death.

And he cannot know: So that he may leave no room for doubt, but that he may obstruct all the cracks of sophistries, he adds that the natural man cannot know the things which are of the Spirit. In spiritual matters, therefore, free will is utterly dead and is destitute of all power or efficacy. Thus at Rom: 8. Paul says: The sense of the flesh is not subject to the law of God: Neither indeed can it be. And Christ says. Iohan: 6: No one can come to me unless my father has drawn him.
