Sed non impertit eis iustitiam & vitam; Inhabitatio autem significat Deum per Spiritum sanctum occupare corda hominum, et eos purgare à peccato, liberare à morte & potestate Satanae: eisque impertiri vitam, iustitiam, laeticiam, & aeternam beatitudinem. Hoc ergò immensum Dei beneficium grato pectore celebremus, & studio sè caveamus ne securitate, aut peccatis contra conscientiam tantum hospitem à nobis abigamus.

Si quis, inquit, templum Dei corrumpit: corrumpit eum Deus. Gravissimas hic addit minas, ut tantò vehementius permoveat nos, ut nobis non scandalis et contentionibus turbantibus Ecclesiam caveamus. Si quis violet suo scelere aulam magni cuiusdam principis vel imperatoris, gravissimo adficitur supplicio. Sic sciat se gravissimas daturum paenas Deo, qui sacratissimum aeterni Dei templum violaverit. Homines tantum corpus occidunt, animam occidere non possunt. Deus autem quando decrevit perdere hominem, corpus & animam coniicit in ignem aeternum. Haec omnium gravissima paena omnes pios movere debet ne quis turbet Ecclesiam.

Nemo seipsum decipiat. Si quis

## 3:18-20
among you seemeth to be wise in this world, let him become a fool, that he may be wise. For the wisdom of this world is foolishness with God. For it is written: He taketh the wise in their own craftiness; And again: The Lord knoweth the thoughts of the wise, that they are vain.

Again Paul inculcates and warns that no one should think arrogantly of himself, and attribute to himself more wisdom than is fitting. For it is a foul error by which a man basely imposes upon himself when anyone arrogates to himself singular wisdom: since without the light of the Spirit there is horrible darkness in the human mind. When those who are dangerously bedridden and at the point of death boast that they are perfectly well, we judge them to be seized by frenzy: so those who attribute wisdom to themselves labor under a far more dangerous frenzy, when the densest gloom occupies their mind. Pelagius deceives himself, who arrogates to himself free will and the faculty by which he can fulfill the law. The Pharisees deceive themselves, when they attribute to themselves a righteousness from which they are most alien. Sennacherib basely imposes upon himself, in that he glories in his wisdom: by which he had occupied kingdoms. He also dissuades us from affecting a singular opinion of wisdom in the world: but rather that we should with a great Spirit bear the contempt of the world and the profane judgment. If any man among you seems to be wise, let him become a fool that he may be wise. Paul does not command that you should act insane in the manner of a fool, or that you should cast off all humanity and decency. He does not command that you should play the buffoon or imitate a Cynic philosopher. But since the judgment of the world is profane and perverse: it calls trickery, deceit, craftiness, and wickedness wisdom: conversely, it calls piety stupidity and folly.

So that what Polycarp, an old man of 99 years, prefers—to be burned by fire rather than to sacrifice three grains of incense to idols—it calls extreme madness: what Eleazar prefers—to die rather than to pretend that he is eating swine's flesh—it holds for detestable stupidity. Therefore Paul warns that there is no reason to care about the judgment of the world, that before it we seem foolish and fatuous: indeed, it ought to be pleasing to us that the world judges us in this way.

For the wisdom of this world is foolishness before God. This is a most weighty saying in which the Apostle shows the distinction between the judgment of the Spirit and human judgment: and it agrees with the saying of Christ. Whatever is sublime before men is an abomination before God. Luke 16. Likewise, the sense or thought of the flesh is enmity against God. Rom: 8. Man admires his own inventions, in the doctrine concerning God, in worship, in government, and in whole life. But whatever man admires, that is an abomination before God, for reason fashions religions without the word, nay, against the word: As Gideon, Aaron, Jeroboam, Numa Pompilius, Varro, Hesiod, Homer: And all wise men outside the Church: And indeed the frenzies of the Gentiles in sacred rites demonstrate it to be most true, that the wisdom of men is foolishness before God.

Then in government, reason admires its own cunning: Pharaoh devises various ways by which he wishes to oppress the Church: First by burdens, then by the doubling of bricks, then through the midwives: Finally by the drowning of infants. And yet the Church is preserved: he himself, however, with his Egyptians is drowned. Ahithophel devises a cunning plan by which he turns the mind of the people away from King David, and gives counsel concerning oppressing him: But David escapes. Ahithophel breaks off his life with a noose. And the counsels of all men which are not governed by the word of God and the leading of the Holy Spirit, the more cunning they are, the more they have of impiety and wickedness.

Many think it to be a singular wisdom, not to mix oneself in the disputation concerning religion; To collude with both sides: To find buskins: To decline all dangers of confession: To simulate and dissimulate everything: To incline oneself to the side of the ship more happily; Not to offend the wills of the powerful: Into the favor of the powerful to deny the faith, and to conform themselves to the world: But this is not only foolishness before God, but also impiety and a most atrocious crime. And for the most part, such turncoats, Eceboluses, Sisyphuses, Therameneses, καὶ ἀλλοπροσαλλοι stumble more heavily, and fall into τραγικοτέρας calamities than simpler people, who openly profess the truth. Therefore, this most serious saying must be observed: The wisdom of this world is foolishness with God. From this it follows that there is no free will in spiritual matters. For foolishness before God can know neither God nor His will.

Indeed, God abominates the wandering thoughts of the mind which inflict insult upon Him. But the highest and most excellent power of the mind and will of men is foolishness before God. It is impossible, therefore, that the mind and will of an unregenerate man should cooperate in any way in the conversion of man, which must be done according to the word of God. He brings forward testimony from Job. Chap: 5. And from Psalm: 94. By which he proves that God opposes the cunning counsels of the wise, and catches and binds the crafty in their own wisdom, just as the example of the princes of the Medes in Daniel shows: Who are caught in their own snare: Likewise, Haman, Ahithophel, Eutropius under Arcadius and others: Pharaoh, Antiochus, Epiphanes, Diocletian attempted with most astute counsels to destroy the Church and oppress the truth, Licinius, Julian: But not only were their counsels vain, but they themselves perished by their own counsels. The Lord knows, says David, that the thoughts of men are vain. For no counsel prevails against the Lord. Paul the Third, Roman Pontiff, and his successors agitated various counsels with monarchs and most powerful kings so that they might erase the entire name of the Church: but all their thoughts were vain. The Church remains and is divinely defended: But the pontiffs have descended to the underworld.

Latin:

inter vos videtur esse sapiens, in hoc seculo stultus fiat, ut sit sapiens. Nam sapientia huius mundi, stulticia est apud Deum. Scriptum est enim: Qui capit sapientes in versutia sua; Et rursus: Novit dominus cogitationes sapientum quòd vanae sunt.

Rursus inculcat & monet Paulus, ne quis arroganter de se sentiat, ac tribuat sibi plus sapientiae quàm par sit. Faedus enim est error quo sibi turpiter imponit homo cum quis arroget sibi sapientiam singularem: cum sine luce Spiritus horrendae tenebrae sint in mente humana. Cum periculosè decumbentes & animam agentes iactitant serectè valere, phrenesi eos correptos esse iudicamus: sic longè periculosius laborant phrenesi qui tribuunt sibi sapientiam, cum densissima caligo occupet mentem illorum. Fallit seipsum Pelagius, qui arrogat sibi liberum arbitrium & facultatem qua possit implere legem. Fallunt sese Pharisaei, cum tribuunt sibi iustitiam à qua sunt alienissimi. Turpiter imponit sibi Sennacherib, quòd gloriatur de sua sapientia: qua regna occupaverit. Dehortatur etiam ne singularem sapientiae opinionem in mundo adfectemus: sed ut potius magno Spiritu mundi contemptum & prophanum iudicium feramus. Si quis inter vos sapiens esse videtur fiat stultus ut sit sapiens. Non iubet Paulus ut fatui more insanias, aut omnem exuas humanitatem & honestatem. Non iubet ut morionem agas vel cynicum Philosophum imiteris. Sed cum prophanum & perversum sit mundi iudicium: Praestigias, dolos, versutiam, nequitiam vocat sapientiam: Contra pietatem vocat stoliditatem & stultitiam.

Ut quod Polycarpus 99. annorum senex mavult igne cremari, quam tria granathuris sacrificare Idolis, extremam vocat dementiam: Quod Eleazarus mavult mori, quam simulare quod vescatur carne suilla, pro detestanda habet stulticia. Idcirco Paulus monet non esse curandum mundi iudicium, quod coràm eo stulti & fatui videamur: Imògratum nobis esse debet quod mundus sic de nobis iudicat.

Sapientia enim huius mundi est stultitia coram Deo. Gravissimum est hoc dictum in quo Apostolus ostendit discrimen inter iudicium Spiritus & humanum: Et congruit cum dicto Christi. Quidquid sublimè est coràm hominibus abominatio est coràm Deo. Lucae 16. Item, sensus seu cogitatio carnis est inimicitia adversus Deum. Roma: 8. Homo admiratur sua inventa, in doctrina de Deo, in cultu, in gubernatione, & in tota vita. Sed quidquid homo admiratur, id est abominatio coràm Deo, fingit enim ratio religiones absque verbo imò contra verbum: Ut Gedeon, Aaron, Ierobeam, Numa, Pompilius, Varro, Hesiodus, Homerus: Et omnes sapientes extra Ecclesiam: Et sanè furores Ethnicorum in sacris demonstrant verissimum esse, quod sapientia hominum sit stultitia coràm Deo.

Deinde in gubernatione admiratur suam calliditatem ratio: Pharao excogitat varias vias, quibus vult premere Ecclesiam: Primum oneribus, deinde duplicatione laterum, de inde per obstetrices: Tandem submersione infantum. Et tamen servatur Ecclesia: ipse verò cum suis Aegyptiis submergitur. Achitophel callidum excogitat consilium quo avertit populo animum à Rege Davide, & dat consilium de eo opprimendo: Sed David evadit. Achitophel laqueo abrumpit sibi vitam. Et omnium hominum consilia quae non reguntur verbo Dei & ductu Spiritus sancti, quo sunt callidiora, hoc plus habent impietatis & scelerum.

Multi putant singularem esse sapientiam, non miscere sese disputationi de religione; Colludere cum utraque parte: Invenire cothurnos: Declinare omnia pericula confessionis: Simulare & dissimulare omnia: Inflectere se ad latus navis faelicius; Non offendere potentum voluntates: In gratiam potentum abnegare fidem, & sese mundo conformare: Sed non solum stultitia haec est coram Deo, sed etiam Impietas & scelus atrocissimum. Et plerumque huiusmodi Cothurni, Eceboli, Sisyphi, Theramenes, καὶ ἀλλοπροσαλλοι gravius impingunt, & in τραγικοτέρας calamitates incidunt quàm simpliciores, qui apertè profitentur veritatem. Observandum igitur est hoc gravissimum dictum: Sapientia huius mundi stultitia est apud Deum. Hinc sequitur nullum esse liberum arbitrium in spirtualibus. Stultitia enim coràm Deo nec Deum nec ipsius voluntatem cognoscere potest.

Imò Deus abominatur errantes mentis cogitationes quae ipsum contumelia adficiunt. At sapientia hominum summa & praestantissima vis mentis & voluntatis est stultitia coràm Deo. Impossibile est igitur ut mens & voluntas hominis non renati aliquid cooperetur in conversione hominis, quam oportet iuxta Dei verbum fieri. Adducit testimonium ex Iob. Cap: 5. Et ex Psalm: 94. Quibus probat Deum adversari callidis consiliis sapientum, & vafros in sua sapientia capere ac constringere, quemadmodum ostendit exemplum principum Maedorum in Daniele: Qui suo se capiunt laqueo: Item, Haman, Achitophel, Eutropius apud Arcadium & alii: Astutissimis consiliis conati sunt delere Ecclesiam & opprimere veritatatem Pharao, Antiochus, Epiphanes, Diocletianus, Licinius, Iulianus: Sed non solum irrita fuerunt ipsorum consilia, verum etiam ipsi suis consiliis perierunt. Novit dominus, inquit David, quòd cogitationes hominum vanae sunt. Non enim valet consilium contra Dominum. Paulus tertius Rom: Pontifi: & successores eius varia agitarunt consilia cum Monarchis & potentissimis regibus ut universum nomen Ecclesiae delerent: sed vanae fuerunt omnes illorum cogitationes. Manet & divinitus defenditur Ecclesia: Sed pontifices descenderunt ad inferos.

## 3:21-22
Therefore let no one glory in men: For all things are yours, whether Paul, or Apollo, or Cephas: or the world, or life, or death, or things present, or things to come: All are yours, and you are Christ's, and Christ is God's.

Paul finally concludes this exhortation to the pursuit of concord, appending still a notable argument from the amplitude and majesty of the kingdom of Christ, and the communion of all the saints. In those things which pertain to the universal Church and to individual pious persons, and which serve for the salvation of all, no one ought to glory peculiarly, as if they were their own. But all ministers and Apostles, Paul, Apollo, Cephas, indeed the whole world and all creatures pertain to the whole Church and to individual pious persons. Therefore, no one ought to boast particularly in this or that minister, or in any man, or in any creature, or to contend about it. Paul wishes us, in the most excellent gifts of God, to look not to men, but to the Son of God himself who has bestowed such ministers upon the Church: furthermore, that regard should be had not only for ourselves but for the whole Church. For we are one body, and all members of Jesus Christ. Therefore, just as we have been co-opted into the society of the kingdom of Christ: so we ought not to begrudge others this communion of heavenly goods.

Paul openly testifies here that neither the Apostles nor any ministers are lords of the Church, but rather that the Church is the lady of all ministers, as much of Prophets and Apostles as of Bishops and pastors. Therefore, the Roman Pontiff, cardinals, Bishops, and prelates exercise tyranny, who exalt themselves above the Church, attempt to impose laws upon her, prescribe dogmas of faith for her, snatch away from her the power of judging, impose burdens upon her against her will without the word of God, and demand obedience from her outside of the ministry. That tyranny is therefore to be refuted by the saying of Christ, The kings of the Gentiles exercise lordship over them: but you shall not be so. Luc: 22.

Here also the most ample riches of the saints and of those believing in Christ are to be weighed. He testifies Paul, that all things are ours, not only all gold and silver, not only the Turkish empire and the kingdom of the Gauls, but the whole world, and finally life and death themselves and all creatures. Reason judges that there is nothing more vain than this boasting. For what group in the world is pressed by greater poverty and lack of things than Christians? Who are exposed to the hatreds of all; they have no fixed seat anywhere: they wander the globe as most miserable exiles. But what Paul affirms is most true. That he who believes in Christ is the lord of the whole world: for through Christ is the possession of the world: lost through Adam, it is restored to us: and every creature is subjected to the dominion of the sons of God: all things are compelled to serve our salvation. Nor do Christians labor under the lack of any thing: through invocation they can obtain all things from the eternal Father. Whatever you ask the Father in my name (says Christ) he will give to you. Ioan: 16. Item Psal: 34. There is no lack for those who fear him. But those who fear the Lord have not lacked any good thing. Jacob says to Esau gen: 38: take I pray these things: For I have all things. Psal: 23. The Lord is my shepherd, I shall lack nothing. Thus Paul Ro: 8. If God is for us who is against us: who also did not spare his own son, but gave him for us: how will he not give all things to us with him. And Ro. 4. he says: that the promise was made to Abraham, that he would be the heir and lord of the world.

Let us therefore magnify and gratefully celebrate these most ample riches, heaven and earth, the inheritance and possession of which the Son of God has procured for us. We have not yet been introduced into full possession, nor has the power over all things been handed over to us: because we are still minors, and we need guardians, on account of the infirmity of our flesh. God therefore distributes individual things to us, according as He Himself knows them to be salutary for us. Augustine says we have all things in hope, not in reality. In the regeneration, the full possession of the whole world will be handed over to us.

From this it is gathered, when one of the rich denies alms and the necessities of life to a Christian, he commits theft: because he denies to the Christian what is owed to him by the right of the kingdom of Christ. If you have not fed him, says Ambrose, you have killed him: For all things are the faithful's: But what? Is it permitted for Christians to occupy the goods of the rich and the impious? By no means: for if they attempt this, they are not Christians. According to the spiritual kingdom of Christ, all things are indeed the faithful's: but they ought to wait until they are introduced into possession by God Himself. For God has also established the kingdoms of the world: and in it He has distinguished the ownership of things. You shall not steal, He says. Therefore, under the pretext of piety, the goods of others are not to be invaded, but one must abstain from everything that belongs to another. When the impious indeed use even a grain of salt, or a drop of water, they do so from their own goods, and acquired by right, they commit theft before God: because they usurp those things which are of the children of God, but the impious, because they are alienated from God, have no right to any creature of God. He permits them, however, the possession of things in the world, so that He may manifest the riches of His goodness even toward the impious.

Latin:

Itaque nemo glorietur in hominibus: Omnia enim vestra sunt, sive Paulus, sive Apollo, sive Coephas: sive mundus, sive vita, sive mors, sive praesentia, sive futura: Omnia vestra sunt, vos autem Christi, Christus autem Dei.

Concludit tandem Paulus hanc adhortationem ad concordiae studium, subnectens adhuc insigne argumentum ab amplitudine & maiestate regni Christi, & communione omnium sanctorum. Quae ad universam Ecclesiam & singulos pios pertinent, & omnium saluti serviunt, in iis nemo peculiariter, tanquam propria essent, gloria ridebet. At omnes ministri & Apostoli, Paulus, Apollo, Caephas, imò totus mundus et omnes creaturae ad totam Ecclesiam & singulos pios pertinent. Nemo ergò in hoc velillo ministro, aut in ullo homine, aut in ulla creatura peculiariter gloriari, aut de ea contendere debet. Paulus vult nos in praestantissimis donis Dei respicere non ad homines, sed ad ipsum Dei filium qui tales ministros Ecclesiae est largitus: deinde non tantum nostri sed totius Eccle: rationem haberi. Unum enim corpus sumus, & omnes membra Iesu Christi Ut ergò nos ad societatem regni Christi cooptati sumus: ita hanc communionem coelestium bonorum aliis invidere non debemus.

Aperte testatur hic Paulus nec Apostolos nec ullos ministros, esse dominos Ecclesiae, sed potius Ecclesiam dominam esse omnium ministrorum, tàm Prophetarum & Apostolorum quàm Episcoporum & pastorum. Tyrannidem ergò exercent Pontifex Roma: cardinales Episcopi, & praelati, qui sese efferunt supra Ecclesiam, conantur ei ferre leges, praescribunt ei fidei dogmata, eripiunt ei iudicandi potestatem, imponunt invitae onera absque Dei verbò, postulant ab ea obedientiam extra ministerium. Refutanda est igitur ista tyrannis dicto Christi, Reges gentium dominantur: vos autem non sic. Luc: 22.

Hic etiam expendendae sunt amplissimae opes sanctorum & in Christum credentium. Teslatur Paulus, Omnia esse nostra, non solum omne aurum & argentum, non solum imperium, Turcicum, & regnum Galliarum, sed universum mundum, ipsam denique vitam & mortem & omnes creaturas. Ratio existimat hac gloriatione nihil esse vanius. Quis enim coetus in mundo maiore egestate & inopiarerum premitur quàm Christiani? qui omnium odiis sunt expositi; nuspiam certam sedem habent: ut miserrimi exules in orbe oberrant. Sed verissimum est quod Paulus adfirmat. Credentem in Christum, dominum esse totius mundi: per Christum enim possessio mundi: per Adamum amissa nobis restituitur: et universa creatura dominio filiorum Dei est subiecta: omnianostrae saluti servire coguntur. Neque ullius rei indigentia laborant Christiani: per invocationem omnia ab aeterno patre impetrare possunt. Quicquid petieritis patrem in nomine meo (inquit Christus) dabit vobis. Ioan: 16. Item Psal: 34. Non est inopia timentibus eum. Timentes autem dominum non indiguerunt ullo bono. Iacob inquit ad Esau gen: 38: accipe quaeso ista: Nam ego omnia habeo. Psal: 23. Deus pastor meus, nihil mihi deerit. Sic Paulus Ro: 8. Si Deus pro nobis quis contra nos: qui etiam proprio filio non pepercit, sed dedit eum pro nobis: quomodo non omnia nobis cum illo daret. Et Ro. 4. dicit: Abrahamo factam esse, promissionem, quod sit futurus haeres & dominus mundi.

Amplissimas igitur has opes coelum & terram, quarum haereditatem & possessionem filius Dei nobis comparavit magnifaciamus & grati celebremus. In Plenam quidem possessionem nondum introducti sumus, nec omnium rerum potestas nobis tradita est: quia impuberes adhuc sumus, & tutoribus egemus, propter carnis nostrae infirmitatem. Deus igitur nobis singula distribuit, pro ut ipse novit ea nobis esse salutaria. Augustinus inquit habemus omnia in spe, non in re. In regeneratione plena totius mundi possessio nobis tradetur.

Hinc colligitur, cum quis ex divitibus denegat Christiano eleemosynam, & vitae necessaria, furtum committit: quia denegat Christiano, quod ei iure regni Christi debetur. Si non pavisti inquit Ambrosius, occidisti: Omnia enim sunt fidelium: Sed quid? nunquid licet Christianis occupare divitum & impiorum bona? nequaquam: hoc enim si tentaverint non sunt Christiani. Iuxta spirituale Christi regnum omnia quidem sunt fidelium: sed expectare debent donec ab ipso Deo in possessionem introducantur. Deus enim etiam mundiregna stabilivit: & in eo distinxit rerum dominia. Non furtum facies inquit. Non igitur praetextu pietatis aliorum bona invadenda sunt, sed abomni alieno abstinendum est. Cum impii quidem vel grano salis, velgutta aquae utuntur, de bonis propriis, & iure acquisitis, coram Deo furtum committunt: quia usurpant ea quae sunt filiorum Dei, Impii verò quia à Deo sunt alieni, nihil iuris in ullam Dei creaturam habent. Permittit autem illis possessionem rerum in mundo, ut divitias bonitatis suae etiam erga impios manifestet.

## 3:23
But you are Christ's: and Christ is God's. As all creatures serve your salvation and necessity: so you individually ought to serve the glory and majesty of Christ, who prepared such great riches for you, and take care lest you disturb or tear apart the Church of Christ with contentions, which scandals turn to the reproach of Christ. But Christ is God's, namely the only-begotten son, who with the greatest zeal directs all things to the glory of the eternal father.

Latin:

Vos autem estis Christi: Christus autem Dei. Ut omnes creaturae vestrae serviunt saluti & necessitati: Ita vos singuli gloriae & maiestati Christi, qui vobis tantas paravit opes servire debetis, & cavere ne contentionibus turbetis aut laceretis Ecclesiam Christi, quae scandala in Christi contumeliam vergunt. Christus autem Dei est scilicet unigenitus filius, qui summo studio omnia ad gloriam aeterni patris dirigit.

## 3:23 Places of Doctrine
Places of Doctrine.

1. Concerning the infirmity of the saints, that great sins may cling to the saints. Paul attributes this title to the Corinthians, that they are sanctified in Jesus Christ. And yet there existed among them contentions, dissensions, and rivalries.

2. With what prudence the Church should be established. We ought to accommodate ourselves to the capacity of the hearers: and deliver the first elements to the more unlearned, and always have regard for the infirm. Just as a nurse gives milk to an infant, she does not immediately burden the weak stomach of the infant with solid food.

3. Concerning the distinction between Christ and the Apostles or other ministers. Christ is the lord of the ministry and is efficacious through it: But the Apostles are only external ministers.

4. Concerning the efficacy of the ministry: the labor of those teaching in the Church is not empty, but God gives the increase, and through the word gathers a Church to Himself.

5. That God will compensate the labors of all pious ministers with a most ample reward. Everyone, he says, will receive his reward according to his work.

6. Concerning the unique foundation of our faith: Which is our Lord Jesus Christ: Therefore outside of Christ there is no salvation: And he who denies either the person or the office of Christ is a stranger to the house of God and has no part in the kingdom of Christ.

7. Concerning the diversity of gifts in the Church. There is a great dissimilarity between those who retain the foundation: For one builds gold upon it: Another stubble and hay.

8. Concerning the distinction between heresy and error: Heresy is when one departs from the foundation, and the articles of faith are corrupted, and a false opinion is pertinaciously defended against the word of God.

Error, however, is when one does not depart from the foundation: But in other parts of doctrine a man hallucinates, yet he does not pertinaciously defend the error against the word of God.

9. Concerning the cross and afflictions, both of the teachers and of the hearers, in whom both the kind of doctrine and the sincerity of faith ought to be tested, as silver in the fire.

10. Concerning the indwelling of the Holy Spirit: That the pious are the temple of God, and the Spirit of God dwells in them.

11. Concerning the horrible punishment that awaits all who tear the Church apart with contentions and dissensions, and stir up scandals in it. The Lord will destroy him: says the Apostle.

12. That the wisdom of the world is foolishness before God. Therefore, the holy judgments of the Spirit must always be distinguished from the profane judgments of the world. And from this it follows that there is no free will in man regarding spiritual matters. For God abominates the wisdom of the human brain.

13. That Apostles and Pastors are not lords of the Church. But rather the Church is the lady of all ministers.

14. That a Christian or believer is the lord and heir of the whole world and of all creatures. He has a right to the thing, but not yet in the thing.

Latin:

Loci Doctrinae.

1. De infirmitate sanctorum, quod magna peccata haereànt in sanctis. Tribuit Paulus Corinth: hunc titulum quod sint sanctificati in Iesu Christo. Et tamen existebant inter eos contentiones, dissidia, aemulationes.

2. Qua prudentia instituenda sit Ecclesia. Accomodare nos debemus ad captum auditorum: & rudioribus prima tradere elementa, & semper infirmorum habere rationem. Sicuti nutrix infantem lacte potat, non cibo solido mox onerat imbecillem infantis ventriculum.

3. De discrimine inter Christum & Apostolos seu alios ministros. Christus est dominus ministerii & per illud est efficax: Sed Apostoli tantum sunt externi ministri.

4. De efficacia ministerii: non est inanis labor docentium in Ecclesia, sed Deus dat incrementum, & per verbum colligit sibi Ecclesiam.

5. Quòd amplissima mercede Deus sit compensaturus omnium piorum ministrorum labores. Unusquisque, inquit, iuxta opus suum mercedem accipiet.

6. De unico fundamento fidei nostrae: Quod est dominus noster Iesus Christus: Ergò extra Christum non est salus: Et qui vel personam vel officium Christi negat alienus est à domo Dei & non habet partem in regno Christi.

7. De diversitate donorum in Ecclesia. Magna dissimilitudo est inter eos, qui retinent fundamentum: Alius enim aurum super aedificat: Alius stipulam & faenum.

8. De discrimine inter haeresin & errorem: Haeresis est cum disceditur à fundamento, & articuli fidei corrumpuntur, falsaque sententia contra Dei verbum pertinaciter defenditur.

Error verò est cum non disceditur à fundamento: In aliis verò doctrinae partibus homo hallucinatur, nec tamen errorem pertinaciter contra Dei verbum defendit.

9. De cruce & adflictionibus, cum doctorum tum auditorum, in quibus & genus doctrinae & synceritatem fidei, tanquam argentum in igne probari oportet.

10. De inhabitatione Spiritus sancti: Quòd pii sint templum Dei, & Spiritus Dei habitet in eis.

11. De horribili poena quae manet omnes qui contentionibus & dissidiis distrahunt Ecclesiam, & scandala in ea excitant. Corrumpet eum dominus: Inquit Apostolus.

12. Quod mundi sapientia sit stultitia coràns Deo. Distinguenda igitur semper sunt sancta Spiritus iudicia, à Prophanis mundi iudiciis. Atque hinc sequitur nullum esse liberum arbitrium in homine quo ad Spiritualia. Abominatur enim Deus sapientiam humani cerebri.

13. Quòd Apostoli & Pastores non sint domini Ecclesiae. Sed potius Ecclesia sit domina ommum ministrorum.

14. Quòd Christianus seu fidelis, sit dominus & haeres totius mundi & omnium creaturarum. Ius habet ad rem, sed nondum in re.

## 4:1 Argument
CHAPTER IV.

Latin:

CAPUT IIII.

## 4:1
Let a man so account of us, as of the ministers of Christ, and stewards of the mysteries of God. Moreover it is required in stewards, that a man be found faithful.

Paul does not yet make an end of chastising the Corinthians on account of the contentions and rivalries, by which one preferred himself to another. For he sees what an irreparable damage this plague brings to the Church of Christ. Therefore, he again exhorts individuals in the Church to modesty and the pursuit of concord: and he chastises one by one the ministers who were exalting themselves on account of their gifts: First, he warns the whole Church not to judge rashly concerning the excellence or the rewards of a minister, but to look only to this, whether he serves faithfully; the rest he leaves to the judgment of God. Then he warns the teachers of the Church themselves not to proudly exalt themselves on account of their gifts, but rather to acknowledge from whom they received the gifts, and in whose honor they ought to use them. That he may the more easily obtain this from them, he commemorates the hardships, dangers, and infinite calamities with which God has burdened the ministers of the Church and especially the Apostles, so that they might be as it were προφυλάκτυκα which might ward off the disease of pride and insolence. Finally, he explains with what a fatherly spirit he embraces them, and with what counsel he sent Timothy to them.

He had shown before the distinction between God the author of the ministry, and the ministers: and he had said that neither he who plants nor he who waters is anything: but only God who bestows and effects salvation is all things. Lest this statement be taken sinisterly by some, for the despising of the ministry of the Apostles:

For the levity of the human mind easily strikes against either side: it either attributes more to ministers than is right, or it holds them in too contemptuous a manner: it teaches in what place the ministers of the Church are to be held. No one ought to acknowledge us as lords or authors of the Church and ministry: but let a man so esteem us as ministers of Jesus Christ, and stewards of the mysteries of God. Apostles and Pastors are not ministers of kings or political Magistrates: but of the highest king our Lord Jesus Christ: for they serve his spiritual kingdom by preaching the Gospel and distributing the sacraments. Nor indeed is there a greater or more glorious office on earth, than to serve Christ the king, in those things which pertain to his eternal glory, and the perpetual salvation of the Church. Nor is there any doubt that a most ample reward is laid up in heaven for those who serve Christ the lord of heaven and earth. They call the whole doctrine of Jesus Christ, the sacraments and all the benefits of the mediator, mysteries. For this wisdom and these spiritual gifts of the kingdom of Christ are unknown to all human reason: and only revealed from heaven through the son. The Apostles and all ministers of the Church are stewards of these mysteries, for through them God makes known his will to us: through them he calls us to repentance: through them he remits sins to us: By their voice and ministry he kindles faith and righteousness in us, and works salvation in us.

Therefore, we receive the highest benefits from God through the ministry of the Apostles. And for that reason, they are worthy of all reverence and honor on account of so sublime a work: nor ought we to measure these things by the excellence of the gifts, or the rank of the office: for the duties are diverse, and the gifts are diverse. But [we ought to measure them] by the truth and efficacy of the divine word. God works salvation as much by the voice of Timothy, or Ignatius, as by the ministry of the highest Apostle, Paul. Therefore, it ought to be enough for us when a minister of the Church proves himself faithful in his office.

This is required, that a minister be found faithful: as if he were to say, it is not required of ministers that they all be instructed with equal or highest gifts: but this one thing, that they be faithful and rightly invest the talent which they have received from the Lord for interest. Now these four things pertain to faithfulness.

I. First, that one rightly hold the doctrine of the Church, be fit for teaching, not be ignorant of the struggles of the Church, and have a zeal for learning and inquiring into heavenly truth. For what one is ignorant of, one cannot teach. While a man professes medicine which he has never learned, he is an impostor and deservedly pays the penalties of perfidy. Thus, when someone has not learned the doctrine of the Church, nor reads the Prophetic and Apostolic writings: and yet undertakes the office of a pastor of the Church, he is a perfidious impostor.

II. Secondly, that he labor diligently, in good faith and conscience. Let him not omit the labors of his vocation:

Let him not flee from troubles; let him not decline struggles; let him not play with the tricks of sophisms: let him not hide his opinion with ambiguous generalities: let him not impose upon the unlearned common people: but let him faithfully, candidly, and with a good conscience teach, confess, and do all things. Let him not collude with either side: let him not dissemble his faith. Because Pelagius plays with tricks and generalities, he is not a faithful teacher.

III. Thirdly, constancy is required, so that a minister may not allow himself to be moved from the profession of truth and the just dispensation of the mysteries by any threats, any dangers, any adversities: let him accuse the sins of all equally: let him offer the gratuitous remission of sins to all equally: and let him always do what is of his office.

IIII. Fourthly, for faithfulness, piety is required, so that all things in the ministry may be referred to the glory of the eternal God and the salvation of the Church, let us not seek either our own gain, or our own honor: lest we also, by an unseemly life, either derogate from our morals or our doctrine, or be a stumbling block to our hearers. When a minister of the word provides this faithfulness, nothing more can be required of him.

Latin:

Sic aestimet nos homo, tanquam ministros Christi & dispensatores mysteriorum Dei. Caeterum hoc requiritur in dispensatoribus, ut quis fidelis inveniatur.

Nondum facit finem Paulus castigandi Corinthios propter contentiones & aemulationes, qua alius alii sese anteferebat. Videt enim quam irreparabile damnum haec pestis det Ecclesiae Christi. Rursus igitur ad modestiam & studium concordiae hortatur singulos in Ecclesia: ac singillatim castigat ministros, qui se propter dona efferebant: Primum totam monet Ecclesiam ne temere iudicet de excellentia, vel praemiis ministrum, sed ad hoc solum respiciat num quid fideliter serviat; caetera Dei iudicio permittat. Deinde monet ipsos doctores Ecclesiae ne se propter dona superbè efferant, sed potius agnoscant à quo dona acceperint, & in cuius honorem ea usurpare debeant. Hoc ut tantò facilius impetret ab eis commemorat aerumnas, pericula, & infinitas calamitates, quibus oneravit Deus ministros Ecclesiae et in primis Apostolos, ut veluti προφυλάκτυκα essent quae superbiae & insolentiae morbum arcerent. Tandem quàm paterno animo eos complectatur, & quo consilio Timotheum ad ipsos miserit exponit.

Ostenderat antea discrimen inter Deum authorem ministerii, & inter ministros: & dixerat nec eum qui plantat nec eum qui rigat esse aliquid: sed solum Deum qui largitur & efficit salutem esse omnia. Hoc dictum ne sinistrè à quibusdam accipiatur, ad contemnendum ministerium Apostolorum:

Levitas enim humani ingenii in utramque partem facilè impingit: aut plus tribuit ministris quam par est, aut nimis contemptim illos habet: docet quo loco habendi sunt ministri Ecclesiae. Tanquam dominos vel authores Ecclesiae & ministerii nemo nos agnoscere debet: sed sic aestimet nos homo tanquam ministros Iesu Christi, & dispensatores mysteriorum Dei. Apostoli & Pastores non sunt regum aut politici Magistratus ministri: sed summi regis Domini nostri Iesu Christi: eius enim spirituali regno serviunt praedicando Evangelion & distribuendo sacramenta. Nec sanè maius aut gloriosius munus est in terris, quàm Christo regi servire, in iis quae ad aeternam ipsius gloriam, & perpetuam Ecclesiae salutem pertinent. Nec dubium est amplissimam illis in coelis repositam esse mercedem, qui Christo domino coeli & terrae serviunt. Mysteria vocant totam doctrinam Iesu Christi, sacramenta & omnia beneficia mediatoris. Haec enim sapientia & haec dona spiritualia regni Christi, ignota sunt universae rationi humanae: & tantum de caelo per filium revelata. Horum mysteriorum dispensatores sunt Apostoli & omnes ministri Ecclesiae, per illos enim Deus patefacit nobis suam voluntatem: per illos vocat nos, ad paenitentiam: per illos remittit nobis peccata: Illorum voce & ministerio accendit in nobis fidem & iustitiam, & operatur in nobis salutem.

Summa ergò beneficia à Deo accipimus ministerio Apostolorum. ideoque omni reverentia & honore digni sunt propter tam sublime opus: neque haec metiri debemus ex praestantia donorum, vel muneris gradu: diversa enim sunt officia, & diversa dona. Sed ex veritate & efficacia verbi divini. Tàm Deus operatur salutem voce Timothei, vel Ignatii, quàm ministerio summi Apostoli Pauli. Satis ergò nobis esse debet, cum minister Ecclesiae fidelem se praestat in officio.

Hoc requiritur ut fidelis sit minister: quasi dicat, non requiritur à ministris ut omnes paribus vel summis donis sint instructi: sed hoc unum ut sint fideles & talentum quod acceperunt a domino rectè collocent ad usuram. Ad fidelitatem autem pertinent haec quatuor.

I. Primum ut rectè quis teneat doctrinam Ecclesiae, sit idoneus ad docendum, non sit ignarus certaminum Ecclesiae & habeat studium discendi & inquirendi veritatem coelestem. Quòd enim quis ignorat docere non potest. Manes dum medicinam profitetur quam nunquam didicit, impostor est & meritò dat paenas perfidiae. Sic cum quis non didicit doctrinam Ecclesiae, nec legit scripta Prophetica & Apostolica: & tamen munus pastoris Ecclesiae suscipit, impostor est perfidus.

II. Secundò ut diligenter, bona fide & conscientia laboret. Non omittat labores suae vocationis:

non fugiat molestias; non detrectet certamina; non ludat praestigiis sophismatum: non occultet suam sententiam ambiguis generalitatibus: non imponat rudi plebeculae: sed fideliter, candidè & bona conscientia omnia doceat, confiteatur & agat. Non colludat cum utraque parte: non dissimulet suam fidem. Pelagius quia Strophis & generalitatibus ludit, non est fidelis doctor.

III. Tertiò requiritur constantia, ut minister nullis minis, nullis periculis, nullis adversitatibus patiatur se dimoveri à professione veritatis & iusta mysteriorum dispensatione: ommum ex aequo accuset peccata: omnibus ex aequo offerat gratuitam remissionem peccatorum: & semper faciat quod sui est muneris.

IIII. Quartò ad fidelitatem requiritur pietas, ut omnia in ministerio ad aeterni Dei gloriam & Ecclesiae salutem referantur, non quaeramus vel lucrum nostrum, vel honorem nostrum: ne etiam inhonesta vita vel moribus, vel doctrinae derogemus, vel auditoribus simus offendiculo. Hanc fidelitatem cum praestat minister verbi, nihil amplius ab eo requiri potest.

## 4:3
But to me it is a very small thing that I should be judged by you or by any human day.

By his own example he teaches that neither ought the hearers rashly to assume for themselves judgment concerning the gifts or labors of ministers: nor ought ministers to be greatly solicitous concerning the censures of the common people, provided they themselves are conscious of a right and pious will: For it belongs to the Son of God alone, Jesus Christ our Lord, to judge concerning the conscience, labors, and rewards of both teachers and hearers in the Church; It is a small thing to me (he says) if I be judged by you; This is, I do not greatly care whether you set me before other teachers, or set me after, or whether you extol me to the heavens with praises, or speak of me contemptuously. For neither will your encomiums increase my reward: Nor will your contempt diminish it in the heavens. However, these things are not to be taken as if Paul does not care about the judgments of men concerning himself; or neglects his reputation. For it has been truly said: That he is cruel who neglects his reputation. But since he is well conscious to himself both of the purity of his doctrine and of the honesty of his life, he says that he does not anxiously inquire what the hearers judge concerning his own gifts and labors. Paul sees that the desire for vain glory is a great impediment to rendering faithfulness in the ministry. For those who always wish to be looked up to and praised by their hearers, these are often compelled to speak to the will of the people, are easily impelled to scatter new dogmas, and do not dare to freely tax the sins of men. He warns, therefore, that this vain desire for glory must be cast away.

He calls it a human day: The praises of the world, and the applause of the theater. When the eyes of all men are turned toward a man celebrated for virtue: And the mouths of all proclaim someone. Paulus Aemylius, having destroyed the kingdom of the Macedonians and captured Perseus, carried in a triumphal chariot together with his sons into the capitol, and celebrated by the mouth of all as a glorious victor, is celebrated by a human day: That is, he is adorned by human testimony, just as Herod, sitting at Caesarea before the tribunal in his silver garment, with the people shouting that they were hearing the voice not of a man but of a God, is judged by a human day. But these human praises do not help at all before God: Indeed, they are the most fleeting and vain dreams of honors. Therefore, Paul wishes faithful ministers to care nothing for these things.

Latin:

Mihi verò minimum est, ut à vobis iudicer vel ab ullo humano die.

Exemplo suo docet nec auditores debere sibi iudicium de donis vel laboribus ministrorum temerè sumere: nec ministros de vulgi censuris magnopere debere esse solicitos, modo ipsi sibi rectae & piae voluntatis sunt conscii: Solius enim filii Dei Iesu Christi domini nostri est iudicare de conscientia, laboribus & praemiis cum doctorum tum auditorum in Eccle; Parum mihi est (inquit) si à vobis iudicer; Hoc est non magnopere curo sive me aliis doctoribus proponatis, sive post ponatis, sive me laudibus in coelum efferatis, sive contemptim de me loquamini. Nam nec encomia vestra augebunt mercedem meam: Nec contemptus vester eam minuet in coelis. Non autem haec ita accipienda sunt, ac si Paulus hominum de se iudicia non curet; aut famam negligat. Verè enim dictum est. Eum esse crudelem qui negligat famam. Sed cum sibi & de puritate doctrinae & de honestate vitae bene sit conscius, quid de ipsius donis & laboribus iudicent auditores dicit se non anxiè inquirere. Videt Paulus cupiditatem inanis gloriae magnum esse impedimentum fidelitatis praestandae in ministerio. Qui enim suspici & laudari semper volunt à suis auditoribus, hi coguntur saepè ad populi voluntatem loqui, facile impelluntur ad spargenda nova dogmata, non audent liberè taxere peccata hominum, Monet ergo hanc inanem cupiditatem gloriae abiiciendam esse.

Humanum diem nominat: Encomia mundi, & adplausus theatri. Cum omnium hominum oculi in hominem virtute celebrem convertuntur: Et omnium ora aliquem praedicant. Paulus Aemylius deleto regno Macedonum, & capto Perseo, triumphali curru, una cum filiis invectus in capitolium, et omnium ore gloriosus victor celebratus, ab humano die celebratur: Hoc est humano testimonio est ornatus, sic Herodes Caesareae pro tribunali sedens in sua veste argentea, populo clamante se non hominis sed Dei audire vocem ab humano die iudicatur. Nihil verò iuvant haec Encomia humana coràm Deo: Imò sunt fugacissima & vanissima honorum somnia. Vult igitur Paulus ministros fideles ista nihil curare.

## 4:4
But neither do I judge myself: For I am indeed conscious of nothing in myself, yet in this I am not justified.

He says that he neglects not only the judgments of others concerning himself, but also that he does not even make a judgment concerning his own labors or gifts, for it is a sublime office pertaining to the majesty of the Son of God alone, to judge concerning a man's conscience, fidelity, labors, counsels, endeavors, dangers, struggles, hardships, patience, thoughts, and actions, and to decree just rewards. I know indeed that I good things to serve God and the Church with faith and the conscience of a right will: I am not conscious to myself of any fraud or crime: But in this I am not justified before God: Who demands from me much more than I provide or can provide. For the judgment of God is spiritual: But I am carnal. He who ought to judge exactly concerning all the counsels, thoughts, and actions of man, it is necessary for him to understand the whole judgment of the law as spiritual: But this is possible to no one on earth except the omnipotent Son of God. Therefore no one can pass a full and exact judgment concerning man, except him to whom the Father has handed over all judgment; the testimony here is to be observed that the justice of a good conscience does not justify a man before God. Although, says Paul, with the help of the Holy Spirit I maintain a good conscience, and in faith I strive for good works: yet in this I am not justified. Therefore no one of the saints, on account of good works, although they proceed from faith and are kindled by the Holy Spirit in the pious, is just before God: But Paul and all others are in need of another justice, namely the obedience of Jesus Christ, which is imputed to us through faith.

Latin:

Sed neque me ipsum iudico: Nihil equidem mihi conscius sum, sed in hoc non sum iustificatus.

Non tantum aliorum de se iudicia negligere se dicit, sed etiam ne se quidem iudicium de suis laboribus aut donis facere, sublime enim officium est ad solius filii Dei maiestatem pertinens, iudicare de hominis conscientia, fidelitate, laboribus consiliis, conatibus, periculis, certaminibus, aerumnis, patientia, cogitationibus & actionibus, & iusta decernere praemia, Scio equidem me bona fide & conscientia rectae voluntatis servire Deo & Ecclesiae: Non sum mihi conscius ullius fraudis, aut sceleris: Sed in hoc non sum iustificatus cor àm Deo: Qui multò plura à me fiagitat quam ego praesto aut praestare possum. Iudicium enim Dei est spirituale: Ego autem carnalis. Qui exactè iudicare debet de omnibus consiliis, cogitationibus, & actionibus hominis, eum necesse est totum iudicium legis spirituale intelligere: Hoc autem nemini in terris est possibile nisi omnipotenti filio Dei. Nemo ergò plenum & exactum de homine iudicium ferre potest, nisi is cui pater omne tradidit iudicium; testimonium hic observandum est quòd iustitia bonae conscientiae non iustificet hominem coràm Deo. Etsi, inquit Paulus, auxilio Spiritus sanctitueor bonam conscientiam, & in fide studeo bonis operibus: tamen in hoc non sum iustificatus. Nullus ergò sanctorum propter bona opera licet ea ex fide proficiscantur, & à Spiritu sancto accendantur in piis, est iustus coràm Deo: Sed Paulus & omnes alii indigent alia iustitia, videlicet obedientia Iesu Christi, quae nobis per fidem imputatur.

## 4:5
But he who judges me is the Lord: Therefore do not judge before the time: Until the Lord comes: Who will illuminate the hidden things of darkness, and will manifest the counsels of hearts: Then shall every man have praise of God.

In order to deter the Corinthians from the rashness of judging the Apostles and ministers, he teaches that all judgment belongs to our Lord Jesus Christ, who is the judge of the living and the dead: And to whom the Father has given all judgment: And that that last day on which the Lord is to come for the judgment of the world is imminent. Therefore, the office of Jesus Christ is not to be invaded, nor is judgment to be rashly precipitated before the last day. This is a sublime article of our faith. That Jesus Christ, God and man, is the judge of the living and the dead, and that that last day is imminent, in which the whole human race will be set before the tribunal of Jesus Christ, and the thoughts and deeds of all hearts will be revealed: So that concerning the individual counsels, thoughts, endeavors, and deeds of individual men, a final judgment may be made in the sight of God, of all the angels, and of the whole creation: And finally, that those who have done good may come forth into the resurrection of life; but those who have done evil into the resurrection of judgment. Therefore, let similar sayings concerning the final judgment be referred here, as Eccles: 12. God shall bring every work into judgment, with every secret thing, whether it be good, or whether it be evil. Item: 2: Corinth: 5. For we must all appear before the judgment seat of Christ; that every one may receive the things done in his body, according to that he hath done whether good or evil. Rom: 14. We shall all stand before the judgment seat of Jesus Christ: For it is written, As I live, saith the Lord, every knee shall bow to me, and every tongue shall confess to God. And first it is to be observed, that the scripture says all hidden thoughts will be revealed; just as Christ also testifies. Matth: 10.Luc: 12. There is nothing covered, that shall not be revealed: There is nothing hidden that shall not be known. Therefore let no one hope that he will perpetually conceal his hypocrisy, fraudulent counsels, secret crimes, and hidden machinations: But let everyone determine that all the most secret counsels will be conspicuous in the final judgment, not only to God, but also to the creature. And therefore the whole life is to be so instituted, and all counsels so directed, that we may know that all things are done in the sight of the most high God, and that they are at some time to be revealed even to the whole world.

Then, he says, shall every man have praise of God. He who seeks true praise ought not to seek the encomiums or applause of men: For human testimonies are full of vanity; often a man slanders good deeds through envy: Often he proclaims crimes as if they were illustrious virtues through flattery. But as the false proclamations of one praising do not heal an evil conscience: So the reproach of one reviling does not wound a good conscience: As August: elegantly said. Human encomiums, therefore, are not to be greatly cared for. And especially because The world judges wrongly concerning the whole ministry of the word; a faithful pastor of the Church ought neither to seek praise from men very much, nor to look for it anxiously: But every pious person ought to look toward God and His final judgment in all actions: And to determine certainly that all good deeds will have just praise before God in the final judgment: And that God will give us the most ample testimony concerning all good works in the sight of the whole creation: According to the remarkable promise of Christ: He who shall have confessed me before men; I will confess him before my heavenly Father and before the angels of God: Luke 12.Matthew 10.

Latin:

Qui autem me iudicat dominus est: Quare nolite ante tempus iudicare: Donec venerit dominus: Qui illuminabit occulta tenebrarum, & manifestabit consilia cordium: Tunc unicuique laus erit à Deo.

Ut deterreat Corinthios à temeritate iudicandi Apostolos & ministros, docet omne iudicium competere domino nostro Iesu Christo, qui est iudex vivorum & mortuorum: Et cui pater omne iudicium dedit: Et ultimum illum diem quo dominus ad iudicium mundi venturus est instare. Non ergò invadendum esse munus Iesu Christi, nec ante extremum diem temerè praecipitandum iudicium. Hic sublimis est fidei nostrae articulus. Quòd Iesus Christus Deus & homo sit iudex vivorum & mortuorum, quodque instet extremus ille dies, in quo totum genus humanum sistetur ante tribunal Iesu Christi, & revelabuntur omnium cordium cogitationes & facta: Ut de singulis consiliis, cogitationibus, conatibus, gestis singulorum hominum fiat ultimum iudicium in conspectu Dei, omnium angelorum et totius creaturae: Ac tandem qui bonum fecerunt, prodeant in resurrectionem vitae; Qui verò malum fecerunt in resurrectionem vitae. Huc ergò similia dicta de extremo iudicio referantur, ut Eccles: 12. Deus in iudicium adducet omne opus, & omnem rem occultam, sive quid bonum sive malum fuerit. Item: 2: Corinth: 5. Oportet nos omnes manifestari coràm tribunali Iesu Christi ut quisque recipiat in corpore pro eo quod fecit sive bonum, sive malum. Rom: 14. Omnes sistemur ante tribunal Iesu Christi: Scriptum est enim, Vivo ego dicit dominus, mihi flectetur omne genu, & omnis lingua confitebitur Deo. Ac inprimis observandum est, quod scriptura dicit omnes occultas cogitationes revelatum iri; Quemadmodum & Christus testatur. Matth: 10.Luc: 12. Nihil est opertum, quod non manifest abitur: Nihil est occultum quod non cognoscetur. Nemo ergò speret se suam hypocrisin, fraudulenta consilia, arcana scelera, & occultas machinationes per petuò celaturum esse: Sed quisque statuat arcanissima quaeque consilia in extremo iudicio non solum Deo, sed & creaturae fore conspicua. Ideoque universa vita sic instituenda est, omniaque consilia sic dirigenda, ut sciamus omnia geri in conspectu altissimi Dei, & aliquando etiam toti mundo ea revelanda esse.

Tunc inquit unicuique laus erit à Deo. Qui veram laudem expetit, non hominum Encomia, vel adplausus quaerere debet: Humana enim testimonia plena sunt vanitatis, saepè benefacta per invidiam calumniatur homo: Saepè scelera tanquam praeclaras virtutes per adsentationem praedicat. Ut verò falsa praeconia laudantis non sanant malam conscientiam: Sic bonam conscientiam non vulnerat conviciantis opprobrium: Ut August: eleganter dixit. Humana igitur Encomia non magnopere sunt curanda. Ac inprimis quia mundus perperam iudicat de toto ministerio verbi, fidelis pastor Ecclesiae, laudem ab hominibus nec valde expetere, nec sollicitè quaerere debet: Ad Deum verò, & ultimum eius iudicium singuli pii in omnibus actionibus respicere debent: Ac certò statuere omnia benefacta iustam apud Deum laudem habitura in extremo iudicio: Et Deum nobis in conspectu totius creaturae amplissimum de omnibus bonis operibus daturum testimonium: Iuxta insignem Christi promissionem: Qui me confessus fuerit coràm hominibus; Confiteboreum coràm patre meo coelesti & coràm angelis Dei: Luc: 12.Matth: 10.

## 4:6
These things indeed brothers, I have transferred figuratively to myself and Apollos, for your sake: that in us you may learn, not to think above that which is written: that one may not be puffed up above another and against another.

Because Paul cherishes a good hope concerning the amendment of the teachers who had exalted themselves too arrogantly, he spares them, nor does he criticize them by name: He proposes all things, however, figuratively in this way, so that in his own person and that of Apollos he might express an example of how teachers ought to conduct themselves in the Church: And that no one ought to exalt himself against another. To puff up, is high and proud To bear a spirit against and above others: to yield to no one: but to prefer oneself and one's own opinion to all. Samosatenus is puffed up against Firmilianus: John of Antioch is puffed up against Cyril: Dioscorus against Flavian, Chrysostom against Epiphanius: Rufinus against Jerome. Jerome against Augustine: and there are countless examples of this most grave sin in the Church, by which most sad dissensions have arisen. Paul therefore warns that individuals should think modestly of themselves: that they should not proudly exalt themselves, that they should not pertinaciously defend their own opinions, if the truth is more clearly demonstrated by others.

Latin:

Haec verò fratres figuratè in me & Apollo transtuli, propter vos: ut in nobis discatis, non supra id quod scriptum est sentire: ne unus supra alium & contra alterum infletur.

Paulus quia de doctorum, qui arrogantius sese extulerant, emendatione spem bonam fovet, parcit eis, nec perstringit eos nominatim: Omnia autem sic figuratè proponit, ut in sua & Apollo persona exemplum exprimat, quomodo doctores in Ecclesia se gerere debeant: Quodque; nemo se debeat contra alium efferre. Inflare, est altos & superbos Spiritus gerere contra et supra alios: nemini cedere: sed omnibus sese & suam sententiam praeponere. Samosatenus inflatur contra Firmilianum: Ioannes Antiochenus infiatur contra Cyrillum: Dioscorus contra: Flavianum, Chrysostomus, contra Epiphanium: Ruffinus, contra Hieronymum. Hieronymus contra Augustinum: & innumera sunt exempla huius gravissimi peccati in Ecclesia, eo quò tristissima dissidia coorta sunt. Monet igitur Paulus, ut singuli modestè de se sentiant: non superbè se efferant, non pertinaciter suas defendant sententias, si ab aliis liquidius monstretur veritas.

## 4:7
For who made you superior? And what do you have that you did not receive? But if you did receive it, why do you boast as if you had not received it?

He proves from the efficient cause of the gifts that one ought not to be proud of gifts against one's brothers. You, he says, have not adorned yourself with those gifts by which you excel others: but you have received all things from God: Therefore you ought not to be proud in them, as if you had them from yourself: nor ought you to use them to the insult of God, and the detriment of the Church: but rather, by how much greater the gifts with which you are instructed by God, by so much the more humbly you ought to conduct yourself, and with a more ready mind serve the Church, and with greater subjection and piety prove your gratitude to God. Augustine in several places confesses that he owes much to this Pauline sentence: for being admonished by this, he cast off and corrected his error, which he previously defended: namely, that the faith by which we believe in God was not a gift of God, but was from us in us. But being convinced by this testimony, as he himself confesses, he corrected that opinion, and confessed also that faith is a gift of God. This notable example of modesty in Augustine ought always to be in the sight of all doctors of the Church, lest they be ashamed to confess if they have slipped anywhere; and lest they pertinaciously defend errors when the truth has become known. I shall transcribe the words of Augustine: De praedestinat: Sancto: lib: 1. Capit: 3. For what have you that you did not receive? But if you received it, why do you boast as if you had not received it? By which principal testimony I was also convinced, when I similarly erred, thinking that the faith by which we believe in God was not a gift of God, but was from us in us, and that through it we obtain the gifts of God. And a little later: This testimony therefore does not allow any of the faithful to say, I have faith which I did not receive. From this testimony of Paul, therefore, with Augustine as interpreter, it is convinced that all gifts, and even faith itself, exist in man from God; therefore, there is nothing to boast about, since nothing is ours, as Cyprian rightly said.

Latin:

Quis enim te eximium fecit? Quid verò habes quod non accepisti? si autem accepisti quid gloriaris tanquam non acceperis?

Acausa efficiente donorum probat, non esse donis superbiendum contra fratres. Tu inquit teipsum non ornasti illis donis quibus antecellis alios: sed omnia à Deo accepisti: Non igitur iniis superbire debes, tanquam ea à teipso haberes: neques in contumeliam Dei, & detrimentum Ecclesiae uti debes: quin potius quò maioribus à Deo donis es instructus, hoc et submissius tegerere, & promtiore animo Ecclesiae inservire, & maiore subietione & pietate tuam gratitudinem Deo probare debes. Augustinus in aliquot locis fatetur se huic sententiae Paulinae plurimum debere: hac enim admonitus abiecit & correxit errorem suum, quem ante defendebat: quòd videlicet fides qua credimus in Deum, non esset donum Dei, sed a nobis esset in nobis: Verum hoc testimonio conviclus ut ipse fatetur, correxit istam sententiam, & fassus est etiam fidem esse donum Dei. Hoc insigne exemplum modestiae in Augustino omnibus doctoribus Ecclesiae semper in conspectu esse debet, ne pudeat eos fateri sicubi lapsi sunt; Et ne pertinaciter defendant errores, cum innotuit veritas. Verba Augustini adscribam: De praedestinat: Sancto: lib: 1. Capit: 3. Quid autem habes quod non accepisti, si autem accepisti, quid gloriaris, quasi non acceperis? Quo praecipuo testimonio etiam convictus sum, cum similiter errarem putans fidem qua in Deum credimus, non esse donum Dei, sed à nobis esse in nobis, & per illam nos impetrare Dei dona. Et paulò post: Hoc ergò testimonium non sinit quenquam fidelium dicere habeo fidem quam non accepi: Ex hoc ergò testimonio Pauli, interprete Augustino convincitur, omnia dona, atque ipsam etiam fidem à Deo existere in hominein nullo ergò gloriandum est, quando nihil est nostrum, ut recte dixit Cyprianus.

## 4:8
Now you are full: now you are made rich: you have reigned as kings without us: And I would to God you did reign: that we also might reign with you.

Paul still chastises the false persuasion of the Corinthians, because they too quickly arrogate to themselves a full knowledge of spiritual things, and think that they have already arrived at the goal, and have overcome all struggles, and are all but reigning: when they ought rather to acknowledge their own great ignorance and infirmity: to progress daily in the study of learning heavenly mysteries: to exercise themselves daily in piety, to wrestle against sin, death, the devil, and the flesh: and thus in faith to contend toward the spiritual kingdom of Christ, which we shall possess only after this life.

Now you are full and rich: That is, you presume yourselves to be full and rich in the knowledge of God, when very much is still lacking to you: and you have perceived only a taste of the mysteries of God.

Now you reign: That is, you dream that you have already overcome the world and hell: but you are still sold under sin: you still stick in the flesh: Satan constantly lies in wait for you: sin reduces you into servitude: Therefore you do not yet reign, which I would indeed wish for you: that it might be permitted for us also to possess the kingdom in heaven: but you must still fight and struggle against the flesh and Satan.

For I think that God has set forth us the apostles last (of all men), as though appointed to death: For we are made a spectacle unto the world, and to angels, and to men.

By the example of the apostles he demonstrates that the Church cannot yet boast of having attained victory, and of having occupied the kingdom: Certainly the victory has been won for us and the heavenly kingdom prepared through Christ: But we have not yet obtained this glory in our own power. We are still running in the stadium, we have not yet attained the palm. We must constantly struggle with the flesh, with the world, with sin, with Satan, with an evil conscience, and with calamities of every kind. Therefore, we must not be carnally proud, just as if we had overcome all the dangers and snares of Satan. And for this purpose the most wise and most merciful God has imposed such countless calamities and afflictions upon His Church, so that we might not grow insolent, so that we might not give ourselves over to security, so that we might not be proud of spiritual gifts, but that we might live perpetually in the fear of God. To illustrate this sentiment, Paul brings forward the example of the apostles and testifies before all other men that the Apostles were afflicted in the world with the greatest miseries, hardships, dangers, and calamities. After our Lord Jesus Christ, whom the world killed most cruelly by lifting him onto the cross, no men were so harshly treated and vexed in the world as the Apostles, just as the history of Paul in the Acts testifies. And someone might wonder what the reason is why God allows his dearest sons and most faithful ministers to be treated so cruelly in the world. But the answer is ready: It is the will of God that those whom he has called to the fellowship of eternal life should become conformed to the image of his son: And that all should enter into the kingdom of heaven through many tribulations: And by how much greater gifts of the Holy Spirit he adorns his own, by so much the more he presses and exercises them with harsher hardships: Then to restrain insolence and security from them: And to stir up in them from time to time an ardent invocation: And to make the knowledge of himself more illustrious in them.

Latin:

Iam saturati estis: iam divites facti estis: sine nobis regnum adepti estis: Atque utinam regnaretis: ut & nos vobiscum regnemus.

Castigat adhuc Paulus Corinthiorum falsam persuasionem, quòd nimis celeriter arrogent plenam spiritualium rerum cognitionem, & existiment se iam pervenisse ad metam, & superasse omnia certamina, & tantum non regnare: cum potius magnam & inscitiam & infirmitatem suam agnoscere deberent: quotidie progredi in studio discendi mysteria coelestia: quotidie se se exercere in pietate, luctari contra peccatum, mortem, diabolum & carnem: atque ita in fide contendere ad spirituale Christi regnum, quòd post hanc vitam primum possessuri sumus.

Iam saturati & ditati estis: Id est, praesumitis vos saturos & divites esse in cognitione Dei, cum plurimum vobis adhuc desit: & gustum tantum perceperitis mysteriorum Dei.

Iam regnatis: Id est, somniatis vos iam superasse mundum & infernum: sed venundati adhuc estis sub peccato: haeretis adhuc in carne: Satan adsiduè vobis insidiatur: peccatum redigit vos inservitutem: Nondum igitur regnatis, quòd sanè vobis optarem: ut & nobis liceret regno potiri in coelo: sed pugnandum adhuc vobis est & luctandum contra carnem & Satanam.

Existimo enim quòd Deus nos Apostolos postremos (omnium hominum) posuerit, tanquam morti destinatos: Quia theatrum facti sumus mundo, angelis & hominibus.

Apostolorum exemplo demonstrat Ecclesiam nondum gloriari posse de adepta victoria, & & occupato regno: Certò quidem parta nobis est victoria & paratum regnum coeleste per Christum: Sed in nostra potestate nondum hanc gloriam obtinemuus. Nos adhuc currimus in stadio, palmam nondum adepti sumus. Adsiduè nobis luctandum est cum carne, cum mundo, cum peccato, cum Satana, cum mala conscientia, & cum omnis generis calamitatibus. Non igitur carnaliter superbiendum est, perinde ac si omnia pericula & insidias Satanae superassemus. Atque hoc consilio tàm innumeras calamitates & adflictiones imposuit Ecclesiae suae sapientissimus & clementissimus Deus, ne insolescamus, ne securitatinos dedamus, ne donis spiritualibus superbiamus, sed perpetuò in timore Dei vivamus. Ut hanc illustret sententiam Paulus, Apostolorum exemplum adducit, & testatur ante omnes alios homines, Apostolos summis miseriis, aerumnis, periculis, & calamitatibus conflictari in mundo. Post dominum nostrum Iesum Christum quem mundus sublatum in crucem necavit omnium crude dissimè, nulli homines adeò duriter excepti atque vexati sunt in mundo atque Apostoli, sicuti historia Pauli in actis testatur. Ac miretur aliquis quid sit causae cur Deus filios carissimos, & ministros fidelissimos tàm crudeliter sinat tractari in mundo. Sed expedita est responsio: Voluntas Dei est ut quos vocavit ad societatem vitae aeternae conformes fiant imagini filii ipsius: Utque omnes per multas tribulationes ingrediantur in regnum coelorum: Acquò maioribus donis Spiritus sancti ornat suos, hoc etiam durioribus aerumnis premit atque exerceteos: Tum ut arceat ab eis insolentiam et securitatem: Et subinde excitet in eis ardentem invocationem: Et sui noticiam in ipsis illustriorem faciat.

## 4:9
He says the Apostles were made a spectacle to men and angels. For the struggles and hardships and punishments of the Apostles were conspicuous in the whole world. Monarchs, princes, all peoples and nations strove with their greatest strength to oppress and destroy the Apostles along with their doctrine. And just as men destined for death are accustomed to be brought out into a theater and thrown to the most savage beasts: So the Apostles in the theater of the world, in which even the angels are spectators, were exposed to the most savage tyrants, and to the most rabid multitude of the impious. Therefore, the Apostles have not yet attained glory and the kingdom: But if the Apostles, who received the first fruits of the spirit, do not yet obtain the kingdom, much less can the remaining pious disciples of the Apostles boast that they have fought completely with the Devil and the world. From this, therefore, let us learn first that we must not securely presume as if no snares, no struggles, no dangers are to be feared by us: But that we must live perpetually in the fear of God, must wrestle with Satan and the flesh, and must implore the help of God, so that at length we may be able to possess a joyful victory. But as we are a theater in the world for ignominy: So we shall be a theater in the final judgment for every creature with immense glory. Thence it ought to be gathered that the most grave miseries and afflictions of the ministers and of the Church are not signs of divine wrath, or proofs of false doctrine, but rather testimonies of the certainty of the doctrine: Since it is necessary that the Apostles truly think thus about God, as they teach: Since on account of this doctrine they endure every most cruel punishment with an admirable constancy of mind. And also that the pious afflicted are paternally loved by God, since he chastises them as sons and makes them conformable to Christ and the Apostles.

Latin:

Apostolos dicit theatrum factos hominibus & angelis. Certamina enim & aerumnae, & supplicia Apostolorum in toto orbe fuerunt conspicua. Monarchae, principes, omnes populi & nationes summis viribus conati sunt Apostolos cum ipsorum doctrina opprimere ac delere. Ac sicuti homines destinati murti in theatrum produci solent, & saevissimis bestiis obiici: Ita Apostoli in theatro orbis terrarum, in quo etiam angeli sunt spectatores, obiecti sunt saevissimis tyrannis, & rabiosissimae multitudini impiorum. Nondum ergò Apostoli adepti sunt gloriam & regnum: Si verò Apostoli, qui primitias spiritus acceperunt, nondum obtinent regnum, multò minus reliqui pii discipuli Apostolorum gloriari possunt se cum Diabolo & mundo prorsus depugnasse. Hinc ergò discamus primùm non esse securè praesumendum quasi nullae insidiae, nulla certamina, nulla pericula nobis sint metuenda: Sed perpetuò in timore Dei vivendum, cum Satana & carne luctandum, & Dei auxilium, ut tandem laeta victoria potiri possimus, implorandum esse. Ut autem theatrum sumus in mundo ad ignominiam: Ita theatrum erimus in extremo iudicio omni creaturae cum ingenti gloria. Deinde colligi hinc debet gravissimas aerumnas & adflictiones ministrorum & Ecclesiae non esse signa irae divinae, vel documenta falsae doctrinae, sed potius testimonia certitudinis doctrinae: Siquidem necesse est Apostolos verè sic de Deo sentire, ut docent: Cum propter hanc doctrinam crudelissima quaeque supplicia admiranda constantia animi perferant. Atque etiam pios adflictos paternè diligi à Deo, siquidem ut filios castigat & Christo atque Apostolis eos efficit conformes.

## 4:10
We are fools on account of Christ: But you are prudent in Christ: We are weak: but you are robust: You are You are glorious, but we are inglorious: Even unto this hour we hunger, we thirst, we are naked, we are buffeted, we wander without a certain home, and we labor, working with our own hands. When we are reviled, we bless: when we suffer persecution, we bear it patiently: when we are defamed, we entreat: we are made as the filth of the world, and are esteemed as the offscouring of all things even unto this day.

In the Apostles themselves Paul shows how the pious ought not to exalt themselves on account of gifts, nor seek any glory in the world: We Apostles, he says, even if we have attained notable wisdom through the Holy Spirit: yet in the world we are held as fools, on account of Christ whom we preach. Just as Festus cries out with a loud voice, You are mad, Paul. Acto. 26. but we do not care for this ignominy. You are prudent in Christ: for you have attained the wisdom of the Spirit: but you must not be proud in it: nor ought you to affect the glory of prudence in the world.

We are weak, as those who are attacked from without and within: You meanwhile are robust, less do you feel the temptations than we Apostles: but beware lest you think you excel the Apostles in gifts. For under the infirmity of the Apostles lies hidden the immense strength of Christ. He then commemorates the ignominy, hunger, thirst, nakedness, blows, exiles, persecutions, curses, and the rest, which the Apostles sustain on account of the ministry of the Gospel. These are most grave voices when he says that the Apostles are esteemed in the world as καθάρματα καὶ περιψήματα This is, as if they were esteemed as piacula and excrements in the world: by the removal of which God might be appeased toward the world.

Καθάρματα and περιψήματα are called men who have so offended God by some atrocious crime, that God is angry at some whole nation, or even at the whole world, and cannot be appeased unless such piacula or purgamenta are removed. Thus Oedipus, Adrastus, and others were held as ἀλάστωρες among the nations. In 2 Samuel, Chapter 21: When a most grave famine pressed upon the land of Judea, and David consulted the Lord, the seven sons of Saul were held as καθάρμοι, & παλαμναίοι: And by these being taken away to the cross, God was reconciled to the land of Judea. Therefore Paul indicates that the world feels this way about the Apostles, that it judges them to be καθάρματα καὶ ἀλάστωρας, on account of whom God is angry at the whole human race, for the reason that they prohibit the worship of the gods, and bring into the world a new kind of of the doctrine: As if God, on account of them and their doctrine, sends in calamities of every kind, wars, fires, sterilities, seditions, the ruin of the Roman empire, slaughters, plagues, famines, and evils of every kind: And that God cannot be appeased unless the Apostles and their doctrine are removed from the world. Since, therefore, the judgments of the world concerning the Apostles themselves are so bitter, it can easily be gathered that the Apostles could neither seek nor hope for empty glory and applause in the world. Therefore, the disciples of the Apostles ought to cast away entirely every desire for worldly glory: and they ought rather to induce this into their mind, that on account of the doctrine of the Apostles, they should be willing to sustain most bitter hatreds and extreme insults with a great spirit and to bear them patiently.

Non haec I do not write these things to put you to shame, but to admonish you as my beloved children. For even if you have countless tutors, you do not have many fathers. For in Christ Jesus I have begotten you through the Gospel. I exhort you, therefore, be imitators of me. For this reason I have sent to you Timothy, who is my beloved and faithful son in the Lord, who will call to your memory

Latin:

Nos stulti propter Christum: Vos autem prudentes estis in Christo: Nos infirmi sumus: vos autem robusti: Vos gloriosi estis: nos verò inglorii: Usque in hanc horam esurimus, sitimus, nudi incedimus, colaphis caedimur, sine certa sede vagamur, & laboramus, operantes manibus nostris. Cum proscindimur conviciis, benedicimus: cum persecutionem sustinemus, patienter ferimus: cum maledictis incessimur, obsecramus: tanquam excrementa mundi facti sumus, veluti omnium piaculum in hunc usque diem aestimamur.

In ipsis Apostolis ostendit Paulus, quomodo pii non debeant sese efferre propter dona, nec ullamin mundo gloriam quaerere: Nos Apostoli, inquit, etiamsi insignem sapientiam adepti simus per Spiritum sanctum: tamen in mundo pro fatuis habemur, propter Christum quem praedicamus. Quemadmodum Festus alta voceclamat, Insanis Paule. Acto. 26. hanc verò ignominiam non curamus. Vos prudentes estis in Christo: sapientiam enim Spiritus adepti estis: sed in ea superbiendum vobis non est: neque gloriam prudentiae in mundo adfectare debetis.

Nos imbecilles sumus, ut qui foris & intus oppugnamur: Vos interea robusti estis, minus sentitis tentationum, quàm nos Apostoli: sed cavete ne putetis vos antecellere Apostolis donis. Sub infirmitate enim Apostolorum ingens robur Christi latet. Commemorat de inde ignominiam, famem, sitim, nuditatem, colaphos, exilia, persecutiones, maledicta & caetera, quae sustinent Apostoli propter ministerium Evangelii. Gravissimae voces sunt cum dicit Apostolos in mundo aestimari tanquam καθάρματα καὶ περιψήματα Hoc est, veluti piacula & excrementa aestimari in orbe: quibus sublatis Deus orbi placari possit.

Καθάρματα ac περιψήματα dicuntur homines, qui atroci aliquo scelere ita Deum offenderunt, ut toti alicui nationi, vel etiam toti orbi irascatur Deus, nec placari possit nisi talibus piaculis seu purgamentis sublatis. Sic oedipus Adrastus & alii tanquam ἀλάστωρες apud gentes habiti fuerunt. In 2. lib: Samuel: Capit: 21. Cum fames gravissima premeret terram Iudaeam, & David consuleret dominum, septem filii Saul tanquam καθάρμοι, & παλαμναίοι sunt habiti: Atque his in crucem sublatis reconciliatus est Deus terrae Iudaeae. Indicat ergò Paulus mundum ita sentire de Apostolis, quòd iudicet eos esse καθάρματα καὶ ἀλάστωρας, propter quos Deus toti generi humano irascatur, eò quòd prohibeant cultum deorum, & invehant in orbem novum genus doctrinae: Quasi Deus propter illos & illorum doctrinam immittat omnis generis calamitates, bella, incendia, sterilitates, seditiones, ruinam imperii Romani, clades, pestes, fames & omnis generis mala: Nec posse Deum placari nisi Apostolis & eorum doctrina sublatis è mundo. Cum ergò tàm acerba sint iudicia mundi de ipsis Apostolis, facilè colligi potest, Apostolos in mundo inanem gloriam & adplausum quaerere aut sperare non posse.
