Ergò et discipuli Apostolorum omnem cupiditatem mundanae gloriae prorsus abiicere: & hoc potius in animum inducere debent quòd propter doctrinam Apostolorum acerbissima odia, & extremas contumelias & magno animo sustinere & patienter ferre velint.

Non haec scribo ut vos rubore suffundam, sed ut vos dilectos meos filios admoneam. Etsi enim innumeros habeatis paedagogos, non tamen multos patres. Nam in Christo Iesu per Evangelium ego vos genui. Hortor igitur vos, Imitatores mei estote. Propter hoc enim misi vobis Timotheum, qui est filius meus dilectus & fidelis in domino, qui vobis in memoriam revocabit vias

## 4:17-19
my ways in Christ, as I teach everywhere in every Church. Some are puffed up, as though I were not coming to you. But I will come to you quickly, if the Lord wills, and I will know not the speech of those who are puffed up, but the power.

The Apostle finally concludes the vehement and sharp rebuke by which he censured the contentions, dissensions, and pride of the Corinthians: and at the same time he has uprooted the persuasion of human wisdom, as the root of all those evils. Now, in order to mitigate their spirits somewhat after the sharp castigation, he advises with what affection he did it. Paul did not wish to put the Corinthians to shame or to affect them with ignominy, but to admonish them as sons regarding what is just, salutary, pious, holy, and pleasing to God. He then testifies that he embraces his hearers with paternal στοργῇ, as those whom he has begotten in Christ through the Gospel: This is, he has led them by the preaching of the Gospel to this happiness, so that from sons of Satan they have been co-opted into sons of God. He calls himself a father, however: just as Abraham is also called the father of many nations, namely by doctrine, ministry, instruction, and example. He also explains with what counsel he sent .

Timothy his colleague, certainly so that he may recall to their memory the doctrine which they received from Paul, and what the character, life, and custom of Paul are in all the Churches. For it matters a great deal for the retaining of the purity of doctrine that the doctrine of the Apostles be repeatedly recalled and inculcated: and that the example of the entire Apostolic life and custom be perpetually held in view. He promises then that he will come to the Corinthians, and will openly chastise and repress the puffed-up teachers, who were abusing the absence of Paul to disturb the Church and to show off their own erudition.

Latin:

meas in Christo, quomodo ubique in omni Ecclesia doceam. Inflati sunt aliqui, quasi ad vos non sim venturus. Veniam autem celeriter ad vos, si dominus voluerit, & cognoscam non sermonem inflatorum, sed virtutem.

Absolvit tandem Apostolus vehementem & acrem repraehensionem, qua contentiones, diffidia, & fastum Corinthiorum taxavit: & simul persuasionem humanae sapientiae, tanquam radicem omnium istorum malorum evulsit: Nunc ut post acrem castigationem aliquomodo mitiget animos eorum, monet quo adfectu id fecerit. Non voluit Paulus pudefacere, velignominia adficere Corinthios, sed tanquam filios admonere, quid sit iustum, salutare, pium, sanctum & Deo placens. Testatur deinde se paterna στοργῇ complecti suos auditores, ut quos in Christo per Evangelium genuerit: Hoc est, praedicatione Evangelii ad hanc foelicitatem perduxerit, ut ex filiis Satanae cooptati sint in filios Dei. Nominat autem se patrem: sicuti & Abraham appellatur pater multarum gentium, scilicet doctrina, ministerio, institutione & exemplo. Exponit etiam quo consilio miserit.

Timotheum collegam suum, nimirum ut revocet illis in memoriam doctrinam quam à Paulo acceperunt, & qui sint Pauli mores, vita, & consuetudo in omnibus Ecclesiis. Plurimum enim refert ad retinendam doctrinae puritatem subinde repeti & inculcari doctrinam Apostolorum: & totius vitae & consuetudinis Apostolicae exemplum perpetuò in conspectu habere. Promittit deinde se venturum esse ad Corinthios, & coràm castigaturum & repressurum inflatos doctores, qui absentia Pauli ad turbandam Ecclesiam & ostentandam suam eruditionem abutebantur.

## 4:20
For the kingdom of God does not consist in speech, but in power.

This sentence of Paul is very significant, by which he represses men puffed up on account of eloquence: And he teaches that it is not enough in the Church to be eloquent and talkative: But that it is necessary for the Spirit and faith to shine in the heart. The kingdom of God, that is, the salvation of the whole Church, does not depend upon talkative or eloquent speech: But upon the power of the Holy Spirit: By which God regenerates men to eternal life: And makes them partakers of all the benefits of the mediator. Let power be understood as the very potency of God, by which He works salvation in men. This power of God does not consist in eloquent speech, but in valid and strong truth against which not even the gates of hell can prevail: And this is the efficacious power of God, not in those who chatter much about the Gospel: But who embrace the doctrine of Christ with true faith, overcome the terrors of death and of Satan; Burn with zeal for propagating the truth; And demonstrate by their whole life that they are ruled by the Spirit of God: they are constant in confession: With a brave heart they endure hardships and dangers: In these the Gospel of Jesus Christ is not a vanishing or empty speech, but much more the power and efficacy of God, bringing forth the most abundant fruits of the kingdom of Christ. Therefore, not only empty chatter is to be looked at in the kingdom of Christ, but in the first place the power and efficacy of the word is to be considered, how the Holy Spirit works salvation in hearts and builds the Church.

Latin:

Non enim regnum Dei consistit in sermone, sed in virtute.

Valde insignis est haec Pauli sententia, qua reprimit homines inflatos propter eloquentiam: Ac docet non satis esse in Ecclesia esse facundum & loquacem: Sed oportere Spiritum & fidem lucere in corde. Regnum Dei, hoc est, salus totius Ecclesiae, non pendet à loquaci seu facundo sermone: Sed à virtute Spiritus sancti: Qua Deus regenerat homines ad vitam aeternam: Et facit eos participes omnium beneficiorum mediatoris. Virtus intelligatur ipsa Dei potentia, qua operatur in hominibus salutem. Haec virtus Dei non in diserto sermone, sed in valida & forti consistit veritate, contra quam nec portae inferorum praevalere possunt: Estque haec Dei virtus efficax non in iis qui multa garriunt de Evangelio: Sed qui vera fide doctrinam Christi amplectuntur, vincunt terrores mortis & Satanae; Ardent Zelo propagandi veritatem; Et tota vita demonstrant quòd regantur à Spiritu Dei: sunt constantes in confessione: Forti animo perferunt aerumnas et pericula: In his Evangelium Iesu Christi non est evanescens aut inanis sermo, sed multò magis virtus & efficacia Dei, proferens uberrimos fructus regni Christi. Non ergò tantum inanis garrulitas spectanda est in regno Christi, sed in primis virtus & efficacia verbi consideranda, quomodo Spiritus sanctus in cordibus operetur salutem & aedificet Ecclesiam.

## 4:20 Places of Doctrine
Places of Doctrine.

1. Concerning the amplitude and majesty of the office, which Apostles and pastors bear in the human race: That they are, namely, ministers of the supreme king Christ, and stewards of the mysteries of God.

2. That from all ministers this alone is required, that they be faithful: Faithfulness, however, comprises

1. A moderate knowledge of doctrine, and that you be fit for teaching.

2. Diligence, and a good conscience.

3. Constancy and patience.

4. Piety, by which we refer all things to the glory of God and the salvation of the Church.

3. That human judgments concerning our labors and struggles are not to be made much of, but that one must always look to the judgment of God.

4. The righteousness of a good conscience is not a righteousness on account of which we please God for eternal life.

5. That our Lord Jesus Christ is the judge of the whole world, and that he is to reveal the most hidden counsels of hearts, and all secrets, and in the final judgment is to adorn each one with just praise.

6. That men have absolutely nothing from themselves: But have received all gifts from God: Therefore faith also is a gift of God: Nor can a man of himself by his own powers believe the Gospel. Rightly Cyprian, that all may be given to God: Since nothing is ours, therefore no one ought to be proud or insolent in his gifts: But to contribute all gifts both to the glory of God and to the utility of the Church.

7. That it is not to be presumed, as long as we dwell in this infirmity of the flesh, as if we had arrived at the full knowledge of Christ, so that nothing is lacking to us, and there is no need for further study: And as if no struggle remained for us any longer: As if we had already attained the kingdom and eternal happiness: But rather to acknowledge our immense infirmity:

We must prepare ourselves for the most serious struggles: to fear the constant snares of Satan: And in faith, hope, and patience to strive for the kingdom of God.

8. Concerning the greatest miseries, hardships, struggles, and dangers of the Apostles and ministers of the Gospel: That on account of the profession of doctrine they are exposed to all the injuries of the world: And destined for slaughter. There is therefore no reason why they should hope for any glory or favor in the world.

9. Concerning the profane, sacrilegious, and insane judgment of the world: That it execrates the Apostles and Pastors, the greatest benefactors of the human race, as ἀλάστορας & καθάρματα. Conversely, it kisses, admires, and adores the plagues and deaths of the human race as the greatest benefactors.

10. That the kingdom of God does not consist in chatter, but in the virtue and efficacy of the Holy Spirit, by which the power of Satan is broken.

Latin:

Loci Doctrinae.

1. De amplitudine & maiestate muneris, quod Apostoli & pastores gerunt in genere humano: Quòd nimirum sunt ministri summi regis Christi, & dispensatores mysteriorum Dei.

2. Quòd ab omnibus ministris hoc solum requiratur ut sint fideles: Fidelitas autem complectitur

1. Mediocrem noticiam doctrinae, & ut sis ad docendum idoneus.

2. Diligentiam, & bonam conscientiam.

3. Constantiam & patientiam.

4. Pietatem, qua omnia ad gloriam Dei & salutem Ecclesiae referamus.

3. Humana iudicia de nostris laboribus & certaminibus non magni facienda esse, sed semper ad Dei iudicium respiciendum esse.

4. Iustitiam bonae conscientiae, non esse iustitiam propter quam Deo placeamus ad vitam aeternam.

5. Quòd dominus noster Iesus Christus iudex sit totius mundi, quodque is revelaturus sit occultissima cordium consilia, & omnia arcana, & in extremo iudicio unumquemque iusta laude sit ornaturus.

6. Quòd homines prorsus nihil habeant à seipsis: Sed omnia dona acceperint a Deo: Ergò & fides est donum Dei: Nec potest homo ex sese propriis viribus credere Evangelio. Rectè Cyprianus ut totum detur Deo: Quando nihil est nostrum, Ergò nemo in donis suis superbire aut insolescere debet: Sed omnia dona & ad Dei gloriam, & ad Ecclesiae utilitatem conferre.

7. Non esse praesumendum quamdiu in hac infirmitate carnis versamur, quasi pervenerimus ad plenam Christi cognitionem, ita ut nihil desit nobis, nullo studio amplius sit opus: Ac quasi nullum amplius nobis restet certamen: Quasi regnum & foelicitatem aeternam iam simus adepti: Sed potius ingentem nostram infirmitatem agnoscere:

Ad gravissima certamina nos praeparare: Insidias Satanae adsiduas metuere: Et in fide, spe, & patientia ad regnum Dei contendere debemus.

8. De summis miseriis, aerumnis, certaminibus & periculis Apostolorum & ministrorum Evangelii: Quòd propter doctrinae professionem expositi sint omnibus mundi iniuriis: Et destinati mactationi. Non est igitur quòd ullam sperent in mundo, vel gloriam vel favorem.

9. De profano, sacrilego & insano iudicio mundi: Quòd summos benefactores generis humani Apostolos & Pastores, tanquam ἀλάστορας & καθάρματα execratur. Contra vero pestes & funera generis humani pro summis benefactoribus exosculatur, admiratur, adorat.

10. Quod regnum Dei non consistat in garrulitate, sed in virtute & efficacia Spiritus sancti, qua frangitur potestas Satanae.

## 5:1 Argument
CHAPTER V.

What do you wish? Shall I come to you with a rod, or with love, and a spirit of meekness? It is altogether heard that there is fornication among you: and such fornication, as is not even

Latin:

CAPUT V.

Quid vultis? cum virga ad vos veniam, an cum dilectione, spirituque mansuetudinis? Omninò auditur in vobis scortatio: & talis scortatio, quae neque

## 5:1-5
named among the Gentiles: so that one has taken his father's wife. And you are puffed up, and have not rather mourned, that he who has done such a deed might be taken away from among you. For I indeed, as absent in body, but present in Spirit, have already judged, as though I were present, him who has committed this crime in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, when you are gathered together, and my Spirit, with the power of our Lord Jesus Christ, to deliver such a one to Satan for the destruction of the flesh, that the Spirit may be saved in the day of the Lord Jesus.

In the whole Epistle, Paul sets out to tax and correct the confusion, errors, crimes, and lapses of the Corinthians: therefore, in the 4 prior chapters, he blocked the source of every evil and of dissensions and confusions, condemning the pride of human nature and the presumption and affectation of wisdom. Now he approaches more to the specific nature of the remaining sins. And in this chapter, he taxes the fornication and incestuous custom of the Corinthians: and he excommunicates and delivers to Satan him who had taken his stepmother. He then exhorts the Corinthians that they manifestly exterminate the wicked from the Church: and worship God in sincerity and truth. He then explains that with those who profess themselves members of the Church, and yet pollute themselves with manifest wickednesses, food is not to be taken, nor is any commerce to be had with them.

The sad example of the fall in the Corinthian Church shows that such a Church is not to be imagined on earth which is entirely lacking in every stain, and in which no wickednesses, no scandals, no dissensions are seen. For Satan especially lies in wait for this holy assembly: he tries to deform it and render it suspect to all: and he strives to provoke the wrath of God against this assembly. It is not therefore to be wondered at if sad falls happen in the Church: the families of Noah, of Jacob, of David, were the Church of God: but how sad scandals arose in these families is known. Judas, one of the Apostles, was the betrayer of the only-begotten son of God: let us not therefore dream on earth of a Church which is devoid of every scandal: nor let us desert the good because of the bad, but rather let us tolerate the bad because of the good: nor let us condemn the Church because of the tares: but let us strive that we may be the pure and solid wheat of the Lord.

The sharp chastisement of the Apostle then teaches that the doctrine of the Gospel does not abrogate the honest laws of marriages, nor is the law of nature taken away: but rather all the laws of nature, as those which agree with the decalogue to be established. For Christ did not come to abolish the law but to fulfill it. Since Paul also confesses that the Gentiles abhor such an incestuous custom, he signifies that in the Gentiles not illuminated by the Holy Spirit there remains some light of nature by which they can in some way understand the distinction between honorable and shameful things.

But above all, the Apostolic example of severe excommunication is to be observed in this place. For Paul, while he delivers the incestuous man to Satan, teaches that the sentence of excommunication passed by the true judgment of the Church is not a pontifical tyranny, but a just and necessary severity of Ecclesiastical discipline, which is a part of the ministry of the Spirit.

Therefore, the doctrine concerning excommunication should be repeated in this place. However, civil excommunication must first be distinguished from Ecclesiastical excommunication. For the former is a civil and corporal punishment: such as was deportation among the Romans: now they call it the ban of the empire. The Church does not exercise that. But Ecclesiastical excommunication is done only by the word, and is not a civil punishment: but only a denunciation of divine wrath, and exclusion from the society of the Church. And the ancient Church exercised a double excommunication: the lesser which it called ἀφόριστμον, that is, separation: or suspension; when they suspended either clerics or laymen for some time on account of some offense, the cleric from office and the use of the Lord's supper; the layman from the communion of the Sacraments:

That they might inquire so much the more accurately into committed sins, and explore whether those thus suspended were seriously performing penance,

He called the greater one Anathema. Moreover, the greater Excommunication is a just severity of ecclesiastical discipline, by which either those infected with errors overturning the foundation: Or those defiled by manifest and notorious crimes: And those persevering in these, are publicly excluded by the heralds of the divine word from the society of the Church, are warded off from the communion of the Sacraments, and are delivered to Satan, until they repent and seek pardon for their offenses from God and the Church. Christ commands this excommunication to be exercised in the Church, when He says: If anyone refuses to hear the Church, let him be to you as a Gentile and a tax collector. Matthaei 18. And we have an illustrious example of this excommunication in this chapter.

And because many dispute in the Church that an admonition must be prefixed to all sins, whether they be publicly notorious, or secretly perpetrated and indicated to the pastor, it is clear from this example of Paul, when crimes are manifest to the whole Church, and are a scandal to the entire assembly, that it is not necessary that a private admonition precede: But that the Ministers of the Gospel with the Church have the right of excommunicating those defiled by notorious crimes, and of excluding them from the society of the saints.

For Paul does not preface an admonition: But he simply pronounces that he must be driven out of the Church and delivered to Satan. Therefore the process of which Christ speaks, Matth: 18., is to be understood concerning private offenses and concerning crimes committed secretly. If, he says, your brother sins against you, rebuke him between you and him: If he hears you, you have gained your brother. A different reason applies to those who openly stir up scandals in the Church, and corrupt the whole assembly either by false doctrine or by flagitious morals. Where there is need of medicine immediately, lest the evil creep more widely.

But because the sentence of excommunication is the saddest of all: for Christ says, whatever you shall bind on earth, shall be bound also in heaven: the Minister of the Church ought not to pass this sentence by his own judgment alone, but to permit the censure to the Church at the same time. Whence also in this place the Apostle Paul says: When you are gathered together and my Spirit: And Christ says, if anyone shall refuse to hear the Church. Matthaei 18. Moreover, the Church of Christ is not a gathering famous for a multitude of men, or illustrious by the eminence of Prophets, but one which is gathered in the name of Jesus Christ, professes the uncorrupted doctrine of the Gospel, and studiously cultivates the unity of the Spirit. The judgment of this Church is not to be neglected: nor are members to be taken away from the body of the Church, while the Church herself is either ignorant or not assenting, for although a minister of the word may be a Bishop of great authority, he is not, however, instructed with either royal or praetorian authority, so that he might be able to decide in such great matters by his own judgment alone. Therefore, by his own example, Paul here instructs all heralds of the word that the thunderbolt of excommunication is not to be promulgated except by the judgment of the Church.

Furthermore, Paul warns that one must not indulge in private vengeance or similar affections in the execution of Ecclesiastical discipline. For this would be a most grave wickedness: for this would be to abuse the power granted by Christ to the Church for the destruction of men. And so he says that he has decreed excommunication in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, that is, in the true fear of God, and for the sake of preserving the glory of the name of Jesus Christ.

To deliver a man to Satan for the destruction of the flesh, is to declare that this impenitent man has nothing in common with the Church of Christ, is not a partaker of the benefits of Christ, does not have the hope of eternal life, is not a son of God: but is concluded under sin, and is subject to the power and tyranny of Satan: whose cruelty he is forced to fear at every moment. Therefore, this phrase teaches that the sentence of true excommunication is the most grave and most sad of all. For what could be said to be sadder than for a man to be delivered by the authority of the Church to the power and tyranny of Satan; and to be excluded from all protection of God and participation of the kingdom of Christ? And when God himself affirms: I will curse those who curse you: and I will bless those who bless you, he shows that he will pour out his wrath upon those who are removed from the society of the Church.

Whether the Corinthian incestuous man was soon seized by some grave disease, history does not record. However, the second Epistle hints that he had been affected by great sorrow. And the very phrase to deliver such a man to Satan for the destruction of the flesh, indicates that the sentence of excommunication is not an empty scarecrow, as many men think. Indeed, experience testifies that for the most part, the most grave bodily punishments follow this most grave judgment of the Church.

When Ambrose had struck the scribe of Stilicho with the thunderbolt of excommunication, he was soon, as historians testify, moved in his mind: by which punishment he was admonished and performed penance. Arius, struck by anathema, a little later poured out his life and his intestines into a latrine. When Nestorius was excommunicated by Cyril and the Ephesian synod, it is written that his tongue, with which he had blasphemed Christ the Son of God, rotted away. And often God teaches by illustrious examples that the sentence of the Church in excommunicating the impenitent is not empty.

Furthermore, this phrase warns that Satan cannot attack the pious according to its own will and desire to harm. For the entire Church of Christ is surrounded and encompassed by whole camps of angels, so that the impure and murderous Spirit cannot harm it. David says: The angel of the Lord shall encamp round about them that fear him, Psalmo. 34. And Zacha: 2 I will be a wall of fire round about you.

Therefore, let the pious take heed lest they strip themselves of this heavenly protection, and through crimes fall away from the fellowship of the Church, and thus expose themselves to the violence and monstrous tyranny of Satan.

For Satan rages against the impious, who have been handed over to his power, he leads them with his snares into errors and crimes, he lies in wait for them at every moment of their lives, and finally he precipitates them into eternal destruction.

That he says, that the Spirit may be saved in the day of the Lord Jesus Christ: he shows that he hopes for the repentance of the unchaste man: and for this end he marks him with anathema, that being punished in the body he may perform repentance: which if he shall have done, he promises that it will be that the Spirit, That is, the new man who through repentance shall rise again in him, may be saved, even if the hard chastisement of the body shall have been to be endured by him.

Latin:

apud gentes nominatur: ita ut quis patris sui uxorem duxerit. Et vos inflati estis, & non magis lugetis, ut auferatur è medio vestri, qui tale opus patravit. Equidem absens corpore, praesens autem Spiritu, iam decrevi, tanquam praesens essem, eum qui scelus hoc commisit in nomine domini nostri Iesu Christi, congregatis vobis & meo Spiritu ac simul virtute domini nostri Iesu Christi, tradere Satanae in interitum carnis, ut Spiritus salvetur in die Domini Iesu.

In tota Epistola instituit Paulus taxare & corrigere confusionem, errores, scelera et lapsus Corinthiorum: In 4. ergò prioribus capitibus fontem omnis mali & dissidiorum, & confusionum obstruxit, damnans humanae naturae superbiam, & sapientiae praesumtionem & adfectationem. Nunc magis ad speciem reliquorum peccatorum accedit. Atque in hoc capite taxat scortationem, & incaestam consuetudinem Corinthiorum: atque eum qui novercam suam duxerat excommunicat & tradit Satanae. Hortatur deinde Corinthios ut manifestè sceleratos exterminent ex Ecclesia: & Deum colant in synceritate & veritate. Exponit deinde quòd cum iis, qui se Ecclesiae socios profitentur, & tamen manifestis sceleribus sese polluunt, non sit capiendus cibus, neque ullum commercium cum eis habendum.

Triste exemplum lapsus in Ecclesia Corinthiaca, ostendit non esse in terris talem fingendam Ecclesiam quae omni prorsus labe careat, & in qua nulla scelera, nulla scandala, nulla dissidia conspiciantur. Satan enim inprimis huic sancto coetui insidiatur: Hunc deformare & omnibus suspectum reddere conatur: atque ergà hunc coetum iram Dei provocare studet. Non ergò mirandum est si tristes accidant lapsus in Ecclesia: familiae Noah, Iacobi, Davidis, fuerunt Ecclesia Dei: sed quam tristia scandala in his familiis sint exortae notum est. Iudas unus ex Apostolis proditor fuit unigeniti filii Dei: Non ergò in terris somniemus Ecclesiam, quae omnis scandali sit expers: nec propter malos deseramus bonos, sed potius malos propter bonos toleremus: Nec damnemus Ecclesiam propter Zizania: sed nos operam demus ut purum & solidum domini frumentum simus.

Castigatio deinde acris Apostoli docet doctrina Evangelii non abrogari honestas coniugiorum leges, neque tolli ius naturae: sed potius omnes leges naturae, ut quae congruant cum decalogo stabiliri. Christus enim non venit solvere legem sed implere. Cum etiam Paulus fatetur gentes abhorrere à tali incaesta consuetudine, significat in gentibus non illuminatis à Spiritu sancto restare aliquod lumen naturae quo discrimen honestorum & turpium aliquomodo intelligere possint.

Inprimis verò exemplum Apostolicum severae excommunicationis hoc loco est observandum. Paul: enim dum incestum tradit Satanae docet sententiam excommunicationis vero Ecclesiae iudicio latam non esse pontificiam tyrannidem, sed iustam & necessariam severitatem Ecclesiasticae disciplinae, quae sit pars ministerii Spiritus.

Doctrina igitur de excommunicatione hoc loco repetatur. Discernenda est autem primum ex communicatio civilis ab ex communicatione Ecclesiastica. Illa enim est poena civilis & corporalis: Qualis fuit apud Romanos deportatio: Nunc imperii bannum vocant. Illam non exercet Ecclesia. At Ecclesiastica ex communicatio fit tantum verbo, & non est civilis poena: Sed tantum denunciatio irae divinae, & exclusto à societate Ecclesiae. Ac vetus Ecclesia duplicem exercuit ex communicationem: Minorem quam vocavit ἀφόριστμον, id est, separationem: Vel suspensionem; Quando vel clericos vel laicos propter aliquod delictum aliquamdiu suspenderunt clericum ab officio & usis coenae domini; Laicum à communione Sacramentorum:

Ut tantò accuratius in commissa peccata inquirerent, & explorarent num sic suspensi seriò poenitentiam agerent,

Maiorem vocavit Anathema. Est autem Excommunicatio maior iusta Ecclesiasticae disciplinae severitas, qua vel infecti erroribus fundamentum evertentibus: Vel polluti manifestis & notoriis sceleribus: Et in his per severantes, publice per verbi divini praecones excluduntur à societate Ecclesiae, arcentur à communione Sacramentorum, & traduntur Satanae, donec resipiscant & à Deo & Ecclesia veniam delictorum petant. Hanc excommunicationem iubet Christus exerceri in Ecclesia, cum inquit: Si quis Ecclesiam audire noluerit, sit tibi veluti Ethnicus & publicanus. Matthaei 18. Atque huius excommunicationis illustre exemplum in hoc capite habemus.

Ac quia multi disputant in Ecclesia, omnibus peccatis sive ea publicè sint notoria, sive clam perpetrata et pastori indicata, praemittendam esse admonitionem, ex hoc Pauli exemplo liquet, quando scelera sunt manifesta toti Ecclesiae, & scandalo sunt universo caetui, non esse necesse ut privata admonitio praecedat: Sed Ministros Evangelii cum Ecclesia ius habere notoriis sceleribus pollutos excommunicandi, & à societate sanctorum excludendi.

Paulus enim non praemittit admonitionem: Sed simpliciter pronunciat, eum pellendum esse ex Ecclesia & Satanae tradendum. Processus ergò de quo Christus loquitur, Matth: 18. De privatis offensionibus, & de sceleribus clàm commissis intelligendus est. Si, inquit, peccaverit in te frater tuus, argue eum inter te & ipsum: Site audierit, lucratus es fratrem tuum. Alia ratio est eorum qui palam excitant scandala in Ecclesia, & totum caetum vel falsa doctrina, vel flagitiosis moribus corrumpunt. Ubi statim medicina est opus ne malum latius serpat.

Quia verò sententia excommunicationis omnium est tristissima: Christus enim inquit, quidquid ligaveritis in terris, erit ligatum & in coelo: Minister Ecclesiae non suo solius arbitrio sententiam hanc ferre debet, sed Ecclesiae simul permittere censuram. Unde & hoc loco Paulus Apostolus inquit: Congregatis vobis & meo Spiritu: Et Christus inquit, si quis Ecclesiam audire noluerit. Matthaei 18. Est autem Ecclesia Christi, non caetus hominum multitudine clarus, aut Prophetarum eminentia illustris, sed qui in nomine Iesu Christi congregatus est, profitetur incorruptam Evangelii doctrinam, & unitatem Spiritus studiose colit. Huius Ecclesiae iudicium non est negligendum: neque à corpore Ecclesiae membra sunt auferenda, ipsa Ecclesia vel ignorante vel non adsentientes Minister quoque verbi licet sit magnae authoritatis Episcopus, non tamen instructus est vel regia vel praetoria authoritate, ut suo solius arbitrio in tantis rebus possit statuere. Suo ergo exemplo instituit hic Paulus omnes verbi praecones, fulmen excommunicationis non nisi de sententia Ecclesiae promulgandum esse.

Monet praeterea Paulus non esse indulgendum privatae vindictae aut similibus adfectibus in executione disciplinae Ecclesiasticae. Hoc enim nefas esset gravissimum: Hoc enim esset abuti potestate à Christo concessa Ecclesiae ad hominum perniciem. Itaque inquit se decrevisse excommunicationem in nomine domini nostri Iesu Christi, Hoc est, in vero Dei timore, & pro conservanda gloria nominis Iesu Christi.

Tradere hominem Satanae ad interitum carnis, est denunciare quòd homo iste impaenitens nihil habeat commune cum Ecclesia Christi, non sit particeps beneficiorum Christi, non habeat spem vitae aeternae, non sit filius Dei: sed sit conclusus sub peccato, & subiectus potestati & tyrannidi Satanae: cuius saeviciam singulis momentis metuere cogitur. Itaque phrasis haec docet sententiam verae excommunicationis omnium esse gravissimam & tristissimam. Quid posset enim dici tristius, quàm hominem tradi authoritate Ecclesiae potestati & tyrannidi Satanae; & excludi ab omni tutela Dei & participatione regni Christi? Ac cum ipse Deus adfirmat: maledicam maledicentibus tibi: & benedicam benedicentibus tibi, ostendit se iram suam effusurum in eos qui à societate Ecclesiae sunt remoti.

An incestus Corinthiacus gravi aliquo morbo mox sit correptus, non tradit historia. Secunda autem Epistola innuit ingenti moerore eum adfectum fuisse. Atque ipsa phrasis tradere hominem Satanae ad interitum carnis, indicat excommunicationis sententiam non esse inane terriculamentum, ut multi homines cogitant. Imò experientia testatur plerumque gravissimas poenas corporales sequi gravissimum hoc iudicium Ecclesiae.

Cum Ambrosius scribam stilliconis excommunicationis fulmine feriisset, mox ille, ut historici testantur, motus est mente: qua poena admonitus poenitentiam egit. Anathemate percussus Arrius, paulò post, vitam & intestina in latrinam effudit. Nestorio excommunicato à Cyrillo & synodo Ephesina lingua scribitur computruisse, qua Christum filium Dei blasphemaverat. Ac saepe Deus illustribus exemplis docet non esse inanem sententiam Ecclesiae in Excommunicandis impaenitentibus.

Adhaec monet haec phrasis quòd Satanas in pios non possit grassari pro suo arbitrio & cupiditate nocendi. Circumvallata est enim universa Christi Ecclesia & integris angelorum castris circumdata, ut impurus & homicida Spiritus ei nocere non possit. David inquit: Castrametatur angelus domini in circuitu timentium eum, Psalmo. 34. Et Zacha: 2 Ego ero murus igneus in circuitu vestro.

Caveant ergò pii ne hoc coelesti praesidio sese nudent, & per scelera excidant societate Ecclesiae, & sic exponant sese violentiae & immani tyrannidi Satanae.

In impios enim, qui eius potestati sunt traditi, grassatur Satanas, ducit eos laqueis suis in errores & scelera, singulis momentis vitaeipsorum insidiatur, & tandem praecipitat eos in aeternum exitium.

Quòd dicit, ut Spiritus salvus sit in die domini Iesu Christi: ostendit se sperare hominis incaesti paenitentiam: & hoc fine se notare eum anathemate, ut punitus in corpore agat paenitentiam: quòd sifecerit, promittit fore ut Spiritus, Id est, homo novus qui per paenitentiam resurget in eo, salvus fiat, etiamsi corporis dura castigatio ei sustinenda fuerit.

## 5:6-7
Your glorying is not good: Know you not that a little leaven leaveneth the whole lump? Purge out therefore the old leaven, that you may be a new paste, as you are unleavened.

Paul intermixes a general admonition, and they may be proud and secure, having taken the occasion from the grave fall of the incestuous man: By which the Corinthians could learn that the Devil was lying in wait for them, and that they themselves were carrying about manifold infirmities of the flesh. And he urges that they drive the incestuous man away from them, lest the whole Church be infected by this crime: for crimes, like a contagion, creep very widely. Then he warns that they should worship God with a pious and sincere heart, and repress and even put off impure affections. In this exhortation, however, he uses an allegory taken from the ancient Mosaic rite concerning the feast of the Passover. God commanded through Moses that the Israelites should eat unleavened bread for seven days at the feast of the Passover: And at the beginning of the feast, all leaven had to be purged from the houses. What God signified by this figure, Paul explains in this place. Leaven signifies sin, whether it be an impious dogma or another fall. But as leaven penetrates the whole mass, and with its sharpness infects and inflates it so that it is all leavened: So sin or false doctrine infects and corrupts the whole man: So also one evil man, and contaminating himself with wickedness, infects the whole Church. For just as gangrene creeps in the body: So some scandal creeps in the whole Church. Therefore Paul urges the Corinthians first that they cast out the incestuous man from their assembly; And that they drive away from themselves all who contaminate themselves with wicked deeds, and do not live according to the rule of Jesus Christ.

Then he exhorts those individually converted to Christ through faith to repress the desires of the flesh, and to put off the malice of the old man: For a desire which seems small at the beginning can occupy the whole man, and cast him into destruction. David indulges in lust; this leaven infected the whole lump. Judas indulges in avarice: He is so entangled in this sin that he perishes eternally. The leaven of Arius, Macedonius, Manes, and Pelagius troubled and infected the whole Church. Effort must therefore be made that the leaven of false doctrine and of impious morals be purged from the Church as quickly and as studiously as possible. But what he adds; As you are unleavened: he mingles consolation according to Apostolic custom. The Corinthians certainly had the leaven of depraved desires: And of manifold sins: Nevertheless he affirms that they are unleavened, namely by imputation through faith on account of our Lord Jesus Christ. For this is our shelter by which all our filth is covered: His righteousness and innocence we put on through faith, so that we may appear clean before God. Therefore the Corinthians are unleavened, that is, they lack sin before the judgment of God, namely by imputation through faith in our Lord Jesus. Both things are therefore true: that the Corinthians are unleavened through faith in Christ by imputation, and yet that it behooves them to purge out the leaven. For although the Holy Spirit has begun to restore nature in them, and to renew the deformed image of God: nevertheless, much filth and depraved affections still cling to them, nor have they at once laid aside all the oldness of the flesh. Therefore, it behooves them daily to mortify and put off the old Adam with his desires.

In this statement, Paul warns that one must not wink when false dogma is spread in the Church. As soon as the scorpion appears, it must be crushed, says Jerome: for it very quickly penetrates and infects the whole assembly. He also warns that there is need for severity of discipline in excluding from the Church those who contaminate themselves with manifest crimes. Furthermore, he teaches that sin remains in the saints.

For Christ our Passover has been sacrificed.

He shows the cause which has made us unleavened before God: namely, Christ Jesus the lamb of God slaughtered for our sins, whose justice and obedience is imputed to us. Therefore, by imputation we are without the leaven of sin: although the remnants of the leaven of sins cling to us, which must be purged daily by the Spirit and true repentance.

Moreover, in this place Paul elegantly demonstrates the allegory of the Passover in the Old Testament, which is instituted and described, Exo: 12. Pasah signifies the passing over: for the angel of the Lord passed over all of Egypt, and killed every firstborn among men and cattle in one night. By this most grave punishment, God signified that all Egyptians and the entire posterity of Adam are guilty of death on account of sin.

Through Moses, however, God commanded that individual heads of families in Israel, on the fourteenth day of the first month toward evening, should slaughter a whole lamb lacking every blemish, and with the blood of this slaughtered lamb should stain the doorposts and the upper lintel: then they should eat the flesh roasted by fire with unleavened bread and bitter lettuces.

The lamb is our Lord Jesus Christ, whom the eternal Father appointed as a victim for sin: He was slaughtered for our sins on the altar of the cross. With the blood of this one are stained and sprinkled the hearts of the faithful, on account of which blood the Lord spares them, so that He does not kill them, even if they are transgressors of the law, like other men. For the blood of Jesus Christ cleanses us from all sin. The flesh of the lamb was roasted with fire. Thus, upon Christ the victim, the whole and most ardent wrath of God and the curse of the law was poured out, so that He sweated blood. We eat the flesh of the lamb when we believe with true faith in our Lord Jesus Christ. He who eats my flesh, says Christ, and drinks my blood, remains in me, John 6, by which saying He demands faith from us.

It was not permitted to break the bones of the lamb: because Christ the mediator had to rise from the dead. The whole lamb was to be consumed: that is, one must believe in the whole Christ, God and man. It is not fitting that Christ be divided; nor that the articles of faith be torn apart: he who casts away one article of faith, loses the whole Christ. Unleavened breads signify pure and sincere doctrine, lacking all leaven of human opinions, and pure affections consistent with the law of God, lacking the leaven of carnal desires: bitter lettuces signify the cross, which stirs up in us a desire and appetite for the benefits of Christ: For vexation gives understanding. With loins girded and shoes put on, and with a staff taken into the hands, the lamb was to be eaten in haste. This figure warns us Christians that we are pilgrims in this world, that we ought always to be girded and prepared to migrate from this world, and to seek again the land of promise, our heavenly fatherland: The Apostle Paul teaches in this place that our entire religion is painted by allegory in the figure of the paschal lamb, when he says: Christ our passover is sacrificed. He also warns that the figures of the Old Testament have passed away: and that we now possess the true paschal lamb. If, therefore, the figures of the Old Testament admonished the fathers to purge out the leaven of false opinions and impure affections, much more ought the truth itself, Jesus Christ crucified for us, who has expiated us with his blood and given his Holy Spirit to us, to excite and move us to walk in sincerity of doctrine and holiness of life. From this, an example can be sought of how allegories are to be treated, namely, that individual accommodations should correspond to the analogy of faith. First, the principal heads of heavenly doctrine must be rightly held, then it must be seen where figures and allegories have a place. Nor are all things to be transformed into allegories: but one simple, certain, and perpetual meaning is to be observed in individual verses of Scripture. But above all, it must be attended to that an allegorical interpretation does not anywhere strike against any article of faith.

Therefore let us keep the feast, not with old leaven, neither with the leaven of malice and wickedness: But with the unleavened bread of sincerity and truth.

He still persists in the allegory, and he exhorts the Corinthians, who were reconciled to God through the victim Jesus Christ crucified and resurrected, and liberated not from bodily Egyptian servitude, but from the spiritual tyranny of Satan, to a serious and sincere piety devoid of all malice and hypocrisy. To celebrate a feast day by allegory is to illuminate the glory of God with holy works, faith, patience, liberality toward the poor, invocation, thanksgiving, and every kind of virtue. The old leaven signifies the old depravity of the flesh, which is prone to vices of every kind, just as Paul himself explains: The leaven of malice and wickedness: By which terms he signifies first, opinions of every kind that are impious, and impure desires, luxury, lusts, avarice, emulation: Then also frauds, deceits, and impostures, by which both false dogmas and wicked morals are cunningly covered. These carnal vices he wishes to be purged and avoided: And God to be worshipped in sincerity and truth: That is, by the confession of sound and incorrupt doctrine, and a holy life devoid of all hypocrisy and frauds.

I wrote to you in the Epistle, not to associate with the sexually immoral: Not at all with the sexually immoral of this world, or the greedy, or the swindlers, or the idolaters (this I wish to be understood:) Otherwise you would have to leave the world. But now I have written to you not to associate with anyone who is named a brother, and is either a sexually immoral person, or a greedy person, or an idolater, or a blasphemer, or a drunkard, or a swindler: With such a one you must not even eat. For what have I to do with judging those who are outside? Do you not judge those who are inside the Church? But those who are outside God will judge. Remove the evil from among yourselves.

The Apostle Paul had written to the Corinthians that they should abstain entirely from the commerce of those who were contaminating themselves with crimes against their conscience: And that they should not confirm the impious in their crimes: Then that they themselves or other weak ones might not be infected by the contagion of crimes. But the Corinthians had not correctly grasped the mind of Paul: For they thought that Paul wanted this, that the pious should abstain from all commerce with the wicked and the impious, as if the company of the impious would contaminate us and render us hateful to God.

Paul therefore explains his opinion more clearly: Namely, that he did not speak of fornicators, idolaters, blasphemers, or robbers outside the Church. For if the association of all the impious were to be avoided by the pious, it would be necessary for them to migrate from the world. For the whole world is placed in the evil one: and wicked and impure men meet us everywhere. Thus the pious could exercise no contracts in the world: they could live with no man. For they cannot know whether anyone is free from crimes. Paul therefore warns that he spoke of those fornicators, misers, idolaters, and blasphemers who wish to be adorned with the title of Christians and to enjoy the communion of the sacraments as members of the body of Christ: and meanwhile pollute themselves with crimes that devastate the conscience: by which they demonstrate that they lack all faith, and simulate piety with flagitious hypocrisy. With men of this kind: who are only disgraces to the Church, no association is to be had, nor even food to be taken with them: but they are to be avoided as ἀλάστορες καὶ μιάσματα.

1. First, lest the name of God be ill-spoken of, if such impure men are tolerated in the Church.

2. Secondly, lest the examples of crimes creep more widely, offend the minds of the pious, and be a scandal to us ourselves.

3. Thirdly, that we may not confirm the sinners themselves in impiety and impenitence, but rather invite them to serious repentance by severe discipline. For these most grave reasons Paul commands that the pious in the Church should abstain from the commerce of the wicked who wish to be held as brothers.

Therefore, we first learn here that it is permitted for a pious person to converse in the world even with idolaters and robbers, if necessity so demands. For to the pure all things are pure. A pious husband to whom an impious and idolatrous wife has fallen, should not on that account desert his spouse, nor think that he is contaminated by the crimes of his spouse. But rather let him conclude that the unbeliever is sanctified by the believer. A pious and faithful servant who serves a master who is greedy, impious, and an idolater should not think that he is contaminated by his crimes, nor should he desert his calling: but let him know that to him who is pure, all things are pure. If any pious person contracts through buying, selling, leasing, or hiring with a wicked man: there is no reason for him to fear that he will be contaminated. For it pertains nothing to him what kind of person he is, who is not a member of the Church.

However, when there are men in the assembly of the Church who pollute themselves with external crimes and are a scandal to the Church, one must abstain from their company: and not only should pastors and elders mark them with the sentence of excommunication, but also individual hearers should abstain from their fellowship and company: so that they may indeed understand the judgments of the saints about themselves, and be seriously admonished concerning the penance to be performed. But someone might say, why then did Christ take food with the Pharisees? Is it not permitted for a pastor to associate with sinners? I answer. Christ associated with the Pharisees for this reason, that he might admonish them concerning their gross errors, and have the opportunity of helping them toward serious penance and the acknowledgment of the truth. Thus, when a pastor or any Christian sees that an opportunity is offered to him of admonishing sinners concerning their crimes or errors, and the matter is outside the scandal of the weak, it is entirely permitted for him to associate, take food, converse, and contract with openly impious men, nor is there any reason that he should fear that he will be contaminated by them. Indeed, he ought to hope that he might be able to win some over. However, after two or three admonitions, both heretics and wicked men are to be avoided.

And it must be entirely seen to that we do not connive at their errors or crimes: that we do not dissimulate their sins: that we do not approve of their blasphemies by our silence: that we do not frequent the houses and tables of the impious for the sake of our own belly rather than for the sake of winning over our neighbor: that we do not offend the weak ones of Christ by our perverse example: that we do not confirm the impious in error, and that the zeal of piety in us be not broken by the company of the wicked. It was not said in vain: He who touches pitch will be defiled by it. And evil communications corrupt good manners. And, he who lives near a lame man, learns to limp. Therefore, the company of the impious is to be avoided with great diligence: but when either the duty enjoined upon us, or the glory of God to be asserted, or the salvation of a neighbor to be promoted demands that we associate with the impious, it must be known that to the clean all things are clean. Antiquity guarded this discipline with great diligence and severity, as can be seen in the History of Joseph, who takes food separately from the Egyptians, and in the Evangelist John, where we read that it is not lawful for Jews to associate with Samaritans. And Christ shows the severe discipline of the Church when He says: Let him be to you as a Gentile and a tax collector. Matth: 18. Therefore, Paul looks to this severity when he says: Remove the evil from among yourselves. That is, take away scandals from your assembly: excommunicate the wicked, and flee their commerce.

Latin:

Non bona est gloriatio vestra: An nescitis quòd parum fermenti totam massam fermentat: Expurgate igitur vetus fermentum, ut sitis nova conspersio, sicut estis sine fermento.

Admiscet Paulus generalem admonitionem, ac sint superbi & securi, sumpta occasione à gravi lapsu incestuosi: Quo discere poterant Corinthii Diabolum ipsis insidiari, & ipsos multiplices carnis infirmitates circumferre. Ac urget ut abigant à se incestuosum, ne tota Ecclesia hoc scelere inficiatur: scelera enim velut contagium latissimè serpunt. Deinde monet ut pio & syncero pectore colant Deum, & reprimant atque etiam exuant impuros adfectus. In hac autem adhortatione allegoria utitur sumpta ex veteri ritu Mosaico de festo paschatos. Iussit Deus per Mosen ut Israelitae festo Paschatos septem diebus vescerentur pane infermentato: Et sub initium sesti oportebat omne fermentum ex aedibus purgari. Quid hac figura significaverit Deus, exponit hoc loco Paulus. Fermentum significat peccatum, sive sit impium dogma, sive alius lapsus. Ut autem fermentum totam penetrat massam, & sua acredine inficit & inflat eam ut tota fermentetur: Ita peccatum seu falsa doctrina totum inficit & corrumpit hominem: Ita etiam unus homo malus, & scelere se contaminans totam inficit Ecclesiam. Ut enim gangrena serpit in corpore: Ita scandalum aliquod serpit in tota Ecclesia. Hortatur igitur Corinthios Paulus primùm ut incestuosum hominem eiiciant ex suo caetu; Et pellant àse omnes qui sese sceleribus contaminant, & non secundum regulam Iesu Christi vivunt.

Deinde singulos per fidem ad Christum conversos hortatur ut reprimant carnis adsectus, & exuant veteris hominis maliciam: Quae enim initiò exigua videtur cupiditas, totum hominem occupare, & in interitum coniicere potest. David indulget libidini, hoc fermentum totam infecit massam. Iudas avaritiae indulget: Hoc peccato ita involvitur ut in aeternum pereat. Arrii, Macedonii, Manetis, Pelagii fermentum totam turbavit & infecit Ecclesiam. Danda igitur est opera ut quàm citissimè & studiosissimè fermentum falsae doctrinae, & impiorum morum expurgetur ex Ecclesia. Quod verò addit; Sicut estis infermentati: consuetudine Apostolica immiscet consolationem. Habebant sanè Corinthii fermentum pravarum cupiditatum: Et multiplicium peccatorum: Nihilominus adfirmat eos esse infermentatos, scilicet imputatione perfidem propter dominum nostrum Iesum Christum. Hic enim est umbraculum nostrum quo teguntur omnes nostrae sordes: Huius iustitiam & innocentiam induimus per fidem, ut mundi coràm Deo adpareamus. Infermentati ergò sunt Corinthii, hoc est, carent peccato coràm iudicio Dei, scilicet imputatione per fidem in dominum nostrum Iesum. Utrumque igitur verum est & infermentatos esse Corinthios per fidem in Christum imputatione: Et tamen oportere eos expurgare fermentum. Etsi enim Spiritus sanctus coepit in eis restituere naturam, & instaurare imaginem Dei deformatam: Tamen multum adhuc sordium, & pravorum adfectuum in ipsis haeret, nec semel omnem carnis vetustatem deposuerunt. Itaque oportet eos quotidie mortificare & exuere veterem Adamum cum suis desideriis.

In hoc dicto monet Paulus non esse connivendum quando falsum dogma spargitur in Ecclesia. Ilicò ut apparuerit scorpio conterendus est, inquit Hieronymus: celerrime enim penetrat & inficit totum caetum. Monet etiam severitate disciplinae opus esse in arcendis iis ab Ecclesia, qui manifestis sese contaminant sceleribus. Praeterea docet in sanctis manere peccatum.

Etenim Pascha nostrum mactatus est Christus.

Causam ostendit, quae effecerit nos in fermentatos coràm Deo: Videlicet Christus Iesus agnus Dei mactatus pro nostris peccatis, cuius iustitia & obedientia nobis imputatur. Itaque imputatione sumus sine fermento peccati: Licet reliquiae fermenti peccatorum haereant in nobis, quae quotidiè Spiritu & vera poenitentia sunt expurgandae.

Eleganter autem hoc loco monstrat Paulus allegoriam Paschatos in veteri testamento, quod instituitur & describitur, Exo: 12. Pasah significat transitum: Transivit enim angelus domini totam Aegyptum, & omne primogenitum in hominibus & pecudibus interfecit una nocte. Qua gravissima poena significavit Deus omnes Aegyptios & totam Adae posteritatem esse ream mortis propter peccatum.

Per Moisem autem iussit Deus ut singuli patres familias in Israele decimaquarta die primi mensis sub vesperam mactarent agnum integrum & omni labe carentem, & huius agni mactati sanguine tingerent postes & superius limen: deinde igne adsatam carnem ederent cum pane azymo & amaris lactucis.

Agnus est dominus noster Iesus Christus, quem pater aeternus constituit victimam pro peccato: Hic pro nostris peccatis mactatus est in ara crucis. Huius sanguine tinguntur & adsperguntur corda fidelium, propter quem sanguinem parcit eis dominus, ita ut non interficiat eos, etiamsi sint transgressores legis, ut caeteri homines. Sanguis enim Iesu Christi mundat nos ab omni peccato. Caro agni igne assabatur. Ita in Christum victimam universa atque ardentissima Dei ira & legis maledictio est effusa, ita ut sanguinem sudaverit. Carnem agni edimus, quando vera fide credimus in dominum nostrum Iesum Christum. Qui carnem meam edit, inquit Christus, & bibit meum sanguinem in me manet, Iohannes. 6. quo dicto postulat fidem à nobis.

Non licebat frangere ossa agni: quia Christus mediator resurgere debuit à mortuis. Totus agnus erat absumendus: hoc est, In totum Christum Deum & hominem credendum est. Non oportet dividi Christum; nec lacerari articulos fidei: qui unum fidei articulum proiicit, totum Christum amittit. Panes in fermentati, significant doctrinam puram & synceram, carentem omni fermento humanarum opinionum, & adfectus puros congruentes cum lege Dei, carentes fermento carnalium cupiditatum: amarae lactucae crucem significant, quae ciet in nobis desiderium & appetitum Beneficiorum Christi: Vexatio enim dat intellectum. Accinctis lumbis & indutis calceamentis, & baculo sumpto in manus sestinanter erat commedendus agnus. Haec figura monet Nos Christianos peregrinari in hoc mundo, semper nos debere accinctos & paratos esse ad migrandum ex hoc mundo, & repetendum terram promissionis patriam nostram coelestem: Ita totam religionem nostram per allegoriam pictam esse in figura agni paschalis, docet hoc loco Apostolus Paulus, cum inquit: pascha nostrum immolatus est Christus. Monet etiam veteris testamenti figuras transiisse: & nos nunc verum obtinere agnum paschalem. Si ergò figurae veteris testamenti admonuerunt patres, ut expurgarent fermentum falsarum opinionum, & impurorum adfectuum, multò magis ipsa veritas Iesus Christus pro nobis crucifixus, qui sanguine suo nos expiavit, & Spiritum suum sanctum nobis dedit, nos excitare & movere debet ut in synceritate doctrinae & sanctitate vitae ambulemus. Hinc exemplum peti potest quomodo tractandae sint allegoriae, nimirum ut singulae accommodationes respondeant analogiae fidei. Primum rectètenenda sunt praecipua capita doctrinae coelestis, deinde videndum ubifigurae & allegoriae locum habeant. Nec omnia in allegorias sunt transformanda: sed una simplex, certa & perpetua sententia in singulis scripturae versibus observetur. Inprimis verò attendendum est ne alicubi allegorica interpretatio impingat in aliquem fidei articulum.

Itaque festum celebremus, non in fermento vetustatis, neque in fermento maliciae & versutiae: Sed in infermentatis synceritatis & veritatis.

Persistit adhuc in allegoria, & Corinthios per victimam Iesum Christum crucifixum & resuscitatum Deo reconciliatos, & non ex corporali servitute Aegyptiaca, sed ex Satanae spirituali tyrannide liberatos hortatur ad seriam & synceram pietatem omnis malitiae & hypocriseos exortem. Festum diem celebrare per allegoriam est sanctis operibus, fide, patientia, liberalitate in pauperes, invocatione, gratiarum actione & omni genere virtutum illustrare Dei gloriam. Fermentum vetustum significat veterem pravitatem carnis, quae ad omnis generis vicia est proclivis, sicuti ipse Paulus exponit: Fermentum maliciae & nequitae: Quibus vocabulis primùm omnis generis impias opiniones, & impuras cupiditates, luxuriam, libidines, avaritiam, aemulationem: Deinde & fraudes, dolos & imposturas, quibus & falsa dogmata & scelerati mores callidè teguntur, significat. Haec vicia carnalia vult expurgari, & vitari: Et Deum coli in synceritate & veritate: Hoc est, sanae & incorruptae doctrinae confessione, & sancta & omnis hypocriseos & fraudum experte vita.

Scripsi vobis in Epistola, ne misceamini cum scortatoribus: Non autem prosus de omnibus scortatoribus huius mundi aut avaris, aut praedonibus, aut Idolatris (hoc intelligi volo:) Alioquin oporteret vosè mundo migrare. Nunc autem scripsi vobis ne misceamini, si quis frater nominatur, & est aut scortator, aut avarus, aut Idolatra, aut blasphemus, aut temulentus, aut praedo: Cum hoc neque cibus capiendus est. Quid enim ad me ut iudicem eos qui foris sunt? Nunquit eos qui intra Ecclesiam sunt iudicatis? Qui verò extra sunt eos Deus iudicabit. Auferte malum ex vobis ipsis.

Scripserat Apostolus Paulus Corinthiis ut eorum qui se sceleribus contra conscientiam contaminabant commercio prorsus abstinerent: Et ne impios in sceleribus confirmarent: Tùm ne ipsi vel alii infirmi scelerum contagio inficerentur. Sed Corinthii mentem Pauli non rectè adsecuti erant: Existimabant enim Paulum hoc velle ut pii abstinerent ab omni commercio seceleratorum & impiorum, quasi impiorum consortium nos contaminaret & Deo exosos redderet.

Planius ergò Paulus exponit suam sententiam: Quòd videlicet non sit locutus de siortatoribus, idolatris, blasphemis, praedonibus extra Ecclesiam. Nam si prorsus omnium impiorum commercium fugiendum esset piis, oporteret eos migrare è mundo. Totus enim mundus in maligno est positus: & passim scelerati & impuri homines nobis occurrunt. Ita pii nullos in mundo contractus exercere: Cum nullo homine vivere possent. Scire enim non possunt an quis immunis sit à sceleribus. De iis igitur scortatoribus, avaris, Idolatris, & blasphemis locutum se esse monet Paulus, qui titulo Christianorum ornari, & communione sacramentorum frui volunt tanquam membra corporis Christi: & interea sceleribus vastantibus conscientiam sese polluunt: quibus demonstrant sese omni fide carere, & flagiciosa hypocrisi simulare pietatem. Cum huiusmodi hominibus: qui tantum sunt dedecora Ecclesiae, nullum est habendum commercium, neque etiam cibus cum eis capiendus: sed veluti ἀλάστορες καὶ μιάσματα sunt fugiendi.

1. Primum ne nomen Dei malè audiat, si tàm impuri homines tolerentur in Ecclesia.

2. Secundò, ne scelerum exempla serpant latius, offendant piorum animos, & nobis ipsis sint scandalo.

3. Tertiò, ne ipsos peccatores in impietate & impaenitentia confirmemus, sed potius severa disciplina ad seriam paenitentiam invitemus. His gravissimis de causis iubet Paulus ut pii in Ecclesia à commertio sceleratorum qui pro fratribus haberi volunt abstincant.

Primum ergò hic discimus quòd pio liceat in mundo conversari etiam cum Idolatris & praedonibus, si ita postulet necessitas. Mundis enim omnia sunt munda. Pius maritus cui impia & Idolatrica contigit uxor, non propterea deserat coniugem, nec existimet se contaminari sceleribus coniugis. Sed potius statuat infidelem sanctificari per fidelem. Pius & fidelis minister qui servit domino avaro, impio et Idolatrae non existimet se contaminari eius sceleribus, nec deserat suam vocationem: Sed sciat sibi mundo omnia esse munda. Si quis pius emptione, venditione, locatione, conductione contrahit cum homine scelerato: non est quòd metuat se contaminari. Nihil enim ad eum pertinet qualis sit is, qui non est membrum Ecclesiae.

Quando autem in coetu Ecclesiae sunt homines qui externis sceleribus sese polluunt & scandalo sunt Ecclesiae, ab illorum consuetudine est abstinendum: nec tantum pastores & seniores sententia excommunicationis eos notare debent, sed etiam singuli auditores ab eorum consortio & consuetudine abstinere debent: ut nimirum intelligant sanctorum de se iudicia, & de agenda paenitentia seriò admoneantur. Sed dicat aliquis cur ergò Christus cibum sumpsit cum pharisaeis? An non licet pastori conversari cum peccatoribus? Respondeo. Christus ideò conversatus est cum pharisaeis, ut eos de crassis erroribus admoneret, & occasionem haberet eos iuvandi ad seriam paenitentiam et agnitionem veritatis. Sic quando pastor vel quivis Christianus, videt oblatam sibi esse occasionem admonendi peccatores de suis sceleribus vel erroribus, & res est extra scandalum infirmorum, omnino licet ei conversari, cibum capere, colloqui & contrahere cum hominibus palam impiis, nec est quòd metuat se ab illis iri contaminatum. Imo sperare debet quòd aliquos lucrari possit. Post duas autem veltres commonefactiones vitandi sunt cum haeretici, tum scelerati homines.

Et omninò videndum est, ne ad eorum errores vel scelera conniveamus: ne peccata illorum dissimulemus: ne silentio nostro illorum blasphemias adprobemus: ne potius nostri ventris causa, quàm lucrandi proximi gratia domos & mensas impiorum frequentemus: ne imbecilles Christi pravo nostro exemplo offendamus: ne impios in errore confirmemus, & ne in nobis studium pietatis malorum consortio frangatur. Non frustra dictum est: Qui tetigerit picem, inquinabitur ab ea. Et corrumpunt bonos mores colloquia prava. Et, qui iuxta claudum habitat, claudicare discit. Magna igitur diligentia vitanda est consuetudo impiorum: quando vero vel munus nostrum nobis iniunctum, velgloria Dei adserenda, vel salus proximi promovenda postulat ut cum impiis versemur, sciendum est quòd mundis omnia sint munda. Magna diligentia & severitate hanc disciplinam custodivit antiquitas, ut videre est in Historia Iosephi, qui seorsim ab Aegyptiis cibum capit, & in Evangelista Ioanne, ubi legimus fas non esse Iudaeis, conversari cum Samaritanis. Et Ecclesiae severam disciplinam monstrat Christus cum inquit: Sit tibi veluti Ethnicus & publicanus. Matth: 18. Ad hanc ergò severitatem respicit Paulus cum inquit: Auferte malum ex vobis ipsis. Hoc est, scandala tollite ex vestro coetu: excommunicate sceleratos, & fugite illorum commercium.

## 5:7 Places of Doctrine
Places of Doctrine.

1. That in the Church of Jesus Christ not only are there great infirmities, but also atrocious crimes are committed and most sad scandals are excited, as the Examples of Aaron, Gideon, the Benjaminites, David, Reuben, and the incestuous Corinthian teach.

2. An illustrious and most grave example of excommunication, which testifies that excommunication is a necessary part of the ministry: And how it is to be exercised against those who are openly flagitious and impenitent by the judgment of the Church.

3. An allegorical exposition of the Passover commanded in the Old Testament, and what God signified by the command concerning the eating of unleavened bread.

4. That Jesus Christ is the victim slaughtered for us: That He might expiate our sins and reconcile us to God.

5. The doctrine concerning good works.

6. That with those who wish to be held as brothers in the Church and to enjoy the communion of the sacraments: While meanwhile they pollute themselves with external crimes, the pious and those who truly fear the Lord ought not even to take food.

Latin:

Loci Doctrinae.

1. Quòd in Ecclesia Iesu Christi non tantum magnae sint infirmitates, sed etiam atrocia scelera committantur & tristissima scandala excitentur, ut Exempla Aaronis, Gedeonis, Beniamitarum, Davidis, Ruben, Corinthii incestuosi docent.

2. Illustre & gravissimum exemplum excommunicationis, quòd testatur excommunicationem esse necessariam partem ministerii: Et quomodo ea sit exercenda contra palàm flagiciosos & impaenitentes iudicio Ecclesiae.

3. Allegorica expositio Paschatos in veriteri testamento mandati, & quid Deus significarit mandato de edendo pane azymo.

4. Quòd Iesus Christus sit hostia mactata pro nobis: Ut nostra peccata expiaret & nos Deo reconciliaret.

5. Doctrina de bonis operibus.

6. Quòd cum iis qui fratres in Ecclesia haberi & communione sacramentorum frui volunt: Interea verò sese polluunt externis sceleribus, pii & verè timentes dominum ne cibum quidem capere debent.

## 6:1 Argument
CHAPTER VI.

Dare any of you, having a matter against another, go to law before the unjust, and not before the saints? Do you not know that the saints shall judge the world? And if the world shall be judged by you, are you unworthy to judge the smallest matters?

Do you not know that we shall judge angels? Why then not things that pertain to the present life? If therefore you have controversies concerning things pertaining to this life, you appoint those who are of no account in the Church as judges.

Paul proceeds in this chapter to the reproof of other vices which were flourishing in the Corinthian Church. Therefore, just as in the previous chapter he taxed lusts, so here he reproves the zeal for contention, and that they carry their lawsuits to unjust men outside the Church. And the Greek nation has a bad reputation in history for having been more studious of contentions than of truth. Paul corrects this foul vice here: and there are three notable members in this chapter.

The first is, as I have already said, a grave reproof that the Corinthians exercise lawsuits and contentions among themselves: And that they carry them to impious and unjust men outside the Church.

In the second place, he transfers the hypothesis to the thesis and intersperses a general exhortation, that they should studiously avoid crimes and flagrant sins of every kind: Since indeed the wicked shall not be participants of the inheritance of eternal life. In this place, however, he mixes in consolation concerning the washing and remission of sins and concerning sanctification: That this most serious cause may move them to avoid crimes and to a serious pursuit of good works.

Thirdly, he repeats the commandment concerning avoiding lusts: And that they should not, under the pretext of liberty, indulge in carnal affections.

Therefore, that the Apostle in the first place gravely censures contentions and lawsuits in the political court, it is not to be thought that he condemns the political order, judgments, the hearing of cases, or the referral of controversies to the political Magistrate: Which error of the Anabaptists is worthy of grave reprehension. Indeed, Paul approves the whole political order, Rom: 13. And he testifies that the Magistrate is a minister of God for wrath against those who perpetrate evil. He approves, therefore, of judges and judgments: And it is permitted for a Christian man to plead cases in court, to pronounce law for litigants, and even to refer civil controversies to the political Magistrate. The Lord sends away from himself to a judge the young man who was asking Christ to compel his brother to the division of inheritances with him: Who, he says, has appointed me a judge between you?

What, therefore, someone says, does Paul censure in the Corinthians if it is permitted for the pious to litigate in court?

I answer. First, Paul censures that they did not rather settle civil controversies among themselves peacefully and compose them, rather than refer them to the political Magistrate, who is a stranger to the Church: For it is shameful for Christians, who ought to be bound together among themselves by the bond of mutual love, to carry on lawsuits and contentions among themselves: For from this the nations take the occasion of blaspheming the name of God and the Church of Christ. Furthermore, it is foolish to refer the cognizance of your controversy to impious and unjust men, when you can have pious arbitrators among the brethren in the Church. For in the saints there is a great light of true wisdom: The fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom: And the saints are illuminated by the Holy Spirit: And they have before their eyes the word, which is a lamp to their feet: There is also in the saints a true and unfeigned zeal for justice, truth, and concord. But the impious outside the Church are agitated by various errors, so that they do not always see what is just: Hilary said most gravely in book 5, De Trinitate: Impiety truly has nothing of wisdom in itself, and the fear of God, which is the beginning of wisdom, where it is lacking, takes away with it every beginning of prudence: nor does a true zeal for justice and concord exist in them: But they are led by depraved affections, they burn with , and in all things they study their own gain and honor, and often take pleasure from the discord of men.

It is therefore a great ignorance to refer controversies to men outside the Church, when pious and holy arbitrators can be had in the Church. He calls the saints believers, who although they have manifold infirmities and sins, yet because they have been washed by the faith in the blood of Jesus Christ, the obedience of the Son of God is imputed to them, and they have been sanctified by the Holy Spirit, who kindles new, holy, and in a certain way law-conforming motions in them, are truly holy before God both by imputation and by inchoation. But he calls the impious outside the Church unjust: as those who are still submerged in sins, and who study injustice. Nor indeed are only the wicked like Harpalus, Demosthenes, Catilina, Verres, unjust, but even those who simulated a study of justice like Aristides, Conon, Solon, Fabricius, Camillus, Cicero, were truly unjust: for they sought their own emoluments rather than the glory of God and the utility of their neighbor. Nor is there any reason why we should seek true justice among those who are not ruled by the guidance of the Holy Spirit, since they are slaves of Satan and of impure affections. For this reason Paul names them despised in the Church, as if he were to say: Although outside the Church some Gentiles are raised to the very heavens with praises on account of their wisdom and justice, like Aristides, Socrates, Xenophon, Solon, Themistocles, Laelius, Cato: Yet the Church of God does not hold them in that place: Because they are destitute of the light of the divine word, and are not ruled by the guidance of the Holy Spirit.

Paul adds to his rebuke two most grave reasons, from a comparison of greater things. ( Saints they shall judge the world, he says How much more fit are they to settle controversies concerning earthly goods: the saints shall even judge the angels, the unclean Spirits: Why therefore should they not judge controversies concerning bodily goods. That the saints are to be judges of the world and of Satan with Christ, is evident from the saying of Christ. Matth: 19. You shall sit upon seats judging the twelve tribes of Israel. Item: That they may receive you into everlasting dwellings. Item: The son of man shall come with a multitude of angels and elect. The highest judge of the world indeed is Christ. But the saints shall stand by Christ and according to the word of God shall condemn impious men and impure Spirits.

Therefore there shall be a remarkable change of affairs. For in the world the saints are the most abject and most miserable of all men, who as the worst of men are condemned by the impious with a cruel sentence to punishments of every kind. But in the final judgment in turn the saints shall occupy seats, judgment, and with a most grave sentence shall condemn the world to eternal destruction. Decius with a cruel sentence condemned Lawrence to the fire: But in the final judgment Lawrence shall stand by the side of Christ the judge, and shall pass a sentence of eternal damnation upon Decius. With this remarkable consolation, therefore, let the pious strengthen themselves, especially when they are dragged to the tribunals of the powerful, and are condemned to death by dire sentences.

The second argument is that the saints are to judge Satan with all his angels: for they are kept for judgment: and Christ will deliver Satan under our feet. Therefore, much more will the saints be able to judge controversies concerning earthly matters and those pertaining to this life.

Secondly, the Apostle reproves the Corinthians because they are more eager for contention than is fitting for Christians. A Christian ought rather to suffer injury and to overlook and forgive it, than to litigate with ignominy and detriment to our religion in the forum, and indeed before a Magistrate or judge who is an adversary to our religion. Therefore, Paul does not prohibit or disapprove of civil offices, nor does he forbid altogether that we should bring cases before a legitimate Magistrate. For if it is lawful for you to reclaim your property legitimately, and a suitable judge is given to you, you ought not to defraud your own by your negligence or superstition. Nor should your excessive indulgence confirm the malice of men. But Paul commands that we should prudently consider when it is necessary to appeal to a political judge, and when it is not necessary; on account of trivial matters we ought not to cause trouble either for ourselves or for others. When the judge is an enemy of your religion, it is great folly to bring a lawsuit before him, so that you create a greater danger for yourself. Especially when the controversy is not with an Epicurean or a Gentile, but with a brother who professes the same Christ with you, religion must be spared, lest it be ill-spoken of on account of our contentions.

I say to your shame: Is there not among you a wise man? Not even one, who can judge between his brother and his brother? But brother litigates with brother, and this before the infidels. Therefore now indeed there is altogether a defect in you, that you have litigations among yourselves. Why do you not rather suffer injury? Why do you not rather receive damage? But you do injury and inflict damage, and that to brothers.

He sharply rebukes those litigating before a political magistrate, because they do not rather appoint arbitrators from the brothers of the same religion, so that the controversy may be settled privately, and without reproach to the Christian name. But above all, he severely censures the authors of injuries and controversies, and warns them to abstain from injuries, and not to inflict damage upon a neighbor, lest they fall from grace and be deprived of the inheritance of eternal life: For manifest injustice cannot stand with faith. Rather, he says, it was fitting for you to suffer injury, and to dissimulate it, and to leave vengeance to God to commit: For the Christian religion demands this. But you inflict injury upon others and cause damage to others. That fights against the 5th and 7th commandments. And this sin of yours is so much the more grave: Because you inflict injury upon brothers, whom you ought to have helped with every duty. For he who harms the least brother, harms Christ himself. Just as the Son of God testifies: Whatever you have done, whether good or evil, to one of these least ones, you have done to me. No man indeed is to be afflicted with injury, but he who harms a brother sins more gravely than he who is injurious to a Gentile or a Turk: Although this one also sins.

Latin:

CAPUT VI.

Audet aliquis vestrúm negocium habens cum altero, iudicium subire apud iniustos, Et non apud sanctos. An ignoratis quòd sancti mundum iudicabunt? Et si per nos iudicatur mundus, indigni ne estis qui de minimis iudicetis?

An nescitis quòd angelos iudicabimus? Cur ergò non quae ad praesentem vitam pertinent? Si ergò controversias habueritis de rebus ad vitam pertinentibus, eos qui nullius precii sunt in Ecclesia, constituitis iudices.

Progreditur Paulus in hoc capite ad repraehensionem aliorum viciorum quae in Corinthiaca Ecclesia vigebant. Ut ergò in proximo capite libidines taxavit, Ita hic repraehendit contentionis studium, & quòd lites suas deferant ad homines iniustos extra Ecclesiam. Ac Graeca natio malè audit in historia quòd contentionum quàm veritatis fuerit studiosior. Hoc verò tetrum vicium corrigit hic Paulus: suntque tria insignia membra in hoc capite.

Primum est ut iam dixi, gravis repraehensio quòd Corinthii inter sese exerceant lites & contentiones: Eaque ad homines impios & iniustos extra Ecclesiam deferant.

Secundo loco hypothesin transfert ad thesin & generalem interspergit adhortationem, ut omnis generis scelera & flagicia studiosè vitent: Siquidem scelerati haereditatis vitae aeternae non sunt futuri participes. Hoc verò loco miscet consolationem de ablutione & remissione peccatorum atque de sanctificatione: Ut haec causa gravissima permoveat eos ad vitanda scelera & ad serium studium bonorum operum.

Tertio repetit praeceptum de vitandis libidinibus: Et ne sub praetextu libertatis indulgeant carnalibus adfectibus.

Quod ergò Apostolus primo loco taxat graviter contentiones & lites in iudicio politico, non est putandum quòd damnet, ordinem politicum, iudicia, cognitionem causarum, delationem controversiarum ad Magistratum politicum: Qui Anabaptistarum error gravi reprehensione dignus est, Imò Paulus totum ordinem politicum comprobat, Rom: 13. Et testatur Magistratum esse ministrum Dei ad iram erga eos qui malum perpetrant. Probat ergò iudices & iudicia: Et licet Christiano homini causas agere in foro, ius dicere litigantibus, atque etiam controversias civiles ad politicum Magistratum deferre. Adolescentem qui petebat à Christo ut cogeret fratrem ad divisionem haereditatum cum ipso, ablegat dominus à se adiudicem: Quis me inquit, constituit iudicem inter vos?

Quid ergò inquit, aliquis reprehendit Paulus in Corinthiis si piis licet litigare in foro?

Respondeò.
