For Paul pronounces the innocent party to be free. However, the deserted person ought not to absolve himself by his own judgment and take upon himself the liberty of contracting another marriage. But let him seek absolution from the Ecclesiastical consistory, or from the ministry, or from the political magistrate. From this foundation of Paul it is clear that with a good conscience a second marriage can be granted to the innocent deserted party, by an Ecclesiastical or political Judge, if the deserter contumaciously resists the laws. Moreover, it befits the deserted and innocent party to await the time defined by the laws.

But God has called us in peace For what do you know, O wife, whether you will save your husband, or what do you know, O husband, whether you will save your wife.

He returns here to the preceding exhortation, that the faithful party should not dissolve the bond of marriage on account of religion: He says, God has called us in peace, as if he were saying: You, the faithful party, shall not give occasion to either husband or wife to depart out of impatience, nor shall you desert your spouse, but you ought to strive with the greatest care for concord, and avoid all occasions of dissension. By your modesty, piety, moderation, and every kind of duty, you ought to bind the soul of your spouse to yourself. For to this end God has called us, that we might live among ourselves as closely and as peacefully as possible. He adds an argument from the effect and utility of cohabitation. Perhaps, he says, the faithful will win over the unfaithful spouse: just as Peter also says. Let wives be obedient to their husbands, so that if any do not believe the word, they may be won over without a word by the conduct of their wives, while they see your chaste conduct in fear. Moreover, a spouse ought to desire nothing greater than that the partner of their life should also become a participant in eternal salvation. Although, therefore, many contentions are accustomed to arise from dissension in religion, nevertheless those are to be endured rather than the marriage dissolved, on account of this hope, that perhaps we shall win over the unfaithful partner of our life. This opinion of Paul is to be understood concerning those who are already in marriage and dissent concerning religion. The case is different when counsel is being taken about entering into marriage: for then the consideration of religion is to be held as the most important, nor is it to be agreed to in any way that such a partner of life should be joined to us in marriage who dissents from us in religion.

For this would be to tempt God; or not to care for religion. And God most severely forbade through Moses that the Israelites should join their sons in marriage to the daughters of the Canaanites, or of foreign nations, and He adds the reason. For they will seduce my sons, that they may commit fornication after strange gods. They will incline (He says) your hearts, that you may walk after their gods. And the most sorrowful examples of Solomon, Ahab, Joram, and the like teach how great a danger it is to take a spouse dissenting from us in religion. And dissension in religion between spouses is a tinder for perpetual quarrels, contentions, and discords. Therefore God is not to be tempted. But Paul speaks of those who are already in marriage, and are of a different religion, while one is illuminated by the Gospel: the other sticks in the darkness of errors, because of this dissension the marriage is not to be dissolved: but rather it is to be hoped and God is to be prayed to, that one may be able to win the other to Christ through pious conversation.

Latin:

& ipsa consenserit cum ipso habitare, ne dimittat eam: Et mulier, quae maritum habet infidelem, & ipsi placuerit habitare cum ipsa, ne dimittat eum. Nam vir infidelis sanctificatur per mulierem: Et uxor infidelis sanctificatur in viro, alioquin liberi vestri immundi essent: Nunc autem sunt sancti.

Primùm attendendum est, quanta verecundia & timore tantus Apost: in suo ministerio versetur. De quibus certa & expressahabet mandata à Christo, ea διαρρηδὴν praecipit, & magna severitate exigit. Domino enim sine omni tergiversatione obtemperandum est. Quae autem dominus expressis verbis non mandavit, illa in persona domini non vult proferre: Exponit tamen, quid ipse sentiat, ut fidelis Apostolus Iesu Christi. Ac saepè casus incidunt in Ecclesia, de quibus voluntas domini precisè & in specie determinata non est; pius tamen & fidelis pastor, qui tantum respicit Dei gloriam, aedificationem Ecclesiae, & hominum salutem, & consilia sua dirigit ad normam verbi divini, salutare potest dare consilium.

Cùm ergò quintò interrogassent Corinthii, num propter religionis diversitàtem liceret facere divortia, & haud dubiè dissensio in religione, & contentiones inter coniuges, & desertiones pepererit multas, ostendit Paulus, quae sua sit sententia. Nimirum propter dissensionem in religione non esse dimittendam, nec deserendam coniugem, modòipsa manere velit. Diversa enim religio non dissolvit foedus coniugii: quòd Deus vult esse perpetuum & insolubile. Observandum est igitur hoc praeceptum Apostoli, ne quis praetextu religionis vel expellat, vel deserat coniugem. Ac ne scrupulos relinquat in conscientia, docet fideles maritos vel uxores, consortio & cohabitatione infidelium vel uxorum vel maritorum non contaminari. Infidelis inquit vir, sanctificatur in uxore fideli. Non potest hoc loco sanctificatio accipi pro reconciliatione & renovatione per Spiritum sanctum: Infidelis enim non sanctificatur hoc sensu per fidelem. Iustus enim sua fide vivet. Et in die illa erunt duo in uno lecto, alter adsumetur, alter relinquetur. Necesse est igitur intelligi haec verba de legali seu civili sanctificatione: Infidelis uxor sanctificatur, id est, nihilominus legitimum est matrimonium, etiamsi alter coniugum sit infidelis: Licet fideli sine laesione conscientiae habitare cum infideli, nec est quòd metuat, nec contaminetur per infidelem. Mundis enim omnia sunt munda; Et per verbum & orationem fide libus omnes creaturae sanctificantur: Hoc est usus earum fit licitus & sanctus.

Probat hanc sententiam ab effectu, quia liberi illorum coniugum, qui in religione dissentiunt sint sancti. Si coniugium propter dissensionem in religione esset impurum: Etiam liberi essent immundi, id est, non legitimi. At liberi habentur pro sanctis seu legit timè natis: Ergò & coniugium talium est legitimum & sanctum. Manifestum est igitur quod Paulus hoc loco sanctum nominat, licitum, legitimum, purum, concessum, sicuti in legeres sanctae dicebantur lege concessae: Immundae autem & communes, quae lege erant prohibitae. Violenter depravat Calvinus haec Pauli verba; siquidem interpretatur de spirituali sanctificaticne, et abolitione male dictionis. Et contendit liberos fidelium esse sanctos ab utero, hoc est exemptos maledictioni: Quia peculiarem habeant praerogativam sanctorum liberi ex promissione, Ero Deus seminis tui. Verùm aliena est haec interpretatio à mente Pauli, nec est ἀνάλογα fidei. Universa enim sacra scriptura testatur, omnes tàm sanctorum quàm impiorum liberos nasci obnoxios peccato & maledictioni legis. Eramus omnes, inquit Paulus, naturae filii irae: Et Ioan: 3. Nisi quis renatus fuerit ex aqua & Spiritu, non intrabit in regnum Dei. Et Baptista dicit, nolite dicere patrem habemus Abraham: Potest enim Deus ex lapidibus his filios Abrahae excitare. Item non ex sanguinibus, neque ex voluntate carnis, neque ex voluntate viri sed ex Deo nati sunt. Et David natus ex sanctissimis parentibus, de se inquit. Ecce in iniquitatibus conceptus sum, & in peccatis concepit me mater mea. Non igitur hoc vult promissio: Ero Deus tuus & Deus seminis tui: Quòd sanctorum liberi ab utero sint sancti: Sed Ahrahae & toti eius posteritati promittit Deus omnia bona, sed ita ut fide sibi hanc promissionem adplicent. Nec Isaac quidem de hac promissione gloriari potuisset, si mansisset incircumcisus. Cogitandum est etiam duplex esse semen Abrahae, aliud carnale, aliud spirituale. Semen Abrahae spirituale sunt, qui per Spiritum sanctum renascuntur & imitantur vestigia fidei Abrahae. Hos praecipuè respicit promissio, et offert illis aeternae & praesentis vitae bona. Aliud est carnale semen, quod ex carne Abrahae ducit originem. ut Esau, Absalon, Annas, Caiphas, & Iudaeiomnes. Et his quidem Deus benefecit, & eos magnis ornavit beneficiis propter Abraham, sed propter carnis praerogativam, neminem annumeravit sanctis, quin à singulis postulavit fidem. Aliena igitur est Calvini interpretatio à Pauli loco.

Si autem infidelis separatur: Separetur: Non est in servitutem redactus in his vel frater vel soror.

De altero casu nunc erudit conscientias, si pars infidelis propter religionem nolit cohabitare fideli coniugi, discedat & dissolvat matrimonium: quid tum faciendum erit parti fideli & innocenti? Respondet Paulus, frater aut for or in hoc casu non est redacta in servitutem, quasi dicat: Non propterea abiiciat fidelis pars religionem: nec metuat suae conscientiae, quasi ea hoc casu captiva teneatur: libertas enim, in quam Christus nos vindicavit nullo casu eripi potest fideli. Pars ergò deserta extra culpam est, & siopus est coniugio propter conscientiam, licet innocenti & fideli parti aliud contrahere matrimonium. Paulus enim pronunciat innocentem partem esse liberam. Non autem iudicio proprio persona deserta sese absolvere & libertatem aliud matrimonium contrahendi sibi sumere debet. Sed absolutionem à consistorio Ecclesiastico, sive à ministerio, sive à politico magistratu petat. Ex hoc fundamento Pauli liquet bona conscientia parti innocenti desertae concedi posse coniugium alterum, à Iudice Ecclesiastico vel politico, si de sertor contumaciter repugnet legibus. Partem autem desertam & innocentem decet expectare tempus à legibus definitum.

In pace autem vocavit nos Deus Quid enim scis tu mulier, num virum, salvabis, aut quid scis tu vir, num uxorem salvabis.

Redit bîc ad praecedentem adhortationem, ne pars fidelis propter religionem dissolvat foedus coniugii: In pace inquit vocavit nos Deus, quasi ditat: Tu pars fidelis non dabis occasionem vel marito, vel uxori, ut ex impatientia discedat, neque tu deseres coniugem, sed summa cura concordiae studere debes, & omnes dissensionum occasiones vitare. Tua modestia, pietate, moderatione & omni genere officiorum coniugis animum tibi devincire debes. Adhoc enim vocavit nos Deus, ut quàm coniunctissimè & placidissimè inter nos viveremus. Addit argumentum ab effectu & utilitate cohabitationis. Fortassis inquit, fidelis infidelem coniugem lucrabitur: quemadmodum & Petrus inquit. Uxores obtemperent suis maritis, ut si qui non credunt verbo, per uxorum conversationem lucrifiant sine verbo, dum vident castam vestram conversationem in timore. Nihil autem maius optare debet coniux, quàm ut vitae socius aeternae etiam salutis fiat particeps. Etsi igitur multae contentiones oriri solent ex dissensione in religione, tamen ferendae sunt illae potius, quàm dissolvendum matrimonium, propter hanc spem, fortassis nos lucrifacturos sociam vitae infidelem. Haec Pauli sententia de iis, qui iam in coniugio sunt et de religione dissentiunt, intelligenda est. Alia ratio est cùm consilium tractatur de ineundo matrimonio: tum enim vel praecipua est habenda ratio religionis, nec ullo modo adsentiendum est, ut talis vitae socia nobis matrimonio iungatur, quae in religione à nobis dissentiat.

Hoc enim esset tentare Deum; vel non curare religionem. Ac Deus per Moisem severissimè vetuit, ne Israelitae filiis suis matrimonio iungerent filias Cananeorum, aut exterarum gentium, & causam adiicit. Illae enim seducent filios meos, ut scortentur post Deos alienos. Inclinabunt (inquit) corda vestra, ut ambuletis post Deos earum. Ac exempla tristissima Salomonis, Achab, Ioram, & similium docent, quanti sit periculi, ducere coniugem dissentientem à nobis in religione. Ac dissensio in religione inter coniuges fomes est perpetuarum litium, contentionum & dissidiorum. Non igitur tentandus est Deus. De iis autem loquitur Paulus, qui iam sunt in matrimonio, & diversae sunt religionis, dum alius illuminatur Evangelio: alius in tenebis errorum haeret, propter hanc dissensionem non est dissolvendum matrimonium: sed potius sperandum & Deus orandus, ut alter alterum Christo per piam conversationem possit lucrari.

## 7:17
But as God has distributed to everyone: and as the Lord has called everyone, so let him walk, and so I command in all the Churches:

He intersperses a general precept here, from which also to make a judgment concerning other similar controversies so that they may, it is certainly to be diligently considered in what kind, state, and condition of life the Lord has called us, and what gift God has bestowed upon each one. If anyone is by nature of such impeded speech that he can scarcely be understood, if this person aspires to offices either in the Church or in the Republic, which for the most part are to be administered by speech: or if anyone is of a very weak body, and aspires to the most burdensome labors of warfare, he will scarcely be considered of sound mind. Thus, if anyone wishes to abstain from marriage, and to vow chastity, when he perceives that he is destitute of the gift of chastity, and was born for marriage, he is insane. Therefore, individuals ought to consider with what gift they have been adorned by God, and they ought to use it rightly. This also must be seen, in what condition and state the Lord has called us. For it is necessary that that condition not be displeasing to the Lord, in which He has called us to the fellowship of eternal life through the Gospel. It is therefore permitted to us to remain in it with a good conscience, until the Lord, according to His kindness, shall have transferred us to another kind of life or condition: This is great and Apostolic wisdom. For very many men sin and err in this, that they think this or that kind of life, this or that condition, is an impediment to them, so that they are less able to cultivate piety. Many think thus, that if I were not married, then I would wish to embrace the Gospel: And to serve God promptly. Another thinks, that if I were not under paternal authority: or If I were not in this office, then I would wish to publish a confession. And hence it is that many frequently change their condition and for the most part for the worse: Many desert their calling, others marriage, others the commonwealth, others the ministry, others struggles: And they hope that they will live with a more tranquil conscience in a new kind of life: But they are shamefully mistaken: in that station in which the Son of God has placed us, one must serve faithfully and fight bravely. Nor must one be concerned in whatever state we may be: If only we cultivate true piety, whether you are a master, or a minister, or a celibate, or a husband, or learned, or an unlearned person, or a citizen, or a rustic, or a soldier, or a farmer, or a king, or a consul, or a subject, or whether you are free, or a slave, no thing can hinder you in religion. For if anyone tries to force you to impiety or crimes, you can publish a confession and suffer. And the kingdom of God does not consist in external conditions or things which serve this life, but in truth, Spirit, faith, piety, and patience. It is worthy of observation that he says he commands in the same way in individual Churches. For he warns that he does not accommodate or bend his doctrine to the various desires or customs of men, but everywhere repeats the same doctrine, proposes the same law to all, offers the same consolation to all, and gives one counsel to all.

Latin:

Coeterum quemadmodum unicuique partitus est Deus: & quemadmodum unumquemque vocavit dominus, sic ambulet, & sic praecipio in omnibus Ecclesiis:

Generale hîc interspargit praeceptum, ex quo & de aliis similibus controversiis iudicium facere possint, nimirum diligenter considerandum esse, in quo genere, statu & conditione vitae dominus nos vocaverit, & quale donum Deus unicuique impertitus sit. Si quis natura adeò sit impeditae linguae, ut vix possit intelligi, hic si adfectat officia vel in Ecclesia vel in Republ: quae ut plurimum oratione sunt ad ministranda: vel si quis admodum imbecilli sit corpore, & adfectet gravissimos militiae labores, is vix sanae mentis habebitur. Ita si quis velit abstinere à coniugio, & vovere castitatem, cùm sentiat se destitui dono castitatis, & natum esse ad coniugium, in sanus est. Singuli igitur considerare debent, quo dono à Deo sint ornati, eoque rectè uti debent. Etiam hoc videndum est, in qua conditione & statu nos vocaverit dominus. Necesse est enim illam conditionem non displicere domino, in qua nos ad aeternae vitae consortium per Evangelium vocavit. Licet ergò nobis in ea manere bona conscientia, donec dominus pro sua benignitate nos ad aliud vitae genus, vel conditionem transtulerit: Magna haec & Apostolica est sapientia. Plurimi enim homines in eo peccant & errant, quòd existimant hoc velillud vitae genus, hanc vel illam conditionem impedimento sibi esse, quò minus pietatem colere possint. Multi sic cogitant quòd si non essem maritus, tum vellem amplecti Evangelion: Et promptè servire Deo. Alius cogitat, quòd si non essem sub patria potestate: aut si non essem in hac functione, tùm vellem edere confessionem. Atque hinc est, quòd multi subindè mutant conditionem & plerumque indeterius: Multi deserunt suam vocationem, alii coniugium, alii rem publicam, alii ministerium, alii certamina: Et sperant se tranquilliore conscientia victuros in novo genere vitae: Sed hallucinantur turpiter: in ea statione, in quam filius Dei nos collocavit, fideliter serviendum & fortiter pugnandum est. Nec curandum est in quocunque simus statu: Si modò veram pietatem colamus, sive sis herus, sive minister, sive caelebs, sive maritus, sive doctus, sive Idiota, sive civis, sive rusticus, sive miles, sive agricola, sive rex, sive consul, sive subditus sis, sive liber, sive servus sis, nulla res teimpedire potest in religione. Si enim quis te ad impietatem vel scelera cogere conatur, confessionem edere & patipotes. Et regnum Dei non consistit in externis conditionibus vel rebus, quae huic vitae serviunt, sed in veritate, Spiritu, fide, pietate & patientia. Dignum est observatione, quòd dicit se eodem modo in singulis praecipere Ecclesiis. Monet enim se non accommodare vel inflectere suam doctrinam ad varias hominum vel cupiditates vel mores, sed ubique eandem repetere doctrinam, omnibus eandem proponere legem, omnibus eandim offerre consolationem, omnibus unum dare consilium.

## 7:18-19
Was any man called being circumcised? Let him not seek to remove the foreskin. Was any man called in uncircumcision? Let him not be circumcised. Circumcision is nothing, and uncircumcision is nothing, but the keeping of the commandments of God.

He applies the general precept to other cases, namely that one should not be concerned whether one was called in uncircumcision or in circumcision. If any man, he says, is called being circumcised, let him not seek to remove the foreskin: Let him not think that he will be nearer to the kingdom of Christ, or more fit to receive the benefits of Christ, if he were a Gentile: Let him remain a Jew, let him not put on Gentile customs. Again, let not a Gentile think that he will be more prepared for the kingdom of Christ if he were circumcised, but let him remain in his condition and state, and let him pursue serious piety.

For neither is circumcision anything, nor uncircumcision: That is, they neither promote men to the kingdom of God, nor do they hinder them. The kingdom of God does not consist in those external rites. But the keeping of the commandments of God. I understand here the whole doctrine of the Apostles, not only νομικῶς concerning the ten commandments. For the commandments of God are, first, be converted to me and I will be converted to you: And this is my beloved son, hear him. By these divine commandments, if anyone obeys, he is fit for the kingdom of Christ and is a partaker by faith of all his benefits. Therefore, those external things are not to be cared for much, but effort must be given so that we may obey the divine will.

Latin:

Circumcisus quis vocatus est, ne accersat praeputium: In praeputio quis vocatus est, ne circumcidatur: Circumcisio est nihil: Et praeputium est nihil: Sed observatio mandatorum Dei.

Praeceptum generale accommodat ad alios casus, videlicet non esse curandum, sive quis in praeputio, sive in circumcisione vocatus sit. Si quis inquit, circumcisus est vocatus, non accersat praeputium: Non existimet se viciniorem fore regno Christi, aut magis idoneum esse ad beneficia Christi percipienda, si esset gentilis: Maneat Iudaeus, non induat gentiles mores. Rursus gentilis non existimet se magis expeditum fore ad regnum Christi, si esset circumcisus, sed maneat in sua conditione & statu, & seriam pietatem sectetur.

Nam nec circumcisio, nec praeputium quidquam sunt: Id est, nec promovent homines ad regnum Dei, nec eos impediunt. In externis illis ritibus non consistit regnum Dei. Sed observatio mandatorum Dei. Totam Apostolorum doctrinam hîc intelligo, non tantum νομικῶς de decem praeceptis. Mandata enim Dei sunt, primùm convertimini ad me & ego convertar ad vos: Et hic est filius meus dilectus, hunc audite. His mandatis divinis, siquis pareat, is idoneus est ad regnum Christi & particeps est fide omnium beneficiorum eius. Non igitur externa illa multùm curanda sunt, sed opera danda est, ut voluntati divinae pareamus.

## 7:20-25
Let each one remain in that calling in which he was called.

He repeats the general precept placed above: That the condition of life is not to be changed, namely on account of religion: As if you could pursue piety more conveniently in that kind of life than in this present one. Levity, impatience, and greed often impel men to change their kind of life, and many pretend religion for their own affections: But the Apostle answers that the condition or state of life is not to be changed: For it is all the same, provided you seriously do penance and believe the Gospel. The Apostle calls a calling not some impure kind of life, or one openly impious: As fornicators live an impure life: Usurers pursuing base gains, Nuns, Monks lead a wicked and impious kind of life. Men ought to lay aside these crimes and impiety, but the Apostle names an honest kind of life granted by God a Calling: Because God has called [them] by his word to this kind of life: In the sweat of your face you shall eat your bread. One is the calling of the celibate, another of the married: Another is one of a king, another of a subject: one of a servant, another of a Lord: one of a schoolmaster, another of a minister of the Gospel: one of a teacher, another of a hearer. Therefore, in whatever calling or state we are called by the Lord, in it we ought to remain, and faithfully serve, nor desert or change it under the pretext of religion. Here it is accustomed to be disputed, whether it is permitted for us to change our calling and to migrate from place to place, and also to institute another kind of life. Many exercising mechanical arts, bearing poverty and unhappy successes impatiently, desert their calling and subsequently change their condition of life, but for the most part for the worse. Many out of impatience desert their seats, but while they flee the frost, they are overwhelmed by snow. Therefore, the Holy Scripture in many places, in the proverbs of Solomon, in Psalm: 37: in Ecclesiastes and elsewhere gives us counsel, and exhorts, that we each remain in that calling and station, patiently tolerate miseries, dangers and difficulties, and commit every outcome to God, hope in the Lord and do good and inhabit the land, and seek a living honestly. Item, Decline from evil and do good and inhabit for ever and ever. Therefore, the affection of impatience is to be repressed, and the condition or seat is not to be rashly changed. But if indeed some grave necessity is imposed upon you, as if for the labor of the ministry the hearers are unwilling to pay as much as they could easily, so that you might honestly sustain your family, if with convenient health, in You cannot use this passage if some people try to burden your conscience, and especially if the listeners wish to hear you, or have persecuted you. Then indeed it is permitted to change both your seat and your condition. Christ says, if they have persecuted you in one city, flee to another. Or if God himself has called you elsewhere, and has offered that opportunity so that you may be able to change your place with great fruit for the Church, and you perceive that it is the merciful will of God that you transfer yourself elsewhere, then you act piously if you follow God who is calling, but beware, lest you follow your own desires, lest you look to your own profit or honor: But the glory of God and the salvation of the Church, and be a stumbling block to no one: Do nothing against piety, do nothing against justice.

Ambrose was a soldier, and he led an army: which calling is far removed from the calling of ministers. But when he is elected Bishop by the Church of Milan, and from the admirable consent of the whole people perceives the will of God, he obeys and from a soldier becomes a Bishop. Ambrose did not act against the precept of Paul. For the Apostle forbids this, that we should change our calling under the pretext of religion and out of impatience: It is another thing when God himself calls us to a new kind of life.

Were you called being a slave do not care: but if you can become free, rather make use of it.

For he who is called in the Lord, being a servant, is the Lord's freeman. Likewise also he that is called, being free, is Christ's servant. You are bought with a price; be not the servants of men. Brethren, let every man, wherein he is called, therein abide with God.

The general rule handed down above and repeated here, he now adapts to the condition of servants. Without a doubt the Corinthians disputed whether it was necessary for servants who wished to become Christians to be manumitted: whether servitude would hinder faith in Christ. Therefore the Apostle instructs consciences also concerning this matter, and teaches that servitude does not hinder religion and faith in Christ: a servant can remain in his servitude, and nonetheless believe in Christ with his whole heart and cultivate piety. A master can also retain a servant in servitude, and nonetheless believe in Christ, and promise true religion to the servant. For servitude is an external and civil matter, doing nothing for religion, which offers us spiritual liberty.

And thus again Paul distinguishes here between the spiritual kingdom of Christ, and external matters or civil conditions. He also approves by his testimony the law of nations concerning slaves and chattels, and other political matters. Furthermore, he advises that if we can obtain freedom for ourselves, we should strive for it, and enjoy freedom rather than allow ourselves to be oppressed by perpetual servitude. It is therefore permitted to change one's condition of life for the better, if a noble opportunity is offered to us by God, and if that can be done without detriment to the Church or anyone else, and without a wound to the conscience. Paul also advises that if any happiness or convenience is offered to us by God, it should neither be morosely rejected nor lazily neglected, but accepted and used with thanksgiving. If God bestows work and dignities upon you, do not madly cast them away, but enjoy the blessing of the Lord: If the Lord bestows good health upon you, do not madly afflict it with immoderate fasts and vigils, but use the gift of God for His glory. If you can acquire freedom, strive for it: For there are already enough miseries and hardships in the world: there is no reason why we should increase troubles for ourselves. It is sufficient, says Christ, for the day its own affliction. And Solomon: Eccles: 7. In a happy time, be of a joyful mind. Therefore, the monks were foolish, who without cause heaped troubles upon themselves, and often tempted God.

He who is called in the Lord as a slave, is the Lord's freedman. Here he teaches spiritual freedom which Christ acquired for us, is in no way hindered by civil servitude. If therefore it is not permitted to hope for liberty, nothing is to be cared for: since indeed spiritual liberty is established for us: he is a freedman of the Lord, who is freed from the tyranny of sin, death, Satan, and hell, is gifted with the Holy Spirit, and is free from Mosaic laws and human traditions, and possesses liberty in Jesus Christ of approaching God and hoping for eternal life.

Likewise, he who is called free, is a servant of Christ. Here he warns that men who are free in Christianity are in no better condition, nor do they have a prerogative over servants. But they are bound to serve Christ just as servants are. A civilly free man is a servant of Christ, if he approaches the Church. This is, he ought to turn all his counsels, efforts, labors, wealth, and whatever he has received from God, toward illustrating the glory of Christ and building up the Church, and let him not think that he has more license than any base servant.

You have been bought with a price, do not become servants of men. From the dignity of the efficient and meritorious cause of our liberty, he exhorts us that we should guard the liberty which we possess in Christ. You have been bought, he says, with a great price: not with gold nor with silver, says Peter, but with the precious blood of the only-begotten Son of God. It is right, therefore, that we should studiously guard a good bought at such a price. And he teaches that it is not to be permitted that we should give ourselves into slavery to men, or so bind ourselves to them that we must live at their beck and call. For the desires of men are various: And there is great inconstancy of wills; one must therefore take care, lest with a wound to the conscience we be compelled to serve the will of men. But he who dedicates his labor either to a certain master or to a certain Church, he does not become a slave of men, but is a minister of God: And the sweetest and most noble liberty of all is to serve Jesus Christ. When he commands that one should remain in the calling with God: He warns that the eyes must always be cast upon God: And that His will must be regarded, lest we attempt anything against it.

Concerning virgins however I have no commandment of the Lord, but I give counsel, as one who has obtained mercy from the Lord to be faithful. I think therefore that this is good because of the present necessity, that it is good for a man so to remain. Are you bound to a wife, do not seek a release, are you loosed from a wife, do not seek a wife.

To the other questions of the Corinthians, what concerning virgins is to be determined, whether daughters are to be given in marriage, or whether they are truly to be supported perpetually at home outside of wedlock; Paul now responds. And first he modestly distinguishes between a counsel, which he imparts in good faith, and a command of the Lord. For the command of the Lord must be obeyed with a ready mind, without any evasion or deliberation: but we are not bound to the counsel of men, but it is placed in our own judgment whether we wish to follow it or to enter upon another course. The Papists wickedly abuse this distinction: for they pretend that divine commands differ among themselves in such a way that some are precepts for all, while others are counsels given to those aspiring to perfection. Then they pretend that those commands, if anyone says to his brother racha, he is liable to judgment: Item, Do not swear at all: Item, if anyone looks at a woman to lust after her: Item, if anyone strikes you on the right cheek, turn the other to him, are not commands for individuals, but only proposed as counsels for the more perfect. This error utterly obscures the spiritual judgment of the law, which requires from individuals an internal and spiritual and in all respects absolute obedience. Far different is the mind of Paul, who says of the individual commands of the Lord that the law is spiritual.

But concerning those things which are not defined by the command of the Lord, but are left to our own judgment, he says that he will faithfully communicate his counsel, as because to the Lord he has obtained this grace, that he may build up the Church in good faith. In what place of the earth we wish to live, what arts, whether liberal or mechanical, we wish to practice, what kind of food or clothing to use: Whether we wish to live in celibacy or marriage: God has permitted this to our own judgment, and in these matters it is lawful for us to choose and determine what has pleased us and has seemed to be to our advantage. If these things had to be defined by commandments, it would have been necessary for God to address individual men. You, cobbler, you, tailor, you, preacher, you, schoolmaster. But God is content with a general precept. You shall love the Lord your God and your neighbor as yourself: And in the sweat of your face you shall eat your bread: And honor your father and your mother, that you may be long-lived upon the earth. Those things which are subject to reason He permits to our judgment and that of our parents. Therefore, it is not to be demanded that God should reveal His will to us from heaven in individual deliberations, but we shall pray to God that He may show right counsels and offer excellent opportunities: Then parents and pious men are to be brought into counsel. And your conscience ought to determine that your work pleases God, which you have undertaken in the fear of the Lord. Thus in this passage Paul says that he does not have a commandment, and therefore that no one is bound to obey: but that he is imparting a counsel, which he himself feels to be most convenient. I think, he says, that it is good for a man so to remain: This is: More convenient. I think it is, if virgins remain unmarried and abstain from marriage, and he adds the reason for this counsel of his, on account of the present necessity. Paul considers to what various dangers the pious are exposed: That dangers, prisons, losses of property, and dire punishments are imminent for them. For undergoing these miseries, the unmarried are more unencumbered than the married. He also sees many in exiles and hardships broken by the love of spouses and children and failing from the truth: That therefore they might have fewer temptations, he counsels that he who is outside of marriage, and without a wound of conscience, can lack marriage, let him not contract matrimony. And it was burdensome for pious parents to give away daughters among the nations, where few were approaching the true religion.

Paul does not say that celibacy is a holier way of life than marriage: By no means: But he says that the unmarried have fewer troubles and afflictions in the flesh. Therefore, with respect to the most difficult time of the Church, he imparts this counsel.

But lest anyone seek a release from a spouse under this pretext, he forbids that anyone tear himself away from a spouse, to whom he is bound by an indissoluble covenant. He who is in matrimony, let him remain in it. For marriage does not hinder religion, but is a school of the Holy Spirit. But if anyone is released from a spouse, let him not seek a wife. Let him enjoy that liberty and convenience which comes to him. But so great is the weakness and

the inconstancy of the human will, so that everyone repents of their own lot. Those to whom God has given a companion in life would desire to be freed from the bond of matrimony. Those who are outside of marriage think themselves more unhappy than others. Paul censures this fickleness and advises that one's present state should be considered good, and that the offered opportunity and convenience should be used excellently: and that we should not commit ourselves to increasing our miseries by indulging our desires.

Latin:

Unusquisque in ea vocatione, in qua vocatus est, maneat.

Repetit superius positum generale praeceptum: Non esse mutandam vitae conditionem, scilicet propter religionem: Quasi in illo vitae genere commodius sectari possis pietatem, quàm in hoc praesenti. Levitas, impatientia, & cupiditas saepè impellit homines, ut genus vitae mutent, & multi praetendunt suis adfectibus religionem: Verùm Apostolus respondet, non esse mutandam conditionem vel statum vitae: Perinde est enim, modò seriò agas poenitentiam & credas Evangelio. Vocationem vocat Apostolus non aliquod impurum vitae genus, aut palàm impium: Ut scortatores impuram vitam vivunt: Usurarii turpia lucra sectantes, Moniales, Monachi genus vitae ducunt improbum & impium. Haec scelera & impietatem deponere debent homines, sed honestum & a Deo concessum vitae genus, nominat Apostolus Vocationem: Quòd Deus verbo suo ad hoc vitae genus vocaverit: In sudore vultus tui vesceris pane tuo. Alia est vocatio coelibis, alia mariti: Alia regis, alia subditi: Alia servi, alia Domini: Alia Ludimoderatoris, alia ministri Evangelii: Alia doctoris, alia auditoris. In quacunque ergò vocationè vel statu à domino vocamur: In ea permanere debemus, et fideliter servire, nec eam praetextu religinis deserere vel mutare. Hîc disputari solet, an liceat nobis mutare vocationem & de loco in locum migrare, atque etiam aliud genus vitae instituere. Multi mechanicas artes exercentes, paupertatem & infelices successus impatienter ferentes, deserunt suam vocationem & subinde mutant vitae conditionem, sed plerumque in deteriorem. Multi ex impatienia deserunt suas sedes, sed dum fugiunt pruinam, nive obruuntur. Sacra ergò scriptura in multis locis, in proverbiis Salomonis, in Psalm: 37: in Ecclesiaste & alibi consilium dat nobis, & hortatur, ut singuli in ea vocatione et statione maneamus, aerumnas, pericula & difficultates patienter toleremus, & eventum omnem Deo committamus, spera in domino & fac bonitatem & inhabita terram, & victum quaere honestè. Item, Declina à malo et fac bonum et inhabita in seculum seculi. Reprimendus igitur est adfectus impatientiae, & non temerè mutanda conditio aut sedes. Quòd si verò gravis aliqua necessitas tibi imponatur, ut si pro labore ministerii tantum solvere nolint auditores cum possent facilè, ut tuam familiam honestè sustentare possis, si commoda valetudine, in isto loco uti non potes, si conantur aliqui tuam gravare conscientiam, & inprimis, si auditores te audire voluerint, aut te persecuti fuerint. Tùm sanè licet & sedem & conditionem mutare. Christus inquit, site persecuti fuerint in unacivitate, fugite in aliam. Aut si ipse Deus te aliò vocaverit, et eam obtulerit occasionem, ut cum magno fructu Ecclesiae locum mutare possis, & perspicias Dei esse clementem voluntatem, ut te alio transferas, tùm piè facis, si vocantem Deum sequaris, sed cave, ne tuas sequaris cupiditates, ne tuum spectes lucrum vel honorem: Sed gloriam Dei & salutem Ecclesiae, & neminisis offendiculo: Nihil contra pietatem, nihil contra iustitiam facias.

Ambrosius miles fuit, & duxit exercitum: quae vocatio longè distat à vocatione ministrorum. Cùm vero ab Ecclesia Mediolanensi in Episcopum eligitur, & ex admirabili consensu totius plebis perspicit Dei voluntatem, paret & ex milite fit Episcopus. Non fecit Ambrosius contra praeceptum Pauli. Apostolus enim hoc vetat, ne praetextu religionis & ex impatientia mutemus vocationem: Aliud est cùm ipse Deus nos vocat ad vitae genus novum.

Servus vocatus es ne cures: Si tamen liber fieri potes, magis utere.

Qui enim in domino vocatus est servus, libertus domini est. Similiter & liber vocatus, servus est Christi. Precio redempti estis, ne fiatis servi hominum. Unusquisquè in quo statu vocatus est, fratres, in ea maneat apud Deum.

Regulam generalem superiùs traditam & hîc repetitam, nunc accommodat ad conditionem servorum. Haud dubiè disputarunt Corinthii, an necesse esset servos, qui fieri velint Christiani, manumitti: Nùm servitus impediret fidem in Christum. Erudit igitur Apostolus etiam hac de re conscientias, & docet servitutem non impedire religionem & fidem in Christum: servus in sua servitute manere potest, & nihilominus toto pectore credere in Christum & colere pietatem. Dominus etiam servum in servitute retinere potest, & nihilominus in Christum credere, & servo veram religionem promittere. Externa enim & civilis res est servitus, nihil ad religionem faciens, quae nobis offert spiritualem libertatem.

Atque. ita rursus distinguit hîc Paulus inter Spirituale regnum Christi, & externas res seu civiles conditiones. Approbat etiam suo testimonio ius gentium de servis & mancipiis, & aliis rebus politicis. Caeterum monet, si libertatem nobis comparare possimus, ut annitamur, & libertate potius fruamur, quàm perpetua servitute premi nos sinamus. Licet ergo vitae conditionem in melius mutare, si divinitus nobis offeratur praeclara occasio, idque sine Ecclesiae aut ullius detrimento, & sine vulnere conscientiae fieri potest. Monet etiam Paulus, si qua felicitas vel commoditas divinitus nobis offeratur, eam nec morosè repudiandam, nec oscitanter negligendam esse, sed cum gratiarum actione acceptandam & usurpandam. Si opus & dignitates largitur tibi Deus, non furenter eas abiicias, sed fruere benedictione domini: Si bonam valetudinem tibi largitur dominus, non furenter eam adfligas immodicis ieiuniis & vigiliis, sed utere dono Dei ad gloriam ipsius. Si libertatem acquirere potes annitere: Satis enim aliàs miseriarum & aerumnarum est in mundo: non est, quòd ipsi nobis augeamus molestias. Sufficit, inquit Christus, diei adflictio sua. Et Salo: Eccles: 7. Tempore felici, sis animo laeto. Stolidi igitur fuerunt monachi, qui sine causa molestias sibi ipsi cumularunt, & saepè Deum tentarunt.

Qui in domino vocatus est servus, libertus est domini. Hîc docet spiritualem libertatem quam Christus nobis acquisivit, nihil impediri servitute civili. Si igitur non licet sperare libertatem, nihil est curandum: siquidem Spiritualis libertas nobis constat: libertus domini est, qui est liberatus ex tyrannide peccati, mortis, Satanae & inferni, est donatus Spiritu sancto, & est liber à legibus Mosaicis, & traditionibus humanis, & libertatem possidet in Iesu Christo adeundi Deum & sperandi vitam aeternam.

Similiter, qui liber vocatus est, servus est Christi. Hîc monet homines liberos in Christianismo non esse meliore conditione, nec habere praerogativam prae servis. Sed perindè ad serviendum Christo devinctos esse atque sunt servi. Civiliter liber servus est Christi, siaccedat ad Ecclesiam. Hoc est, omnia sua consilia, conatus, labores, opes & quidquid à Deo accepit, ad Christi gloriam illustrandam & aedificandam Ecclesiam convertere debet, non existimet se plus habere licentiae, quàm servus quispiam vilis.

Precio redempti estis, nolite fieri servi hominum. A dignitate causae efficientis & meritoriae nostrae libertatis, nos hortatur, ut libertatem, quam in Christo possidemus, tueamur. Magno inquit precio redempti estis: non auro neque argento, inquit Petrus, sed precioso sanguine unigeniti filii Dei. Aequum est igitur, ut bonum tanto emptum precio studiosè tueamur. Ac docet non esse committendum, ut nos hominibus in sernitutem dedamus, aut illis nos ita obligemus, ut ad illorum nutum nobis sit vivendum. Variae enim sunt hominum cupiditates: Et magna inconstantia voluntatum; Cavendum igitur, ne cum vulnere conscientiae cogamur servire hominum voluntati. Qui autem vel certo domino vel certae Ecclesiae operam suam addicit, is non fit servus hominum, sed est minister Dei: Et omnium suavissima & nobilissima libertas est servire Iesu Christo. Cum, iubet manendum in vocatione apud Deum: Monet semper oculos in Deum coniiciendos esse: Et eius voluntatem respiciendam, ne quid contra eam tentemus.

De virginibus autem mandatum domini non habeo, consilium autem do, ut qui misericordiam consecutus sum a domino, ut fidelis sum. Existimo igitur hoc bonum esse propter instantem necessitatem, quòd bonum sit homini sic manere. Alligatus es conugi, ne quaeras solutionem, solutus es a coniuge, ne quaeras coniugem.

Adalias quaestiones Corinthiorum, quid de virginibus sit statuendum, num elocandae sint filiae, an verò perpetuò alendae domi extra coniugium; Respondet nunc Paulus. Ac primùm modestè distinguit inter consilium, quod bona fide impertiat, & inter mandatum domini. Nam domini mandato, sine omni tergiversatione & deliberatione, prompto animo est obtemperandum: Ad consilium verò hominum non sumus adstricti, sed in nostro arbitrio est positum, num illud sequi, vel aliam rationem inire velimus. Pontificii flagiciosè abutuntur hac distinctione: fingunt enim divina mandata ita inter se differre, ut alia sint praecepta omnibus, alia sint consilia data perfectionem adfectantibus. Deinde fingunt illa mandata, si quis dixerit fratri racha, reus est iudicii: Item, Ne omninò iuretis: Item, si quis aspexerit mulierem ad concupiscendam eam: Item, si quis te percusserit in dexteram maxillam, obverte illi & alteram, non esse mandata singulis, sed tantum ut consilia proposita perfectioribus. Hic error prorsus obscurat spirituale legis iudicium, quod a singulis requirit internam & spiritualem & omnibus numeris absolutam obedientiam. Longè alia est mens Pauli, qui de singulis mandatis domini dicit lex spiritualis est.

De iis autem, quae mandato domini definita non sunt, sed nostro arbitrio sunt relicta, dicit se fidele communicaturum consilium, ut quia domino hanc gratiam est nactus, ut bona fide aedificet Ecclesiam. Quo terrarum loco velimus vivere, quas artes, vel liberales vel mechanicas velimus exercere, quo genere ciborum, aut vestimentorum uti: Num in caelibatu vel coniugio vivere velimus: Nostro arbitrio permisit Deus, & in his nobis licet eligere & statuere, quod placuerit & ex re nostra visum fuerit. Haec si mandatis fuissent definienda, oportuisset Deum singulos alloqui homines. Tu sutor, tu sarctor, tu concionator, tu Ludimoderatoreris. Verùm Deus contentus est generali praecepto. Diliges dominum Deum tuum & proximum, sicut teipsum: Et in sudore vultus tai vesceris pane tuo: Et honora patrem & matrem tuam, ut sis longaevus super terram. Quae rationi subiecta sunt nostro & nostrorum parentum permittit arbitrio. Non igitur postulandum est, ut Deus in singulis deliberationibus de coelo nobis patefaciat suam voluntatem, Sed Deum or abimus, ut monstret recta consilia, & offerat praeclaras occasiones: Deinde parentes & pii homines in consilium sunt adhibendi. Et conscientia tua statuere debet opus tuum placere Deo, quod in timore domini suscepisti. Ita hoc loco Paulus dicit se non habere mandatum, idcircò neminem adstrictum esse ad obediendum: consilium autem se impertiri, quod ipse sentiat esse commodissimum. Existimo inquit, quod bonum sit homini sic manere: Hoc est: Commodius esse puto, si virgines innuptae maneant & abstineant à coniugio, & addit causam huius sui consilii propter instantem necessitatem. Considerat Paulus quàm variis periculis expositi sint pii: Quòd immineant illis pericula, carceres, amissiones facultatum, dira supplicia. Ad has miserias subeundas, expeditiores sunt coelibes, quàm coniugati. Videt etiam multos in exiliis & aerumnis, amore coniugium et liberorum frangi et deficere à veritate: Ut igitur minus haberent tentationum, consulit, ut qui extra coniugum est, et sine vulnere conscientiae, coniugio carere potest, non contrahat matrimonium. Et piis parentibus grave erat elocare filias, inter gentes, ubi pauci ad veram religionem accedebant.

Non dicit Paulus coelibatum esse sanctius vitaegenus, quàm coniugium: Nequaquam: Sed coelibes dicit minus habere molestiarum & adflictionum incarne. Respectu igitur difficilimi temporis Ecclesiae, hoc impertit consilium.

Ne quis autem hoc praetextu quaerat solutionem à coniuge, vetat ne quis avellat se à coniuge, cui foedere indissolubile est vinctus. Qui in matrimonio est, in eo permaneat. Coniugium enim non impedit religionem, sed schola est Spiritus sancti. Si quis autem solutus est à coniuge, non quaerat uxorem. Fruatur illa libertate & commoditate, quae illi obvenit. Verùm tanta est imbecillitas &

inconstantia voluntatis humanae, ut unumquemquè sortis suae paeniteat. Quibus dedit Deus vita sociam, cuperent se vinculo matrimonii liberatos esse. Qui sunt extra coniugium, eo putant se infeliciores caeteris esse. Hanc levitatem taxat Paulus & monet praesentem statum boni consulendum, et oblata occasione & commoditate praeclarè utendum esse: et non committendum ut cupiditatibus nostris indulgentes miserias nostras adaugeamus.

## 7:28
If indeed you have taken a wife, you have not sinned: And if a virgin has married, she has not sinned: but such as these will have affliction in the flesh. But I spare you.

He indeed imparts counsel, but he compels no one to follow it: and he does not even wish for the conscience to be bound by this counsel. For he leaves it to the judgment of each person to decide what will be most convenient for himself. For everyone feels most of all by what necessity he is pressed, and what he can bear. But if, he says, you have taken a wife, or a virgin has married a husband, he will not cast this scruple into the conscience: For it is lawful for all to contract marriage. But they are going to have afflictions of the flesh: exiles with a spouse and children are to be feared, and various kinds of persecutions on account of religion. And in this matter I wish to spare you, so that you might have as few temptations as possible.

But if it so pleases your mind to enter into matrimony and to endure the afflictions of the flesh, you have not sinned: for the matter is placed in your own judgment. And you will have to pray so much the more ardently that God may mitigate the miseries and the affliction, and may grant patience and constancy in the acknowledged truth.

Latin:

Si verò uxorem duxeris, non peccasti: Et si virgo nupserit, non peccavit: adflictionem autem in carne habebunt tales. Ego autem vobis parco.

Consilium quidem impertit, sed neminem cogit ut id sequatur: ac ne conscientiam quidem hoc consilio adstrictam esse vult. Relinquit enim uniuscuiusque arbitrio, quid iudicet sibi fore commodissimum. Quisque enim sentit potissimùm, qua prematur necessitate, & quid ferre possit. Quòd si inquit duxeris uxorem, aut virgo nupserit viro, non in, iiciet hoc scrupulum conscientiae: Omnibus enim est licitum contrahere matrimonium. Adflictiones autem carnis habituri sunt: timenda sunt exilia cum coniuge & liberis, & varia persecutionum genera propter religionem. Et hac in re vobis parcere superem, ut quàm minimum haberetis tentationum.

Sed si ita placet animo vestro inire matrimonium & sustinere carnis adflictiones non peccastis: res enim posita est in vestro arbitrio. Et tanto ardentius orandum vobis erit, ut Deus mitiget aerumnas, & adflictionem, & largiatur patientiam, & constantiam in agnita veritate.

## 7:29-31
This I say, brothers, the time that remains is contracted: therefore those who have wives, let them be as though not having them: and those who mourn, as though not mourning: and those who rejoice, as though not rejoicing, and those who buy, as though not possessing: and those who use this world, as though not abusing it. For the figure of this world passes away.

The Apostle shows what goal the pious ought always to have before their eyes in every deliberation concerning these worldly things, namely, that it must be considered that this time which we spend in this world is short and meager: we must depart from here. Therefore, our whole heart ought not to be occupied with the cares of worldly things, but we ought to prepare ourselves daily for eternal communion with God, and to serve the glory of God perpetually. He who always keeps this goal in view lives in the world as though he were not in the world: for his mind and πολιτεύμα in the heavens is. And whether he obtains or loses worldly things, he is nevertheless affected in the same way toward religion, and in all things he sustains himself with the hope of eternal life. Those who have spouses, let them be as though they had none, as if he were saying: Let them not place their highest happiness in the fact that they have convenient companions of life: let them consider that they must one day depart from spouse and children. And thus let them promptly serve the Lord, as if they did not have spouses. Let them prefer the love of God to the love of spouses. Those who mourn, let them be as though they were not mourning, that is, let them not be completely broken by grief on account of the death of a husband, or spouse, or parents, or children. But let them moderate their sorrow with the hope of the future resurrection, and that they are to live forever with the Lord in the heavens. Those who rejoice, let them be as though they were not rejoicing. This is, Those who enjoy happiness, receive benefits from God and rejoice in them: let them not place their highest blessedness in this temporal happiness, but let them know that it will pass shortly, and that various miseries are to be expected here at every moment. And therefore, in joy itself, God must be feared at the same time, and humbly invoked, lest He allow us to slip: Those who buy, he says, as though not possessing. We cannot be without contracts as long as we are in this life. But Christians ought to use these in such a way that they do not allow themselves to be entirely occupied by purchases: nor should they place their chief happiness in the possession of earthly goods: but let them assiduously consider that he must migrate from here, and that all things must be left behind. Let them therefore use and enjoy the riches granted by God, with thanksgiving: and let them always be prepared to relinquish them. If anyone having entered upon a journey into a happy and blessed fatherland, should happen upon an inn on the way, not entirely inconvenient: he acts prudently if he enjoys it with a joyful mind, and gives thanks to God, and in a certain way refreshes his limbs wearied from the labor of the journey. But if anyone is so delighted by the foreign inn, that he forgets his sweetest and most blessed fatherland, truly he is entirely foolish. Thus we are pilgrims in this world: if riches and other comforts of this life happen to us: if a convenient lodging is granted: let us enjoy the goods granted by God, but let us beware, lest we allow our soul to be so occupied by riches and the comforts of this life, that we forget eternal life. The rule of Christ ought always to be in our sight, beware lest your hearts be weighed down with care, concerning the necessities of this life. Watch therefore and pray at all times, that you may be worthy to escape all these things, and to stand before the son of man, and with Paul we ought always to desire, I desire to be dissolved and to be with Christ. In sum, we ought to place the highest good and highest happiness, not in the perishable and fleeting goods of this world, but in the perpetual happiness of eternal life. For the figure, That is, glory, form, riches, comforts, and whatever is dear in the world passes away in the flesh, nothing is stable, nothing is perpetual. Therefore it is not the highest good.

Latin:

Hoc dico, fratres, tempus, quod reliquum est, contractum est: itaque qui habent uxores, sint tanquam non habentes: & qui lugent, tanquam non lugentes: Et qui gaudent, tanquam non gaudentes, Et qui emunt, tanquam non possidentes: & qui mundo hoc utuntur, tanquam non abutentes. Transit enim figura huius mundi.

Ostendit Apostolus, quem scopum pii in omni deliberatione de hisce mundanis rebus semper ante oculos habere debent, nimirum cogitandum breve et exiguum esse hoc tempus, quod degimus in hoc mundo: migrandum nobis est hinc. Non igitur totum cor nostrum occupari debet curis rerum mundanarum, sed ad aeternam cum Deo consuetudinem nos indies praeparare, & Dei gloriae perpetuò inservire debemus. Hunc scapum, qui semper intuetur, is in mundo vivit, tanquam non esset in mundo: nam animus eius & πολιτεύμα in coelis est. Et sive obtineat, sive amittat res mundanas, eodem modo tamen erga religionem est adfectus, & in omnibus se sustentat spe vitae aeternae. Qui coniuges habent, sint tanquam non habentes, quasi dicat: Non in eo ponant summam felicitatem, quòd habent commodas vitae socias: cogitent discedendum aliquando esse à coniuge & liberis. Atque ita promptè serviant domino, ac si non haberent coniuges. Dilectionem Dei, amori coniugum praeponant. Qui lugent, sint tanquam non lugentes, hoc est, non planè frangantur luctu, propter obitum mariti, vel coniugis, vel parentum, vel liberorum. Sed moderentur dolori spe futurae resurrectionis, & quòd apud dominum in caelis per petuò sint victuri. Qui gaudent, sint tanquam non gaudentes. Hoc est, Qui felicitate fruuntur, beneficia à Deo accipiunt & in iis gaudent: non ponant in hac temporali felicitate summam beatitudinem, sed sciant eam brevi transituram, & singulis momentis varias aerumnas hîc expectandas esse. Ideoque in ipso gaudio simul metuendus est Deus, & submissè invocandus, ne sinat nos labi: Qui emunt inquit, tanquam non possidentes. Contractibus carere non possumus, quandiu sumus in hac vita. His autem sic uti debent Christiani, ut non patiantur se totos occupari emptionibus: nec in possessione terrenorum bonorum praecipuam ponant felicitatem: sed adsiduè cogitent sibi hinc migrandum, & omnia reliquenda esse. Utantur igitur & fruantur opibus à Deo concessis, cum gratiarum actione: & semper ad relinquendum ea, sint parati. Si quis iter ingressus in patriam felicem & beatam, incidat in itinere in diversorium, non omninò incommodum: prudenter facit, si eo fruitur animo laeto, & Deo gratias agit, & membra ex labore profectionis defatigata, quodammodo refocillat. Si quis verò ita delectetur peregrino diversorio, ut dulcissimae & beatissimae patriae obliviscatur, nae ille totus est fatuus. Sic in hoc mundo peregrinamur: si opes & alia huius vitae commoda contingunt: si commodum conceditur hospitium: fruamur bonis à Deo concessis, sed caveamus, ne animum nostrum opibus et huius vitae commodis ita occupari patiamur, ut aeternae vitae obliviscamur. Semper nobis in conspectu esse debet regula Christi, cavete ne graventur corda vestra cura, de huius vitae necessariis. Vigilate autem & in omni tempore orate, ut digni sitis, qui effugiant ista omnia, & stare possitis ante filium hominis, & cum Paulo semper optare debemus, Cupio dissolvi & esse cum Christo. In summa, summum bonum & summam felicitatem, non in caducis, & pereuntibus huius mundi bonis, sed in vitae aeternae perpetua felicitate ponere debemus. Figura enim, Id est, gloria, forma, opes, commoda, & quidquid carum est carni in mundo transit, nihil est stabile, nihil perpetuum. Non igitur est summum bonum.

## 7:32-34
I want you to be without care: the unmarried man is anxious about the things of the Lord, how he may please the Lord. But he who marries a wife cares for the things of the world, how he may please his wife. There is a difference between a wife and a virgin. The unmarried woman cares for the things of the Lord, that she may be holy in body and Spirit: But she who has married a husband cares for the things of the world, how she may please her husband.

He explains the reason why he dissuades widows and virgins from matrimony: Namely, that they may be able to serve the Lord more expeditiously. Not that the celibacy of either virgins or widows is a holier kind of life than marriage, as foolish monks have feigned, but lest they be hindered in the worship of religion in such a great mass of persecutions. Paul shows his fatherly spirit toward the Corinthians: That he desires them to follow true piety without any trouble and impediment: The unmarried man, he says, cares for the things of the Lord: He speaks of him who has the gift of continence: He can more expeditiously pursue those things which pertain to religion and ministry: If exile encroaches, there is no reason he should fear the complaints of a spouse or children: If he is led into prison, there is no reason he should be broken by the love of a spouse: if a confession must be made, it is not necessary that he fear lest he bring his spouse and children into danger: But in a certain way, free from the cares of this age, he can make a free and eager confession. A husband indeed ought to make a confession with no less eagerness than if he were unmarried: And to prefer the glory of the divine name to the love of a spouse and children: But in few does this fortitude and constancy of mind shine. Without doubt Paul saw the saddest examples of defections: That husbands, broken by the love of spouses and children, whom they saw cast into the most atrocious dangers by their confession, denied the truth, or cast away the ministry of the Spirit: Likewise, that many matrons, fearing the offense of their husbands, cast away the profession of the Gospel and returned to Ethnic impiety, for faith is not of all. Because therefore such various impediments were then impending, Paul persuades that he who is not bound by marriage should enjoy the granted liberty, and be wholly in this, that he may please the Lord Jesus Christ.

The unmarried man, he says, cares for the things that are of the Lord: Doubtless the unmarried man, who has the gift of continence, who has been converted to the faith, who indeed burns with zeal for piety. Jeremiah and the Baptist were not married: For both taught the Church in a most difficult time, and

he could more conveniently perform the duties of the ministry, and more easily bear the hardships which occurred. They were wholly intent on this, that they might enlarge the kingdom of Christ. But he who takes a wife, cares for the things that are of the world, how he may please his wife: Paul does not speak of Sardanapaluses, who serve the lust and foolish desires of silly women: But he speaks of pious husbands who are converted to God: Upon these lies the solicitude of how they may be able to nourish, cherish, and defend their spouse and children. These are often hindered in the course of religion by the love of their spouses: They often omit necessary duties of piety, lest they kindle perpetual strife and quarrels in marriage: They often, for the sake of their spouses, either collude with the impious, or connive at manifest impiety, or approve of Idols. Therefore, that the pious may be free from temptations of this kind, especially when the Church was first being born among the nations, and pious spouses could scarcely be had, Paul persuades them to abstain from marriage. He persuades the virgins of the same. There is, he says, a great difference between a spouse and a virgin: Namely, as far as liberty is concerned. A virgin can follow the true religion with greater liberty than a wife who has an unfaithful and morose husband.

The virgin cares for the things that are of the Lord: Namely, she who has the gift of chastity, and burns with a sincere zeal for piety, that she may be holy in body and Spirit: As if he were to say: Thus I persuade virginity and celibacy, so that those who wish to follow this counsel of mine may abstain from all uncleanness and impurity: Let them not burn with the flames of lust, let them not pollute themselves with illicit effusions of seed, but let them serve the Lord in true chastity and holiness.

She who is married cares for the things of the world, how she may please her husband. Paul does not disapprove of the zeal in a wife to comply with and please her husband according to God's commandment, but he indicates that for pious wives, very grave impediments to piety are often presented when the anger and offense of a husband are feared, when for the sake of the husband's favor, either idols are approved, or the confession of truth is hidden, or a necessary duty of piety is omitted. Therefore, so that they may not be entangled in these temptations, he advises that virgins who have the gift of continence should abstain from marriage.

Latin:

Volo autem vos sine cura esse: caelebs solicitus est de iis, quae domini sunt, quomodo placeat domino. Qui verò uxorem ducit, curat ea, quae sunt mundi, quomodo placeat uxori. Discrimen est inter uxorem & virginem. Innupta curat ea, quae sunt domini, ut sit sancta corpore & Spiritu: Quae verò nupsit marito, curat ea, quae sunt mundi, quomodo placeat viro.

Causam exponit, cur viduis & virginibus dissuadeat matrimonium: Nimirum ut expeditius domino servire possint. Non quod caelibatus vel virginum vel viduarum sit vitae genus sanctius, quàm coniugium, ut stolidi monachi finxerunt, sed ne in tanta persecutionum mole in religionis cultu impediantur. Animum suum paternum ostendit Paulus erga Corinthios: Quòd cupiat eos sine omni molestia & impedimento se qui veram pietatem: Caelebs inquit curat ea, quae domini sunt: De eo loquitur, qui donum habet continentiae: Is expeditius potest ea, quae ad religionem & ministerium pertinent, sectari: Si ingruit exilium, non est quòd vereatur coniugis vel liberorum querelas: Si ducitur in carcerem, non est quòd frangatur amore coniugis: si edenda est confessio, non necesse est ut metuat, ne coniugem & liberos adducat in periculum: Sed quodammodo libera curis huius seculi liberam & alacrem potest edere confessionem. Maritus quidem debebat non minori alacritate edere confessionem, quàm si caelebs esset: Et gloriam nominis divini anteponere amori coniugis & liberorum: Sed in paucis lucet haec fortitudo & constantia animi. Haud dubiè vidit Paulus tristissima exempla defectionum: Quòd mariti fracti amore coniugum & liberorum, quos viderunt confessione in atrocissima pericula coniici, abnegarint veritatem, aut proiecerint ministerium Spiritus: Item, quòd maltae matronae veritae maritorum offensionem abicerint Evangelii professionem & redierint ad impietatem Ethnicam, non enim omnium est fides. Quia igitur tum tam varia imminebant impedimenta, suadet Paul; ut qui matrimonio alligatus non est, libertate concessa fruatur, & totus in hoc sit, ut placeat domino Iesu Christo.

Caelebs inquit curat ea, quae sunt domini: Nimirum caelebs, qui donum habet continentiae, qui ad fidem conversus est, qui verò pietatis zelo ardet. Ieremias & Baptista non fuerunt mariti: Uterque enim & difficilimo tempore docuit Ecclesiam, &

commodius potuit obire partes ministerii, & facilius ferre aerumnas, quae obtigerunt. Toti in hoc fuerunt, ut regnum Christi amplificarent. Qui verò ducit uxorem, curat ea, quae sunt mundi, quomodo placeat uxori: Non loquitur Paulus de Sardanapalis, qui serviant libidini & stultis capiditatibus muliercularum: Sed de piis & ad Deum conversis maritis loquitur: His sollicitudo incumbit, quomodo coniugem & liberos nutrire, fovere & defendere possint. Hi saepè impediuntur in cursu religionis, amore coniugum: Saepè omittunt necessaria pietatis officia, ne perpetuas lites & rixas in matrimonio accendant: Saepè in gratiam coniugum, aut colludunt cum impiis, aut connivent ad manifestam impietatem, aut ad probant Idola. Ut igitur liberi sint pii ab huiusmodi tentationibus, praesertim cum nascente primùm Ecclesia inter gentes, pii coniuges vix haberi possint, suadet Paulus, ut matrimonio abstineant. Idem suadet et virginibus. Magnum inquit discrimen est inter coniugem & virginem: Scilicet quò ad libertatem attinet. Virgo maiore libertate sequi potest veram religionem, quàm uxor, quae maritum habet infidelem & morosum.

Virgo curat ea, quae domini sunt: Nimirum, quae donum habet castitatis, & flagrat syncero pietatis studio, ut sancta sit corpore & Spiritu: Quasi dicat: Sic suadeo virginitatem et caelibatum, ut qui hoc meum consilium se qui volunt, ab omni immundicie & impuritate abstineant: Non flagrent flammis libidinum, non polluant se illicitis effusionibus seminis, sed in vera castitate & sanctitate serviant domino.

Quae nupsit, curat ea, quae mundi sunt, quomodo placeat marito. Non improbat Paulus in uxore studium obsequendi & placendi marito iuxta Dei praeceptum, sed indicat saepè piis uxoribus, obiici gravissima impedimenta pietatis, quando ira & offensio mariti timetur, quando in gratiam mariti, vel adprobantur Idola, vel occultatur veritatis confessio, vel omittur necessarium pietatis officium. Ne igitur his tentationibus implicentur, suadet, ut matrimonio abstineant virgines, quae continentiae donum habent.

## 7:35
This however I say for your own benefit, not that I may cast a snare upon you: But that I may show what is honorable, and how you may more easily adhere to the Lord without distraction.

He intersperses a necessary exception, that each one should examine himself, whether he can follow this counsel of Paul without a wound and danger to his conscience. Paul is not ignorant that few men in the world are instructed with the gift of chastity: The Apostle is not ignorant of what kind the incitements of lusts are in miserable and corrupt nature, what kind the snares of the Devil are, how great the security and torpor of men is in prayer. And if therefore he has set forth his counsel concerning preserving chastity with singular faith: yet because not all receive this word, as Christ says, he testifies explicitly that he does not place a snare upon consciences: That he does not compel either virgins or widows to bind themselves by a vow of chastity: Which the insane and impure and wicked Roman pontiffs have done: But that he leaves it entirely free to them, whether they wish to marry or to abstain from marriage. For he has only set forth a convenient way of life, and how one, instructed with the gift of chastity, may be able to adhere to the Lord perpetually without distraction.

Si quis but if anyone thinks that these things do not befit his virgin, if the time of marrying passes by, and it is necessary that it be done so, let him do what he wills, he does not sin: let them be joined in marriage. But he who stands firm in his heart, not having necessity, but has power of his own will, and has decreed this in his heart, that he may keep his own virgin, does well. Therefore he who gives her in marriage, does well: but he who does not give her in marriage, does better.

The Apostle, being very solicitous that the Corinthians might rightly perceive his mind, often repeats both his faithful counsel and the added exception, that he might cast a snare upon no one's conscience, and snatch away from no one the liberty which he possesses in the Lord. Therefore he repeatedly inculcates that those who contract marriage, or give their daughters in marriage, do not sin: for marriage is granted to all men. He also warns parents that they should diligently weigh both the gifts of their children and what necessity itself demands. Children are indeed in the power of their parents: but nevertheless, parents ought not to force unwilling children either to marriage or to celibacy: nay, they ought also to consult the conscience of their children. If, he says, it is necessary that it be done so: as if he were to say: if a parent perceives that a daughter cannot be without marriage without danger to her chastity, let him by all means give her in marriage and know that he does not sin.

But he who is firm in his own judgment: That is, he who perceives that his daughter does not greatly desire marriage, as one who is adorned with the gift of chastity, and sees that no necessity is imposed upon him of giving her in marriage daughter, he does well: For he rightly provides for both his own tranquility and quiet and that of his daughter.

And here we have an excellent testimony that the will and consent of parents must by all means be present for the marriages of children, and that children are in the power of their parents. However, parents ought to use this power in the fear of God and moderately, and by no means turn it into tyranny. Above all, they ought to provide for the consciences of their children rightly and with a fatherly spirit.

That he says those who do not give their daughters in marriage do better than those who do give them: it is not to be taken as if they perform a duty more pleasing to God, or as if there is greater holiness in celibacy than in marriage: but that he provides better for himself and his own, with respect to present necessity and impending persecution. He who does not give her away will have more tranquility and quiet, and fewer temptations and troubles.

A wife is bound by the law as long as her husband lives: but if her husband has fallen asleep, she is free, let her marry whom she wishes, only in the Lord. But she will be happier if she remains so, according to my judgment indeed. I think, however, that I also have the Spirit of God.

Just as he did not take away from virgins the freedom of marrying, although he communicated the counsel concerning celibacy: so that he might not cast a snare upon consciences: So also he instructs widows that they are prohibited by no law from being able to marry, if they are in need of matrimony.

As long as the husband lives, she is bound by the law. That is, the indissoluble covenant of matrimony lasts as long as both parties live, but with the husband taken from the living, the widow is entirely free. Let her marry whom she will, only in the Lord: This is, in the fear of the Lord, and with the serious invocation of the Son of God, Jesus Christ. For without the blessing of Jesus Christ, marriage does not turn out happily. Without any obscurity, Paul most plainly approves of second marriages here. Wherefore Tertullian, Jerome, and others, who either condemned or inveighed against second marriages, gravely hallucinated and sinned in that, because they contradicted the doctrine of the Holy Spirit.

That the Apostle says that the widow will be more blessed if she remains so, is not to be understood that she is therefore more acceptable to God, that she merits greater grace before God, or is nearer to the kingdom of Christ; as monks corrupt the place of Paul: But he speaks of earthly and bodily blessedness: She will be more blessed, that is, she will have fewer troubles: She will undergo fewer dangers, she will enjoy greater tranquility: she will be able to pursue piety with greater freedom. And so she acts prudently if she guards the offered happiness, but if indeed he feels that he is in need of marriage, let him marry, and let him firmly resolve that he is not sinning. Lest the pious should despise the counsel of Paul, as if it proceeded from the prudence of the flesh, he testifies that he has the Spirit of God, as one who is an Apostle of Jesus Christ.

Latin:

Hoc autem ad vestram utilitatem dico, non ut laqueum vobis iniiciam: Sed ut ostendam, quid sit honestum, & quò faciliùs domino sine divulsione adhaerere possitis.

Necessariam interspergit exceptionem, ut quisquè se ipsum examinet, num sine vulnere & periculo conscientiae hoc Pauli consilium se qui possit. Non ignorat Paulus paucos homines in mundo dono castitatis instructos esse: Non ignorat Apostolus qualia sint in misera & corrupta natura incitamenta libidinum, quales sint insidiae Diaboli, quanta sit hominum securitas & torpor in precatione. Et si igitur singulari fide suum consilium exposuit de servanda castitate: tamen quia non omnes capiunt verbum hoc, ut Christus inquit, disertè testatur se non ponere laqueum conscientiis: Se non adigere vel virgines, vel viduas, ut sese voto castitatis adstringant: Quod insani & impuri & scelerati pontifices Romani fecerunt: Sed omninò relinquere se illis liberum, sive velint nubere, sive abstinere a matrimonio. Se enim tantum ex posuisse commodam vitae rationem, & quomodo quis instructus dono castitatis perpetuò sine distractione domino queat adhaerere.

Si quis verò existimat haec non convenire suae virgini, si tempus nubendi praetereat, & sic fieri oportet, quod vult faciat non peccat: iungantur matrimonio. Qui verò stat firmus, in corde suo non habens necessitatem, potestatem autem habet propriae voluntatis, & hoc decrevit in corde suo, ut servet suam virginem, bene facit. Itaque qui elocat nuptum, benefacit: Qui verò non elocat nuptum, melius facit.

Apostolus admodùm sollicitus ut Corinthii eius mentem rectè percipiant saepè, repetit & fidele suum consilium, & adiunctam exceptionem, quòd nullius conscientiae iniiciat laqueum, nemini eripiat libertatem, quam possidet in domino. Subinde igitur inculcat, eos qui matrimonium contrahunt, aut filias suas elocant, non peccare: Coniugium enim omnibus hominibus est concessum. Monet etiam parentes, ut diligenter expendant & dona liberorum, & quid ipsa postulet necessitas. Sunt quidem liberi in potestate parentum: sed tamen invitos liberos, nequè ad coniugium, neque ad caelibatum cogere debent parentes: imò & conscientiae liberorum consulere debent. Si inquit ita necesse est fieri: quasi dicat: si animadvertit parens, filiam sine periculo pudicitiae matrimonio carere non posse, omninò elocet eam & sciat se non peccare.

Qui verò firmus est in sua sententia: Hoc est, qui animadvertit filiam non admodum expetere matrimonium, ut quae dono castitatis sit ornata, & videt nullam sibi imponi necessitatem elocandi filiam, ille bene facit: Nam & suae & filia tranquillitati & quieti rectè consulit.

Atque hîc praeclarum habemus testimonium, quòd ad liberorum matrimonia, parentum voluntas & consensus omninò accedere debet, quodque liberi sint in potestate parentum. Hac autem potestate parentes in timore Dei & moderatè uti debent & nequaquam eam in tyrannidem convertere. In primis conscientiae liberorum rectè, & paterno animo consulere debent.

Quòd dicit eos, qui non elocant filias nuptum, melius facere quam illos, qui elocent: non est sic accipiendum, quasi Deo gratius officium praestent: aut quasi maior sit sanctitas in coelibatu, quàm in matrimonio: sed quòd meliùs sibi & suis consulat, respectu praesentis necessitatis, & impendentis persecutionis. Plus ille, qui non elocat, tranquillitatis & quietis habiturus est: & minus tentationum & molestiarum.

Uxor alligata est lege, quanto tempore vivit maritus eius: si autem dormierit vir eius, libera est, cui voluerit nubat, tantum in domino. Felicior autem erit, si sic manserit, iuxta meam quidem sententiam. Existimo autem & me habere Spiritum Dei.

Quemadmodum virginibus non ademit nubendi libertatem, licet consilium de caelibatu communicarit: ne laqueum conscientiis iniiceret: Ita & viduas instruit nulla lege eas prohiberi, quò minùs nubere possint, si indigent matrimonio.

Quandiu maritus vivit, lege alligata est. Id est, Indissolubile faedus matrimonii durat, quandiu utraque pars vivit, Marito autem è vivis sublato, libera est prorsus vidua. Cui voluerit nubat, tantum in domino: Hoc est, in timore domini, & cum seria invocatione filii Dei Iesu Christi. Nam sine benedictione Iesu Christi, coniugium non cedit feliciter. Sine omni obscuritate planissimè adprobat hîc Paulus secundas nuptias. Quare Tertulianus, Hieronymus & alii, qui vel damnarunt, vel insectati sunt secundas nuptias, graviter in eo hallucinati sunt & peccarunt, quòd Spiritus sancti doctrinae contradixerunt.

Quòd dicit Apostolus, beatiorem fore viduam, si sic manserit, non est intelligendum, quòd eò acceptior sit Deo, quòd maiorem gratiam apud Deum mereatur, aut vicinior sit regno Christi; Ut monachi Pauli locum corrumpunt: Sed de terrena & corporali beatitudine loquitur: Beatior erit, id est, minus habebit molestiarum: Minus subibit periculorum, maiore tranquillitate fruetur: maiore libertate pietatem sectari poterit. Itaque prudenter facit, si oblatam felicitatem custodiat, Quòd si verò sentiat se indigere coniugio nubat, & certò statuat se non peccare. Ne pii adspernantur consilium Pauli, tanquam ex prudentia carnis profectum, testatur se habere Spiritum Dei, ut qui sit Apostolus Iesu Christi.
