## 7:35 Places of Doctrine
Places of Doctrine.

1. The first place is concerning marriage, that it is an indissoluble covenant of one male and one female. And that it is lawful for the pious to live in marriage with a good conscience: And that neither party ought to desert the other, but to provide the due benevolence. And that marriage is to be entered into not only for the sake of offspring, but also to avoid lusts.

2. That celibacy is a lawful and indifferent thing: especially if one has the gift of continence from God.

3. That pious spouses ought sometimes to be free for fasting and more ardent prayer and to abstain for a time. But at the same time to take care lest they be tempted by Satan.

4. That there is a distinction between the commandment of God, and the counsel of the Apostles or pastors: The commandment of God must be obeyed without any tergiversation and deliberation. But the counsel of the Apostles or pastors does not impose upon us a necessity of obeying, but leaves freedom, and exhorts that we examine our conscience and strengths and take them into counsel.

5. On account of a difference of religion, a spouse is neither to be deserted nor driven away. For the marriage covenant between spouses of different religion is valid.

6. That which Paul says, that the unbelieving spouse is sanctified by the believing spouse, and that the children of the faithful are holy: It is not to be understood concerning spiritual sanctification: But that it is lawful for the faithful spouse to cohabit with the unbelieving spouse without a wound to the conscience, and to nourish the children of both.

7. That a person deserted by a spouse and who is innocent is rightly absolved by a judge from the deserting party: And that another marriage is to be granted to him, if he has need of it. For he is free, according to the testimony of Paul.

8. Individuals ought to remain in that calling in which they were called: A legitimate and honest way of life is not to be changed on account of religion.

9. That the kingdom of God is spiritual and does not consist in external ceremonies or rites: But in the observation of the commandments of God, that is, that we obey the law and the Gospel.

10. When an opportunity is divinely offered to change a harsh way of life for the better, one must strive for it: And we must not foolishly heap miseries and hardships upon ourselves.

11. Concerning the defending of Christian liberty, which has been purchased for us at a great price, namely, the blood of the only-begotten Son of God.

12. Concerning the hardships and afflictions of spouses: which those who are endowed with the gift of continence are indeed permitted to avoid: But those who are destitute of this gift must take care, lest they fall into the snares of Satan.

13. A notable rule, which ought to govern our whole life, all contracts, and all our deliberations and actions: Namely, that we must use the world and worldly things in such a way that we never prefer them to salvation, that they do not hinder piety, and do not occupy our heart: but that we always look toward God, and prepare ourselves for the migration from this life to the heavenly fellowship.

14. Paul here disapproves of the impious and sacrilegious vows of monks concerning perpetual chastity, because he does not wish a snare to be cast upon consciences.

15. Paul here also condemns the papal law concerning the celibacy of the ministers of the word. For he testifies in the Holy Spirit that it is better to marry than to burn: And to avoid lusts, he wishes that each should have his own wife.

16. Paul also approves of second marriages.

Latin:

Loci Doctrinae.

1. Primus locus est de coniugio, quod sit foedus unius maris et foeminae indissolubile. Quodque piis liceat bona conscientia vivere in coniugio: Et quòd neutra pars alteram de serere debeat, Sed debitam praestare benevolentiam. Et quòd non tantum sobolis causa, sed etiam ad vitandas libidines ineundum sit matrimonium.

2. Quòd coelibatus sit res licita & media: praesertim si quis habeat à Deo donum continentiae.

3. Pios coniuges debere aliquando ieiunio & ardentiori precationi vacare & sese ad tempus continere. Sed simul cavere ne tententur à Satana.

4. Quod sit discrimen inter praeceptum Dei, & consilium Apostolorum vel pastorum: Mandato Dei sine omni tergiversatione & deliberatione obtemperandum est. Sed consilium Apostolorum vel pastorum non imponit nobis parendi necessitatem, sed relinquit libertatem, & hortatur, ut nostram conscientiam & vires examinemus & in consilium adhibeamus.

5. Propter religionis diversitatem nec de serendam nec à se abigendam esse coniugem. Valet enim foedus coniugii inter coniuges diversae religionis.

6. Quod Paulus dicit infidelem sanctificari per fidelem coniugem, & fidelium liberos esse sanctos: Non de spirituali sanctificatione intelligendum est: Sed quòd liceat sine vulnere conscientiae fideli cohabitare infideli coniugi, & liberos utriusque enutrire.

7. Quod persona deserta à coniuge & innocens, iure absolvatur per iudicem à parte de sertrice: Quodque ei concedendum sit alterum matrimonium, si eo indiget. Libera est enim teste Paulo.

8. Singuli in ea vocatione, in qua vocati sunt manere debent: Legitimum & honestum vitae genus non est mutandum propter religionem.

9. Quod regnum Dei spirituale non consistat in externis ceremoniis, vel ritibus: Sed in observatione mandatorum Dei, id est, ut legi & Evangelio obediamus.

10. Cùm divinitus offertur occasio durum vitae genus in melius mutandi, annitendum esse: Et non stolidè cumulandas nobis esse miserias et aerumnas.

11. De tuenda libertate Christiana, quae magno precio, nimirum sanguine unigeniti filii Dei nobis est comparata.

12. De aerumnis & adflictionibus coniugum: quas licet quidem iis declinare, qui dono continentiae sunt instructi: Sed qui hoc dono destituuntur, cavere debent, ne incidant in laqueos Satanae.

13. Regula insignis, quae totam nostram vitam, omnes contractus, & omnes nostras deliberationes & actiones gubernare debet: Nimirum sic mundo & rebus mundanis utendum esse, ut eas nunquàm anteponamus saluti, ut ea non impediant pietatem, non occupent cor nostrum: sed semper ad Deum respiciamus, & nos ad migrationem ex hac vita ad caelestem consuetudinem, praeparemus.

14. Impia & sacrilega vota monachorum de castitate perpetua improbat hîc Paulus, quia non vult conscientiis iniici laqueum.

15. Pontificiam etiam legem de caelibatu ministrorum verbi, damnat hîc Paulus. Testatur enim in Spiritu sancto meliùs esse nubere, quàm uri: Et ad vitandas libidines, vult ut singuli proprias habeant coniuges.

16. Adprobat etiam Paulus secundas nuptias.

## 8:1 Argument
CHAPTER VIII.

Latin:

CAPUT VIII.

## 8:1-2
Now concerning those things that are offered to idols, we know that we all have knowledge. Knowledge puffs up, but charity edifies: If anyone, however, thinks that he knows anything, he knows nothing yet, as

Latin:

De iis autem, quae idolis offeruntur, scimus quòd omnes scientiam habemus. Scientia inflat, charitas autem aedificat: Si quis autem videtur sibi scire aliquid, nec quidquam novit, quemadmodum

## 8:3-4
it is necessary to know. But if anyone loves God, this one is known by him: Therefore concerning foods which have been sacrificed to idols, we know that an idol is nothing in the world, and that there is no other God, except one.

In this 8th Chapter the Apostle treats a new argument: For he teaches the Corinthians concerning the true use of Christian liberty, and censures its untimely use, with the stumbling block of a neighbor. The Corinthians had perceived the doctrine handed down by Paul concerning Christian liberty, that the conscience of Christians cannot be captivated by any laws, that idols were nothing, that to the clean all things were clean: But they were abusing this knowledge and liberty rather for the stumbling block of a neighbor, than for the consolation of their own conscience and the edification of the Church. Paul therefore reproves this abuse, and teaches with what piety, modesty, love of neighbor, and circumspection the pious ought to use their liberty and knowledge of spiritual things. By divine law it was prohibited that the sons of Israel should eat Idolothyta, That is, those things which had been sacrificed to Idols. And that law had most grave causes. For God demands confession: he prohibits the approval of Idols, he warns that we should abstain from Idols and Idolaters, lest we be invited to impious cults. It was therefore customary in the Church, when the Israelitic as well as the Christian, to avoid the sacrifices of the Gentiles and to abstain from things sacrificed to idols. Various cases, however, occurred; often Gentiles converted to the Christian faith were invited by their Gentile relatives to banquets, in which things sacrificed to idols were set before them: Often a pious wife of a Gentile husband was compelled to be present at the husband's banquets: Hence various disputes and controversies and questions were stirred up. Paul therefore instructed them with the knowledge of liberty: that the earth is the Lord's: and to the pure all things are pure. Therefore there is no need for a long inquiry as to what is a thing sacrificed to idols, what has been brought from the meat market. But because some were proudly abusing this liberty, Paul restricts it and recalls it to the rule of Love, which like a standard ought to govern the whole army of virtues. And this is the sum of the opinion of Paul and of the whole eighth chapter. Idols are nothing at all, and a thing sacrificed to idols is nothing: but to the pure all things are pure, and it is lawful for Christians to use all of God's creatures with thanksgiving. Therefore no scruple ought to be cast into our consciences. But when we notice that a brother can be harmed and offended by our action, we ought not to proudly display our knowledge, nor petulantly use our liberty: but rather to consult the infirmity of our neighbor, and to beware of his offense: for the salvation of our neighbor ought to be more important to us than the free use of external things. Paul, however, mixes into this doctrine a sharp castigation of arrogance. For from this source the abuse of liberty is accustomed to flow.

We know, he says, that we all have knowledge: by mimesis he recites the proud voice of the Corinthians, by which they boasted: we are all enlightened, we are all taught by the Lord, therefore we all have knowledge, that an idol is nothing. And although it is true that all Christians are enlightened by God, and excellent gifts are seen in the saints: nevertheless there is a great difference among the pious: one has more, another less light. And the greater part in the Church is always of the weak. Therefore one should not boast so proudly. Knowledge, says Paul, puffs up: love builds up: as if he were to say: The Kingdom of God does not consist in cognition; it is not enough for you to have known many things: but also individual things must be referred to the glory of God and the salvation of one's neighbor. Many use the knowledge of religion for pride: Therefore, one should rather strive for love, which always builds up one's neighbor. If anyone, he says, seems to know something: he does not yet know: He taxes the empty persuasion of wisdom as in the whole Epistle: and recalls them to the knowledge of their own infirmity. It is not enough to know something in general, but at the same time all circumstances must be perceived. And the fall of human wit is most easy. Therefore there is nothing safer or better than to think humbly of oneself, and always to pray to the Lord that He may rule us with His holy Spirit and show us salutary counsels. He who loves God, this one is known by God: We ought rather to glory in this, that we are known by God through Christ as members of the household, than that we know many things.

But he who loves God and his neighbor, this one is known by God: For he is led by the Holy Spirit, who kindles in him the love of God and of his neighbor. Before all things, therefore, one must strive for the love of one's neighbor, and one must always consider what is expedient for the Church.

Now concerning things sacrificed to idols, we know: After the rebuke, he returns to the proposed question, and first he refutes the pretext of the Corinthians. We know (he says) that an idol is nothing in the world, and that there is only one God. Therefore, there is no reason why we should fear idols or things sacrificed to idols. Paul answers. It is indeed true that an idol is nothing, and that there is only one God: But not all have an equal knowledge of the truth, therefore one must see not only what is permitted to you, but also what is expedient for the Church. The doctrine of the Church, that there is only one God, and that the other deities of the nations fashioned outside the Church or even within the Church itself are nothing, should be attentively observed in this place.

Latin:

oportet scire. Si quis autem diligit Deum, hic cognitus est ab eo: De escis igitur, quae idolis sacrificatae sunt, scimus quòd nihil est idolum in mundo, & quòd nullus est Deus alius, nisi unus.

In hoc 8. Capite Apostolus novum tractat argumentum: Docet enim Corinthios de vero usu libertatis Christianae, & taxat eius intempestivum usum, cum offendiculo proximi. Perceperant Corinthii doctrinam à Paulo traditam de libertate Christiana, quòd Christianorum conscientia nullis legibus captivari possit, quòd idola nihil essent, quòd mundis omnia essent munda: Verùm hac scientia et libertate abutebantur potiùs ad offendiculum proximi, quàm ad consolationem suae conscientiae et aedificationem Ecclesiae. Reprehendit igitur hunc abusum Paulus, & docet qua pietate, modestia, dilectione proximi, & circumspectione pii sua libertate & scientia rerum spiritualium uti debeant. Lege divina prohibitum erat, ne filii Israel ederent Idolothyta, Id est, ea, quae Idolis sacrificata erant. Et habuit illa lex gravissimas causas. Postulat enim Deus confessionem: prohibet approbationem Idolorum, monet ut abstineamus ab Idolis & Idolatris, ne ad impios cultus invitemur. Usitatum igitur in Ecclesia fuit, cùm Israelitica tum Christiana Ethnica sacrificia vitare & Idolothytis abstinere. Varii autem casus inciderunt, saepè ad fidem Christianam conversi gentiles, invitati fuerunt à cognatis Ethnicis ad convivia, in quibus idolothyta adponebantur: Saepè uxor pia mariti Ethnici cogebatur interesse conviviis mariti: Hinc variae disputationes & controversiae & quaestiones motae sunt. Paulus igitur instruxit eos cognitione libertatis: quòd domini sit terra: & mundis omnia sint munda. Ideò non opus esse longa inquisitione, quid sit Idolothytum, quid è macello allatum. Quia verò hac libertate quidam superbè abutebantur, restringit eam Paulus & revocat eam ad regulam Dilectionis, quae veluti vexillum totum exercitum virtutum regere debet. Estque haec summa sententiae Pauli & totius octavi capitis. Idola omninò nihil sunt, & Idolothyton nihil est: mundis verò omnia sunt munda, et Christianis licet omnibus Dei creaturis uti cum gratiarum actione. Idcircò nostris conscientiis nullus scrupulus iniici debet. Cùm verò animadvertimus fratrem nostro facto posse laedi & offendi, scientiam nostram non debemus superbè ostentare, nec libertate petulanter uti: sed potius infirmitati proximi consulere, & eius offensionem cavere: potior enim nobis esse debet salus proximi, quàm externarum rerum liber usus. Immiscet autem huic doctrinae Paulus acrem castigationem arrogantiae. Ex hoc enim fonte manare solet libertatis abusus.

Scimus inquit quòd omnes cognitionem habemus: per mimesin recitat superbam vocem Corinthiorum, qua iactarunt: omnes sumus illuminati, omnes summus docti à domino, omnes ergò scientiam habemus, quod nihil sit idolum. Et si autem verum est omnes Christianos illuminari à Deo, et excellentia dona conspici in sanctis: tamen magnum est discrimen inter pios: alius plus, alius minus lucis habet. Et semper imbecillium maior pars est in Ecclesia. Non ergò tam superbè gloriandum est. Scientia inquit Paulus inflat: dilectio aedificat: quasi dicat: Regnum Dei non consistit in cognitione; non satis est te multa novisse: sed etiam singula ad Dei gloriam & proximi salutem referenda sunt. Multi ad superbiam utuntur scientia religionis: Potius igitur dilectioni est studendum, quae semper aedificat proximum. Si quis inquit videtur scire quid: nondum novit: Inanem sapientiae persuasionem taxat ut in tota Epistola: & revocat eos ad congnitionem propriae infirmitatis. Non satis est nosse aliquid in genere, sed simul omnes circumstantiae perspiciendae sunt. Et facilimus est lapsus humani ingenii. Ideò nihil est tutius aut melius quàm submissè de se sentire, et semper orare dominum ut nos regat suo sancto Spirituet monstret salutaria consilia. Qui diligit Deum, hic cognitus est à Deo: Potius in eo gloriari debemus quod nos noti simus Deo per Christum tanquam domestici, quàm quod nos multa cognoscamus.

Qui verò diligit Deum & proximum, hic cognitus est à Deo: Ducitur enim à Spiritu sancto, qui in ipso accendit dilectionem Dei et proximi. Ante omnia igitur studendum est dilectioni proximi, & semper considerandum, quid expediat Ecclesiae.

De escis igitur sacrificatis idolis scimus: Post correptionem redit ad propositam quaestionem, & primùm diluit Corinthiorum praetextum. Nos scimus (inquit) quòd idolum nihil sit in mundo, & quòd tantum unus sit Deus. Ergò non est, quòd vereamur idola vel idolothyta. Respondet Paulus. Verùm quidem est idolum esse nihil, & unum tantum esse Deum: Sed non omnes parem habent cognitionem veritatis, ideò non tantum, quid liceat tibi, sed etiam quid expediat Ecclesiae, videndum est. Doctrina Ecclesiae, quòd unus tantum sit Deus, et quòd caetera numina gentium conficta extra Ecclesiam vel etiam in ipsa Ecclesia nihil sint, hoc loco attentè observetur.

## 8:5-6
For even if there are those who are called gods, whether in heaven or on earth: As there are many gods, and many lords. Yet for us there is one God the Father, from whom are all things and we in Him: And one Lord Jesus Christ through whom are all things and we through him. But there is not knowledge in all.

Paul explicitly distinguishes between the knowledge of God in the Church and the counterfeit religion by which fictitious deities are worshipped among the nations. Therefore, let this notable distinction between the true Church and other sects be diligently observed. The Church acknowledges the true God revealed in the Church, who is one, and from whom are all things: the nations outside the Church worship various deities, which are nothing, and can neither help nor harm.

1. Furthermore, the nations outside the Church are ignorant of the merciful will of God revealed in the Gospel: and so they can place no hope in God. But the Church understands the most merciful will of God, that for the sake of Christ he is willing to remit sins to those who repent freely.

2. It also hands down the doctrine that there are distinct persons in the divinity, God the Father from whom are all things, and the Son of God, Jesus Christ.

3. Thirdly, the doctrine concerning creation is touched upon here, that all things which have been made were made through the Son.

4. Fourthly: the doctrine concerning the end of man created is proposed to us: namely, that this is the chief end of man, that he may serve the praise and glory of the divine name, and perpetually celebrate the wisdom, justice, and omnipotence of God.

But knowledge is not in all: As if he were to say: Although this clear knowledge of God shines in the Church, and Christians have been freed from the darkness of Gentile idol-mania: yet there is a great dissimilarity among Christians: Many are ignorant, many are unrefined, many are weak: Therefore, consideration must always be had for these, rather than displaying a great knowledge of liberty in an untimely manner. And this is Paul's principal response to the pretext of the Corinthians.

But some with conscience of the idol, even until now eat as food sacrificed to idols, and their conscience being weak is defiled. But food does not commend us to God. For neither if we eat do we abound: Nor if we do not eat do we have less.

He indicates how the conscience of the weak is wounded by the abuse of liberty? Namely, when someone is weak, and has not yet grasped the doctrine concerning Christian liberty, and fears lest he injure his conscience by the eating of foods which have been sacrificed to idols, and nevertheless imitates the example of another who understands that idols are nothing, and eats of things sacrificed to idols, this person wounds his own conscience: For whatever is not done from faith is sin. And he who eats against his conscience, both doubts concerning religion, and despises God. Therefore, one must take care lest we offend by an untimely use of liberty the weak brother: Rather, we must strive to confirm him by our moderation, to instruct him in doctrine, and to strengthen him in faith. He calls it the conscience of an Idol, when someone fears out of weakness that he might be contaminated by the eating of things sacrificed to idols. Conscience ought to be ruled entirely by the law of nature, as well as by the express word of God: And according to this norm, either to approve things rightly done, or to condemn things done otherwise. But there are many errors in the human mind. Often men do not recognize sins, which nevertheless are most grave: Often they fear wounds of conscience where there is no danger. However much a man may understand in religion, he must always take care not to undertake anything against his conscience. For he who judges something to be unclean, to him it is unclean. And it is a most grave sin to despise the wrath of God. First, therefore, the clear word of God must be consulted, whether God has prohibited anything in it: That which we understand to be prohibited by God must by no means be attempted. Then, if we doubt about any matter, it is better to abstain than to undertake anything with a doubting conscience: For this would be to tempt God. Often, however, men pretend that they are hindered by conscience from performing this or that duty, when they are rather commanded to do so by the express word of God. The petulance of these men must be gravely censured and refuted by the word. For conscience must always be ruled by the word of God.

The Libertines have feigned that no crimes are sins before God, provided that one does not in his own conscience. accuse, then they loosen the reins to their desires, and attempt to remove the judgment of conscience. But these hold the knowledge of God in unrighteousness: and their sin lies at the door, until it is awakened by the law, therefore let us always know that conscience ought to be ruled by the word of God. Whatever is against the word of God, this defiles the conscience. Then Paul argues with arguments, and exhorts those more learned in religion, that they should restrict the use of liberty for the sake of the weak. Food, he says, and drink does not render us more acceptable to God: nor are we richer, nor poorer in the kingdom of God, whether we eat, or abstain. For it is an external thing. Deservedly therefore we omit the use of liberty, when we see that the necessity of a brother demands it. Paul always urges that external things are to be distinguished from the Spiritual kingdom of Christ, which is righteousness, peace and joy, in the Holy Spirit.

See to it, that in some way your power does not place a stumbling block for the weaker ones. For if anyone sees you, who have knowledge, sitting in the temple of an Idol, will not his conscience, who is weak, be built up to eat things sacrificed to Idols? And the weak brother will perish by your knowledge, for whom Christ has died.

This is the principal sentiment of this chapter: That our liberty and power must not be abused, but we must take care with zeal, lest we be a stumbling block to anyone. For we ought always to be mindful of the commandment: you shall love your neighbor as yourself. And we ought to have regard not only for ourselves, but for the whole body of Christ.

A scandal given, therefore, is not only some external crime, or deed, or dogma against the word of God, but also the untimely use of liberty, by which the conscience of a neighbor is wounded or led into error.

If, he says, the weak one sees you reclining in the sanctuary of an Idol, his conscience will be built up. That is, he will be invited, he will be moved, to eat together of the food sacrificed to idols, even if he does not have that knowledge which you have. Thus, when Peter withdrew himself from the company of the Gentiles, Barnabas also was led into error at the same time. For the examples of teachers in the Church draw hearers along with great force.

But it is most grave that he says: And your weak brother perishes by your knowledge. For the Apostle indicates that when anything is undertaken against conscience, then the Holy Spirit is shaken off, and faith is extinguished. He then exaggerates the sin from the magnitude of the price by which we have been redeemed. Brothers are to be highly esteemed and in no matter to be offended, for whom Christ has died. But Christ died for the brothers: Therefore, we ought by no means to offend in any matter a man bought at such a dear price. Indeed, since Christ did not hesitate to die for the brothers and for us ourselves, what is more equitable than that we should restrict the use of our liberty, so that we do not hinder the salvation of the brothers?

Latin:

Etsi enim sunt, qui dicuntur dii, sive in coelo, sive in terra: Quemadmodum sunt dii multi, & domini multi. Nobis tamen unus est Deus pater, ex quo sunt omnia & nos in ipsum: Et unus dominus Iesus Christus per quem sunt omnia & nos per ipsum. Sed non in omnibus est cognitio.

Disertè distinguit Paulus inter noticiam Dei in Ecclesia & commentitiam religionem, qua fictitia numina inter gentes coluntur. Hoc ergò insigne discrimen inter veram Ecclesiam & alias sectas diligenter observetur. Ecclesia agnoscit verum Deum patefactum in Ecclesia, qui est unus, & a quo sunt omnia: Gentes extra Ecclesiam colunt varia numina, quae nihil sunt, nec iuvare nec nocere possunt.

1. Praeterea gentes extra Ecclesiam ignorant voluntatem Dei clementem in Evangelio patefactam: Itaque spem nullam in Deum ponere possunt. Ecclesia verò intelligit Dei clementissimam voluntatem, quòd propter Christum gratis paenitentiam agentibus, velit remittere peccata.

2. Doctrinam etiam tradit, distinctas esse personas in divinitate, Deum patrem ex quo sunt omnia, & filium Dei Iesum Christum.

3. Tertiò doctrina de creatione hîc attingitur, quòd omnia, quae facta sunt, per filium sint facta.

4. Quartò: doctrina de fine hominis conditi nobis proponitur: Nimirum hunc esse praecipuum finem hominis, ut serviat laudi & gloriae nominis divini, & perpetuò celebret sapientiam, iustitiam, & omnipotentiam Dei.

Sed non in omnibus est cognitio: Quasi dicat: Etsi in Ecclesia haec clara Dei noticia lucet, et Christiani ex tenebris Ethnicae idolomaniae liberati sunt: magna tamen est dissimilitudo Christianorum: Multi sunt ignari, multi rudes, multi infirmi: Horum igitur semper est habenda ratio potius, quam intempestivè ostentanda magna scientia libertatis. Estque haec principalis responsio Pauli ad praetextum Corinthiorum.

Aliqui verò conscientia idoli, etiamnum ut idolis sacrificata esca vescuntur, & conscientia ipsorum infirma existens inquinatur. Cibus autem nos non commendat Deo. Neque enim etiamsi comedamus abundamus: Neque si non comedamus minus habemus.

Indicat quomodo infirmorum conscientia abusu libertatis vulneretur? Nimirum cum quis infirmus est, nondum percepit doctrinam de libertate Christiana, & metuit ne laedat conscientiam esu ciborum, qui idolis sacrificati sunt & nihilominus imitatur exemplum alterius, qui intelligit Idola nihil esse, & vescitur Idolothytis, hic sauciat suam conscientiam: Quod enim non fit ex fide peccatum est. Et is qui contra conscientiam vescitur, & dubitat de religione, & contemnit Deum. Cavendum est igitur ne intempestivo usu libertatis offendamus imbecillam fratrem: Potius annitendum est ut nostra moderatione eum confirmemus, in doctrina instituamus & in fide corroboremus. Conscientiam Idoli vocat, cum quis metuit ex infirmitate ne esu Idolothyti contaminetur. Debebat omninò conscientia regi cum lege naturae, tum expresso Dei verbo: Et iuxta hanc normam vel adprobare rectè facta: Vel damnare secus facta. Sed multi sunt errores in mente humana. Saepè homines non agnoscunt peccata, quae tamen sunt gravissima: Saepè metuunt vulnera conscientiae, ubi nihil est periculi. Quantumcunque autem intelligat homo in religione, semper cavere debet ne quid contra conscientiam suscipiat. Nam qui iudicat aliquid immundum esse ei est immundum. Et peccatum gravissimum est contemnere Dei iram. Primum igitur, perspicuum Dei verbum est consulendum, num quid in eo Deus prohibuerit: Quod intelligimus à Deo esse prohibitum, nequaquam est tentandum. Deinde si aliqua de re dubitamus, abstinendum potius est, quam ut dubitante conscientia quicquam suscipiamus: Hoc enim esset tentare Deum. Saepè autem praetendunt homines se conscientia impediri, quo minus hoc vel illud praestent officium, cum id potius iubeantur expresso Dei verbo. Horum petulantia graviter est taxanda & refutanda verbo. Semper enim verbo Dei conscientia regi debet.

Libertini finxerunt nulla scelera esse coram Deo peccata, modo quis seipsum in conscientia non accusaret, deinde laxant frena cupiditatibus, & conantur tollere iudicium conscientiae. Sed hi noticiam Dei in iniustitia detinent: & peccatum eorum cubat prae foribus, donec excitetur lege, semper ergò sciamus conscientiam oportere regi verbo Dei. Quidquid est contra Dei verbum, hoc polluit conscientiam. Argumentis deinde agit Paulus, & hortatur doctiores in religione, ut usum libertatis adstringant propter infirmos. Cibus inquit, & potus non reddit nos magis acceptos Deo: nec ditiores, nec pauperiores sumus in regno Dei, sive edamus, sive abstineamus. Est enim res externa. Meritò igitur usum libertatis omittimus, cùm videmus id postulare fratris necessitatem. Semper urget Paulus res externas à Spirituali regno Christi, quod est iustitia, pax & gaudium, in Spiritu sancto esse discernendas.

Videte, ne quodammodo potestas vestra ponat offendiculum infirmioribus. Si enim quis viderit te, qui cognitionem habes, in templo Idoli sedentem, numquid conscientia eius, qui infirmus est, aedificabitur ad edendum sacrificata Idolis? Et peribit infirmus frater tua cognitione, propter quem Christus est mortuus.

Haec principalis est sententia huius capitis: Non esse abutendum nostra libertate & potestate: sed studio sè cavendum, ne cuiquam simus offendiculo. Semper enim memores esse debemus mandati: diliges proximum tuum, sicut teipsum. Et non tantum nostri, sed totius corporis Christi rationem habere debemus.

Scandalum igitur datum est, non tantum externum aliquot scelus, aut factum, aut dogma contra verbum Dei, sed etiam intempestivus usus libertatis, quo proximi conscientia vulneratur aut in errorem inducitur.

Si inquit infirmuste viderit accumbentem in sacrario Idoli, ipsius conscientia aedificabitur. Id est, invitabitur, permovebitur, ut una comedat de Idolothyto, etiam si non habeat eam cognitionem, quam tu habes. Sic cùm Petrus subducebat se ex commèrcio gentium, simul & Barnabas inducebatur in errorem. Exempla enim doctorum in Ecclesia magna, vi pertrahunt auditores.

Gravissimùm est autem, quòd dicit: Et perit infirmus frater tuus tua scientia. Indicat enim Apostolus, cùm quid suscipitur contra conscientiam, tum excuti Spiritum sanctum, & extingui fidem. Exaggerat deinde peccatum à magnitudine precii, quo redempti sumus. Magnifaciendi & in nulla re offendendi sunt fratres pro quibus Christus est mortuus. Sed pro fratribus mortuus est Christus: Ergo nequaquam tam caro precio emptum hominem, ulla in re offendere debemus. Imò cum Christus non dubitaverit mori pro fratribus & pro nobis ipsis, quid est aequius quam ut usum libertatis nostrae adstringamus, ne salutem fratrum impediamus?

## 8:12
When you thus sin against the brothers and wound their weak conscience, you offend against Christ.

Another exaggeration of the offense and the stumbling block, from the effect. When you wound the weak conscience of the brothers, you not only harm men, and indeed those redeemed by the blood of Christ, which is surely most grave: but you also inflict an atrocious injury upon the Son of God himself. For he had already received the weak in faith: he had already grafted the weak into his own body, and acknowledged him as his own member: indeed, he had purchased and enslaved him to himself with his own precious blood: therefore, when you overturn them by your rashness so that they fall away from the faith, do you not inflict damage upon the body of Christ, and inflict an atrocious insult upon the Lord? Therefore, it must be guarded against with the highest religion, lest by an untimely use of liberty we be a stumbling block to the weak. But we must accommodate ourselves to the capacity of the weak, and seek their salvation rather than our own liberty, knowledge, and we ought to show our power, which we possess in the Lord. The voice of Paul agrees with the sublime saying of Christ: Whatever you did to one of these least ones, you did to me. Likewise, whatever you did not do to one of these least ones, you did not do to me. Than which saying nothing more grave can be said, both for deterring men from sin, and for exciting them to virtue and the love of the neighbor.

Latin:

Quum sic peccatis in fratres & vulneratis ipsorum conscientiam infirmam, in Christum delinquitis.

Alia exaggeratio delicti & offendiculi, ab effectu. Quum fratrum imbecillam conscientiam vulneratis, non tantum homines laeditis, & quidem sanguine Christi redemptos, quod sanè est gravissimum: verumetiam ipsum filium Dei atroci iniuria adficitis. Is enim infirmum in fide iam susceperat: is in severat iam infirmum corpori suo, & pro membro suo agnoscebat: imò sanguine suo precioso comparaverat & mancipaverat eum sibi: ergo cum evertitis vestra temeritate ita ut deficiat à fide, an non corpori Christi damnum infertis, & dominum atroci contumelia ad ficitis? Summa igitur religione cavendum est, ne intempestivo usu libertatis offendiculo simus infirmis. Sed nos ad captum infirmorum accomodare, & illorum potius quaerere salutem, quàm libertatem, scientiam, & potestatem nostram, quam in domino possidemus ostentare debemus. Congruit vox Pauli cum sublimi dicto Christi: Quidquid uni ex minimis his feceritis, mihi fecistis. Item, quidquid uni ex minimis his non fecistis, mihi non fecistis. Quo dicto nihil gravius dici potest, cum ad deterrendum homines à peccato, tum ad excitandum ad virtutem & proximi dilectionem.

## 8:13
Wherefore if food scandalizes my brother, I will not eat meat forever, lest I scandalize my brother.

Paul concludes from the preceding sentence, because it is most grave to afflict Christ Jesus with injury, that one should rather abstain forever from the eating of meats, than that by the untimely use of liberty, we should be a stumbling block to the brother for whom Christ has died. And he explains with what spirit he himself is affected, so that he may invite us also to the imitation of his example.

Latin:

Quapropter si esca scandalizat fratrem meum, non edam carnem in aeternum, ne fratrem meum scandalizem.

Concludit Paulus ex praecedenti sententia, quià sit gravissimum Christum Iesum iniuria adficere, potius in aeternum abstinendum esse ab esu carnium, quam ut usu libertatis intempestivo, fratri pro quo Christus est mortuus simus offendiculo. Et exponit quo ipse sit ad fectus animo, ut & nos ad sui exempli imitationem invitet.

## 8:13 Doctrines of the Place
Doctrines of the Place.

1. The principal point in this chapter is the doctrine concerning the use of Christian liberty, that in it pious prudence must be applied, and always for the salvation of the weak we must take counsel and take heed, lest we wound the conscience of any by indifferent things, nor arrogantly display the knowledge of liberty.

2. The second is concerning the love of neighbor: which ought to shine before all our counsels, endeavors, actions, and deliberations. For this everywhere looks to edification.

3. The third concerning the fruit of good works: When we love God and neighbor, from that we can gather, as from an effect, that we are known by God, cherished, loved, and ruled by him.

4. The fourth concerning the acknowledgment of the true God revealed in the Church, that namely there is one God, the eternal father of our lord Jesus Christ: and our lord Jesus Christ: from which father and son the Holy Spirit is never torn away, and that idols in the world are absolutely nothing.

5. The fifth, the doctrine concerning creation. Paul testifies that all things are from God, and were founded through the son, therefore all things did not flow together by chance from the atoms of Democritus.

6. The sixth concerning the end of the created world: Paul says that all things were created into him, that is, into his own glory and praise: therefore individual things ought to serve his glorious name. But in the first place man is destined for the praise and glory of God.

7. The seventh: That nothing is to be undertaken against conscience, and that he, who against conscience does something, he falls from grace and perishes.

8. Eighth: That food and drink do not commend us to God. For the kingdom of God does not consist in external rites or ceremonies: but it is life and righteousness and peace in the Holy Spirit. Therefore, in order to be most acceptable to God, one must look to his word, as to what he demands of us. Therefore it is permitted to us to use any food with thanksgiving: and it is a foul error that the Roman pontiff, under penalty of death, commands distinctions of foods, just as if the whole of religion were situated in food and drink.

9. Ninth concerning scandal and indeed that which is given. Now scandal given is either some external act against the law of God, or a false dogma fighting against sacred scripture, or an untimely use of liberty, by which the pious are both offended and seduced, and in them the Holy Spirit is saddened.

10. Tenth: That Jesus Christ died for us and also for the weak, and those who wound the consciences of the brethren, sin against the Lord Jesus Christ.

Latin:

Loci Doctrinae.

1. Praecipuus in hoc capite locus est doctrina de usu libertatis Christianae, quòd in eo pia sit adhibenda prudentia, & semper saluti infirmorum consulendum & cavendum, ne rebus mediis ullius conscientiam vulneremus, neque scientiam libertatis arroganter ostentemus.

2. Secundus est de dilectione proximi: quae omnibus consiliis, conatibus, actionibus, & deliberationibus nostris praelucere debet. Haec enim passim spectat aedificationem.

3. Tertius de fructu bonorum operum: Cùm nos diligimus Deum & proximum, inde colligere possumus, utpote ab effectu, quòd Deo simus noti, ab eo foveamur, diligamur, regamur.

4. Quartus de agnitione veri Dei patefacti in Ecclesia, quòd nimirum Unus sit Deus, aeternus pater domini nostri Iesu Christi: & dominus noster Iesus Christus: a quo patre & filio Spiritus sanctus nunquam divellitur, quòdque idola in mundo prorsus nihil sint.

5. Quintus, doctrina de creatione. Paulus testatur omnia ex Deo esse, & per filium esse condita, non ergò casu ex atomis Democriti confluxerunt omnia.

6. Sextus de fine conditi mundi: Paulus dicit omnia in ipsum, Id est, in ipsius gloriam & laudem condita esse: singula igitur ipsius glorioso nomini servire debent. In primis verò homo laudi & gloriae Dei destinatus est.

7. Septimus: Quòd nihil contra conscientiam sit suscipiendum, & quòd is, qui contra conscientiam agit aliquid, excidat gratiam & pereat.

8. Octavò: Quòd cibus & potus nos non commendent Deo. Nam regnum Dei non consistit in externis ritibus vel ceremoniis: sed est vita & iustitia & pax in Spiritu sancto. Ut ergò Deo acceptisimus, ad ipsius verbum respiciendum est, quid à nobis flagitet. Ergò licet nobis quovis cibo uti cum gratiarum actione: & foedus error est, quòd pontifex Roma: sub paena capitis mandat ciborum discrimina, perinde ac si tota religio sita esset in cibo & potu.

9. Nonus de scandalo & quidem dato. Est autem scandalum datum, aut externum aliquod factum contra legem Dei, aut falsum dogma pugnans cum sacra scriptura, aut intempestivus usus libertatis, quo & offenduntur & seducuntur pii, & in ipsis contristatur Spiritus sanctus.

10. Decimus: Quòd Iesus Christus pro nobis atque etiam pro infirmis sit mortuus, & qui vulnerant fratrum conscientias, in dominum Iesum Christum peccent.

## 9:1 Argument
CHAPTER IX.

As he taught in the eighth chapter that in the use of liberty one must spare the conscience of the weak: so in the ninth chapter he urges the same, his own example to the whole Church proposing. For he commemorates with what faith and readiness of mind he conducts himself in the ministry: that although he is free and has power in many things, yet he has not usurped it, but has always accommodated himself to the weaker ones, and even to his own disadvantage has always sought the salvation of the hearers and the edification of the Church. Having found an occasion, he indeed mixes in the doctrine concerning the reward to be given to the ministers of the Gospel: But this is the scope of the whole ninth chapter: And if Paul had great liberty and power in eating, and drinking, in taking a wife, in demanding a stipend according to the constitution of Jesus Christ, in omitting circumcision and in other things: yet he usurped none of these, lest he should be an offense to any man: so it also behooves us to be affected toward our brothers, that we should rather concede from our right of liberty, than that we should offend anyone: Indeed this is the true liberty of the Spirit, to be able to lack and abstain from all things when the matter demands it, so that we may gain some for Christ.

Latin:

CAPUT IX.

Ut in octavo capite docuit, in usu libertatis parcendum esse conscientiae infirmorum: Ita in nono capite idem urget, suum exemplum toti Ecclesiae proponens. Commemorat enim qua fide & animi promptitudine versetur in ministerio: quòd etsi sit liber & in multis rebus habeat potestatem, tamen eam non usurpaverit, sed semper sese accommodaverit infirmioribus, et cum suo etiam incommodo quaesiverit semper salutem auditorum & aedificationem Ecclesiae. Nactus occasionem miscet quidem doctrinam de mercede danda ministris Evangelii: Verùm hic scopus est totius capitis noni: Et si Paulus magnam habuerit libertatem & potestatem in edendo, & bibendo, in duxenda uxore, in poscendo stipendio iuxta constitutionem Iesu Christi, in omittendo circumcisionem & in aliis: tamen nihil horum usurpavit, ne ulli homini esset offendiculo: ita & nos erga fratres adfectos esse decet, ut potius concedamus de iure nostro libertatis, quàm ut offendamus quemquam: Imò haec vera est Spiritus libertas, posse omnibus rebus carere & abstinere cum res postutat, ut aliquos lucremur Christo.

## 9:1-2
Am I not an Apostle? Am I not free? Have I not seen Jesus Christ our Lord? Are not you our work in the Lord? If I am not an Apostle to others, certainly I am to you. For the seal of my Apostleship you are in the Lord. This is my defense to those who judge me.

In order to illustrate his example more clearly, that he did not usurp his liberty, he first commemorates the amplitude of his office, the knowledge of liberty, the glory of revelation. I am, says the Apostle, an Apostle of Jesus Christ: therefore I could use great liberty and power before others in the Lord. For after the office of mediator, there is no more sublime office on earth than the office of the Apostles: To no order of men did Christ grant greater power on earth than to the Apostles: to whom he handed over the keys of the kingdom of heaven, and gave the power of casting out demons, and healing every kind of sick person. I am also free, as if he were to say: I certainly understand the doctrine concerning Christian liberty, I know that I have been liberated through Christ, not only from sin, death, Satan, the wrath of God and all evils, but also from all Mosaic laws and human traditions. And I, among the Apostles most of all, both by doctrine and by examples, have illustrated this doctrine concerning Christian liberty. I can also boast of the prerogative that I saw the Lord Jesus with my own eyes 1. Cor: 15. Act: 22. Act: 23.Act: 26. which did not happen to the fathers, nor to the holy kings, nor to the prophets: and otherwise it happened to very few of the elect.

I know that I excel many by this prerogative: And yet I do not abuse either my authority or my liberty, but I accommodate myself to the capacity of the weak. How much less ought they to abuse their liberty, who are placed in a far inferior rank? Paul then appeals to the very edification of the Corinthian Church: As a most certain proof, both of Paul's fidelity and of his great office and excellent gifts. This apology he says he opposes to those who judge him, that is, who spoke with little reverence about Paul the Apostle. This is indeed the most convenient method of all, both for refuting the detractions of the malevolent, and for demonstrating one's own faith and office: Namely, to exhibit a Church rightly instructed by our ministry, and well constituted: For thus our work itself, he says, bears testimony of our labor. The Church constituted by Moses, Samuel, David, Jehoshaphat, Isaiah, Hezekiah, Jeremiah, Nehemiah bears testimony, with what faith these men labored in the Church, and what God has wrought through these men. This is my apology, says Paul, as if he were to say: I shall not contend much with my calumniators: The Church itself, built by my ministry, bears living testimony concerning me. And thus he censures the false apostles, because they attribute much to themselves, boast greatly, and display their liberty in an untimely manner: And yet they produce little fruit in the Church.

Have we not power to eat and to drink? Have we not power to lead about a sister, a wife, as well as other apostles, and as the brethren of the Lord, and Cephas? Or I only and Barnabas, have not we power to forbear working (with our hands?)

By the examples of the other apostles he teaches that he is endowed with a notable liberty of eating any food and drink, of leading about a spouse, and of living from the ministry of the Gospel. Since, however, he does not use all these things, as he could by the best of rights, he clearly demonstrates that he values the salvation of the weak and the edification of the Church of Christ more than the use of his own liberty. And thus by his own notable example he teaches that, when the conscience of the weak is endangered, we ought rather to yield from our right of liberty than to urge our right with the scandal of the brethren: especially when nothing is taken away from the glory of God, nor does our salvation suffer any impediment or loss.

The Mosaic law having been abrogated, it is granted to the Church that it may eat any food: For the earth is the Lord's, and the fullness thereof: And every creature of God is good, which is received with thanksgiving.

From this passage it is also manifest that marriage is honorable for all, and prohibited to no order of men. For Paul testifies that most of the Apostles, and especially the brothers of the Lord, James the Less, Simeon, and Jude Thaddeus, and Peter, had wives, and led them about in their travels and ministry. It is certain, therefore, that it is a doctrine of demons that the Roman Pontiff and the pontifical Bishops prohibit legitimate marriage to priests.

He also adds that he has the power not to perform mechanical labors, and to live only from the ministry of the Gospel. For the laborer is worthy of his hire. Since, therefore, the Apostles and pastors are compelled to serve the whole Church with the most difficult labor of teaching and administering the sacraments, equity itself demands that they be nourished by the stipends of the Church. For thus also our Lord Jesus Christ ordained: And the Apostles undoubtedly demanded sustenance from their hearers, so that they might be free for studies and prayers, and they abstained from mechanical labors. Paul, however, in order to demonstrate all the more clearly that he did not carry about the doctrine of the Gospel for the sake of gain, but only sought the glory of God and the edification of the Church, did not demand a stipend, nor was he a burden to any congregation: But he provided for himself the necessities of life with his own hands. Barnabas followed the example of Paul. By this example again he teaches that he did not use his right: But the glory of God, and the edification of the Church he has preferred far above the use of his own liberty: Which affection of piety he wishes other teachers of the Church to imitate.

Who serves at his own charges? Who plants a vineyard, and does not eat of its fruit? Who feeds a flock, and does not eat of the milk of the flock? Do I say these things only in a human manner? Does not the law also say these things? For it is written in the law of Moses: You shall not muzzle the ox that treads out the grain. Is it for oxen that God is concerned? Does He not say this for our sake? For it was written for our sake: that he who plows, ought to plow in hope: And he who threshes in hope, ought to be a partaker of his hope.

There are two serious reasons why Paul treats the passage concerning the bestowing of stipends and food upon the ministers of the Gospel somewhat more copiously and vigorously. The first is, that he may so much the more illustrate his own abstinence in the use of liberty, when he relinquishes those things which he could demand by the best of rights, and thus inflame his hearers to the imitation of his example. The second is, that he may cut off the occasion for evil men to abuse the example of Paul, who are accustomed to slander and traduce the ministers of the Gospel demanding the due reward of their labors. The manifest enemies of the Gospel not only give no stipends to pious pastors, but furthermore persecute them with every kind of punishment.

In the Church and among the hearers of the heavenly word, many are found who are either Epicureans from the herd of swine, or who simulate piety through hypocrisy. These provide food for the ministers of the Gospel and their children and families most grudgingly and peevishly. They frequently shout that pastors are greedy, that they cannot be satisfied: everywhere they subtract and deduct from the revenues attributed to the Church, and they kill many miserable pastors and their families with hunger. Therefore, so that Paul may refute this injustice, impiety, and ingratitude, and take care that no one abuses the example of Paul for that calumny, or denies a just reward to any pastor: he treats this passage at length and gravely concerning the stipends to be given to pious pastors.

First, he argues from the example of human affairs. No one serves as a soldier at his own expense. The pastor of the Church serves as a soldier for Christ and the Gospel: therefore let him be nourished by a just stipend. He who plants a vineyard, enjoys the grapes. Therefore, let the pastor planting the vineyard of the Lord have food from his own labor. The shepherd of sheep enjoys the milk, and has a certain reward: therefore the spiritual pastor, who presides over the flock and the clergy of the Lord, must entirely be nourished and sustained with his whole family.

Secondly, he argues from the testimony of God. He says that the Holy Scripture itself, which ought to be the norm of all our actions, commands that the mouth of the ox that treads out the grain should not be bound: signifying that the one laboring a just reward must be granted. As to what he says, does God care for oxen? He does not deny the universal providence of God, by which God provides for individual creatures. For the sayings are well known: Psalm: 147. Who gives food to all flesh, who gives to the beasts their food and to the young ravens that call upon him. Likewise: Look at the birds of the air: For they do not sow nor reap, nor gather into barns: And your heavenly father feeds them, Matt: 6. But he warns that this law was not written for the sake of oxen only, but rather for our sake, so that we might learn from it that the laboring minister is not to be defrauded of food and a just reward. If God wills that the ox treading the grain be nourished from the crop. Therefore it is much more the will of God that the plowman should plow in hope, and receive the fruit of his labors: And that the reapers and threshers should become partakers of the crops. Thus also it is most equitable that the ministers of the Gospel, who serve the Church with the word, and are compelled to neglect their own domestic affairs, should be fed and sustained with necessary stipends.

If we have sown spiritual goods for you, is it a great thing if we reap your carnal ones? If others are partakers of this power over you, why not rather we? But we have not used this power: But we suffer all things, lest

Latin:

Annon sum Apostolus? Annon sum liber? Nunquid Iesum Christum dominum nostrum vidi? Annon opus nostrum vos estis in domino? si aliis non sum Apostolus, certè vobis sum. Nam sigillum mei Apostolatus vos estis in domino. Haec mea sit defensio erga eos, qui me diiudicant.

Ut magis illustret suum exemplum, quòd non usurpaverit suam libertatem, primùm commemorat amplitudinem sui muneris, cognitionem libertatis, gloriam revelationis. Ego, inquit Apostolus sum Iesu Christi: itaque magna libertate & potestate prae caeteris in domino uti possem. Nullum enim, post mediatoris officium, sublimius munus est in terris, quàm officium Apostolorum: Nulli ordini hominum maiorem potestatem in terris concessit Christus, quàm Apostolis: quibus tradidit claves regni coelorum, & dedit potestatem eiiciendi daemonia, & sanandi omnis generis aegrotos. Sum etiam liber, quasi dicat: Ego sanè intelligo doctrinam de libertate Christiana, scio me per Christum liberatum esse, non solum à peccato, morte, Satana, ira Dei & omnibus malis, sed etiam ab omnibus legibus Mosaicis & traditionibus humanis. Et ego inter Apostolos omnium maximè, & doctrina & exemplis, hanc doctrinam de libertate Christiana illustravi. Gloriari etiam de praerogativa possum, quòd dominum Iesum meis oculis vidi 1. Cor: 15. Act: 22. Act: 23.Act: 26. quòd nec patribus, nec sanctis regibus, nec prophetis contigit: & alioquin paucissimis electis contigit.

Hac praerogativa scio me multos antecellere: Et tamen non abutor mea vel authoritate vel libertate, sed me accommodo ad infirmorum captum. Quantò minus abuti debent sua libertate, qui gradu longè inferiori positi sunt? Provocat deinde Paulus ad ipsam Ecclesiae Corinthiacae aedificationem: Tanquàm documentum certissimum, & fidelitatis Pauli & magni muneris & excellentium donorum. Hanc apologiam dicit se opponere iis, qui ipsum diiudicent, id est, qui parum reverenter de Paulo Apostolo loquebantur. Est sanè haec omnium commodissima ratio, & refutandi malevolorum obtrectationes, & demonstrandi suam fidem & munus: Nimirum exhibere Ecclesiam rectè eruditam nostro ministerio, & probè constitutam: Sic enim ipsum opus nostrum, dicit de nostro labore testimonium. Ecclesia constituta à Moyse, Samuele, Davide, Iosaphath, Iesaia, Hiskia, Hieremia, Nehemia testimonium dicit, qua fide isti laborarint in Ecclesia, & quae Deus per isto homines sit operatus. Haec mea est apologia inquit Paulus, quasi dicat: Non multum contendam cum meis calumniatoribus: Ipsa Ecclesia ministerio meo aedificata, de me vivum dicit testimonium. Atque ita perstringit pseudo apostolos, quòd multum sibi tribuant, valdè glorientur, libertatem intempestivè ostentent: Et tamen exiguum producant fructum in Ecclesia.

An non habemus potestatem edendi & bibendi: An non habemus potestatem circumducendi sororem uxorem, quemadmodum & reliqui Apostoli, & fratres domini & Cephas? An tantum ego & Barnabas potestatem non habemus, non laborandi (manibus?)

Exemplis aliorum Apostolorum docet se instructum esse insigni libertate vescendi quolibet cibo & potu, circumducendi coniugem, & ex ministerio Evangelii victitandi. Cùm autem his omnibus non utatur, ut optimo iure posset, liquidò demonstrat se pluris facere salutem infirmorum, & Ecclesiae Christi aedificationem, quàm suae libertatis usum. Atque ita suo insigni exemplo docet, cùm periclitatur infirmorum conscientia, debere nos potiùs de nostro iure libertatis cedere, quàm cum scandalo fratrum ius nostrum urgere: Praesertim cùm nihil decedit gloriae Dei, nec salus nostra ullum patitur impedimentum vel damnum.

Abrogata lege Mosaica, concessum est Ecclesiae, ut quolibet cibo vescatur: Domini enim est terra, & omnis plenitudo eius: Et omnis creatura Dei bona est, quae cum gratiarum actione percipitur.

Ex hoc etiam loco manifestum est, coniugium honorabile esse omnibus, & nulli ordini hominum prohibitum. Testatur enim Paulus plerosque Apostolos & inprimis fratres domini, Iacobum minorem, Symeonem, & Iudam Thaddeum, ac Petrum habuisse coniuges, easque in peregrinationibus & ministerio circumduxisse. Certum est igitur doctrinam esse daemoniorum, quòd Roma: Pontifex & Episcopi pontificii prohibent sacerdotibus legitimum coniugium.

Addit etiam se potestatem habere, non exercendi operas Mechanicas, & tantum ex ministerio Evangelii victitandi. Dignus est enim operarius mercede sua. Cùm ergò Apostoli & pastores servire cogantur toti Ecclesiae difficilimo labore docendi, & administrandi sacramenta, ipsa aequitas postulat, ut stipendiis Ecclesiae alantur. Sic enim & dominus noster Iesus Christus ordinavit: Et Apostoli haùd dubiè poposcerunt alimenta à suis auditoribus, ut studiis & precationibus vacare possent, abstinuerunt ab operis mechanicis. Paulus autem, ut tantò liquidius demonstraret se non quaestus gratia circumferre doctrinam Evangelii, sed tantùm quaerere gloriam Dei & Ecclesiae aedificationem, non poposcit stipendium, nec ulli caetui fuit oneri: Sed propriis manibus vitae necessaria sibi comparavit. Pauli exemplum secutus est Barnabas. Hoc rursus exemplo docet se non usum suo iure: Sed gloriam Dei, & aedificationem Ecclesiae longè antetulisse usui suae libertatis: Quem pietatis ad fectum alios Ecclesiae doctores vult imitara.

Quis militat propriis stipendiis? Quis plantat vineam, & non comedit ex fructibus eius? quis pascit gregem, & non vescitur lacte gregis? Num haec tantum humano more loquor? Annon & lex haec dicit? Scriptum est enim in lege Mosis: Bovi trituranti non obligabis os. Num curae est Deo de bobus? Annon propter nos haec dicit? propter nos enim scriptum est: quòd, qui arat, in spe arare debeat: Et qui triturat sub spe, spei suae particeps esse debeat.

Duae sunt graves causae, cur Paulus locum de tribuendis stipendiis & alimentis ministris Evangelii paulo copiosius & nervosius tractat. Prima est, ut tantò magis illustret suam abstinentiam in usu libertatis, cùm relinquat ea, quae optimo iure flagitare posset, atque ita auditores suos ad imitationem sui exempli accendat. Altera est, ut praescindat occasionem abutendi exemplo Pauli malis hominibus, qui ministros Evangelii poscentes debitam mercedem laborum calumniari & traducere solent. Hostes manifesti Evangelii, non solum nulla dant stipendia piis pastoribus, sed insuper eos persequuntur omni genere suppliciorum.

In Ecclesia autem & inter auditores verbi coelestis multi reperiuntur, qui aut Epicurei de grege porci sunt, aut hypocrisi simulant pietatem. Hi egerrimè & morosissimè praebent alimenta ministris Evangelii & eorum liberis & familiis. Subinde vociferantur, avaros esse pastores, non posse eos expleri: Passim subtrahunt & deducunt de reditibus Ecclesiae attributis, & multos miseros pastores & eorum familias enecant fame. Hanc ergò iniustitiam, impietatem & ingratitudinem ut refellat Paulus, & caveat, ne quis ad istam caluminiam exemplo Pauli abutatur, aut ulli pastori deneget iustani mercedem: Prolixè & graviter hunc locum tractat de stipendiis dandis piis pastoribus.

Primùm argumentatur ab exemplo rerum humanarum. Nemo propriis militat stipendiis. Pastor Ecclesiae militat Christo & Evangelio: alatur igitur iusto stipendio. Qui vineam plantat, fruitur vuis. Pastor ergò plantans vineam domini, habeat ex labore suo alimenta. Pastor ovium lacte fruitur, et certam habet mercedem: spiritualis ergò pastor, qui gregi & clero domini praeest, omninò alendus & sustentandus est cum tota sua familia.

Secundò argumentatur à testimonio Dei. Ipsa inquit sacra scriptura, quae omnium actionum nostrarum norma esse debet, praecipit, ut bovi trituranti non obligetur os: Significans labor anti iustam mercedem esse concedendam. Quòd dicit, num boves curae sunt Deo? Non negat providentiam Dei universalem, qua Deus singulis creaturis prospicit. Nota sunt enim dicta: Psalm: 147. Qui dat escam omni carni, qui dat iumentis escam ipsorum & pullis corvorum invocantibus eum. Item: Intuemini volucres coeli: Quia non ferunt neque metunt, neque convehunt in horrea: Et pater vester coelestis alit illas, Matt: 6. Sed monet istam legem non esse boum causa tantum scriptam, sed magis propter nos, ut inde disceremus, labor antem ministrum alimento & iusta mercede non esse defraudandum. Si bovem tritur antem de segete nutriri vult Deus. Ergò Dei voluntas multò magis est, ut agricola sub spe aret, & laborum fructum percipiat: Utque messores & trituratores frugum fiant participes. Sic & ministros Evangelii, qui serviunt Ecclesiae verbo, & interearem familiarem negligere coguntur, aequissimum est ali & necessariis stipendiis sustentari.

Si nos vobis spiritualia bona seminavimus, an magnum est, quòd carnalia vestra messuerimus? Si caeteri potestatis erga vos participes sunt, cur non magis nos? Sed non usurpavimus hanc potestatem: Sed omnia sufferimus, ne

## 9:12
we give an offense to the Gospel of Christ.

The third argument is from a comparison of greater things. Spiritual things are infinitely more excellent, namely the word of God, the knowledge of the true God, the knowledge of the mediator, consolation against death, sin, and Satan, the distribution of the sacraments, absolution from sins, the doctrine of how one might arrive at eternal life, and the whole kingdom of Christ, than carnal and earthly goods, such as lodging, food, drink, clothes, money, and the necessities of this life. Since, therefore, we Apostles impart spiritual goods to you, equity itself commands that you in turn communicate to us the necessities of this life. This is a most weighty argument, which all pious people ought to seriously weigh, and stir themselves to gratitude toward their pastors. It cannot be expressed by the voice of any man how great is the ingratitude of that man who denies his pastor a just reward.

If others are partakers: The fourth is an argument from the example of other teachers: who both receive stipends and sustenance from the Church, and indeed from the Corinthian one: whence Paul infers that he can do so much more justly because he is ὀικης ἡς and in a certain way the first founder, who laid the first foundations of that Church.

But he returns here to his purpose; that he does not use this liberty and power as much as he could: and he subjoins the final cause, with what intention he did this, not that he might hunt for empty glory, but that he might take heed in every way, lest he should place any stumbling block for the Gospel of Jesus Christ. So that all might understand that Paul does not seek what is his own, but what is of Jesus Christ.

Do you not know, that those who perform sacred rites, eat from the sacrifice? Those who stand by the sanctuary, have a share in the sanctuary?

This is the fifth argument, drawn from the example of the priests and Levites who, when they were sacrificing, slaughtering the victim, and serving the altar, according to the law had their share of the offerings. Now the glory of the new testament is greater and has greater brightness than the old testament: And the pastors of the Churches, by teaching the people, sustain a more difficult duty than the priests and Levites slaughtering victims. It is just, therefore, that they be nourished in the ministry. God most diligently commanded in the Mosaic law that food be provided to the priests and Levites: so that they might be able to be free for the reading of scripture. Hence Paul commands us to seek the doctrine, by what piety pastors and ministers in the new testament are to be nourished.

For so also the Lord ordained, that those who those who preach the Gospel, should live from the Gospel. I, however, have used none of these.

The sixth and principal argument is this, from the authority and constitution of the Son of God, our Lord Jesus Christ. He is altogether impious who dares to infringe or slander the constitution or ordinance of our Lord Jesus Christ. But Jesus Christ himself, the head, redeemer, and savior of the Church, and author of the καὶ βραβευτής ministry, brought this law and thus ordained: That those who preach the Gospel, should live from the Gospel: That is, that they be nourished by the Church and the hearers with honest stipends, by which they may be able to sustain themselves and their family. Without doubt, Paul looked to the sermon of Christ, Matth: 10. The laborer is worthy of his hire. And Christ repeated this law and ordinance several times in his sermons. It is therefore most just to seek honest and necessary stipends for nourishing a family in return for the labor of teaching in the Church.

Latin:

quod offendiculum demus Evangelio Christi.

Tertium argumentum est à comparatione maiorum. In infinitum praestantiora sunt Spiritualia, scilicet verbum Dei, agnitio veri Dei, noticia mediatoris, consolatio contra mortem, peccatum, Satanam, distributio sacramentorum, absolutio à peccatis, doctrina quomodo quis pervenire possit ad vitam aeternam, & totum regnum Christi, quàm carnalia, & terrena bona, ut sunt hospicium, cibus, potus, vestes, pecunia, huius vitae necessaria. Cùm igitur nos Apostoli vobis spiritualia bona impertiamus, ipsa aequitas iubet, ut vicissim nobis communicetis huius vitae necessaria. Gravissimum est hoc argumentum, quod omnes pii seriò expendere debent, & sese ad gratitudinem erga pastores excitare. Nullius hominis voce exponi potest, quanta sit ingratitudo eius hominis, qui denegat suo pastori iustam mercedem.

Si caeteri participes sunt: Quartum est argumentum ab exemplo aliorum doctorum: qui & accipiant ab Ecclesia & quidem Corinthiaca stipendia & alimenta: unde Paulus infert se multò iustius id facere posse eò quòd sit ὀικης ἡς & quodammodo primus conditor, qui prima fundamenta eius Ecclesiae iecerit.

Redit autem hîc ad suum institutum; se non usum esse ista libertate & potestate, ut maximè potuerit: & subnectit causam finalem, quo consilio hoc secerit, non ut inanem gloriam aucuparetur, sed ut omnibus modis caveret, ne ullum offendiculum poneret Evangelio Iesu Christi. Ut omnes intelligerent Paulum non quaerere quae sua sint, sed quae Iesu Christi.

An nescitis, quòd ii, qui sacra faciunt, ex sacrificio comedunt? Qui sacrario adsistunt, partem in sacrario habent?

Quintum hoc est argumentum, ductum ab exemplo sacerdotum & Levitarum qui cum sacrificarent, mactarent victimam, & servirent altari, secundum legem partem suam habebant de oblationibus. Iàm novi testamenti gloria maior est & maiorem habet claritatem, quàm vetus testamentum: Et pastores Ecclesiarum, docendo populum, difficilius sustinent munus, quàm sacerdotes & Levitae mactantes victimas. Aequum est igitur ut in ministerio alantur. Diligentissimè praecepit Deus in lege Mosaica, ut alimenta praeberentur sacerdotibus & levitis: ut lectioni scripturae vacare possent. Hinc Paulus iubet nos petere doctrinam, qua pietate pastores & ministri in novo testamento sint alendi.

Sic enim et Dominus ordinavit, ut hi qui Evangelion annunciant, de Evangelio vivant. Ego tamen nullo horum sum usus.

Sextum & praecipuum est hoc argumentum ab authoritate & constitutione filii Dei domini nostri Iesu Christi. Impius omninò est, qui audet infringere aut calumniari constitutionem seu ordinationem domini nostri Iesu Christi. Ipse autem Iesus Christus caput, redemptor & salvator Ecclesiae, & author καὶ βραβευτής ministerii, tulit hanc legem & sic ordinavit. Ut hi, qui annunciant Evangelion, ex Evangelio vivant: Hoc est, ab Ecclesia & auditoribus honestis stipendiis alantur, quibus se & familiam sustentare possint. Haud dubiè respexit Paulus ad concionem Christi, Matth: 10. Dignus est operarius mercede sua. Et Christus hanc legem & ordinationem aliquoties in suis concionibus repetivit. Iustissimum est igitur, petere honesta & necessaria stipendia ad alendam familiam pro labore docendi in Ecclesia.

## 9:15
I, however, have used none of these: he says. He repeats his purpose: that he certainly abstained from the use of his liberty, when he could have sought, done, and usurped many things by most just right, so that by this example of his he might invite the Corinthians to imitation, so that, namely, they might willingly yield from their own right for the sake of the edification of the Church.

I have not written these things, however, so that it might be done so with me. For I would rather die than suffer that anyone should make my boasting void. For if I preach the Gospel, there is no reason for me to boast. For necessity is laid upon me. But woe to me if I do not preach the Gospel. For if I do this willingly, I have a reward: if unwillingly, a stewardship is entrusted to me.

This is an objection, by which he meets the tacit suspicion of the Corinthians. For because Paul taught so prolixly and with many most weighty arguments brought forward that by the most just right food and stipends are owed to those serving the Gospel, the Corinthians could suspect that Paul had obliquely censured the Corinthians, because they were less grateful toward him, and that under the person of others he is asking for a stipend from them. Therefore, so that he may forestall this sinister suspicion, Paul excepts that he did not write these things with this intention: But rather for the sake of other ministers and the whole Church: lest pastors and ministers be defrauded of their due reward and stipends under the pretext of Paul's example, and lest the hearers of the Gospel show themselves ungrateful or difficult toward the heralds of the word. And so that he may remove every suspicion, he commemorates how much he values this boasting, that he preaches the Gospel freely, It were better for me to die than that any man should make my glorying void. As if he were to say: I value this glorying, that I announce the Evangelion without stipend and freely, more than this life of mine. For Paul sees that a copious reward is laid up for him in the heavens, by which this faithfulness of his will be compensated. If, he says, I preach the Gospel, I have nothing to glory of: for necessity is laid upon me; yea, woe is unto me, if I preach not the Gospel. Here he explains the necessity of his office: That it was enjoined and severely imposed upon him by divine command that he should sound the doctrine of the Gospel in the world. He undoubtedly looks back to the history of his conversion, where Christ spoke to him from heaven, Acto: 9. And expressly said to Ananias: He is a chosen vessel unto me, to bear my name before the Gentiles, and kings, and the children of Israel: And caught up into the third heaven he undoubtedly received a severe command to preach the Evangelion. Therefore he says that necessity is laid upon him, and woe unto him if he does not preach: This is, most grievous punishments would be to be expected by him if he were to omit the preaching. From this passage it is manifest that the form of words is sound, when it is said, Good works commanded by God are necessary. It is necessary that we obey God: for the severe commands of God are by no means to be neglected, or placed in doubt. But that Majoristic appendix, that they are necessary for salvation, is impious and false. For grace alone Of God, the merit of Jesus Christ alone, and faith alone is necessary for salvation. Good works, however, are necessary by reason of the divine command, and they are necessary for the illustration of God's glory on earth, and for the testimony of our faith.

If I do this willingly, he says, I have a reward: The Son of God repays with an abundant reward all the labors of the pious undertaken in faith: But especially for those teaching the Gospel, He has laid up an unfading crown of glory in the heavens. 2. Timoth: 4. Daniel says, those who instruct others unto righteousness shall shine like the sun in the firmament of heaven: Cap: 12. If I do it unwillingly, a dispensation is committed unto me: Even if I were not of a ready mind to teach the Gospel, as the flesh often struggles against the spirit, and turns away from hatreds, exiles, and dangers, which always follow the preaching of the Gospel as inseparable companions: Nevertheless, I could not omit the calling: The dispensation, that is, the ministry of preaching the Gospel, has been entrusted and committed to me. Therefore, whether I perform it with a ready or an unwilling mind, it is altogether necessary that I obey the command of God and the calling imposed upon me.

What then is my reward? That when I preach the Gospel, I may make the Gospel of Christ without charge and without expense:

That I abuse not my power in the Gospel.

The very preaching of the Gospel was commanded to Paul by God: but that he should preach freely and without a stipend, was not commanded to him. Of this his faithfulness and readiness, therefore, he boasts. And this very boasting he calls his wage and reward, as if he were to say: I do not ask for a wage from you. It is a notable reward to me that it is permitted to me to boast against false teachers and slanderers, that the Church has incurred no expenses on my account because of the Gospel, and that I have labored in the ministry for free. He then repeats the final cause of this plan of his, namely, that he might not abuse his power in the Gospel, that he might not in any way hinder the course of the Gospel, or place a stumbling block before any man.

For whereas I am free from all, I have made myself the servant of all: that I might gain the more. And I became to the Jews as a Jew, that I might gain the Jews. To those that are under the law, as if I were under the law, that I might gain them that were under the law.

Here at last the Apostle returns to the principal scope of this chapter. For his own example he proposes to the whole Church that, since he is most free in Jesus Christ, he judges all things to be clean for himself, he is bound to no man in his conscience, and by the Apostolic Spirit he understands the doctrine concerning Christian liberty, he is restricted by no Mosaic laws, by no traditions of men. Nevertheless, as if he had reduced himself into servitude, so that he might gain more for Christ, he proposes his own example to the whole Church to be imitated. But because Libertines and Epicureans, alien to the alacrity of confession, are accustomed to wickedly abuse this testimony of Paul, as if this Paul were teaching here to collude with men of all sects and to connive at all crimes, it is altogether necessary that the false and impious interpretation of the Pauline saying be refuted, and the sound meaning of the Holy Spirit be shown. First, let the entire doctrine concerning Christian liberty be in sight, which is not a barbaric license of sinning, or of doing whatever one wishes, and of obeying no laws, neither divine nor human. The world, through madness, calls this ferocity and petulance liberty, when it is the foulest servitude of all. For he who follows only his own impure desires is a most miserable slave of Satan and of sin, which finally rushes of its own accord into eternal destruction. Just as the Lord teaches: He who commits sin is a slave of sin. But true Christian liberty is that excellent happiness and glory that, through our Lord Jesus Christ, we have been freed we are from sin, from the wrath of God, from the curse of the law, from death, and from the tyranny of Satan, and also we have been gifted with the Holy Spirit who kindles new light, righteousness, and life in us, and restores lost powers so that we may serve God with a spontaneous and free spirit according to His word, and also that no Mosaic law, nor any traditions of men regarding religion can bind our conscience before God, but that all things are pure to the pure, and that every creature of God is good, to be used with thanksgiving. Of this spiritual liberty Christ speaks John 8 If the Son has set you free, you will be truly free, and Paul Gal. 5 Stand fast therefore in the liberty wherewith Christ has called you, and 1 Cor. 7, You have been bought with a great price, do not become the servants of men, and Isa. 52 You were sold for nothing, you shall be redeemed without money: And for the sake of teaching, four degrees of liberty are rightly posited.

The first degree is liberation from sin, from the wrath of God, from the curse of the law, from sin, from death, from the tyranny of the Devil, and from all infernal servitude: And conversely, the imputation of the righteousness of the Son of God and reconciliation with the eternal Father. This liberty is a greater good than to rule over many worlds, and to abound in the abundance of all things. Scripture inculcates this liberty everywhere, as Rom. 6 You are not under the law but under grace: Likewise, Rom. 8 The law of the Spirit of life in Christ Jesus has set me free from the law of sin and death.

The second degree is the gift of the Holy Spirit and the renewal itself of the powers, which the Holy Spirit instructs with new force and liberty so that we no longer acknowledge, invoke, fear, and love God out of the compulsion of the law with a resisting nature, but with a prompt and spontaneous Spirit. Paul speaks of this degree in Rom: 8. For you have not received the spirit of bondage again to fear, but you have received the spirit of adoption of sons, in which we cry Abba Father, and 2. Cor: 3. Where the Spirit is, there is liberty: But we all beholding the glory of the Lord with open face are transformed into the same image from glory to glory, as by the Spirit of the Lord.

The third degree is the liberation from the Mosaic forensic and ceremonial laws. For after the Messiah was exhibited, and the warfare of Jerusalem completed: The whole law of Moses was abrogated and no longer binds those born from the seed of Abraham. Paul speaks of this liberty in Coloss: 2. Let no man judge you in meat or in drink, or in respect of holy days or of the new moons or of the sabbaths, which are a shadow of things to come: But the body is all this which is of Christ and pertains to his spiritual kingdom.

The fourth degree is that no traditions of men regarding religion can bind our conscience before God. Of this degree Paul speaks Coloss: 2. If therefore you have died with Christ from the elements of the world, why, as though living in the world, are you subject to decrees? Do not touch, do not taste, do not handle, which all are consumed and perish by their very use, as being the precepts and doctrines of men.
