Constat Paulum testari, quod omnes, quot quot de hoc pane manducant, participes fiant corporis & sanguinis Iesu Christi, sive sint digni, hoc est, fideles, & Spiritu Dei praediti: Sive sint indigni, hypocritae, securi & expertes fidei. Argumentationem Pauli sic paucis complectimur:

Id quod est participatio seu communicatio corporis Christi, cum eo necesse est verè exhiberi corpus Christi.

Sed panis benedictionis est communicatio corporis Christi.

Ergò cum pane benedicto verè exhibetur corpus Iesu Christi.

Item.

Id quod est participatio corporis Iesu Christi, id est verum & essentiale corpus Christi:

Sed panis benedictus est participatio corporis Christi:

Ergò panis benedictus est verum & essentiale corpus Christi.

Item.

Omnes, qui manducant id, quod est participatio corporis Christi, eos necesse est fieri participes corporis Christi.

Sed multi hypocritae & indigni manducant panem benedictum, qui teste Paulo, est communicatio corporis Christi.

Ergò multi hypocritae participes fiunt corporis Christi.

Item.

Nulla res dici potest participatio corporis Christi, nisi quae sumpta & usurpata iuxta Christi mandatum, corporis ipsius facit nos participes.

Panis benedictus, teste Paulo, est participatio corporis Christi.

Ergò panis benedictus, samptus iuxta Christi institutionem, facit nos vescentes in coena participes corporis ipsius.

IIII. ARGUMENTUM. A Manducatione Indignorum.

Quod si tantum spiritualiter manducaremus carnem Christi per fidem, ut Calvinistae contendunt, & in sacra coena tantum vim & efficaciam absentis corporis Christi perciperemus, & panis benedictus tantum esset symbolum corporis Christi, in coelum evecti & procul à nobis positi, omnino necesse esset statuere indignos, securos, hypocritas & salvifica fide carentes, nequaquam fieri participes corporis & sangùinis domini. Indigni enim & à fide alieni, nequaquam percipiunt vim & efficaciam corporis Christi: Non liberantur à peccato, non vivificantur Spiritu Christi, sed manent in morte & haerent sub ira Dei, exclusi ab omni communicatione beneficiorum Christi: Qui non credit in filium, vitam non videbit, sed ira Dei manet super ipsum, Paulus verò perspicuè docet, non solum fideles, sed & indignos & securos fieri participes corporis Christi in sacra coena dominu Severa enim sententia adfirmat Apostolus Paulus eos, qui indignè de hoc pane edunt, reos fieri corporis Christi. Indignè de hoc pane edere diciteos, qui sese non probant, hoc est, qui sine poenitentia, sine vera contritione & fide temerè & audacter ad mensam domini accurrunt: Hos dicit reos fieri corporis & sanguinis Christi. Hic verò reatus gravissimus non contrabitur, nisi cum inturia infertur corpori & sanguini Christi: Iam si abest corpus & sanguis Christi, & tantum panem & vinum manducant & bibunt indigni, quomodo fiunt rei corporis & sanguinis Iesu Christi? Frivolum est, quod Calvinistae dicunt. Qui imaginem vel mandatum imperatoris contumelia adficit, in ipsum imperatorem contumeliosus esse habetur. Sic qui symbolo corporis Christi abutitur, in ipsum Christum dicitur esse contumeliosus. Non enim hoc tantum dicit Apostolus, quòd indignè manducans, ipsum Christum quodammodo iniuria adfecerit, sed quod reus factus sit corporis & sanguinis Christi. Ille autem alicuius rei reus peragitur, qui ipsam rem contumelio se seu nefariè tractavit. Et quidem hunc reatum ipso esu contrahi ab indignis testatur Paulus: Iudicium inquit sibi edit & bibit, non diiudicans corpus domini. Qui indignè edendo panem & indignè bibendo vinum benedictum, reus fit corporis Christi, & iudicium sibi edit & bibit, ipsum necesse est non solum panem & vinum, sed ipsum corpus & sanguinem Christi edendo & bibendo iniuria & contumelia adficere. Quòd Apostolus clarissima voce indicat, non diiudicans corpus domini, quasi dicat, eò quòd non discernit corpus & sanguinem Christi in sacra coena à communi cibo & potu, habet panem & vinum benedictum, ac si none essent corpus & sanguis domini nostri Iesu Christi, reus fit corporis et sanguinis domini, & provocat adversus se Dei iudicium & iram. Cur Paulus tam atroci sententia gravaret conscientiam eorum, qui indignè ad mensam domini accedunt, si non adesset verè corpus & sanguis Iesu Christi in coena Domini? Quomodo discerni poterit corpus Christi in coena domini, ab aliis cibis, quibus corporalem vitam sustentamus, cum non adsit, sed longissimè à terra absit, in coelo remotissimo? Non dicit Apostolus rem sacram à prophana, non dicit symbolum aut signum corporis à communi pane discernendum esse: Sed corpus domini ab alio cibo discernendum esse. Manifestum est igitur indignos etiam in sacra coena edere corpus Iesu Christi, licet ad iudicium.

Hoc vero demonstrato, quòd indigni edunt corpus Domini, & bibunt eius sanguinem in sacra coena: quemadmodum ex testimoniis Pauli evicimus: evidentissimè colligitur, in coena domini non tantum spiritualiter per fidem manducari carnem Christi: Sed etiam corporaliter, ore corporeo sumi cum pane corpus domini, & panem benedictum esse verum & substantiale corpus domini. Indigni enim & hypocritae non manducant carnem Christi spiritualiter per fidem: prorsus enim destituuntur fide & expertes sunt Spiritus Christi: Nec percipiunt vim & efficaciam corporis Christi, quin potius iudicium sibi edunt, exclusi ab omnibus beneficiis regni Christi: Et tamen manducant corpus Christi, & bibunt eius sanguinem indignè, teste Paulo, necesse est igitur, non tantum spiritualiter efficaciam corporis Christi in sacra coena distribui, sed etiam verum & substantiale corpus Christi in sacra coena adesse, & cum pane benedicto dari omnibus, qui sacra coena ut untur.

Huius argumenti tanta est firmitas & evidentia, ut nulla sophistica labefactari, nullis cavillis obscurari possit. Aliquoties incursionem in hoc argumentum fecerunt Calvinistae, sed statim splendore veritatis repressi, resilerunt. Effugiae primùm quaerunt in voce (indignè). Contendunt Paulum non loqui de hypocritis & fide salvifica carentibus: Sed de infirmis & negligenter ad coenam domini accedentibus: Qui non prorsus ab omni fide sunt alieni, sed tamen non satis sese probant, non satis reverenter ad percipiendum corpus domini accedunt. Hos dicunt reos fieri corporis domini, & iudicium sibi edere. Hîc iam cogitet pius & Deum timens animus, quid Satan quaerat per eiusmodi violentam depravationem verborum Pauli. Si Paulus illos vocat indignos, qui infirma vel exigua fide sunt praediti, & qui minus reverenter accedunt ad mensam Domini, an non omnium piorum animis scrupulus perniciosissimus iniectus erit? An non ex saluberrima medicina merum animae venenum efficient?

Quis nostrum est, quantavis luce & robore fidei sit praeditus, qui non sentiat in lucta suam imbecillitatem?

quis nostrum gloriari audet se satis reverenter ad sumendum corpus Iesu Christi accedere? Quis nostrum non deplorat & suam imbecillitatem & indignitatem? Iam si infirmi indignè edunt de isto pane: Ergò omnibus nobis statuendum erit, quoties ad mensam domini accedimus, nos reos fieri corporis & sanguinis Iesu Christi: cohorresco toto pectore, quoties virulentam istam cavillationem cogito. Ergò omnes edimus nobis iudicium, Etiam nos, qui seriò agimus poenitentiam, dolemus Deum nostris peccatis offensum esse, atque etiam verè credimus in filium Dei mediatorem & amplectimur Evangelion: fateri enim nos oportet ingentem in nobis esse infirmitatem fidei: Et iuxta Calvini interpretationem, infirmi indignè edunt de pane benedicto: Hoc scilicet est consolari infirmorum conscientias. An tibi culpa levis videtur, reum fieri corporis & sanguinis Iesu Christi? An non praestaret prorsus abstinere ab Eucharistiae usu, quàm gravissimo reatu obstringere conscientiam, etiam si non prorsus careas fide? Et quis unquam certos nos reddet cum fructu et in salutem nos uti coena domini? Cùm scire non possumus, an satis firma fide praediti simus, & num dignè accedamus ad mensam domini? Siquidem semper nos fateri oportet fidem languidiorem esse, quàm debebat esse, & multiplici infirmitate circumdatos nos esse. Quò ergò tendat ista Calvini cavillatio de indignis, cordato lectori obscurum non est. Fructum enim omnem, quem ex usurpatione Eucharistiae percipere debebamus, nimirum, ut confirmaretur & aleretur nostra languida fides planè aufert, & summè necessariam consolationem incertam nobis reddit. Detestemur igitur toto pectore perniciosam istam verborum Pauli depravationem. Indignos vocat Paulus impaenitentes, securos, qui sese non explorant, nec fide syncera amplectuntur promissionem gratiae, sed manent in peccatis contra conscientiam, & nihilominus per hypocrisin accedunt ad mensam domini. Paulus enim opponit inter se eos qui indignè de hoc pane edunt: & eos, qui sese explorant. Dicit enim, Si quis indignè de hoc pane edit, fit reus corporis Iesu Christi. Probet autem se ipsum homo, & sic de hoc pane edat. Eum, qui sese exploraverit nimirum vera paenitentia, qui ex animo dolet se peccatis offendisse Deum, & seriò adsentitur Evangelio, non dicit Apostolus reum fieri corporis Christi, Sed cum fiducia iubet eum accedere mensam domini, sive parva, sive magna fide sit praeditus. Indignos ergò intelligit hypocritas & securos, qui sunt expertes motuum poenitentiae, & tamen ad mensam domini accedunt.

Novam indignorum distinctionem fabricavit Eberus antea ignotam Ecclesiae. Alios nimirum indignos esse hypocritas, incredulos, securos, impaenitentes, qui corpus Christi in sacra coena manducent, ad iudicium: alios verò indignos esse ἀθεούς, merè profanos, Ecebolos, prorsus impios, Epicureos, qui totam religionem, vel ignorent, vel prorsus contemnant: Hos dicit non accipere corpus domini, etiamsi verba Christi ad eos sonent. Accipite, comedite, hoc est corpus meum, quia non sint membra Ecclesiae. Haec distinctio & nova, & periculosa, & verbis Pauli contraria est. Paulus enim disertè pronunciat de omnibus indignè manducantibus, quòd rei fiant corporis & sanguinis Iesu Christi, & quòd sibi iudicium edant, eò quòd non discernant corpus domini. Iam ipso Ehero teste, Apostolus non tulisset tam atrocem sententiam de indignè manducantibus, nisi sensisset indignos edere ipsum corpus, & bibere sanguinem Iesu Christi. Ergò cùm de atheis, Ecebolis, & Epicureis, planè impiis Eucharistia utentibus dici non possit, quòd non fiant rei corporis & sanguinis Christi, & quòd sibi non edant, nec bibant iudicium, necesse est fateri quòd tam athei, Eceboli, & planè Epicurei edant corpus & bibant sanguinem Christi, atque hypocritae, securi & infideles Christiani.

Aut demonstrandum erit, quod illi qui minus peccant, nimirum securitate & impoenitentia rei fiant corporis Christi dum, Eucharistia ut untur: Qui vero gravius peccant & prorsus sunt athei, derisores religionis & manifesti hostes Dei, non fiant rei corporis & sanguinis Christi, nec edant nec bibant sibi iudicium, etiamsi ad sacram coenam inter alios Christianos accedant. Et cum authore Paulo Apostolo indigni hoc ipso edant & bibant sibi iudicium quod non discernunt corpus domini, scire velim quomodo athei, Eceboli merè profani & contemptores omnis pietatis magis discernant corpus domini, quam securi, impoenitentes, hypocritae? Et quo tandem fundamento, scripturae nititur haec indignorum distinctio? Certè Spiritus sanctus omnes pronunciat hostes Dei, irae divinae obnoxios, & morti ac Satanae tyrannidi subiectos, quot quot non seriò agunt poenitentiam, nec credunt Evangelio. Qui non credit in filium, vitam non videbit, sed iram Dei manet super ipsum, Ioan: 3.

Qui Spiritum Christi non habet, hic non est eius, Rom: 8. Sive sit hypocrita, sive securus, sive Idolatra, sive atheos sive, Ecebolus, et merè prosanus. Alia quidem peccata aliis sunt graviora.

Verùm omnes, qui à veris poenitentiae motibus alieni sunt, unius generis sunt peccatores, ni mirum mortalibus peccatis obstricti, remoti à beneficii regni Christi. Reiicimus igitur atque explodimus novam istam & falsam indignorum distinctionem, & dicimus cum Paulo: omnes, qui sine vera poenitentia ad mensam domini accedunt, edere corpus & bibere sanguinem Christi sine salutari fructu ad iudicium.

Petulanter admodum finxit Calvinus, corpus Domini in sacra coena offerri quidem hypocritis, securis & indignis, sedrepelli & reiici ab impiis ipsa securitate & diffidentia. Hoc sanè est Apostolo Paulo in faciem contradicere. Is enim disertè dicit, Indignè edens & bibens, iudicium sibi edit & bibit, eò quòd non discernit corpus domini. Si ipso esu iudicium sibi accersit impius, & ipso esu non discernit corpus domini. Ergò non repellit sua diffidentia, sed ore suo accipit corpus domini. Sacramenta enim non pendent à dignitate vel indignitate sumentium, sed à veritate verborum Iesu Christi. In vocabulo (iudicii) quaerunt etiam Calvinistae sophismatum rimas, per quas elabantur. Interpretantur enim de poenis corporalibus & castigatione temporali, non de ira Dei & condemnatione aeterna. Sed frustra & hoc quaeritur effugium. Nam ex Pauli tota concione manifestum est, eum minari iram Dei, praesentes & aeternas poenas, indignè sumentibus. Qui sine exploratione ad mensam domini accedunt, securi & impoenitentes sunt. Impoenitentes verò non tantum temporales merentur castigationes, sed etiam iudicium & mortem aeternam. Et qui à Spiritu Dei rei peraguntur corporis & Sanguinis Iesu Christi, hi certè partem in regno Christi non habent, sed damnationi aeternae sunt obnoxii. Ad quos enim consolatio Pauli pertinet: Nulla est condemnatio his, qui in Christo Iesu sunt: Roma: 8. Item, Christi: Qui credit in filium, non iudicatur, nequaquam tristi hoc fulmine terrendi sunt, quòd rei fiant corporis & Sanguinis Christi. Quòd ergò Paulus dicit, Indignè sumentes Eucharistiam, edere & bibere sibi iudicium, non tantum de temporali castigatione, sed de gravissima Dei ira, & aeterna damnatione, nisi securus, hypocrita & atheos vera poenitentia ad Deum redierit, & fide veniam delictorum impetraverit, intelligendum est. Firmum ergò est nostrum argumentum de manducatione impiorum sumptum, nimirum, quia Paulus testatur indignos, Id est, securos, hypocritas, atheos, Ecebolos et planè impios, cùm ad mensam domini accedunt, edere corpus domini, et bibere eius sanguinem, evidentissimum esse, quòd in sacra coena verum corpus & verus Sanguis Iesu Christi verè adsint; &

quòd panis benedictus sit verum & substantiale corpus, & vinum benedictum sit verus & substantialis Sanguis Iesu Christi, quem digni & indigni pariter ore accipiunt, illi in salutem, hi in iudicium. Argumentationem nostram syllogismis comprehendemus.

Qui in sacra coena reus fit corporis & Sanguinis Iesu Christi, eum necesse est, in ipsa coena praesenti corpori & Sanguini Iesu Christi inferre iniuriam.

Sed indignè sumentes panem & vinum benedictum, rei siunt corporis & Sanguinis Iesu Christi.

Ergò indignè sumentes panem & vinum benedictum, in sacra coena praesenti corpori & Sanguini Iesu Christi contumeliam & iniuriam inferunt.

Alius.

Qui in sacra coena domini edit & bibit sibi iudicium, eò quòd non discernit corpus domini, verè manducat corpus domini.

Sed indignè edens panem benedictum, iudicium sibi edit, eò quòd non discernit corpus domini.

Ergò indignè edens panem benedictum, verè manducat corpus domini.

Alius.

Quod in sacra coena, ipsa manducatione & usu discernendum est à communi cibo, id adsit necesse est.

Sed corpus Iesu Christi, in sacra coena ipsa manducatione discernendum est à communi cibo.

Ergò ut adsit verè corpus Iesu Christi in sacra coena, necesse est.

Alius.

Qui ipsa manducatione non discernit corpus Iesu Christi ab aliis cibis, is haud dubiè manducat corpus domini, ut alium cibum.

Sed hypocritae & securi ipsa manducatione Eucharistiae non discernunt corpus domini.

Ergò hypocritae et securi manducant corpus domini, ut alium cibum.

Alius.

Panis benedictus idcircò dicitur participatio corporis domini, quòd omnes, quotquot manducant istum panem, participes fiant corporis domini.

Sed multi hypocritae, athei, Epicurei, Eceboli, planè impii & profani manducant panem benedictum in sacra coena.

Ergò multi hypocritae athei, securi, impoenitentes, Epicurei, Eceboli et planè impii, participes fiunt corporis & sanguinis Christi.

Haec sunt nostrae sententiae & confessionis de praesentia corporis & sanguinis Iesu Christi, in sacra coena fundamenta, quae non desumpsimus ex humanae rationis argumentationibus aut speculationibus, neque etiam petivimus ea ex procul accersitis, aut violenter contortis scripturae testimoniis, neque ea nituntur authoritate hominum eruditorum & clarorum in Ecclesia: sed ex ipsa sede doctrinae de coena domini huc allata sunt. Tantum verba Iesu Christi planissima, interpretationem Christi clarissimam, testimonia Pauli lucidissima ursimus. Et ex ipso textu Spiritus sancti, in quo erudit Ecclesiam de coena domini, demonstravimus hanc verissimam esse mentem Spiritus sancti, quòd verè & substantialiter adsit in sacra coena corpus & sanguis Iesu Christi: & quòd panis benedictus sit verum & substantiale corpus Iesu Christi, & vinum benedictum sit verus & substantialis sanguis Iesu Christi, quod corpus et quem sanguinem Christi digni edunt & bibunt in salutem & confirmationem fidei: indigni verò edunt & bibunt in iudicium. Ergò filium Dei Dominum nostrum Iesum Christum, mediatorem & redemptorem nostrum, & authorem sacro sanctae coenae rogamus toto pectore, ut per Spiritum sanctum fidem nobis adaugeat, & in hac certa, perspicua & solida veritatis confessione clementer nos confirmet, Amen.

## 11:22 Concerning the Lord's Supper: Chapter V. Refutation of the Objections by Which the Calvinists Oppose the Presence of the
CHAPTER V. Refutation of the Objections by which the Calvinists Oppose the Presence of the Body of Jesus Christ.

The first and most important care of a pious mind ought to be that it draws a sound and clear opinion concerning individual controversies of religion from the word of God, and that it properly fortifies it with indubitable testimonies of the divine word: which it then ought to defend constantly, whatever cavils may be objected; for it is the property of sincere faith to sustain the various insults of Satan, of the world, and of reason, and yet not to be moved from the clear word of God.

The second care of a pious mind then ought to be that it diligently inquires how the cavils of adversaries may be clearly dissolved, and the falsity of them shown. For we are much confirmed in faith when we detect that the opinions of antagonists rest upon no certain foundation. And in the very serious of the truth in the inquiry, the Holy Spirit subsequently kindles a greater light.

After we have therefore proven and fortified with clear and infallible demonstrations of Holy Scripture this pious and sound doctrine concerning the presence of the body and Blood of Jesus Christ: we shall now proceed to the refutation of the sophisms by which the Calvinists and their followers attempt to undermine our confession. For although all the cavils which are accustomed to be brought forward by Zwingli, Calvin, and all men of the same flour have been clearly, vigorously, and validly refuted, to such an extent that the impudence of the Calvinists, who dare to bring back such worn-out trifles into the Church, is worthy of hatred, nevertheless, because Satan does not cease to disturb the little ones of Christ with these sophisms and to obscure the truth of the Church, it is necessary for us to repeat our refutations and to oppose the clear truth to their illusions and sophisms.

I. Objection of the Calvinists.

It is impossible that a true and natural human body be at one and the same time in different or multiple places.

But Christ, sitting at the right hand of the Father, has a true and natural body, consisting of flesh, blood, and bones.

Therefore it is impossible that a true and natural body of Jesus Christ is truly and substantially present in all places in which the holy supper is administered on earth.

Respond:

First, to the major premise. Since in this argument the question is not what is possible for a man or a creature, but what is possible for the only-begotten and omnipotent Son of God, Jesus Christ, the major proposition is not only false, but also impious, sacrilegious, and blasphemous. For our faith holds thus: With God all things are possible, And what is impossible with men, this is possible with God: And nothing is impossible with God. Whence also the first article of our faith, the foundation of our religion, says thus: I believe in God the creator of heaven and earth. Since the impious opinion in the argument contradicts this immovable foundation of our faith, it ought to be rejected by all the pious and held as blasphemous. I say nothing yet about the properties or prerogatives of the human nature of Jesus Christ: I will treat of this matter in its own place, God willing. The major premise of the argument calls the omnipotence of God into doubt: whether God can cause a true and natural human body to be at one and the same time in different and multiple places. Here I expressly affirm that he who denies that God can perform this differs in no way from a pagan man, as one who overturns the chief foundation of the whole Christian religion and of all piety.

For what crumb of true religion will remain, if we establish that those things which seem to be repugnant to the laws of nature are not even possible for God? What hope can be ours, not only against death and hell, which seem to us invincible enemies, but in any necessity, where secondary causes desert us, if we do not believe that with God all things are possible? Or will any of us be able to believe with certainty either the incarnation of the Son, or the resurrection of the dead, with this axiom overturned: That with God all things are possible? Let pious minds therefore attend to what Satan seeks through the Calvinists, namely, the extirpation of all religion and faith.

The somewhat more modest among the Calvinists immediately recoil here, and seek for the state of the dispute to be transposed here. For they say the question is not about the omnipotence of God, but about His will. To these I reply: if the question is only about His will and not about His omnipotence, why then is such an argument woven by you? Certainly there must be a connection of the argument. That which cannot be done, (and as some of the Calvinists speak) Not even God can make it so that one and a natural body is in different and many places. Is this not to derogate from the omnipotence of God? Which if you concede, at least in feigned speech: Therefore explode your argumentation. For with the major proposition overturned, which is σύνεχον of the argument, the whole thing collapses. Others, however, are more impudent, such as Beza and Peter Martyr, who do not hesitate to profess their paganism openly: for without any shame they write and speak in the Church that that universal proposition, which affirms that with God all things are possible, must be restricted. This is truly to contradict the Son of God, Jesus Christ, to his face. And blasphemies of this kind proceed from those who profess themselves to be leaders of the Church.

Then Beza and Martyr descend to the specific case, and in clear words they posit that it is not possible even for God to bring it about that one body should have the nature of a true body and yet be in different and multiple places. And to this they add other things which cannot be done by God: such as what Jerome said not without blasphemy: Although God can do all things, yet he cannot raise up a virgin after her ruin; Item, a triangle cannot be made a quadrangle. And in order to decline in some way the odium of blasphemy, they pretend that these are not signs of weakness, but rather of omnipotence. Is it not therefore manifest that the Calvinists are disputing not about the will of God, but about his very omnipotence? We therefore repeat our confession, and we say that the major proposition is blasphemous. For since God can do all things, it is not only possible, but also easy for him to bring it about that, when he himself wills, one body is in different and many places, and nevertheless retains the nature of a true body. Nor indeed is it only possible for God to bring it about that the glorious body of Christ is in different places: But even if He should wish to bring it about, He can cause the body of Paul, Elijah, or another man to be at one and the same time in different and many places. For He who created heaven and earth from nothing by His word, and established the laws of all nature, would anything be impossible for Him? Constantly, therefore, without any restriction, we retain the axiom: All things are possible with God: And absolutely no word is impossible with God. We do not delay over the blasphemous opinion of Jerome, that God cannot restore a virgin after a fall: We have more faith in Isaiah: Who promises that it will come to pass that even if our sins have been as scarlet, yet we shall be made whiter than snow. Certainly Rahab, Bathsheba, and Magdalene, who after their fall performed penance and believed in the mediator, will be cleaner than many virgins in the world to come. And what fatal necessity would prevent God from being able to make a triangle out of a quadrangle, if He wished?

The Calvinists therefore betray their own heathen impiety when they bring forward such examples. God cannot sin or lie, because He has set forth His will in His word, that He is angry at sin and lying.

Nowhere, however, has God explained that He is unwilling to bring it about that one body should be in different places. It is therefore blasphemy to say that not even God can bring it about that one body should be in different places.

Since, therefore, the major premise in the argument does not hold, the whole fabrication of the cavil collapses of its own accord.

There is no reason for the Calvinists to shout that we are weaving an inept consequence. God can do this or that: Therefore He does it. For we do not argue in this way at all. Those are the usual evasions of the Calvinists. We demonstrate only this here, that it is not impossible for God to bring it about that one body should be in different and multiple places. Which, since we obtain it here, is enough for us: for then the objection of the Calvinists, by which they attacked our confession from the standpoint of impossibility, collapses entirely. That it is the will of God that the body of Christ in the sacred supper, wherever it is administered on earth, should be truly present, we prove not from the omnipotence of God, but from the express word of God, which we have shown above in confirmation of our opinion clearly, and without any obscurity. Therefore, it is a calumny that the Calvinists object that we argue from the power of God to His will; just as if someone were to conclude thus: God could have created a man capable of flight: Therefore He created such a one. Nay, rather, we demonstrate both the will of God and His power individually from His own word.

His will is manifest from the words of the institution of the Supper: his omnipotence is established from the creation of all things and the testimony of Christ. With God all things are possible. Matth: 19. If anyone fully posits the major proposition, he will soon discover its falsehood and impiety: for thus it ought to have been posited. It is impossible with God that one natural and finite body should be at one and the same time in many places. But what pious soul would not immediately shudder at and execrate the impiety of that proposition?

In this argument it is also customary to dispute concerning the properties and prerogatives of the human nature of Jesus Christ. But, because the major proposition, which ought to have been the σύνεχον of the argument, has been overturned, the whole structure of the argument collapses and vanishes, I will not mix in this dispute. For there is no need for a longer discourse, after the sophism has been worn down and trampled underfoot. We openly and ingenuously concede the minor, and we assert and defend it against the Eutychians. We say that Jesus Christ the Son of God, sitting at the right hand of the eternal Father, has a true, natural, and finite body, which consists of flesh, blood, and bones, and retains all its essential properties. But it does not follow from this that his body cannot be present in the Holy Supper, wherever it is administered on earth: Indeed for that is the rule, admitting no restriction. That with God all things are possible. Matt: 19. Wherefore when the omnipotent Son of God said, This blessed bread is my body: We must certainly believe that the natural body of Jesus Christ is truly present, wherever the sacred supper is celebrated according to the institution of Christ.

II. Objection.

It is an essential property of a true and natural human body to be in one place only and not in many at one and the same time.

Jesus Christ sitting at the right hand of the eternal Father has a true and natural body.

Therefore it is an essential property of the body of Christ, now sitting at the right hand of God, to be in one place only and not in many.

Response:

The major premise is not true. For to be in a place is not an essential property of a human body, but an accidental one. For it is not of the very substance of the body. The essential or substantial properties of a human body are to be finite, to be created, to have flesh, blood, bones, limbs, a head, a liver, and veins. But to be in a place or time is not of the essence of a body. Secondly, to be in a place is indeed a property of a human body, according to the elements and infirmities of this world: but who will hinder or forbid God, so that if He wills, He may exempt some body from the laws and elements of this world? It is a property of a human body to be burned in fire, to be drowned in water, to die when food is withdrawn for many days: and yet divine power caused that the bodies of the three companions of Daniel were not burned in the burning furnace: that Peter walked with his body on the sea: that Moses and Elijah lived for 40 days without food. A distinction must therefore be made between the laws of this nature and the omnipotence of God, which is circumscribed by no limits, nor is it bound to any laws of nature.

Although, therefore, the laws of this world demand that one body be in one certain place, these laws of the world nevertheless cannot infringe upon the word of God, which affirms that the body of Jesus Christ is present everywhere, wherever the holy supper of the Lord is administered according to the institution of Christ. Those who subject God to the laws of nature, it is necessary for them to deny all the miraculous deeds of God, of which the holy scripture testifies: nor can these hope for any salvation against sin and death: therefore, let the most certain foundation of our faith always be in sight. With God all things are possible. When therefore God pronounces and reveals something, the laws of universal nature are compelled to yield to His omnipotence.

III. Objection.

The flesh of Jesus Christ is in all things similar to our flesh without sin: Heb: 2.

But our flesh cannot be in many places, but is only in one place.

Therefore also the flesh of Christ is only in one place, nor can it be wherever the supper is administered.

Response:

In this argument something must be said by us, concerning the properties and prerogatives of the human nature of Jesus Christ, and that with the help of the Spirit of God.

First, we clearly and constantly profess that Jesus Christ assumed true and natural human flesh in all things similar to us without sin: He was found in fashion as a man, having taken the form of a servant, Phili: 2. We also confess in Jesus Christ two natures, the divine, which is from eternity, and the human, which was born of the virgin Mary, not confused nor mixed, but united by a hypostatic union, with the essential property of each nature preserved. We also confess that Christ in the time of humiliation took on all the infirmities of human flesh without sin. Furthermore, we affirm that Christ, sitting at the right hand of the eternal Father, retains for all eternity true human flesh, with its essential properties, by which it is distinguished from the divine essence. These things are certain from the testimony Ph: 2. Ph: 3.Heb: 2.Luc: 24. See and touch: For a spirit does not have flesh and bones: therefore, the flesh of Christ is similar to our flesh in all things, as far as the truth of substance and essential properties are concerned. Here, however, it is now asked whether Christ, even in the time of his humiliation, without the abolition of his flesh, could not have performed with his body those things which exceeded all the laws of nature. Then it is asked whether the human nature of Christ did not have sublime prerogatives over the flesh of all men, both on account of the personal union with the divine nature λόγου: and on account of his exaltation in the kingdom and his sitting at the right hand of God. Furthermore, it is asked whether the body of Christ, after it passed from this world to the Father into another life, did not lay aside the elements and infirmities of this age without the abolition of human flesh. When these things have been explained according to the word of God, it will clearly be established that the sophistry of the adversaries has no strength to impugn our confession concerning the true presence of the body and blood of Jesus Christ in the sacred supper.

As regards the first question, therefore, the Evangelical history clearly testifies that Christ, even in the time of his humiliation, did many things with his body, without its abolition, which we cannot imitate with our bodies, and which exceed not only the laws of this world, but also its grasp: By touch he healed the sick: By his voice he raised the dead: He fasted for 40 days and nights: He walked with his feet upon the sea: He was born into the world with the virginity of his mother unharmed. Although, therefore, as regards the substance of nature, namely, of soul and body, flesh, blood, bones, etc., it is similar to our flesh: Yet our nature, as regards virtues, properties, and prerogatives, is not similar in all things to the flesh of Christ: Wherefore when Holy Scripture asserts something about the flesh of Christ, we ought not to make a judgment from our own flesh, whether that could have been done or not; But we ought to assent to the word of the omnipotent and truthful God in all simplicity and obedience.

Furthermore, on account of the sublime and ineffable hypostatic union of the flesh of Christ, with him λόγῳ the eternal God, the flesh of Christ possesses many excellent prerogatives, which cannot and ought not to be attributed to the bodies of other men without idolatry and sacrilege. We do indeed openly confess that we can neither exhaust, nor fully perceive the sublime and arcane mystery of the incarnation of the Son of God, or of the personal union of two natures in Christ in this life. Nor do we gather from the personal union either an equalization of both natures, or the abolition of one, or a transmutation into the other nature, or a commixture. Rather, according to the word of God, we believe that each nature remains and retains its essential properties in all eternity without any confusion or separation. Λόγος is and remains the eternal God, the human nature is and remains a creature forever. But what prerogatives, virtues, and eminences the Holy Spirit attributes to the human nature of Jesus Christ, on account of the hypostatic union, no one can derogate from that nature of Christ without sacrilege and blasphemy. Indeed, it is not permitted for us by our own judgment to invent or attribute to the flesh of Christ properties or glory. But we must remain within the boundaries of the divine word, and this alone is both to be believed and asserted, which the express divine voice testifies concerning the flesh of Christ.

Concerning the prerogatives of the human nature of Jesus Christ.

The first glory and prerogative, therefore, of the flesh of Jesus Christ is that it both sustained, and overcame, and appeased the entire wrath of God kindled by the sins of the whole world: which was possible to no man, and thus to no creature. David says, if iniquities you have observed, Lord, Lord, who shall stand? The entire human race would succumb if God were to pour out all His wrath upon it. Whence He says, I will not kindle all the heat of my wrath: Because I am God, and not man. Christ, however, in His flesh sustained all the wrath of the Father. And He appeased it by His obedience. He did indeed sweat blood in this struggle, and was reduced to the greatest straits, yet He did not succumb to this burden, but appeared a glorious victor. This virtue and glory, however, He did not have from Himself, for since He was a creature, He could not have sustained the whole wrath of God if He had been alone. But He has it from the personal union with λόγῳ the omnipotent, who, when He had made this flesh His own, provided this immense strength to it, so that He could overcome and conquer the most ardent wrath of the Father and the whole curse of the law. For it is not to be thought that the divine nature alone sustained and appeased the wrath of the eternal Father. But the whole person of Christ, God and man according to both natures, underwent this burden, and conferred upon us this immense benefit. The human nature, however, could not have performed this, unless it had been assumed by λόγῳ into the unity of the person, and instructed with divine strength. Here Paul says 2. Corin: 5. God was in Christ, reconciling the world to Himself, not imputing their sins to them. And Ephes: 2. That He might reconcile both in one body to God through the cross, killing the enmity in himself. Rom: 5. For if, when we were enemies, we were reconciled to God by the death of his son, much more now that we are reconciled, shall we be saved by his life.

These testimonies of the Holy Spirit clearly testify that our reconciliation with God was made not only through the divine nature of Christ, but also through the flesh of Christ. And it must be diligently observed that the Apostle, speaking of the glory and benefit of reconciliation, speaks not only in the concrete, that is, through words which signify the whole person, but also in the abstract, that is, through words which signify one nature, namely, human flesh. For he says that Christ reconciled the world to God in his body. Therefore, the flesh of Christ excels the flesh of all men by this most eminent prerogative.

II. The second glory and prerogative of the flesh of Christ is that it deletes, washes away, and takes away sins from our nature, and bestows and even effects righteousness in us. It is clearly a divine work to take away and delete sins, and to render and kindle spiritual and eternal righteousness. I, I am, he says, Jehovah, Iesa: 43. Who delete your sins and iniquities like a cloud. For my own sake, for my own sake I will do it, that I may not be blasphemed. Therefore, human nature could not have effected this either alone or of itself.

But because it is united to the divine nature, it has received this power and glory, that it both washes away sins and bestows righteousness. For the divine nature alone does not take away sins and kindle righteousness: but we must also attribute this huge benefit to the human nature. For the Holy Scripture, brought forth by the mouth of the Holy Spirit, attributes this glory to the flesh and blood of Jesus Christ. 1. John 1. The blood of Jesus Christ cleanses us from all sin. Heb: 9. For if the blood of bulls and of goats and the ashes of a heifer sprinkling the unclean, sanctified to the cleansing of the flesh: how much more shall the blood of Christ, who through the eternal Spirit offered himself without spot to God, cleanse your consciences from dead works, to serve the living God? And Rom: 3. Being justified freely by his grace, through the redemption that is in Jesus Christ, whom he set forth as a propitiation, through faith in his blood. Rom: 5. Much more therefore, being justified in his blood, we shall be saved through him from wrath. Eph: 1. In whom Christ we have redemption through his blood, the forgiveness of sins. These clear and plain testimonies of the Holy Spirit show that the flesh and blood of Jesus Christ have this excellence and prerogative, that it deletes and takes away sins from us, and bestows upon us cleansing and righteousness before God. Not indeed of itself, but by the virtue of which it received from λόγῳ, from whom it was assumed into one person. And again let the pious observe here, that the Apostles speak not only in the concrete, that Christ the man blots out sins, and confers righteousness, but also in the abstract, that is, through words which signify the human nature. For they say, The blood of Jesus Christ cleanses us from all sin: The blood of Jesus Christ justifies us before God. These are locutions not in the concrete, but in the abstract, that is, which speak expressly of the human flesh and blood of Christ. This divine majesty therefore and power of blotting out sins, and of bestowing spiritual righteousness, has been communicated to the flesh of Jesus Christ by λόγῳ.

III. The third prerogative is, that the flesh of Christ takes away death from our nature and restores spiritual and eternal life: which again is a divine property, power and glory. For there is no such power in any creature, that it can destroy and abolish death in man, and restore to him spiritual and eternal life. For it is the work of creation to make alive, as the king of Israel testifies. Am I God, that I can kill and make alive. And Hannah says, God brings down to the underworld and brings back, delivers to death and makes alive. But the holy scripture of the holy spirit expressly affirms that this power is in the flesh of Christ, that it may take away death from our nature, and may bestow and effect everlasting life. For thus Christ says: John 6 I am the living bread, which came down from heaven: if any man eat of this bread, he shall live for ever: And the bread that I will give is my flesh, which I will give for the life of the world. Item, Amen, Amen I say unto you, except you eat the flesh of the son of man, and drink his blood, you have not life in you. He that eateth my flesh, and drinketh my blood, hath everlasting life, and I will raise him up in the last day. For my flesh is meat indeed, and my blood is drink indeed. What could be said here more plainly concerning the most eminent prerogative of the flesh of Christ? namely, that it has the divine power and majesty of quickening men. For he speaks not only of merit, but also of efficacy, application, and communication: Nor does he attribute the power of quickening only to his divinity, but he pronounces concerning his own flesh, that it communicates eternal life to men: nor does he only affirm in the concrete that the son of man quickens others: but in the abstract he ascribes this glory to his own flesh, that it has the power of quickening: which glory it is a sin to ascribe to any creature outside of Christ. Hence it is, that Cyril and the whole Ephesian synod pronounce concerning the flesh of Christ.

If any man does not confess the flesh of Christ to be vivifying, for the reason that it has been made the property of the Word, because it can vivify all things, let him be anathema. And book 4, chapter 14: Since therefore the flesh of the Savior is joined to the Word of God, which is naturally life, it has been made vivifying: when we eat it, then we have life in us, joined to that by which it has been made life.

And Theodoret, Dialogue 2, page 69: We name the body of Christ divine, vivifying, lordly, teaching that it is not the common body of some man: but of our Lord Jesus Christ, who is God and man.

This is a very illustrious prerogative of the flesh of Christ, since it is of divine majesty and power to vivify dead men, and indeed to communicate eternal life. Nor indeed has this glory and majesty been communicated to the man Christ only in such a way that it is permitted only in the concrete to affirm that the man Christ is endowed with the power of vivifying: But also in the abstract, both Scripture and the holy fathers speak that the flesh of Jesus Christ is vivifying.

Whence it is most manifest that there are diverse kinds of communication of both idioms and majesty. For certain idioms are so communicated to another nature, that it is not permitted to express those things in the abstract, but only in the concrete. As when it is rightly said that God has suffered, died, been crucified: God has hungered: Likewise, the Man Christ is from eternity, the Man Christ is God, the Man Christ created heaven and earth. It is not, however, right to say, the Divinity has suffered, died, been crucified. The Divinity has hungered: Likewise, the Humanity of Christ is from eternity, the Humanity of Christ is deity, the Humanity of Christ created heaven and earth. For these phrases would confuse the true distinction of natures in Christ, and would bring back Eutychianism. But there is another kind of communication, when the divine nature λόγῳ. so imparts its divine power, glory, majesty, property, to the assumed flesh, that it is permitted not only in the concrete, but even in the abstract to enunciate these things, as that λόγος, who vivifies all things and possesses the power of vivifying from eternity, so imparts to his flesh this power and majesty, that it is permitted to us according to the holy scripture to say. The flesh of Jesus Christ is vivifying. The body of Jesus Christ is vivifying and confers salvation to the world. A horrible blindness, therefore, impiety, and ignorance it is to wish to measure the properties of the flesh of Christ by the infirmity of other human bodies: And to despoil the flesh of Christ of its glory and majesty, with which λόγος adorned it in the personal assumption.

IV: The fourth prerogative is, that the human nature of Christ breaks and destroys the whole kingdom of Satan and of hell: Which certainly no mere man could otherwise have accomplished. For the power of Satan is horrible and indeed so great that Scripture calls him the lord of the world, and the God of this age. And there is a huge multitude of unclean Spirits. And therefore it was necessary for our mediator to be almighty God, so that he might be superior to Satan, and that you might have certain hope of victory against so monstrous a tyrant. Moreover, Christ overcame Satan, and crushed the whole head of the serpent, not only as God, but also as man. For λόγος the almighty bestowed this huge strength upon his flesh assumed by him into the unity of his person, so that it might prevail over Satan, and destroy all his works. Whence in the first promise it is said. The seed of the woman shall crush the head of the serpent. As if Scripture were saying: true human flesh shall break the whole power of Satan, and shall liberate the human race. Not indeed alone, nor of itself did the flesh crush the head of the serpent: But the flesh of Jesus Christ personally united to the deity λόγου, and receiving divine strength from λόγῳ, was the victor of Satan, and destroyed his tyranny. Which was also signified in the promises. 2. Samuel: 7: I will raise up your seed after you, which shall come forth from your womb, and I will establish his kingdom. The human of Christ he names the flesh the seed of David. That he promises the kingdom of this seed will be firm, he shows that the flesh of Christ will be the victor over Satan, and hell, and all our enemies. Item, Psalm 132. Of the fruit of thy womb, I will set upon thy throne. Therefore, although the flesh of Christ is true flesh, yet it obtains a prerogative which cannot be attributed to the body of any man in the whole world.

V. The fifth glory and prerogative is that the flesh of Jesus Christ, together with the divinity, pours the Holy Spirit into believers and sanctifies them. This is such a great glory that it cannot be attributed to any creature without impiety. For since the Holy Spirit is the eternal God and Lord of all creatures, he is not sent nor given by any creature. But the human nature assumed by λόγῳ has been raised to this glory and majesty, that together with the divinity of Christ it imparts the gift of the Holy Spirit to the faithful. For as he merited this gift for us by his blood: so he also received the faculty and glory of imparting the Spirit. Christ, resurrected from death, breathes upon his Apostles and says: Receive the Holy Spirit.

With this breath of his, flowing from his most holy breast, he truly gave the Holy Spirit, and made it testified that his human nature is endowed with this prerogative, of imparting the Holy Spirit to the faithful. Whence also Peter, Acts 2, says: After he was exalted by the right hand of God and received the promise of the Spirit from the Father, he poured out that which you see. Because he speaks of the exaltation of Christ, it is certain that he signifies his human nature. For the divine was not exalted, but from eternity it was in sublime majesty. But the human nature, with the work of our redemption perfected, ascended to the heavens and was placed at the right hand of the eternal Father. This human nature in Christ, exalted by the right hand of God, the Apostle Peter says received the promise of the Spirit, that is, the promised Holy Spirit from the Father, and poured him out in visible form upon the Apostles. And indeed Christ himself confesses that unless he goes to the Father, that is, unless he has poured out his blood for the world and through death has passed to the Father, the Holy Spirit will not come: but if he goes, then he will send him. He teaches therefore both that he by his death obtained and merited for us the Holy Spirit, and that his human nature possesses this glory, so that it may impart the Holy Spirit to the faithful. The Holy Spirit does not indeed proceed from the flesh or the human nature of Christ. For the Holy Spirit is from eternity almighty God: but the human nature of Christ is and remains a creature, fashioned in the womb of the virgin Mary by the Holy Spirit and by the whole Trinity. But he is sent and given by the human nature of Christ assumed by λόγῳ into the unity of the person. Which John the Baptist also intimates: When he says: I baptize you with water: but after me comes he who is before me, he will baptize you with fire and the Holy Spirit.

VI. The sixth prerogative of the flesh of Christ, that it is the Head of the whole Church, dispersed everywhere throughout the whole world, which is gathered in all ages by the ministry of the word, which cherishes, sustains, guards, rules, preserves, and protects the individual members and fulfills and effects all things in all. This glory and property also belongs to no creature. No Apostle or Prophet can be present to the whole Church and to individual members: No angel also can bring aid to individual pious ones, drive away all dangers, or succor in every necessity. But the humanity of Christ, because it is united to the Logos by a personal union, and because it is constituted the head of the whole Church, is present to all the members of its body, cherishes individual pious ones with its Spirit, sustains, rules, defends, wards off all dangers, and supplies all necessary things. It is present and has all creatures in its hand, and fills all things. For thus its most ample and sweetest promise holds: Wherever two or three are gathered in my name, I am in the midst of them, Matth: 18. And Matth: ult: I am with you all days even to the consummation of the age.

Although these promises are enunciated in the concrete, since he says: I, Christ, God and man, will be with you: Yet it must not be imagined that he promised us only the presence of his divinity, but of his whole person, and even of his flesh, although we do not comprehend it with external senses. And lest we should doubt concerning the presence of his flesh, he instituted the most holy supper, in which with the bread he gives us his body to be eaten and with the wine he gives his blessed blood to be drunk, as a most evident and infallible argument that the whole Christ, God and man, is perpetually present to his Church. And Paul Eph: 1 and 4. when he testifies that Christ fills all things, he speaks significantly concerning his human nature and demonstrates its true presence in the whole Church. For thus he says, He subjected all things under his feet, and gave him as head over all things to the Church, which is his body, his fullness, who fills all in all. It is manifest that the Apostle is speaking of the flesh of Christ: Because he says God raised Jesus from the dead and placed him at his right hand. No one, however, is so unskilled as to think that the divinity was raised from the dead. Paul adds, in order to describe the heavenly glory of Jesus Christ, he subjected all things under his feet. Therefore all creatures are also present and subject to the human nature of Christ raised from the dead. And because he is the head of the whole Church, it is necessary that it be present to individual members. Furthermore, he says that he fills all things in all, that is, that Christ not only works in all the faithful but is also present in them and dwells in them, and imparts eternal salvation; thus also in the fourth chapter he says: He who descended is the same who also ascended above all the heavens, that he might fill all things. That Paul is speaking about the human nature λόγῳ assumed, no one can deny. For the divinity neither descends nor ascends. But the Apostle affirms that this Christ, who ascended above all the heavens, fills all things, and he speaks not only of his operation or efficacy, but of his very presence. Therefore he says he ascended above all the heavens that he might fill all things. How these things can come to pass, that the human nature of Christ, which is finite, might fill all things, we cannot comprehend with our minds: just as we cannot grasp or understand concerning the divinity how it fills all things, for no mass, no extension is to be imagined here. But because the Holy Spirit has revealed these mysteries in the Church through the Apostles, we must altogether assent.

VII. The seventh prerogative of the human nature of Christ is that it is omniscient, it sees and knows all things, and understands the groanings of our hearts. For Paul expressly says that all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge are hidden in Christ Coloss. 1. Not only to the divinity λόγου, but to the whole Christ It is attributed to the person that all the treasures of wisdom are hidden in him. And the disciples, speaking with the Lord after the institution of the supper, say: Behold, now you speak openly and say no proverb; now we know that you know all things, and there is no need for you that anyone should ask you. They do not only attribute this glory of omniscience to the divinity, with the flesh of Christ excluded, but they give this glory to this man Jesus Christ, that he knows all things. Item, Ioan: 21. When Peter had been asked a third time, he answers: Lord Jesus, you know all things: you know that I love you. Peter speaks with Christ, whom he sees before him clothed in human flesh and resurrected from the dead, and he clearly affirms that this man Jesus knows all things, as much future as present. Nor does Jesus refute this, but approves his pious confession. And since the Church adores the flesh of Christ together with λόγῳ and invokes it in every necessity, it is necessary to attribute to it omniscience and the searching of our hearts: otherwise the invocation would be vain. For he is invoked in vain who is ignorant of our groans and necessities, which often we cannot even explain. But what is said in Luke, that Jesus grew in age and wisdom, does not derogate from the omniscience of the human nature of Christ. For the Holy Spirit in that place shows that Christ assumed all the infirmities of the flesh without sin. He was not perfect immediately. A man was born, but a little infant: And yet he was God almighty. He did not show his divine wisdom immediately in infancy, but little by little this light of divine wisdom shone more and more in him, so that he might teach that he was a true man in all things like us without sin. Paul says that Christ will judge even the secret thoughts of hearts on the day of his coming: But it is certain that not only the divine, but also the human nature of Christ will judge the living and the dead, just as Christ testifies. The Father has given all judgment to the Son: because he is the son of man John 5. It is necessary, therefore, that Christ, even according to his humanity, look into the hearts, groans, counsels, thoughts, and desires of all men. Scripture indeed speaks in the concrete when it attributes the knowledge of all things to Christ: but it does not obscurely show at the same time also in the abstract, that is, through words which signify human nature, that it rightly declares this prerogative and glory. For according to his human nature he will judge the thoughts and affections of all men: Therefore also according to his human nature he sees and understands all things.

VIII. The eighth prerogative is that the human nature of Christ, united λόγῳ, has received all power in heaven and on earth, and is truly omnipotent, which glory and majesty otherwise belong to the only and omnipotent It belongs to God. Although the power of angels and spirits in heaven is great, the power of no angel is infinite. But Jesus Christ, according to his humanity, which is united to the Word, received this glory and majesty, so that all things are subject to him, which the Holy Scripture testifies in many places. Matthew, last chapter; Christ says: All power is given to me in heaven and on earth. All power is certainly immense and infinite power. He did not receive this in time according to his divine essence: but λόγος he possessed it from all eternity. For he is of the same essence and power as the Father from all eternity, but according to his humanity he did not obtain this glory perpetually, but it was given to him in time. And all things which the Holy Scripture says Christ received in time must be understood as having been bestowed upon his human nature. Therefore, the human nature received all power. John the Baptist says: The Father loves the Son and has given all things into his hands. John 3. The Father gave all things not only to the divinity, but also to the human nature of Christ. Thus also Psalm 8. You allowed him to be a little lower than God, but you crowned him with glory and honor: you subjected all things under his feet, sheep, oxen, and the beasts of the field. It is manifest that the prophet is not speaking only of the divine nature of Christ, to which the Father subjected all things: but also of the flesh. of Christ. For he says that Christ was for a little while forsaken by God: This certainly must be understood of the flesh of Christ, he soon adds you have crowned him with glory and honor: And you have put all things under his feet. Therefore all things are also subject to the human flesh of Christ. Certainly Christ, even according to his humanity, is the guardian and defender of his Church in all places and at all times, and in every danger and necessity. But how will Christ be able, according to his humanity, to ward off all dangers, to rescue us from all necessities, to protect us against all enemies, and to bestow all good things, if he is not omnipotent also according to his humanity? Truly the government, defense, and custody of the whole Church requires omnipotence. Jesus Christ is to judge the whole world not only according to his divinity, but also according to his humanity: Which certainly cannot be done without omnipotence. For he who does not look into the counsels, thoughts, and groans of all men, who cannot discern true faith from hypocrisy, nor has all creatures in his power, how can he judge the whole world and all souls, and execute the sentence of his judgment, which is to be valid for all eternity? Paul says that Christ, having been raised from death, has been constituted above every name that can be named, not only in this but also in the future century: Who, therefore, will dare to derogate the name and glory of omnipotence from the human nature of Christ? The ancient writers of the Church, from these very fountains of Holy Scripture, have not doubted to attribute omnipotence to the flesh of Christ in the abstract. Cyril, in his work on the true faith to the King, says: When it is said that he received glory, power, and kingdom over all things from God, this (receiving) must be referred to the conditions of humanity. Behold, Cyril clearly affirms that in the abstract the humanity of Christ received power and kingdom over all things. Who, therefore, will deny that Christ is omnipotent according to his humanity? Thus also Ambrose, book 5, on the faith: According to the operation of the divinity, he can subject all things to himself: According to the flesh, he received all things subjected. Likewise, according to the flesh, therefore, all things are delivered to him as subjected. It is manifest, therefore, that it is also correctly said in the abstract that Christ is omnipotent even according to his humanity.

IX. The ninth prerogative of the flesh of Christ is that it is invoked by all creatures, angels and men, with one adoration, since λόγῳ, and he hears the groans and vows of all who rightly invoke him. Invocation and the imploring of aid in every necessity, both spiritual and corporal, is a property and glory befitting only the divine majesty. Moreover, Holy Scripture testifies, not only to the divinity of Jesus that Christ is to be adored and invoked, but also his humanity λόγῳ united by a personal union. The Magi coming from the east adore the infant Jesus lying in the manger: He who had been blind from birth and is restored by Christ. John 9 Falling down he adores Jesus, whose human nature he saw and whose divinity he believed. Nor does Christ rebuke this worship as idolatrous, but approves it as consistent with the word of God. Paul, Phil. 2 says. That Christ took the form of a servant, and was found in habit as a man, and rendered obedience to the Father even unto death. Which words cannot be understood of the divinity of Christ, but must necessarily be understood of the human nature of Christ. Moreover, Paul adds. Therefore God gave him a name above every name, that in the name of Jesus every knee should bow of those in heaven, and above and below the earth, and every tongue should confess that Jesus Christ is Lord, to the glory of the Father. When the Apostle says that a name was therefore given to Christ, because he was obedient to the Father even unto death, he certainly speaks of his human nature, which died and was resurrected. And when he says that a name was given to him, he speaks of the flesh of Christ. For Λόγος he had a name above every name from eternity. But the human nature received this glory in time. To bow the knee in the name of Jesus signifies invocation. Therefore Paul teaches, all men in heaven, and all who live on earth, and all who are under the earth, invoke the human nature of Christ. However, this adoration is not to be estimated in such a way as when the purple of a king is adored along with the king. For help is not sought from the purple, nor does the purple understand the honor which is shown to the king. But Christians seek help and goods, both spiritual and bodily, simultaneously from λόγῳ and from the human nature of Christ. And the human nature understands that this divine honor is being offered to it as well. To Heb: 1. Being made so much better than the angels, as he hath inherited a more excellent name than they. According to the flesh he became better than the angels, and inherited a more excellent name than the angels: so that even according to the flesh he is adored by the angels. Pious antiquity did not hesitate to confess in the abstract that the flesh of Christ is to be adored. Ambrose, On the Holy Spirit, Book 2, Chapter 12: Therefore, by the footstool the earth is understood, and by the earth the flesh of Christ, which we adore today in the mysteries. And which the Apostles adored in the Lord Jesus, as we have said. Cyril indeed says anathema to him who denies that the flesh of Christ is to be adored. If anyone says that the flesh of our Lord is not to be adored as that of a man, the holy Church anathematizes him. Likewise, Athanasius, Oration 5: How would the body of the Lord not be adorable, when the Word, extending his hand, healed? he raised Lazarus, who was feverish, by uttering a human voice, and by stretching out his hands on the cross he prostrated the prince of the air. And in many other places Athanasius, Cyril, Augustine, and other orthodox writers testify that the flesh of Jesus Christ is to be adored: not with a peculiar adoration, distinct from the adoration of λόγου: as Nestorius imagined, that the man Christ is to be co-adored with λόγῳ, as one with another: but that the flesh of Jesus Christ, as λόγῳ united by a personal union, is to be adored with a single λατρείᾳ or invocation with λόγῳ the eternal Son of God. It is manifest, therefore, that even in the abstract this glory and prerogative is to be attributed to the flesh of Christ, that it is to be adored.

Who, therefore, will dare to deny that the properties and divine glory have been conferred upon the flesh of Jesus Christ by λόγῳ?

X. The tenth prerogative of the flesh of Christ is that it sits at the right hand of the eternal Father, and rules over angels and men and all creatures in heaven and on earth. For it is not said of the divinity λόγου that it is placed at the right hand of God: since the Son of God, by his very eternal birth, is of the same essence and is of equal power with the eternal Father. But to the flesh of Jesus Christ this divine glory has been granted and given, that he may sit at the right hand of the eternal God, as Scripture expressly testifies. God raised Jesus from the dead, and placed him at his right hand in the heavenly places above every principality: Christ says. Luc: 22. From this time on the son of man shall sit at the right hand of the power of God. And although Christ speaks here in the concrete; yet he clearly signifies that this glory and divine majesty is granted to his flesh. And therefore the orthodox ecclesiastical writers did not hesitate to ascribe this prerogative even in the abstract to the flesh or body of Jesus Christ. Athanasius, as Theodoret reports, expressly pronounces. Sit at my right hand: it is said of the Lord's body. For if God fills all things, in what seat does he sit? It is the body, therefore, to which the Lord says: sit at my right hand. Likewise, Cyprian. To sit at the right hand of the Father is a mystery of the flesh. And all antiquity expressly confesses this, that the majesty of sitting at the right hand has been granted to the human nature of Christ. But to sit at the right hand of the eternal Father, as the Apostle Paul interprets, is to have been exalted into sublime majesty, and above every principality, power, and throne, and to possess the name which is above every name, not only in this, but also in the future age, for thus The Apostle explains the meaning of this article Eph: 1. Since, therefore, the flesh of Jesus Christ sitting at the right hand of the eternal Father possesses a name and glory above every name that can be named, not only in this age, but also in the age to come: who then will dare to detract from the human nature of Jesus Christ the glory and name of omniscience and omnipotence? For Paul excludes no majesty when he says, above every name. And since sitting at the right hand of the Father signifies equal majesty, honor, glory, power, and authority with the Father, we deservedly, according to Holy Scripture, attribute all these things to the human nature of Christ, which, united λὸγῳ after the work of our redemption was completed, has been placed at the right hand of God. But as for what the Calvinists, enemies of the testament of Jesus Christ, object, that these prerogatives or majesty exceed the capacity of the flesh of Christ, it is very much to be wondered at that the Calvinists are carried away into such impudence that they dare to determine the measure of the capacity of the flesh of Christ from their own brain. Why do they not rather measure the capacity from the omnipotence and truth of God? For the human nature did not snatch this majesty for itself, but the omnipotent and eternal λὸγος bestowed it upon his flesh, which was made the property of the Word, according to his immense wisdom and goodness. Who, therefore, has been the counselor of God? Who has measured the power and wisdom of God? Nor indeed does it follow from this the equalization or confusion of diverse natures in Jesus Christ. For even if the human nature of Jesus Christ has been raised to divine and equal glory and majesty with the Father, it has not, however, been converted or changed into the divine. The diversity and inequality of the natures remains for all eternity.

Λόγος is from eternity: But the human nature began in time, and draws its origin from the womb of the blessed virgin Mary. Λόγος is an eternal spiritual essence: But the human nature of Christ is partly corporeal, partly spiritual, namely the soul, which is not from eternity. The divine nature of Christ is an infinite essence: But the human nature of Christ is a finite essence. Λόγος is the creator of all things: But the human nature of Christ is and remains a creature. Λόγος has life and glory in itself, and had all divine majesty from eternity: But the human nature of Christ received life and all majesty through communication from λόγῳ. The divine nature of Christ sustains the human: But the human is sustained by λόγῳ, and for all eternity it will be subject to God. 1. Corinth: 15. Since this inequality remains for all eternity, and is expressly taught by us, it is a mere calumny that the adversaries shout that an equalization of natures is being made in Christ, since to the human nature in Christ sitting at the right hand of the Father is attributed omnipotence, equal majesty, and glory. For although Holy Scripture testifies to some equalization of glory, power, and majesty, it does not follow from this that the natures themselves are entirely equalized and confused among themselves. It is also a putrid cavil that they shout that the very divinity of Jesus Christ is obscured if those prerogatives are attributed to the human nature of Christ. For it is certain that that glory and majesty belong to no creature alone, but only to the divine majesty: Nor does God give his glory to another. For the human nature of Christ is not other than λόγῳ, but by personal union λόγῳ it is united: And because λόγος he did not only exert his divine glory and majesty in himself, nor did he only preserve it for himself, but he also communicated it to his human nature, by this very fact he revealed and demonstrated his eternal divinity all the more illustriously.

But again they object. That the essential properties of the divine nature can in no way be communicated to the human nature: that omnipotence, omniscience, and substance are essential properties of the divine nature. To this sophism, which the adversaries consider insoluble, I clearly reply: That phrase (essential properties of the divine nature) must be entirely unfolded and distinguished. For that God communicates his goods and properties to creatures, to Angels and to men, is more manifest than that it needs any proof. God communicates to men his wisdom, justice, liberty, life, chastity, joy, according to his good pleasure. God created man, says the scripture, in his own image. This is certainly nothing else than that God has transfused the rays of his wisdom, justice, light, life, and joy into the souls of men: And by this counsel we are redeemed through the mediator son Jesus Christ and are renewed through the holy Spirit, so that we may be made partakers of divine wisdom, justice, and life.

And yet all these goods, justice, wisdom, life, liberty, joy, are not accidents in God, but the divine essence itself. It is therefore said ignorantly that essential properties are not communicated to creatures. The divine essence itself is indeed not so transfused into creatures that creatures also become the divine essence: Nevertheless, God communicates his properties, which they call attributes in the schools, to creatures in such a way that, although in God they are the substance itself, yet when communicated to creatures they are not substance, but ornaments and qualities. It must therefore be entirely distinguished between the communication of essence, which is impossible, and between the communication of properties, which are more correctly called attributes than essential properties. Now since it is manifest that God has communicated his goods both in creation and in renewal, and even now communicates them to men: Why should we call into doubt whether God could communicate his gifts, properties, and majesty to the flesh of Christ? Just as omniscience and omnipotence in God are not certain accidents, but are substance, so also justice, and wisdom, and life, and joy in God are substance, and not accidents. And yet God communicates these gifts to men without any change of his essence. It is manifest, therefore, that omnipotence can also be communicated to the flesh of Christ without confusion of the natures. It cannot indeed be exhausted by us how those goods are in God indeed the substance itself, but when communicated to us are not the substance of God: But concerning this there can be no doubt for us, that God communicates to us those goods of his which in him are substance, as are justice, wisdom, joy, life. For the sacred scripture testifies to this expressly. Therefore, those things which God has revealed in his word, let us embrace with grateful hearts, meditate upon piously, and defend constantly. But those things which have not been revealed, let us not scrutinize rashly. But let us await the heavenly fellowship with God, in which not in a mirror as in this life, but in clear light we shall behold and understand those heavenly mysteries.

That which is said in the minor premise, that omnipotence is an essential property of the divine nature, is said obscurely, inconveniently, and perplexingly. The ancients did not wish to say that accidents or properties exist in God, lest they should seem to establish mutability in the divine nature. And when it is said that the omnipotence of God is nothing other than the divine essence itself being omnipotent, they mean this: that omnipotence is not a certain accident in God, or something mutable. And yet, in order to show some distinction, which could be comprehended at least by thought, between the divine essence itself and the goods of the essence which He communicates to creatures, such as wisdom, justice, joy, and life, they called these the attributes of God. Thus, therefore, according to the custom of the ancient Church, we shall call omnipotence and omniscience attributes rather than essential properties. And since it is manifestly evident that the major premise of the argument cannot be simply conceded, as has been demonstrated, the sophism vanishes entirely.

Now I also respond to the third question that Jesus Christ, after He departed from this world, having been resurrected from death, entered into a new and heavenly life, and then was exalted to the right hand of God, laid aside the elements and infirmities of this age, without the abolition of His flesh. He no longer hungers, thirsts, is fatigued, nor does He need food or drink, nor is it necessary for a body to be heavy and to be carried downward, nor is it any longer necessary for it to be able to be seen, touched, hindered by a vacuum, by the penetration of dimensions, by intervals of places, or by time. For these are the infirmities of this perishing world. But Christ now bears a glorious body, exempt from the infirmities of this world; a stone mass does not hinder him from going out of the sepulcher. A closed door does not prevent him from approaching his disciples: he suddenly vanishes from the eyes of the disciples as often as he wishes, again he offers himself to be seen when and where he wishes, finally with his body he ascends upward into heaven, contrary to the nature of human bodies.

From all these things it is clearly evident that concerning the prerogatives and majesty of the flesh of Christ, one cannot and ought not to make a determination based on the infirmity of our bodies, which are not one person with God, nor yet glorified, but are still subject to the needy elements of this world and to manifold infirmities.

IV. Objection.

Christ Jesus with his body ascended into heaven and sits at the right hand of the Father, from thence he is to come to judge the living and the dead.

Therefore the body of Jesus Christ is not on earth.

I respond:

And if from the solution of the previous sophism, the refutation of this argument can be taken, nevertheless so that the articles of faith may be more clearly understood, and the deceptions refuted, we shall repeat certain things. And first, it is so far from the case that the articles of faith concerning the ascension of Christ into heaven, and his sitting at the right hand, infringe upon the presence of the body of Jesus Christ in the sacred supper, that they rather demonstrate the omnipotence of Jesus Christ, that he can easily perform those things which he said and promised: So that it is very strange, when the universal Church learns the immense glory of Jesus Christ from the articles concerning the ascension of Christ into heaven, and his sitting at the right hand, that the Calvinists and Zwinglians gather from them the infirmity of Christ, and under the pretext of those articles despoil him of both truth and omnipotence. Let us therefore inquire into the true meaning of these articles of faith: The most clear Apostolic writings show it to us. We do not invent an allegory or metaphors in the articles of faith, but we understand them simply as the words sound. Christ truly ascended into heaven, and sits at the right hand of the eternal father. The ascension of Christ does not only signify the disappearance of Christ from the eyes of the disciples, as on the day of the resurrection he disappeared in Emmaus: But as Luke explained in the Acts, Christ was lifted up on high while they were watching, and a cloud took him away from their eyes: And the Angels then explain more clearly, This Jesus was taken up from you into heaven. Visibly, therefore, he changed place, and was translated into heaven. But what? Did he occupy some seat in this visible heaven, among the planets, or above the firmament? Paul says that Christ has passed through all the heavens, and has been raised above all the heavens, and above every name that can be named, both in this age and in the one to come. Therefore, he ascended into this eternal heaven, which he himself on the cross named Paradise, in which the eternal God dwells, and in which angels and holy men, resurrected and translated into heaven, live.
