Ut igitur unius corporis membra pari studio communes operas conferunt ad tuendam & conservandam totius corporis salutem, nulla hîc aemulatio, nulla invidia, nulla dissensio est. Sic & in Ecclesia, quod est corpus Christi mysticum esse debet. Qui Christum induerunt ab omni aemulatione, invidia, dissensione & contentione alienissimi esse debent, & toti in hoc incumbere, ut salutem totius corporis Ecclesiae conservent & tueantur.

Observet pius lector hoc loco testimonium de causa finali & efficacia Baptismi & coenae domoni: Paulus inquit, in uno Spiritu nos omnes in unum corpus Baptizatos esse. Ergò Baptismus in hunc finem à Deo est institutus, ut per eum efficiamur membra corporis Christi, abluamur à peccato, regeneremur per Spiritum sanctum & constituamur haeredes vitae aeternae, quemadmodum & alibi dicitur. Quotquot in Iesum Christum baptizati estis, Iesum induistis. Item, Rom: 6. Anignoratis quod quicunque in Christum Iesum baptizati sumus, in mortem eius baptizati sumus. Cum ipso igitur sepulti sumus per Baptismum in mortem, ut quemadmodum surrexit Christus ex mortuis per gloriam patris, ita & nos in novitate vitae ambulemus.

Non igitur tantum externum est signum Baptismus, quod cives Ecclesiae simus, sed est medium per quod Deus operatur in nobis salutem, & Spiritus sanctus regenerat nos in vitam. Eodem modo & de coena domini pronunciat: In unum Spiritum potati sumus, quasi dicat, Hoc fine instituit filius Dei suam sacrosanctam coenam, & omnibus dat vescendum suum corpus, & bibendum suum sanguinem, ut nobis Spiritum suum sanctum impertiat, & hoc nexu tanquam unius corporis membra nos sibi conglutinet.

Non igitur tantum externum signum est coena domini, quae nos admoneat de passione & morte Christi, sed etiam est medium & organon, per quod filius Dei Spiritum suum nobis impertit, tribuit vitam, alit & confirmat nostram fidem, & obsignat nobis haereditatem vitae aeternae.

Etenim corpus non est unum membrum, sed multa: si dixerit pes, quia non sum manus, ideò non sum de corpore, an propterea non erit ex corpore? Et si dixerit auris, quia oculus non sum, ideò de corpore non sum, an propterea non erit de corpore? Si totum corpus esset oculus, ubi maneret auditus? Si totum auditus, ubi olfactus? Nunc autem posuit Deus membra, unumquodque ipsorum in corpore, quemadmodum voluit. Si igitur omnia unum essent membrum, Ubi corpus? Nunc verò multa quidem membra, corpus verò unum. Non potest autem oculus dicere manui, non indigeo te, aut rursus caput pedibus, mihi non est opus vobis. Imò verò multo magis membra corporis, quae videntur esse imbecillia, sunt necessaria: & quae videntur minus honesta esse corporis, his ampliorem honorem adponimus, & minus decentia nostri maiorem decorem habent. Quae verò decora sunt, non indigent. Sed Deus temperavit corpus membro ignobiliori uberiorem honorem adponens, ne sit diffidium in corpore. Sed invicem alia pro aliis membris eandem sollicitudinem gerant: Et sive patiatur unum membrum, compatiuntur omnia membra: sive glorificetur unum membrum, congaudent omnia membra. Vos autem estis corpus Christi, & membra ex parte.

Copiose & pro lixè ipse Paulus singulas partes similitudinis & institutae collationis exposuit, Ideoque longiore declaratione non est opus. Haec autem totius collationis summa est, sicut mira sapientia constituit Deus & temperavit diversa membra in corpore humano: Sic etiam pro sua admiranda sapientia & bonitate diversis donis ornavit cives Ecclesiae, quare sicut nullae sunt aemulationes, nulla contentiones, nulla dissidia inter membra unius corporis: Sic & inter Christianos nullum dissidium, nulla aemulatio esse debet. Episcopus est veluti oculus Ecclesiae: Ministri verbi tanquam pedes speciosi Evangelizantium pacem.

Non potest Episcopus dicere se non indigere opera ministri verbi. Ac Deus inferioribus civibus suae Ecclesiae tantò confert excellentiora dona, ut omnes decori sint corpori. Utergò membrum pro membro est sollicitum in corpore: Et cum unum laeditur, omnia simul dolent et adsiciuntur? Talis συμπάθεια et inter Christianos esse debet, nemini invidere debent vel altiorem gradum dignitatis, vel excellentiora dona: Sed cogitare quod Deus singulos suo loco constituerit: Et quod nemo inter pusillos Christi, tam sit abiectae sortis, qui non serviat gloriae Dei, et fructum ferat domino. Itaque neminem despicere debemus: Quin potius cum uni Christiano infertur iniuria, omnes dolere: Cum uni gloria & honor contingit, omnes laetari debemus. Talis consensus & concordia si extiterit in omnibus membris corporis Christi, tum nullus locus futurus est contentionibus ac dissidiis.

## 12:28
And some indeed God has placed in the Church, first Apostles, second Prophets, third teachers, then powers, then gifts of healings, helps, governments, kinds of tongues. Are all Apostles? Are all Prophets? Are all Teachers? Are all Are all powers? Do all have the gifts of healing? Do all speak with tongues? Do all interpret? Pursue the better gifts.

This is the fourth argument, by which the Apostle proves that one should not be proud of gifts, nor contend with others through emulation, nor should anyone be deceived, nor should anyone be envied. Because God himself has not placed ministers and offices of one kind in the Church: But according to his wisdom and goodness he has adorned the Kingdom of his son with various offices and gifts. Nor is it placed in the judgment of any man, that he should either adorn himself with gifts, or place himself in this or that position. This is situated in the sole judgment and good pleasure of the most high God: Who understands more rightly what most conduces to the Church, and whom alone it befits to distribute his gifts. Therefore, in true humility and with serious thanksgiving, one must look to the most wise counsel of God, and his most clement will, and in that place where he himself has placed us, one must serve faithfully for the illustration of the glory of God and the edification of the Church.

Then in order he recounts the principal ministries, which the omnipotent God established in his Church, and in the first place he recounts the Apostles, for the reason that these were established as witnesses of his doctrine, life, miracles, travels, death, resurrection, and ascension into heaven. This is the highest office in the Church after the office of the Messiah, to testify concerning the person, doctrine, miracles, death, and resurrection of the exhibited Messiah. They were also adorned with the highest gifts of the Holy Spirit. Therefore, he recounts them in the first place.

An Apostle is a person called immediately by Jesus Christ in the New Testament, so that he may be a witness of the doctrine, miracles, death, and resurrection of Jesus Christ, not bound to a certain place, but sent into the whole world to preach the Gospel concerning Jesus Christ, adorned with the visible grace of the Holy Spirit, and the gift of performing miracles proper to the Church as a testimony that he does not err in doctrine.

A Prophet in the Old Testament is a person called immediately by God to purge the doctrine of the Church, and to propagate the promise concerning the Mediator, and to assist the counsels of political government in the Israelite kingdom, adorned with the gift of predicting future things, and of performing miracles as a testimony that he brought doctrine from God that was beyond doubt.

A Prophet in the New Testament is a person called immediately by God, not for political government in any kingdom, nor bound to a certain place, but sent into the world to purge the doctrine of the Church, and to illustrate the Gospel concerning Jesus Christ, adorned by the Holy Spirit with the gift of predicting future things.

A Doctor in the Church is a person mediately, that is, called by God through men to propagate the doctrine concerning God among men, and to explain the sacred and Apostolic scripture, not occupied with either the government of the Church or the administration of the Sacraments, but faithfully applying himself only to the propagation of the doctrine which he has drawn from the writings of the Prophets and Apostles, and likewise to consolation and exhortation.

Δυνάμεις, that is, powers, he here recounts the ministers of the Church, who were instructed by God with singular virtue and power to drive out demons, to punish hypocrites, and to perform great works in the Church. As Paul by a word blinded Elymas the sorcerer. Ambrose drove the scribe of Stilicho into a frenzy: he does not understand civil power, but spiritual power in the Church, by which certain ministers were instructed by God.

What it is to be endowed with the gift of healings is known. Αντιλήψεις, helps or assistances I refer to the ministry and office of deacons, who took care of the poor, and provided them with subsidies and assistances. Government pertains partly to the Bishop, partly to the presbyters and elders of the Church, to whom the inspection of the Church, the examinations of pastors, the calling of ministers, and the judgment concerning the doctrine and life of both those who teach and those who hear in the Church has been committed. To the Ephesians he recounts more offices. In this place it was sufficient for Paul to show the diversity of gifts and ministries in the Church: which ought to admonish individuals, lest we affect more sublime offices, or more eminent degrees of honors, than those to which we are called by God himself. For thus it pleased the most wise God not to instruct all with equal gifts, nor to place all in an equal degree of dignity, but to place some in the first, others in the second, others in the third place. Therefore let each one remain in his station and adorn his place with humility, faith, diligence, and thanksgiving.

Latin:

Et alios quidem posuit Deus in Ecclesia, primùm Apostolos, secundò Prophetas, tertiò doctores, deinde potestates, deinde dona curationum, auxilia, gubernationes, genera linguarum. Num omnes Apostoli? Num omnes Prophetae? Num omnes Doctores? Num omnes potestates? Num omnes dona curationum habent? Num omnes linguis loquuntur? Num omnes interpretes sunt? Sectamini dona potiora.

Quartum est hoc argumentum, quo probat Apostolus non esse superbiendum donis, nec aemulatione certandum cum aliis, nec quenquam decipiendum, nec cuiquam invidendum. Quia ipse Deus non unius generis ministros et officia posuerit in Ecclesia: Sed pro sua sapientia & bonitate variis officiis & donis exornaverit Regnum sui filii. Nec est in ullius hominis arbitrio positum, ut vel ipse ornet se donis, vel collocet seipsum velhoc vel illo loco. Hoc in solo arbitrio & beneplacito altissimi Dei est situm: Qui rectius intelligit, quid maxime conducat Ecclesiae, & quem solum decet sua distribuere dona. In vera igitur humilitate & cum seria gratiarum actione, ad sapientissimum Dei consilium, & clementissimam eius voluntatem est respiciendum, et eo loco quo ipso nos collocavit, fideliter esse serviendum ad gloriae Dei illustrationem & Ecclesiae aedificationem.

Ordine deinde recenset praecipua ministeria, quae Deus omnipotens in sua constituit Ecclesia, ac primo loco recenset Apostolos, eo quod hi fuerint testes constituti doctrinae, vitae, miracularum, peregrinationum, mortis, resurrectionis & adscensionis eius in coelum. Hoc est summum in Ecclesia officium post Messiae munus, testari de persona, doctrina, miraculis, morte & resurrectione Messiae exhibiti. Summis etiam Spiritus sancti donis fuerunt exornati. Ideò primo loco illos recenset.

Apostolus est persona immediatè à Iesu Christo in novo testamento vocata, ut sit testis docrtinae, miraculorum, mortis & resurrectionis Iesu Christi, non alligata ad certum locum, sed missa in orbem terrarum, ad praedicandum Evangelium de Iesu Christo, ornata visibili, Spiritus sancti gratia, & dono edendi miracula propria Ecclesiae in testimonium, quod non erret in doctrina.

Propheta in veteri testamento est persona immediatè vocata à Deo ad re purgandam doctrinam Ecclesiae, & propagandam promissionem de Mediatore, & ad iuvanda consilia politicae gubernationis in regno Israelitico, ornata dono praedicendi futura, & edendi miracula in testimonium, quod indubiam de Deo doctrinam adferret.

Propheta in novo testamento est persona immediatè vocata à Deo, non ad gubernationem politicam ullo in regno, nec alligata certo loco, sed missa in orbem ad repurgandum doctrinam Ecclesiae, & illustrandum Evangelion de Iesu Christo, ornata à Spiritu sancto dono praedicendi futura.

Doct: in Eccle; est persona mediatè, hoc est, per homines vocata à Deo ad propagandam doctrinam de Deo inter homines, & ad explicandam sacram scripturam & Apostolicam, non occupata vel gubernatione Ecclesiae, vel administratione Sacramentorum, sed tantum doctrinae, quam ex scriptis Prophetis & Apostolicis hausit, propagationi atque item consolationi & exhortationi fideliter incumbens.

Δυνάμεις, id est, potestates, ministros Ecclesiae hic recenset, qui singulari virtute & potestate à Deo instructi sunt pellendi damones, puniendi hypocritas, & magna opera edendi in Ecclesia. Ut Paulus verbo excaecavit Elymam magum. Ambrosius Stilliconis scribam adegit in furorem: non intelligit civilem potestatem, sed spiritualem in Ecclesia, qua certi ministri à Deo instructi fuerunt.

Quid sit praeditum esse dono sanationum notum est. Αντιλήψεις, auxilia seu opitulationes ad ministerium & officium diaconorum refero, qui curam agebant pauperum, iisque subsidia & opitulationes praestabant. Gubernatio partim ad Episcopum, partim ad presbyteros & seniores Ecclesiae pertinet, quibus inspectio Ecclesiae, examina pastorum, vocatio ministrorum, iudicium de doctrina & vita cum docentium tum auditorum in Ecclesia est commissa. Ad Ephesios plura officia recenset. Hoc loco satis fuit Paulo monstrare diversitatem donorum & ministeriorum in Ecclesia: quae singulos admonere debet, ne sublimiora officia, vel eminentiores gradus honorum adfectemus, quàm ad quos ab ipso Deo vocamur. Sic enim Deo sapientissimo placuit non omnes paribus donis instruere, nec omnes in parigradu dignitatis collocare, sed alios primo, alios secundo, alios tertio loco collocare. Ergò quisque in sua statione maneat & locum suum ornet humilitate, fide, diligentia, gratiarum actione.

## 12:28 Places of Doctrine
Places of Doctrine.

1. Concerning spiritual gifts, with which God adorns his Church, that there is a great variety of gifts: that all things proceed from God, not from the free will of man: that individual gifts are to be conferred in the fear of the Lord for the illustration of the glory of God and the edification of the Church.

2. Concerning the servitude of free will: that a man not reborn through the Holy Spirit cannot call Jesus Christ Lord. Moreover, the foundation of faith and of all piety is the acknowledgment of Jesus Christ, that he is our almighty and eternal Lord. Therefore, there is no freedom of the will in spiritual matters: Nor is there any synergy or cooperation of the human will in conversion. For human reason of itself, without the illumination of the Holy Spirit, cannot acknowledge the Lord Jesus. No one knows the Son except the Father, says Christ Matth: 11.

3. That there are three persons of the divinity. God the Father, Jesus Christ the Lord, and the Holy Spirit. That these persons of the divinity are distinguished by their offices. The Father is the person from whom all admirable operations proceed, he supplies the power and efficacy: The Son is the Lord of the Church and governs all ministries: The Holy Spirit is the effector and bestower of all gifts.

4. A most weighty testimony concerning the eternal divinity of the Holy Spirit: inasmuch as Paul affirms that the Holy Spirit effects and distributes all the gifts which are seen in the whole Church.

5. Concerning the final cause and efficacy of the sacraments of the new testament: of Baptism and the Lord's supper, that they are not only bare signs: but are means and organs through which the Holy Spirit works salvation, and regenerates men to eternal life.

6. Concerning the difference of gifts and ministries in the Church: and concerning the sublime degree of dignity, in which God has placed in the Church, first Apostles, then prophets and other ministers.

Latin:

Loci Doctrinae.

1. De donis spiritualibus, quibus Deus exornat suam Ecclesiam, quod magna sit donorum varietas: quod omnia à Deo proficiscantur, non à libero hominis arbitrio: quod singula dona sint in timore domini conferenda ad gloriae Dei illustrationem & Ecclesiae aedificationem.

2. De servitute liberi arbitrii: quod homo non renatus per Spiritum sanctum, Iesum Christum non possit vocare dominum. Est autem fundamentum fidei & omnis pietatis agnitio Iesu Christi, quod sit Dominus noster omnipotens & aeternus. Nulla igitur est libertas arbitrii in spiritualibus: Nec ulla est synergia vel cooperatio humanae voluntatis in conversione. Dominum enim Iesum ratio humana ex sese sine Spiritus sancti illuminatione agnoscere non potest. Nemo novit filium nisi pater, inquit Christus Matth: 11.

3. Quod tres sint personae divinitatis. Deus pater, Iesus Christus Dominus, & Spiritus sanctus. Quod hae personae divinitatis officiis distinguantur. Pater est persona, à qua omnes admirandae operationes proficiscuntur, ille virtutem & efficaciam suppeditat: Filius est Dominus Ecclesiae & omnia gubernat ministeria: Spiritus sanctus est effector & largitor omnium donorum.

4. Testimonium gravissimum de aeterna divinitate Spiritus sancti: siquidem Paulus adfirmat Spiritum sanctum efficere & distribuere omnia dona, quae conspiciuntur in tota Ecclesia.

5. De causa finali & efficacia sacramentorum novi testamenti: Baptismi & coena domini, quod non tantum sint nuda signa: sed sint media & organa, per quae Spiritus sanctus operatur salutem, & regenerat homines ad vitam aeternam.

6. De differentia donorum & ministeriorum in Ecclesia: & de sublimi gradu dignitatis, in quo Deus collocavit in Ecclesia, Primùm Apostolos, deinde prophetas & alios ministros.

## 13:1 Argument
CHAPTER XIII.

And yet I show unto you a more excellent way: If I speak with the tongues of men and of angels, and have not love, I am become as sounding brass or a tinkling cymbal. And if I have prophecy and know all mysteries, and all knowledge: And if I have all faith, so that I could remove mountains, and have not charity, I am nothing.

In this chapter Paul exhorts the Corinthians and the whole Church to true and sincere love of God and neighbor. For this is true piety.

This is the fountain, the spring, and the mother of all virtues: This is the directress of all gifts and duties: This is the unique scope, to which all things must be directed, namely, that we may love God and our neighbor. This is the banner of the kingdom of Christ, which all citizens of the Church ought to follow for the overcoming of Satan with all his works: Therefore he commends love here and prefers it to all gifts. By comparison he adds those gifts and duties, which in this life serve for the edification and propagation of the Church, are to have an end, when God shall be all in all.

First he warns that nothing profits us, even if we speak in various tongues and in eloquence are in a certain way equal to the angels, if true love of God and neighbor is lacking to us. For when this does not exist in a man, it is certain that neither does faith exist in him, nor is that man reconciled to God, nor is he a dwelling place of the Holy Spirit: even if the most excellent gifts shine in him. For he is not going to be a participant in the kingdom of heaven: Indeed, he is going to undergo the greater punishments, by how much greater gifts he was instructed by God, which he did not contribute to the glory of God.

Brass indeed gives forth a sound, but lacks life: Thus the eloquent hypocrite gives forth a sound, but lacks life and Spirit. Thus the knowledge of doctrine and of all mysteries of the intellect helps a man nothing, if he be devoid of love. For a naked knowledge of sacred things does not save a man: But faith, which is effective through love.

But why does Paul say, And if I have all faith, so that I move mountains: But have not love, I am nothing. By this saying, contrary to the mind of Paul, the Papists first abuse it, who attempt to gather from hence that a man is not justified by faith alone, but by faith and love together: And they contend that faith is only a preparation for justification: But that it is perfected by love, and thus by love we are formally just before God. Then also the followers of Major seek from hence a patronage for their error, as if Paul here wished love to be necessary for salvation, and that no one can be justified and saved without love. Likewise, that in the very act of justification the presence of good works is necessary. These corruptions of the Pauline saying are to be entirely refuted. Therefore, to both, and to the Papists and to those patronizing the error of Major, we answer, that in the Apostolic writings it must always be attended to, which heads of doctrine are being explained: For the Apostles do not hand down all things confusedly, but they distinguish matters accurately. Paul is not here dealing with the justification of a man before God: Which doctrine he expounded at Rom: 3. & 4. & Galat: 3.: Where he expressly testified that man is justified by faith alone without works. But in this place he treats of the good works of the reborn and justified, namely of love, which ought to be the moderator of all gifts. Therefore these things are not to be drawn to the article of justification. Augustine distinguishes very skillfully between the one to be justified and the justified: good works, he says, do not precede the one to be justified, but follow the justified. Thus we also distinguish between the justification of man itself: and the judgment concerning the justified man. When it is a matter of justification itself, good works are not to be mixed in. For man is justified before God without the works of the law, freely by faith alone. This is, good works are not the cause, nor the merit, nor ἄιτιον, nor συνάιτιον of justification: They are not the medium apprehending justification: Nor are they even necessary by necessity of presence for justification: but man is justified before God entirely without any condition and necessity of good works by faith alone on account of the mediator Jesus Christ. For the death of Jesus Christ alone is the sole and sufficient cause of our justification: And faith alone is the medium by which we apply to ourselves the benefits of the mediator. And thus faith justifies even when no good works are present, but man is full of sins from the crown of his head to the sole of his foot: yet he believes in Him who justifies the ungodly. But after a man has been justified freely through faith, then good works must altogether follow faith as fruits. For it is impossible that a man should truly establish for himself that all his sins have been forgiven, and that he has been constituted an heir of eternal life, without beginning to love so merciful a God. It is impossible for the Holy Spirit to dwell in anyone, and yet for that man to remain without any love and new motion, for the Holy Spirit is not idle, but stirs up in man motions congruent to God. But if anyone has obtained pardon from God in faith, and yet, being justified, does not begin to love God and to be renewed in mind, then it is most certain that he has fallen away from grace again, has extinguished the spark of faith by security, has expelled the Holy Spirit, and that this man has returned to his vomit after the manner of dogs. Therefore, those sayings of the Apostles are to be understood concerning this examination of faith to be taken from its effect. If I have all faith, but have not love, I am nothing. Likewise, He who does not love, remains in death. Likewise, faith without works is dead. As if you were to say, a man who is without any motion does not live: because life is not without motion, but from this it does not follow that motion is necessarily required for the vivifying of a man. Therefore, it must be accurately seen when the Apostles speak of the act and struggle of faith in justification. they speak, where it apprehends the mediator alone without any work, and relies on this alone in the sight of God: And when they speak of the examination of faith from its effect outside of justification, where faith, unless it be effective through love, is detected to be false and feigned. Therefore, both doctrines must be urged and retained in the Church; And that a man is justified by faith alone without works before God freely on account of the obedience of Jesus Christ. And that love or new obedience must necessarily follow faith in the justified: And that faith cannot be in the justified without the fruit of good works, just as life cannot be without motion, nor can the Sun be without light. So that both statements are most true. Faith without works and without any presence of good works justifies: And faith without good works is nothing, it is dead, it is an empty dream of the heart, but these things are said in a different respect. For that former statement speaks of the act of faith in justification. Where faith is the medium applying to man the benefits of the mediator. But this latter one deals with the examination of faith from its effect in the justified. But the papists are to be detested first, because they feign that love and good works are a partial efficient cause, or even a formal one and a merit of justification, or at least an applicative medium. Since love and new obedience follow as the fruit of justification. These greater ones are also to be detested, because they mix faith and love in the very act of justification, and contend that love is necessary for salvation and justification. Since Paul expressly testifies that salvation and justification consist for us by faith alone without works: it is a false and impious voice that faith without works, or without love, is nothing, when it is a matter of justification. It is an impious and blasphemous voice, it is impossible for a man to be saved by faith alone without works. Therefore, let the justification of man itself be distinguished from the examination of faith in a justified man: Others respond thus, that Paul is speaking here not of justifying faith, which apprehends the whole Christ: But of a particular faith, which they call the faith of signs, which only apprehends the power of Christ in performing miracles. And they prove that by this particle: That Paul says so that I may remove mountains: And it is indeed true that in certain hypocrites and those alien from justifying faith there exist certain gifts, the faith of performing miracles and others. As Matth: 7. they say: Lord, did we not perform virtues in your name? But because Paul prefixed (Even if I have all faith) it is too forced to wish to restrict this saying only to the faith of performing miracles. A more solid response is that this saying must be understood concerning the examination of faith by its effect. in the justified. And as for what Paul says: If I have all faith, but do not have love, I am nothing, it must be known that the argumentation is κατὰ τὸ ἀδυνάτον. That is, by the impossible, so that he may the more validly exclude all sophistry which pretends that faith can shine in a man without love and newness of life. It cannot happen that anyone who is justified has all faith and does not also have love: Thus τῶν ἀδυνάτων it is, to speak with the tongues of Angels: But he posited these things hypothetically for this reason, that he might exclude and refute every simulation of faith which is devoid of all love.

Latin:

CAPUT XIII.

Et adhuc excellentiorem viam vobis demonstro: Si linguis hominum loquar & angelorum, dilectionem autem non habeam, factus sum aes sonans & cymbalum tinniens. Et si habeam prophetiam & noverim omnia mysteria, & omnem scientiam: Et si habeam omnem fidem, adeò ut montes dimoveam, charitatem autem non habeam, nihil sum.

In hoc capite hortatur Paulus Corinthios & totam Ecclesiam ad veram & synceram dilectionem Dei & proximi. Haec enim est vera pietas.

Haec fons, scaturgio & mater est omnium virtutum: Haec rectrix est omnium donorum & officiorum: Hic unicus est scopus, quo omnia dirigenda sunt, nimirum, ut Deum & proximum diligamus. Hoc est vexillum regni Christi, quod universi cives Ecclesiae sequi debent ad debellandum Satanam cum omnibus suis operibus: Itaque dilectionem hîc commendat & omnibus donis praefert. Simulantem per collationem adiungit dona & officia illa, quae in hac vita serviunt, aedificationi et propagationi Ecclesiae, finem habitura esse, cum Deus futurus est omnia in omnibus.

Primum monet nihil nobis conducere, etiamsi variis linguis loquamur & eloquentia angelis simus quodammodo pares, si desit nobis vera dilectio Dei & proximi. Haec enim cum non existit in homine, certum est nec fidem in eo existere, nec hominem istum esse reconciliatum Deo, nec esse domicilium Spiritus sancti: etiamsi dona in ipso fulgeant excellentissima. Non enim est futurus particeps regni coelorum: Imò tanto maiores poenas subiturus est, quo maioribus donis à Deo fuit instructus, quae non contulit ad gloriam Dei.

Aes sonum quidem edit, sed vita caret: Ita hypocrita facundus sonum edit, sed vita et Spiritu caret. Sic cognitio doctrinae & omnium mysteriorum intellectus nihil iuvat hominem, si sit expers dilectionis. Nuda enim rerum sacrarum scientia non salvat hominem: Sed fides, quae per dilectionem est efficax.

At cur dicit Paulus. Et si omnem fidem habeam adeò, ut montes dimoveam: Dilectionem autem non habeam, nihil sum. Hoc dicto contra mentem Pauli abutuntur primùm pontificii, qui hinc colligere conantur, non sola fide iustificari hominem, sed simul fide & dilectione: Et contendunt fidem tantum esse praeparationem ad iustificationem: Dilectione autem eam perfici, & sic dilectione nos coram Deo formaliter iustos esse. Deinde & Maioris asseclae patrocinium sui erroris hinc petunt, quasi Paulus hîc voluerit dilectionem esse necessariam ad salutem, nec posse quenquam iustificari & salvari sine dilectione. Item, in ipso actu iustificationis praesentiam bonorum operum esse necessariam. Hae corruptelae dicti paulini omninò refutandae sunt. Utrisque ergò, & pontificiis et Maioris errori patrocinantibus respondemus, In scriptis Apostolicis semper attendendum esse, quae doctrinae capita explicentur: Non enim confusè omnia tradunt Apostoli, sed distinguunt accuratè materias. Non iam hîc agit Paulus de iustificatione hominis coram Deo: Quam doctrinam ad Rom: 3. & 4. & Galat: 3. exposuit: Ubi disertè testatus est hominem sola fide absque operibus iustificari. Hoc vero loco agit de bonis operibus renatorum & iustificatorum, nimirum de dilectione, quae omnium donorum moderatrix esse debet. Non ergò haec trahenda sunt ad articulum iustificationis. Scitè admodum distinguit Augustinus inter Iustificandum & Iustificatum: bona opera, inquit, non praecedunt iustificandum, sed sequuntur iustificatum. Sic & nos distinguimus inter ipsam hominis iustificationem: Et iudicium de homine iustificato. Cùm de ipsa iustificatione agitur, non miscenda sunt bona opera. Homo enim absque operibus legis, gratis sola fide iustificatur coram Deo. Hoc est, bona opera non sunt causa, nec meritum, nec ἄιτιον, nec συνάιτιον iustificationis: Non sunt medium apprehendens iustificationem: Neque etiam necessaria sunt necessitate praesentiae ad iustificationem: sed prorsus absque omni conditione & necessitate bonorum operum homo iustificatur coram Deo sola fide propter mediatorem Iesum Christum. Sola enim mors Iesu Christi, est unica & sufficiens causa nostrae iustificationis: Et sola fides est medium, quo nobis adplicamus beneficia mediatoris. Atque ita iustificat fides etiam cùm nulla adsunt bona opera, sed homo plenus est peccatis à vertice capitis usque ad plantam pedis: credit autem in eum qui iustificat impium. Post quam verò homo per fidem gratis iustificatus est, tum omninò bona opera tanquam fructus fidem sequi debent. Impossibile est enim ut homo verè statuat sibi remissa esse omnia peccata, & se esse haeredem vitae aeternae constitutum, ut non incipiat tàm clementem diligere Deum. Impossibile est in aliquo habitare Spiritum sanctum, & tamen hominem istum manere sine omni dilectione & novo motu, Spiritus sanctus enim ociosus non est, sed excitat in homine motus congruentes Deo. Quod si quis in fide impetravit veniam apud Deum: Et tamen iustificatus non incipit diligere Deum & renovari mente, tum certissimum est eum rursus excidisse gratia, securitate extinxisse fidei scintillam, expulisse Spiritum sanctum & hominem istum more canum rediisse ad vomitum. De hac igitur fidei exploratione ab effectu sumenda, intelligenda sunt illa Apostolorum dicta. Si omnem fidem habeam, dilectionem autem non habeam, nihil sum. Item, Qui non diligit, manet in morte. Item, fides sine operibus mortua est. Ut si dicas, homo, qui sine omni motu est, non vivit: quia vita non est absque motu, sed hinc non sequitur ad vivificandum hominem, necessariò requiri motum. Accuratè igitur videndum est, quando Apostoli de actu & lucta fidei in iustificatione loquuntur, ubi sola absque omni opere mediatorem adprehendit, & hoc solo nititur in conspectu Dei: Et quando loquuntur de exploratione fidei ab effectu extra iustificationem, ubi fides, nisi sit efficax per dilectionem, falsa & simulata esse: deprehenditur. Utraque ergò doctrina urgenda & retinenda est in Ecclesia; Et quod sola fide absque operibus coram Deo gratis propter obedientiam Iesu Christi iustificetur homo. Et quod dilectio seu nova obedientia necessariò sequi debeat fidem in iustificato: Et quod fides non possit esse in: iustificato absque fructu bonorum operum, sicut: vita non potest esse absque motu, nec Sol esse potest: absque lumine. Adeò utraque sententia est verissima. Fides sine operibus & sine omni praesentia bonorum operum iustificat: Et fides sine bonis operibus nihil est, mortua est, inane somnium cordis est, sed diverso respectu haec dicuntur. Illa enim sententia de actu fidei in iustificatione loquitur. Ubi fides est medium adplicans homini beneficia mediatoris. Haec verò posterior agit, de exploratione fidei ab effectu in iustificato. Detestandi verò sunt primùm pontificii, quod fingunt dilectionem & bona opera esse partialem causam efficientem, aut etiam formalem et meritum iustificationis, aut saltem medium adplicativum. Cum dilectio & nova obedientia sequetur ut fructus iustificationem. Maior istae quoque detestandi sunt, quod miscent fidem & dilectionem in ipso actu iustificationis, & contendunt dilectionem esse necessariam ad salutem & iustificationem. Cùm Paulus disertè testetur salutem & iustificationem nobis constare, sola fide absque operibus: falsa & impia vox est fidem absque operibus, vel absque dilectione nihil esse, cùm de iustificatione agitur. Impia & blasphema vox est, impossibile est hominem salvari sola fide absque operibus. Distinguatur igitur ipsa hominis iustificatio, ab exploratione fidei in homine iustificato: Alii sic respondent, Paulum hîc loqui non de fide iustificante, quae totum adprehendit Christum: Sed de fide particulari, quam fidem signorum vocant, quae tantum potentiam Christi in edendis miraculis adprehendit. Idque probant hac particula: Quòd Paulus dicit adeò ut montes transferam: Et verum quidem est in hypocritis quibusdam & à fide iustificante alienis existere dona quaedam, fidem edendi miracula & alia. Ut Matth: 7. dicunt: Domine an non in nomine tuo virtutes edidimus? At quia Paulus praemisit (Etiamsi omnem fidem habeam) coactius est tantum ad fidem edendi miracula hoc dictum restringere velle. Solidior est responsio, hoc dictum intelligendum esse de exploratione fidei ab effectu in iustificato. Quodque Paul: dicit: Etsi omnem fidem habeam, dilectionem autem non habeam, nihil sum, sciendum est argumentationem esse κατὰ τὸ ἀδυνάτον. Id est, per impossibile, ut tantò validius omnem sophisticen, quae fingit fidem in homine lucere posse absque dilectione & vitae novitate excludat. Fieri non potest, ut quis iustificatus, habeat omnem fidem et non etiam habeat dilectionem: Sic τῶν ἀδυνάτων est, loqui linguis Angelorum: Sed ideò haec posuit hypotheticè, ut omnem fidei simulationem, quae omnis dilectionis expers est, excluderet & refutaret.

## 13:3
If I distribute all my goods for the food of the poor, and if I deliver my body so that I may burn, but do not have charity, I gain no profit.

The Apostle teaches that all the remaining duties of a Christian man, such as remarkable liberality toward the poor, constancy in undergoing dangers, confessions, and others, are without any fruit if they do not proceed from true love, which is the fountain, parent, and scope of all virtues and duties. The reason is manifest, because virtues which are destitute of love are also devoid of faith: And as they are expressed only by human powers, they are not kindled by the Holy Spirit: Thus they are mere simulations, they are not directed to the glory of God and the utility of the neighbor: But they only seek the shadow of glory before men. Therefore they do not please God nor are they true virtues, nor do they have any reward before God, but they belong to the catalog of works, of which Christ says, Amen I say to you, they have already received their reward.

Love is long-suffering, kind: Love envieth not: Love dealeth not perversely, is not puffed up, is not ambitious, seeketh not her own, is not provoked to anger, thinketh no evil, rejoiceth not in iniquity: But rejoiceth with the truth. Beareth all things, believeth all things, hopeth all things, endureth all things, love never faileth.

He institutes here a prolix commendation and description of true love, so that to perform it he may excite and kindle the Corinthians and all who are studious of true piety. For the foundation of true virtue is love and the scope of all the commandments of God: It is the fortification and bond of concord: Therefore it ought to shine before all counsels and actions and be the directress of the whole life. For love is the true obedience of the heart and of all the powers of man, kindled by the Holy Spirit, and agreeing with all the commandments of God, rendering to each his own as much to God as to man. It is indeed true, except for Jesus Christ the Son of God, that no man has ever existed, nor is, nor is to come into this world, who has performed or is about to perform such a love, absolute in all its parts. For the whole nature of men is corrupted by sin, All lack the glory of God, All are corrupted, they have turned aside and have become useless.

Neither Abraham, nor Moses, nor Paul had such a love, which would have been the fulfillment of the law: For the law is spiritual, but men, although they are reborn and sanctified, are in part carnal. And therefore the good, which they wish to perform, they cannot. But although it is impossible for men in this life to perform an integral love, nevertheless this scope is to be looked upon by individuals, and the sentence of the law is to be urged, so that it may always be in our sight, what God demands of us, and toward what we ought to strive.

Therefore, let individual pious persons not only apply themselves to demonstrate their sincere faith through true love of neighbor, but also implore the help of the Holy Spirit, so that He may inflame our souls with true and not feigned love. For God is love, and he who abides in love, abides in God. Paul took the praises of love from its properties and effects.

Love is long-suffering: The first fruit of love is patience, which is a virtue ignited by the Holy Spirit, by which someone patiently and moderately endures an insult or injury brought upon them by a neighbor, and for the sake of God and the peace of the Church forgives it, and does not allow themselves to be moved to anger or a desire for vengeance. A notable example of patience was in David, who, although he had grave and great causes for removing Saul, nevertheless spared his life and forgave him atrocious injuries. An illustrious example of patience was also in Moses, whom, although the Israelites often attempted to overwhelm with stones, he nevertheless embraced this people with immense love, and bestowed upon them the highest benefits, interceded for them, and sustained the most grave labors of governance. Thus Samuel, affected by a grave insult from the people of Israel, nevertheless overcame his pain with patience and interceded for them before God. In Paul also there was great patience: For although he was affected by the most grievous insults and injuries by the Jews and the Gentiles, he did not cease, however, to do good to them, and to offer the heavenly treasure to them.

This patience is altogether necessary in the Church, and this virtue is especially necessary for ministers, for the reason that the world is full of malice and petulance: And it treats the faithful heralds of the word very badly: Even in the saints there is great infirmity, one easily harms another either by word or by deed. Love and patience ought to cover and bury these injuries immediately, so that the peace of the Church may be consulted. Jerome was impatient, even harmed by a little word, he immediately conceived an angry mind and often caused a tumult without cause: so also Chrysostom often seethed with impatience, and caused great disturbances in the Church. From this vice, therefore, Paul deters the Church, and shows that it fights against love.

It is kind: The second fruit is beneficence, this is a virtue ignited by the Holy Spirit, by which one is of a ready mind to help and to succor one's neighbor, both friend and enemy, in every necessity with every kind of service which can proceed from us. A notable example of beneficence shone in Joseph, who did good to all his brothers, when they had attempted to destroy him. Beneficent was Obadiah, a minister of King Ahab, who even at the peril of his own life fed and protected the Prophets of the Lord. Barzillai the Gileadite was beneficent, who fed the king in exile with his whole family, and followed him with every kind of service.

Love envieth not: Now he also recites the vices fighting against love, so that the pious may avoid them, lest they show themselves to be strangers to love. Emulation is an affection of the heart, by which one is grieved that another excels, and that he is either equaled or surpassed by him, and therefore desires him to be removed. As Korah and Dathan envy the virtue and glory of Moses and Aaron. Saul envies the glory of David, and desires him to be removed. Arius envies Bishop Alexander. John of Antioch envies Cyril. And this plague wanders most widely in the world and in the Church, and impels very many ambitious minds to stir up dissensions. Eliab envies the virtue and kingdom of David. The false Apostles envy the authority and gifts of the Apostle Paul. By this emulation, therefore, they demonstrated that they were strangers to true love.

Love dealeth not insolently. Περπερεύεσθαι is to conduct oneself insolently and petulantly, which vice fights with love. For this always consults for the tranquility and honor of the neighbor, it adorns and helps the neighbor. But petulance does not have regard for the neighbor, it only indulges its own desire and folly. Therefore, petulance is a vice fighting against the 4th commandment, by which someone, without regard for the neighbor, indulges his own folly and unjust desire, and either harms the reputation of the neighbor with insults, or inflicts injury upon his body. Petulance was prodigious in the Emperor Julian, who snatched away the resources of the Church, and furthermore insulted it, repeating that it was written in their law: That the kingdom of heaven is the poor's: Therefore by this duty he was promoting Christians to the kingdom of heaven.

It is not puffed up: The third vice fighting against love is pride and arrogance, by which someone is puffed up against the neighbor, attributes more to himself than is right: he prefers himself to others, and despises others. Detestable pride was in Nestorius: Who used this foolish and impious voice before the assembly. O Emperor, give me the earth purged of heretics, and I grant heaven to you. John of Antioch is puffed up with arrogance against Cyril: Therefore he was the author of a foul and pernicious dissension in the Ephesian synod. For among the proud there is always contention. Carlstadt, puffed up with arrogance against Luther, stirred up a sad dissension in the Church.

He does not act indecently: Men puffed up with pride observe neither measure nor decorum: But both by indecorous gestures and arrogant speech they betray their own folly, and lose all the grace which they might otherwise obtain by their gifts. For every sign of an elated and proud mind loses all grace, and creates for itself envy and hatred before God and before men. Moreover, there is a wonderful power in modesty for conciliating the benevolence of men. Samosatenus conducts himself indecently, who everywhere displays his arrogance, walks indecently, reads letters in public, so that he may show that he is involved in many affairs. Without doubt, in individual particulars he pricks and lashes the Corinthians, because they were laboring under vices of this kind. They did not study patience, nor beneficence: they burned with emulation, they indulged in petulance, they were inflated with pride, and they conducted themselves indecently in public. Therefore he teaches that these things fight against love, and that all pious men ought to be most alien to vices of this kind.

He does not seek the things that are his own: Fifthly, it fights against love of one's neighbor πλεονεξία, whereby someone studies only his own advantages, without having regard for the necessity of his neighbor. For it is the property of true love to love one's neighbor as oneself: And what you do not wish to be done to you, not to do to another;

Love not only does not seek its own advantages, but is also liberal and beneficent toward the needy even at its own loss. Emperor Maurice, when he could have redeemed 12,000 Roman citizens from a savage tyrant with a small sum of money, being clearly afflicted with , preferred to expose them to the cruelty of the enemy rather than suffer the loss of such a small amount of money.

It is not provoked: That is, it is not irritated, it does not flare up with anger. Where minds are ulcerated, there they are immediately and at a slight moment inflamed to anger. For then all things are taken in the worse part, and in a certain way occasions for becoming angry are sought. But when minds are bound together by the bond of love, place is not easily given to anger, but all things are accepted in the better part. Thus Paul warns that one must always look to brotherly love as to the banner of virtues: And that by this bridle the immoderate affections of the flesh must be restrained and curbed.

It thinks no evil: That is, it does not suspect evil, and does not reckon evil. Men sin most of all by false suspicions. For while they wish to take good care of themselves, they exceed the measure. Theodosius, because of the gift of an apple, holds his wife Eudoxia and the rhetorician Paulinus as suspects: and he indulges in this suspicion to such a degree that he arranges for Paulinus to be killed. Constantine the Great, by calumny and suspicion impelled, ordered his son Crispus, an excellent man, to be killed. Thus many in the Church suspect others of aspiring to their own dignity and position. And so that they may take precautions for themselves too prematurely, they suppress others. Love is a stranger to this vice; it does nothing out of sinister suspicion. The other interpretation is also suitable. Love does not reckon evil: This is, even if a pious person understands that he has been affected by harm in some way, nevertheless he does not make so much of it that he would therefore wish to break the bond of charity or act against the duty of love; rather, he neglects this harm and dissimulates the injury, rather than stirring up disturbances by vindicating his own right.

It does not rejoice over injustice: It is a truly diabolical vice, completely fighting against love. Επιχαιρεκακία, when someone, by the instinct of Satan and the malice of nature, takes delight from another's harm or insult: as the Pharisees rejoice when they see Christ lifted up on the cross; Shimei is affected with joy when he sees David driven into exile, and mocks him with biting sarcasms. Because Epiphanius hates Chrysostom, he rejoices in his calamity and exile. It is a common vice in those who are not led by the Holy Spirit. However, Paul here rebukes the Corinthians, because in contentions and lawsuits they desire to obtain victory in any way possible, even if that happens with injustice and with the loss of one's neighbor. But this is foreign to love, which prefers to lose the case than to obtain victory with injustice.

It rejoices, however, with the truth: A pious man in whom true love shines is more delighted by truth and justice than by his own advantage or honor. If, therefore, he has a dispute with a neighbor concerning an injury inflicted or concerning earthly goods, and the controversy is obscure, he seeks at least the truth. And if it has been shown to him, he willingly acquiesces, and rejoices more in the truth of the judgment than if he had won the case. Thus, if any pious man has been mistaken in his opinion, he does not stubbornly defend his error, he does not wish to obtain his case by any means, whether that happens with scandal to the Church and detriment to the truth, or not: But he rejoices from the heart that the truth has been shown to him, he is more solicitous about the truth than about his own honor. Augustine ingenuously confesses that he had been mistaken in that he thought the beginning of faith in us is from us: And he rejoices with the truth, when, having been admonished by the saying of Paul: What however do you have that you have not received: he understands that faith also is purely a gift of God: he does not stubbornly defend his previously conceived opinion, but prefers to profess his own lapse: than to be deprived of the light of truth.

Thus Martin Luther rejoiced with the truth. For when he had previously been of the opinion that the Magistrate must not be resisted for any reason, nor should a league be made for the sake of defending oneself against the Emperor: being then instructed by experts in law that it is sometimes permitted by the laws to resist: Luther ingenuously confesses that he had not known this was lawful: and because the Gospel does not impugn nor abolish political laws, he agrees that a league can be entered into for the sake of defense. These are notable examples of true modesty and piety. I shall not be reluctant to show the meaning of the Apostolic saying by my own example as well: and to provoke pious minds to imitation. In my Theological examination, which I published to the public two years ago, I had posited that there is no distinction between the remission of guilt and the remission of temporal punishment. And I intended this, that the afflictions of the saints should not be called punishments, but paternal chastisements: For I was looking at the error of the papists, by which they affirm that the temporal punishments of the saints in this life are compensations for a fault, and satisfy in some way the wrath of God. Since this foul error detracts from the glory and office of Jesus Christ, I thought that the afflictions of the saints should not even be named punishments: But some pious and learned pastors admonished me concerning this matter: Therefore I examined this question more diligently, the testimonies of scripture concerning the punishments and afflictions of the pious to be considered, and with the help of the Holy Spirit implored, I observed that the chastisements of the pious can rightly be called punishments, although they are in no way compensations for sin: because they are inflicted on account of sin, and are reminders to perform penance, as the examples of Adam and David teach.

It is therefore most pleasing to me that I have been admonished by pious pastors: and that the truth has been shown to me by divine providence. I also change and amend the whole passage in my examination. I openly affirm: That there is a distinction between the remission of guilt and the remission of temporal punishment. For a greater regard is held by me for eternal and heavenly truth, the glory of God, and the edification of the Church, than for my own reputation. Far be it from me to defend or even maintain a cause to the detriment of the Church. Nay, I rejoice together with the truth that has been shown: Nor do I consider this frank confession to be joined with ignominy: as proud and profane minds are accustomed to judge: but rather I congratulate myself and my hearers on the salutary gain and progress in the acknowledgment of the truth.

Let all the pious therefore beware of detestable pertinacity, which attempts to cloak and excuse errors that are manifest and convicted by the Word of God. For this sin fights against love, since foolish obstinacy is only concerned with its own reputation: and meanwhile it harms the Church greatly by defending what is false. As now Matthias Flacius Illyricus with execrable obstinacy defends the Manichaean delirium. That original sin is a substance: or that original sin is the corrupted nature itself: although he has been convicted by the most evident testimonies of Holy Scripture. But he labors more for his own reputation than for the salvation of the Church: Therefore he does not rejoice with the truth, but shows himself to be a stranger to love.

It Endures All Things.

Στέγειν, signifies to sustain something, just as a pillar sustains a building. Thus it is necessary for pious and prudent governors to sustain many things, which otherwise would collapse. Paul the wise Apostle forgives many infirmities in his colleagues, he dissimulates many things: he calms and heals the irritated minds of many: and everywhere where he notices the building of the Church threatening ruin, he subjects his own shoulders. Jerome, irascible and impatient, would have stirred up a great struggle in the Church, had not Augustine anticipated it with his moderation and prudence.

It Believes All Things.

Paul is not speaking here of the ease or futility of believing just anything, without serious testimony: But he shows here a remarkable virtue, which true love generates, namely, Candor, by which we interpret ambiguous things in a better light, nor do we indulge in blind suspicions: but while we do not have certain proofs of malevolence, we trust that our neighbor wishes us well. And if Saul was the most bitter enemy of David, nevertheless David trusts Jonathan the son of Saul because he loves him, and has no cause to suspect evil of him. King Joash trusts the priests, and commits to their faith the money by which the temple was to be restored: for he did not have cause to suspect them sinisterly. But as Candor is a remarkable virtue, without which it is impossible for colleagues to cultivate peace among themselves: so prudence must be joined to this virtue, lest by the futility of believing we precipitate ourselves into dangers: as Jonathan the brother of Judas Maccabeus, while he trusts Tryphon too much, is miserably slaughtered. Abner, when he immediately has faith in Joab, is killed by him. And the most frequent examples of perfidy in the world have finally produced this verse.

Avoid those whom you believe to be faithful, and you will be safe.

Lest therefore Candor degenerate into futility and the foolishness of believing just anyone, pious prudence must be applied. To the impious and those dissenting from us in religion faith is not to be had: for they are full of deceits and frauds. Where there are great arguments of distrust, we must take care that we do not believe easily. Abner had killed Asahel, the brother of Joab. Therefore, he ought to have been on his guard against the avenger of blood and otherwise a rival. Jonathan knew that Tryphon was an impious man: therefore he ought to have been on his guard against his frauds. And when we see our safety brought into danger, we ought not to commit ourselves to the uncertain faith of others.

It Hopes All Things.

Love from time to time hopes for the amendment of one's neighbor, therefore it acts more gently, it does not immediately run to extremes. As a parent, even if he detects the negligence and petulance of his son, nevertheless does not wish him to be removed, nor does he drive him from the house, but from time to time hopes that the son will return to a sounder mind. And by this hope he acts more gently than the son's offense deserves. Thus David tolerates the vehemence of Joab and Abishai, hoping for amendment. Theodosius absolved the senator Symmachus, who was guilty of treason and who had sung the praises of the tyrant Maximus, and he tolerated him, hoping for amendment.

It Endures All Things.

As he began the commendation of love from patience, so now at the end he repeats the same virtue: that he may admonish us that patience is necessary in every duty of love. For the infirmities of all men are various and manifold: many colleagues are morose and difficult: Many things happen daily beyond our expectation, and against our will. In all these things patience must be shown, lest by impatience we disturb the common peace. But this patience must be prudently moderated: For a pilot ought not to connive at all sins: nor ought a pastor always to dissimulate the sins of his hearers and cover them with silence. Especially enormous vices and notorious sins must be sharply chastised and censured. And that patience is untimely and pernicious which connives at false dogmas, and allows the minds of the simpler ones to be infected with errors, lest tranquility be disturbed.

Love never fails: Some explain it thus: Love is never frustrated, never stumbles, is never useless, it always profits the neighbor: other gifts do not always profit: but are often a destruction to the one having them and to others. As eloquence is often destructive to orators, as to Demades, Hyperides, and others. And this indeed is the meaning that is convenient: But the things which follow show that Paul intends this: This distinguished gift of the Holy Spirit will endure perpetually, and for all eternity: The gift of healing, of prophesying, of teaching others, will have no place in that other blessed life. But love then will be both most pure and most ardent for all. Therefore, one must apply oneself with all strength to this, that we may obtain from God this most excellent gift of all, and that love may shine in you as purely as possible.

Latin:

Etsi distribuero in alimenta pauperum omnes facultates meas, etsi tradam corpus meum ita ut ardeam, charitatem autem non habeam, nihil utilitatis capio.

Docet Apostolus reliqua officia omnia Christiani hominis ut liberalitatem insignem in pauperes, constantiam in subeundis periculis, confessiones, & alia absque omni fructu esse, si non proficiscantur ex vera dilectione, quae est fons, parens & scopus omnium virtutum & officiorum. Ratio est manifesta, quia virtutes, quae destituuntur dilectione, etiam expertes sunt fidei: Et ut tantum viribus humanis exprimuntur, non à Spiritu sancta accenduntur: Ita merae sunt simulationes, non diriguntur ad gloriam Dei et utilitatem proximi: Sed tantum captant umbram gloriae coram hominibus. Non ergò placent Deo nec sunt verae virtutes, nec ullam habent apud Deum mercedem, sed pertinent ad catalogum operum, de quibus Christus dicit, Amen dico vobis, iam perceperunt mercedem suam.

Dilectio est longanimis, benefica: Dilectio non aemulatur: Dilectio non agit insolenter, non insidiatur, non inflatur, non agit indecenter, non quaerit quae sua sunt, non accenditur ira, non cogitat malum, non gaudet ob iniustitiam: Congaudet autem veritati. Omnia sustinet, omnia credit, omnia sperat, omnia suffert, dilectio nunquam excidit.

Prolixam hîc instituit commendationem et descriptionem verae dilectionis, ut ad eam praestandam excitet & accendat Corinthios & omnes verae pietati studiosos. Fundamentum enim verae virtutis est dilectio & scopus omnium praeceptorum Dei: Munimentum & vinculum est concordiae: Itaque omnibus consiliis & actionibus praelucere & totius vitae rectrix esse debet. Est enim dilectio vera obedientia cordis & omnium virium hominis, accensa à Spiritu sancto, & congruens cum omnibus praeceptis Dei, ius suum cuique tribuens tàm Deo quàm homini. Verum quidem est, excepto Iesu Christo filio Dei, nullum hominem unquam extitisse, nec esse, nec in hunc mundum venturum esse, qui talem & omnibus numeris absolutam praestiterit aut praestiturus sit dilectionem. Tota enim hominum natura peccato corrupta est, Omnes carent gloria Dei, Omnes corrupti sunt, declinaverunt & inutiles facti sunt.

Nec Abraham, nec Moses, nec Paulus talem habuerunt dilectionem, quae fuisset legis impletio: Lex enim spiritualis est, at homines licet renati et sanctificati sunt, ex parte sunt carnales. Ideoque bonum, quod volunt perficere, non possunt. Etsi autem impossibile est hominibus in hac vita integram praestare dilectionem, tamen hic scopus singulis intuendus est, & legis sententia urgenda est, ut semper nobis in conspectu sit, quid Deus flagitet à nobis, & ad quid niti debeamus.

Singuli ergò pii non solum dent operam, ut vera dilectione proximi synceram suam fidem demonstrent, verumetiam Spiritus sancti auxilium implorent, ut is inflammet nostros animos vera & non simulata dilectione. Deus enim dilectio est, & qui manet in dilectione, in Deo manet. Encomia dilectionis sumpsit Paulus à proprietatibus & effectibus.

Dilectio est longanimis: Primus fructus dilectionis est patientia, quae est virtus accensa à Spiritu sancto, qua quis patienter & moderatè contumeliam vel iniuriam à proximo illatam perfert, & propter Deum & pacem Ecclesiae condonat, nec se commoveri sinit ad iram vel vindictae cupiditatem. Insigne exemplum patientiae fuit in Davide, qui cùm graves & magnas habuit causas tollendi Saulem, tamen vitae eius pepercit, & iniurias atroces illi condonavit. Illustre etiam exemplum patientiae fuit in Moise, quem cùm Israelitae saepius conati sint lapidibus obruere, tamen ingenti amore hunc populum est complexus, & summis adfecit beneficiis, intercessit pro eis, & gravissimos labores gubernationis sustinuit. Sic Samuel gravi adfectus contumelia à populo Israel, tamen patientia vicit dolorem & intercessit pro eis apud Deum. In Paulo quoque magna fuit patientia: Siquidem gravissimis adfectus contumeliis, & iniuriis à Iudaeis & gentibus, non destitit tamen eis benefacere, & Thesaurum coelestem illis offerre.

Hac patientia omninò opus est in Ecclesia, ac inprimis ministris necessaria est haec virtus, eò quòd mundus plenus est malicia & petulantia: Et pessimè tractat fideles verbi praecones: Etiam in sanctis magna est infirmitas, alius alium vel verbo vel opere facile laedit. Has iniurias dilectio & patientia mox tegere & sepelire debet, ut paci Ecclesiae consulatur. Hieronymus fuit impatiens, vel verbulo laesus, mox concepit iratum animum & saepè sine causa tumultuatus est: sic & Chrysostomus saepè impatientia aestuavit, & magnas turbas in Ecclesia dedit. Ab hoc ergò vitio deterret Ecclesiam Paulus, & ostendit pugnare cum dilectione.

Benefica est: Secundus fructus est beneficentia, haec est virtus accensa à Spiritu sancto, qua quis prompto animo est ad iuvandum & succurrendum proximo, & amico & inimico, in omni necessitate omni genere officiorum, quae à nobis proficisci possunt. Insigne exemplum beneficentiae fulsit in Ioseph, qui omnibus fratribus benefecit, cùm conati fuerint perdere ipsum. Beneficus fuit Obadia minister Achab regis, qui etiam cum periculo vitae suae pavit & protexit Prophetas domini. Beneficus fuit Barsillai Gileadites, qui regem exulantem cum tota familia pavit in exilio, & omni genere officiorum eum est prosecutus.

Dilectio non aemulatur: Nunc etiam vitia cum dilectione pugnantia recitat, ut ea vitent pii, ne ostendant se alienos esse à dilectione. Aemulatio est adfectus cordis, quo quis dolet alium antecellere, & sibi vel aequari vel anteferri, atque ideo sublatum eum cupit. Ut Chore & Dathan invident virtuti & gloriae Mosi & Aaronis. Saul invidet gloriae Davidis, & sublatum eum cupit. Arrius invidet Alexandro Episcopo. Ioannes. Antiochenus invidet Cyrillo. Ac latissime vagatur haec pestis in mundo & in Ecclesia, & plurima ambitiosa ingenia impellit ut dissidia suscitent. Eliab invidet virtuti & regno Davidis. Falsi Apostoli invident authoritati & donis Apostoli Pauli. Hac ergò aemulatione demonstrarunt se à vera dilectione alienos esse.

Dilectio non agit insolenter.Περπερεύεσθαι est insolenter & petulanter sese gerere, quod vitium pugnat cùm dilectione. Haec enim consulit semper tranquillitati & honori proximi, ornat & iuvat proximum. At petulantia non habet rationem proximi, tantum suae indulget cupiditati & stultitiae. Itaque petulantia est vitium pugnans cum 4. praecepto, quo quis non habita ratione proximi, indulget suae stultitiae & iniustae cupiditati, & vel conviciis laedit famam proximi, vel corpori eius iniuriam infert. Petulantia prodigiosa fuit in Iuliano Imperatore, qui Ecclesiae eripuit facultates, & insuper insultavit ei, dictitans, scriptum esse in lege ipsorum: Quod pauperum sit regnum coelorum: Hoc ergò officio se promovere Christianos ad regnum coelorum.

Non inflâtur: Tertium vitium pugnans cum dilectione, est superbia & arrogantia, qua quis inflatur contra proximum, plus tribuit sibi quàm par est: praeponit se aliis, & alios despicit. Detestanda superbia fuit in Nestorio: Qui pro concione hac stulta & impia voce est usus. O Imperator da mihi terram purgatam ab haereticis, & ego coelum tibi tribuo. Ioannes Antiochenus arrogantia inflatur contra Cyrillum: Author igitur extitit faedi & perniciosi dissidii in synodo Ephesina. Nam inter superbos semper est contentio. Arrogantia inflatus Carolostadius contra Lutherum, dissidium triste in Ecclesia excitavit.

Non agit indecenter: Homines elati superbia, nec modum nec decorum servant: Sed & indecoris gestibus & oratione arrogante produnt suam stultitiam, & gratiam omnem amittunt, quam alioquin donis suis obtinere possent. Omne enim indicium elati & superbi animi perdit omnem gratiam, & creat sibi invidiam & odium apud Deum & apud homines. Mira autem vis est modestiae ad conciliandam hominum benevolentiam. Indecenter se gerit Samosatenus, qui passim arrogantiam suam ostentat, indecenter incedit, in publico legit literas, ut ostendat se multis implicitum esse negociis. Haud dubiè in singulis particulis pungit atque perstringit Corinthios, quòd huiusmodi laborarent vitiis. Non studerent patientiae, nec beneficentiae: arderent aemulatione, indulgerent petulantiae, superbia inflarentur, & indecenter sese gererent in publico. Docet igitur haec pugnare cum dilectione, & omnes pios ab huiusmodi vitiis oportere esse alienissimos.

Non quaerit quae sua sunt: Quintò pugnat cum dilectione proximi πλεονεξία, qua quis tantum studet suis commodis, non habita ratione necessitatis proximi. Dilectionis enim verae proprium est, diligere proximum sicut seipsum: Et quod tibi non vis fieri, non facere alteri;

Dilectio non solum non studet suis commodis, sed etiam cum damno suo liberalis & benefica est in egenos. Mauritius imperator cum exigua pecunia 12000. Civium Rom: redimere potuisset à truci Tyranno, nimirum laborans pleonexia, maluit eos obiicere crude litati hostis, quàm tantillae pecuniae iacturam facere.

Non exacerbatur: Id est, non irritatur, non excandescit iracundia. Ubi animi exulcerati sunt, ibi subiò & levi momento ad iram inflammantur. Tum enim omnia in peiorem partem rapiuntur, & quodammodo occasiones irascendi quaeruntur. Cùm verò animi vinculo dilectionis colligati sunt, non facile datur locus irae, sed omnia in meliorem partem accipiuntur. Monet adeò Paulus semper ad dilectionem fraternam, tanquam ad vexillum virtutum respiciendum esse: Et hoc freno immodicos adfectus carnis cohibendos atque frenandos esse.

Non cogitat malum: Id est, non suspicatur malum, & non aestimat malum. Plurimum peccant homines falsis suspicionibus. Dum enim probè sibi cavere volunt, modum excedunt. Theodosius ob donationem pomi, Eudoxiam coniugem & Paulinum Rhetorem habet suspectos: & huic suspicioni adeò indulget, ut Paulinum curet interfici. Constantinus Magnus calumnia & suspicione impulsus, iussit interfici filium suum Crispum praestantem virum. Sic multi in Ecclesia suspicantur alios adfectare ipsorum dignitatem & locum. Utque nimis maturè caveant sibi, premunt alios. Ab hoc vitio aliena est dilectio, nihil facit ex sinistra suspicione. Altera quoque sententia est commoda. Dilectio non aestimat malum: Hoc est, etiamsi pius intelligit se aliquomodo damno adfectum esse: tamen id non facit tanti, ut ideò velit solvere charitatis vinculum, aut contra dilectionis officium facere: potius negligit hoc damnum & dissimulat iniuriam: quàm ut vindicando ius suum, turbas excitet.

Non gaudet ob iniustitiam: Vitium verè Diabolicum est, prorsus pugnans cum dilectione. Επιχαιρεκακία, cum quis instinctu Satanae, & naturae malicia delectationem capit ex alterius vel damno vel contumelia: ut Pharisaei laetantur, cum vident Christum sublatum in crucem: Semei gaudio adficitur cum videt Davidem pulsum in exilium, & mordacibus sarcasmis illudit ei. Quia Epiphanius odit Chrysostomum, laetatureius calamitate & exilio. vulgare vitium est in illis, qui non ducuntur Spiritu sancto. Perstringit autem hic Paulus Corinthios, quod in contentionibus & litibus quo quomodo cupiant obtinere victoriam, etiamsi id fiat cum iustitia & cum damno proximi. Hoc verò alienum est à dilectione, quae mavult cadere causa, quam cum iniustitia obtinere victoriam.

Congaudet autem veritati: Pius in quo lucet vera dilectio, magis delectatur veritate & iustitia, quàm suo commodo vel honore. Quod si igitur lis illi est cum proximo de illata iniuria, vel de bonis terrenis, & controversia obscura est, expetit saltem veritatem. Quae si ei monstrata fuerit, libenter acquiescit, & gaudet potius veritate iudicii, quamsi causam obtinuisset. Ita si quis pius hallucinatus est in sententia, non pertinaciter defendit suum errorem, non quoquo modo obtinere vult suam causam, sive id fiat cum scandalo Eccle: et detrimento veritatis, sive non: Sed ex animo gaudet sibi monstratam esse veritatem, magis de veritate, quàm de suo honore est solicitus. Augustinus ingenuè fatetur se hallucinatum fuisse in eo, quod putaverit, initium fidei in nobis esse ex nobis: Et congaudet veritati, cum admonitus dicto Pauli: Quid autem habes quod non accepisti: intelligit & fidem esse merè donum Dei: non defendit pertinaciter suam prius conceptam opinionem, sed mavult suum profiteri lapsum: quàm veritatis luce destitui.

Sic Martinus Lutherus congavisus est veritati. Cùm enim prius in ea fuisset opinione, Nulla ratione resistendum esse Magistratui, Nec foedus faciendum esse, muniendi sui causa contra Imperatorem: edoctus deinde à peritis iuris, legibus permissum esse resistere nonnunque: Lutherus ingenuè profitetur se nescivisse hoc licere: & quia Evangelion non impugnet, neque aboleat politicas leges, adsentitur defensionis causa foedus iniri posse. Haec sunt insignia exempla verae modestiae & pietatis. Meo quoque exemplo non gravabor ostendere sententiam dicti. Apostolici: & pias mentes ad imitationem provocare. In examine meo Theologico, quod ante biennium in publicum edidi, posueram, non esse discrimen inter remissionem culpae, & remissionem poenae temporalis. Et hoc volebam, adflictiones sanctorum non dicendas esse poenas, sed castigationes paternas: Errorem enim pontificiorum, quo adfirmant poenas temporales sanctorum in hac vita esse compensationes pro delicto, & satisfacere aliquo. modo irae Dei respiciebam. Hic faedus error cùm deroget gloriae et officio Iesu Christi, putabam adflictiones sanctorum ne poenas quidem nominandas esse: Sed aliquot pii & eruditi pastores me hac de re admonuerunt: Diligentius igitur hanc quaestionem expendi, scripturae testimonia de poenis & adflictionibus piorum considerari, & implorato Spiritus sancti auxilio animadverti, Piorum castigationes rectè posse poenas dici, licet nullo modo sint compensationes pro peccato: eo quod propter peccatum infligantur, & sunt commonefactiones ad agendam poenitentiam, ut Adae & Davidis exempla docent.

Gratissimum igitur mihi est, me à piis pastoribus esse admonitum: & divinitus mihi monstratam veritatem. Muto etiam & emendo totum locum in examine meo. Apertè adfirmo: Esse discrimen inter remissionem cuipae & remissionem poenae temporalis. Potior enim apud me ratio habetur aeternae & coelestis veritatis, gloriae Dei, & aedificationis Ecclesiae, quàm existimationis meae Absit ut ego defendam veletiam obtineam causam cum detrimento Ecclesiae. Imò congaudeo veritati monstratae: Neque statuo hanc ingenuam confessionem cum ignominia coniunctam esse: ut superba & prophana ingenia iudicare solent: sed potius de salutari lucro & progressu in agnitione veritatis mihi & meis auditoribus gratulor.

Caveant ergò omnes pii detestandam pertinaciam, quae manifestos et verbo Dei convictos errores palliare, & excusare conatur. Pugnat enim hoc peccatum cum dilectione, Siquidem stolida pertinacia tantum de sua existimatione sollicita est: et interea plurimùm nocet Ecclesiae falsa tuendo. Ut nunc Matthias Flacius Illyricus execranda pertinacia Manichaeum delirium defendit. Peccatum originis esse substantiam: seu peccatum originis esse ipsam corruptam naturam: cùm evidentissimis sacrae scripturae testimoniis sit conuctus. Sed magis ille laborat de sua existimatione, quàm de salute Ecclesiae: Non ergò congaudet veritati, sed ostendit se à dilectione alienum esse.

Omnia Sustinet.

Στέγειν, significat sustinere aliquid, sicuti columna sustinet aedificium. Sic necesse est pios & prudentes guber natores multa sustinere, quae aliâs collapsura essent. Paulus sapiens Apostolus multas infirmitates condonat collegis, multa dissimulat: multorum animos irritatos placat & sanat: & passim ubi animadvertu aedificium Ecclesiae ruinam minari, subiicit ille humeros. Hieronymus iracundus & impatiens magnum in Ecclesia certamen movisset, nisi Augustinus sua moderatione & prudentia antevertisset.

Omnia Credit.

Non loquitur hîc Paulus de facilitate seu futilitate credendi quidvis, sine gravi testimonio: Sed insignem virtutem hîc monstrat, quam generet vera dilectio, nimirum, Candorem, quo ambigua in meliorem partem interpretamur, nec indulgemus caecis suspicionibus: sed dum certa documenta malevolentiae non habemus, considimus proximo eum bene nobis velle. Et si Saul hostis erat Davidis acerbissimus, tamen Ionathae filio Saulis credit David quia diligit eum, & non habet causas malè de eo suspicandi. Ioas rex credit sacerdotibus, & fidei ipsorum committit pecuniam, quatemplum erat instaurandum: non enim habebat causam sinistrè de ipsis suspicandi. Ut autem insignis virtus est Candor, sine qua impossibile est collegas inter se pacem colere: ita prudentia huic virtuti est coniungenda, ne fatilitate credendi nos in pericula praecipitemus: ut Ionathan frater Iudae Maccabei dum nimium credit Tryphoni, miserè trucidatur. Abnerdum statim fidem habet Ioab, ab eo interficitur. Et frequentissima perfidiae in mando exempla hunc tandem pepererunt versum.

Quos credis fidos effuge tutus eris.

Ne igitur Candor in futilitatem & stultitiam credendi cuilibet degeneret, pia prudentia adbibenda est. Impiis & in religione à nobis dissentientibus non est habenda fides: pleni enim sunt dolis & fraudibus. Ubi magna sunt argumenta diffidentiae cavendum est ne facilè credamus. Abner interfecerat Asael fratrem Ioab. Vindicem ergò sanguinis et aliâs aemulum cavere debuisset. Ionathas sciebat Tryphonem esse hominem impium: Itaque fraudes eius cavere de buisset. Ac ubi salutem nostram in discrimen adduci videmus, aliorum incertae fidei nos committere non debemus.

Omnia Sperat.

Dilectio subinde sperat emendationem proximi, ideò lenius agit, non statim decurrit ad extrema. Ut parens etiamsi filii deprehendat negligentiam, & petulantiam: non tamen vult eum sublatum: nec pellit eum ex aedibus: sed subinde sperat filium rediturum ad saniorem mentem: Atque hac spe lenius agit, quàm delictum filii meretur. Sic David tolerat vehementiam Ioab & Abisai: sperans emendationem. Theodosius Symmachum senatorem maiestatis reum, & qui laudes Maximi tyranni decantaverat, absolvit: & toleravit eum, sperans emendationem.

Omnia Suffert.

Ut à patientia exorsus est commendationem dilectionis, ita in fine nunc eandem virtutem repetit: ut nos admoneat in omni officio dilectionis necessariam esse patientiam. Variae enim & multiplices sunt omnium hominum infirmitates: multi collegae sunt morosi & difficiles: Multa quotidie accidunt praeter nostram expectationem, & contra nostram voluntatem. In his omnibus patientia praestanda est, ne impatientia turbemus communem pacem. Haec verò patientia prudenter moderanda est: Gubernator enim non debet ad omnia connivere peccata: nec pastor auditorum suorum peccata semper dissimulare & silentio tegere debet. Inprimis vitia enormia & peccata notoria acriter castiganda & taxandae sunt. Et intempestiva atque perniciosa est patientia, quae ad falsa dogmata connivet, & simpliciorum mentes erroribus sinit infici, ne tranquillitas turbetur.

Dilectio nunquam excidit: Aliqui sic exponunt: Dilectio nunquam frustratur, nunquam impingit, nunquam est inutilis, semper prodest proximo: caetera dona, non semper prosunt: sed saepè sunt exitio habenti & aliis. Ut eloquentia saepè est exitiosa oratoribus, ut Demadi, Hyperiae, & aliis. Et haec quidem sententiae commoda est: Sed quae sequuntur, ostendunt Paulum hoc velle: Hoc insigne Spiritus sancti donum perpetuò, & in omnem aeternitatem duraturum: Donum sanandi, Prophetandi, docendi alios, non habebit locum in altera illa beata vita. Dilectio verò tum omnium erit & purissima & ardentissima. Huc ergò totis viribus incumbendum est, ut hoc omnium excellentissimum donum à Deo impetremus, & dilectio in vobis fulgeat quàm purissima.

## 13:8
Whether there be prophecies, they shall be abolished, or tongues, they shall cease, or knowledge, it shall be destroyed.

He still persists in the comparison of love and other gifts: and shows that love is superior, in that its use endures for all eternity. The others, however, serve only this life. There will be no use for prophecies in eternal life: thus neither will the knowledge of various tongues, or the science of many things, have a place there. For God will be all in all.

Latin:

Sive sint Prophetiae abolebuntur, sive linguae, cessabunt, sive cognitio destruetur.

Persistit adhuc in collatione dilectionis & aliorum donorum: & ostendit dilectionem potiorem esse, eo, quod eius usus in omnem aeternitatem duret. Caetera autem huic tantum vitae serviant. Vaticiniorum usus nullus erit in vita aeterna: sic nec variarum linguarum cognitio, aut scientia multarum rerum isthic locum habebit. Deus enim omnia futurus est in omnibus.

## 13:9-12
For in part we know: and in part we prophesy. But when that which is perfect is come, that which is in part shall be done away. When I was a child, I spake as a child: I understood as a child: I thought as a child: but when I became a man, I put away childish things.
