How he wishes it to be understood, that which he said above, that prophecy and tongues shall be done away, he now explains, namely, not that the knowledge of all things is to perish in eternal life: but that those things shall cease, which served the infirmity of this life. For in the other life, we shall not have need of the elements of this world. One shall not say to another, know the Lord: For all shall know the Lord. Therefore Paul does not mean this, that all knowledge and science is to perish: but that which in this world is obscure, thin, mixed with errors and doubts, shall be most lucid, immune from all error and doubt: For we shall behold God face to face: and we shall know God, even as we are known. Imperfection shall be done away, not the thing of knowledge itself. That which is now abstractive knowledge, shall then be intuitive.

We know in part now. He does not speak of the imperfection of doctrine: as if not all things were revealed to us, which pertain to our salvation: but concerning our weakness and imperfection: because we are imperfect, and cannot bear the brightness of the presence of God: therefore we have need of prophecies, disciplines, knowledge of languages, and various science. And yet all these things are both obscure, and thin, and mixed with our doubts. Therefore these things will be abolished in the other life, and then we are to contemplate God the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit face to face: and without any darkness, without any doubt, without any error we are to know the most lucid truth. At midday and in clear light we know a man much more perfectly than if we were to gaze upon him in the twilight.

When I was a child, I spoke as a child: By his own example he shows how prophecy and knowledge are to cease, namely, as childish thoughts cease in manly age. For then a man both considers more closely, and thinks more seriously, and understands things more fully: Thus in eternal life all things will be more perfect. In this world, although we are reborn, yet we babble like infants about God, about the three persons, about the two natures in Christ, about the glory of the future life.

For we see now through a glass in a dark manner: but then face to face: for now I know in part: but then I shall know, even as also I am known.

Again, by another similitude he declares that the knowledge which will be in eternal life is much more illustrious, firmer, and richer than that which we acquire in this life through the ministry of the word. The Son of God has indeed revealed to us through the Gospel all things in which our salvation consists: and it is permitted to us to acquire through the ministry of the word such a knowledge of God as may suffice for us to obtain eternal life. Nor is it to be imagined here that the doctrine of the Apostles is condemned for obscurity or ambiguity, or that our hope and knowledge are accused of uncertainty. For the doctrine of the Gospel is the most clear, most open, and most firm of all: and from the word of God we have the most certain hope of eternal life. But Paul indicates this, that we do not thoroughly perceive those admirable mysteries of the doctrine of Christ in this life. We hear, we read, and we believe that God is a spiritual and eternal essence, which is present everywhere and fills all things. But who among us can attain to such a mystery by thought and intellect? There is one divine essence: and three distinct persons of the divinity: this exceeds the grasp of human intellect. Holy Scripture testifies that two natures are united in Jesus Christ: the divine, which is begotten from the Father from eternity, and the human, which is similar to our flesh. This is truly an incomprehensible and ineffable mystery, at the consideration of which the angels in heaven stand amazed. Who among us can understand the manner in which all the dead are to be resurrected on the last day? How souls are to return to their own respective bodies. The articles of faith are indeed clear, perspicuous, and indubitable: but the majesty and abundance of heavenly things is incomprehensible to us in this life. Rightly, therefore, Paul compares the ministry of the Gospel to an enigma, that is, to an involved sentence, which contains within itself a hidden and secret meaning. Likewise, he compares it to a mirror, in which the knowledge of God and of His will is represented to us, as much as this life can bear, and is necessary for us to attain eternal life. But it is not permitted for us to gaze upon the essence of God itself in this life. You cannot see my face, He says to Moses: for man shall not see Me and live. But in the other life we shall see God face to face: that is, we shall gaze upon the eternal essence itself in person, without any covering and impediment. Thus, 2. Corinth: 5. says Paul. We are pilgrims away from the Lord: for we walk by faith, not by sight: That is, in this life it is not permitted for us to gaze upon the divine essence itself face to face: This blessedness is reserved for the future life, If therefore the knowledge of God, which exists in us in this life, is compared with that which is to shine in us in the heavenly fellowship, it is truly a riddle and a mirror: for it is much thinner, more languid, and more obscure than that future one will be: very many things now lie hidden and wrapped up, which then in that admirable light will be revealed. But as far as this life is concerned, the knowledge of God, which we obtain from the word, is both most clear and sufficient for attaining eternal life.

Paul says that he knows in part: For he had not yet obtained a full and perfect knowledge of God, such as we are to attain in the heavenly fellowship. He had not yet gazed upon the essence of God itself: He was indeed caught up into the third heaven, and heard ineffable words: but he did not behold what God is like according to his essence, for God dwells in light inaccessible. Since therefore this so immense glory and blessedness is laid up for us in heaven, that before our eyes we are to behold God himself, as he is, God the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, face to face without any wrapping and veil, let us pray to the Lord Jesus, that through his Holy Spirit he may kindle in us an ardent desire for eternal fellowship with God, and may increase it daily:

Now there remain faith, hope, charity: these three: but the greatest of these is charity.

Paul finally concludes his discourse, in which he commended love, and preferred it to all spiritual gifts: and he urges this in particular, that most gifts of the Spirit have a place only in this life: such as faith and hope: but that love will endure for all eternity. That they invent only three Theological virtues from this passage is absurd: piety, fear of God, invocation, thanksgiving, patience, confession of the divine name, zeal, preaching of the word, are indeed Theological virtues, and differ from faith, hope, and love. Paul, however, compares the primary and chief virtues of the spiritual man, namely, faith and hope, as those which have a place only in this life, with love, so that he may commend the latter by its perpetuity, and excite the pious to the pursuit of it.

Faith is a motion kindled in the heart by the Holy Spirit, relying certainly on the word of God, by which with certain confidence we establish according to God's promise that all sins are forgiven us, that God is reconciled to us, that we are constituted heirs of eternal life, and that we shall obtain all the good things which are promised to us in the word. Thus the Epistle to the Hebrews: Faith is the firm confidence of things to be hoped for, and the demonstration of those things which are not seen. God demands this faith from us in this life. And by this as it were instrument He bestows upon us righteousness, the Holy Spirit, and eternal life. For He offers these goods of the kingdom of Christ to us in the word: for the Gospel is the power of God unto salvation to every one that believeth. But by the word brought forth by Himself, God wills that faith be had: and in the believer He works salvation, whence Habakkuk. The just shall live by his faith. Great therefore is the virtue of faith, because it is kindled by the Holy Spirit: it attributes to God the praise of truth: it opposes itself to all arguments brought forth from the necessity of nature: it overcomes death and sin: it lays hold of the mediator with all benefits: it obtains righteousness before God: and it brings peace and joy to the conscience. These such great things, which could not be effected by the power of any creature, are obtained by faith. But it is not to remain in the other life, when the last day shall have shone, then faith will reach the goal, and there will be an end of the struggle of faith: for there will no longer be need for the Word and sacraments: since we shall behold God face to face, and those things which we have believed here, we shall then look upon, and we shall obtain the most ample rewards of faith.

Hope is a motion kindled by the Holy Spirit, leaning upon the expressed word of God, by which with certain confidence we expect the mitigation of miseries in this life, and the hearing of our prayer in every invocation, and finally the certain inheritance of eternal life, whence Paul says Rom: 8., By hope we are saved. The movements are clearly distinct, faith and hope. But they differ in this, that faith is the efficient cause: hope the effect. For from faith apprehending the promise of the Gospel, and acquiescing in the mercy of God, and the intercession of the mediator, hope is born, certainly expecting both deliverance from dangers and the gift of eternal life. And faith expects present goods, such as the remission of sins, reconciliation with God, and the gift of the holy spirit: but hope expects future goods. Hope is therefore an excellent virtue, inasmuch as it is kindled by the holy Spirit, attributing to God the praise of justice, clemency, and truth: overcoming temptations of every kind, strongly apprehending the word of God, and sustaining the soul in the greatest difficulties and dangers. This hope leaning on the word of God differs greatly from the vain hopes or dreams of men, which they fashion for themselves. The hope of the human mind is an affection by which the heart expects and promises to itself a desired good, but on an uncertain argument. Pindar not ineptly names it: the hope of men, the dreams of the waking. For they are for the most part full of vanity. But the hope of Christians is a movement kindled by the holy Spirit, which leans on a certain and infallible word. And so the hope of the pious cannot be frustrated. Hope, says Paul, does not confound: And Psalm 2. Blessed are all they that hope. to me. But hope has a place only in this life. For as Paul says, What a man sees, he does not hope for. But we are going to see God himself in the other life as he is, and to possess all the goods of the kingdom of Christ. Therefore, when that goal has been reached, there will be no need for hope.

Love is an ardent motion in God, kindled by the Holy Spirit, and arising from faith resting in the mediator, by which we truly love God above all things, and our neighbor as ourselves. For we are speaking of love, such as the divine law demands, which is perfect and absolute in all respects. Our nature indeed is so corrupted and weakened by sin, that not only do we not perform complete love, but we do not even sufficiently understand what love properly is. For love signifies a most ardent motion, by which a man rejoices in God, delights in him as the highest good, prefers him to all creatures, and with a most ready mind performs also obedience according to all the commandments, and loves his neighbor as himself for the sake of God. Love of this kind embraces within itself virtues of every sort, and is the fulfillment of the law. Although such love cannot be performed completely by anyone in this life, nevertheless this goal, which the law sets before us, must be kept in view, and the course of one's whole life must be directed toward it, as much as can be done with God helping. Now this love is born from true confidence in God, with the Holy Spirit working it. For after a man discovers how immense the benefits are which he obtains from God freely without any merit, the Holy Spirit kindles in his heart a wonderful love, by which the man takes delight in so merciful and beneficent a God.

Therefore, that Paul asserts here that love is greater than faith and hope: that is indeed most true. Since Paul is looking especially at the fact that love extends itself most widely in its duties: and that it endures for all eternity. Faith and hope deal only with God, and serve our salvation: but Love contemplates God perpetually in all duties, then serves the whole Church, and not only has use in this life, but extends itself to all eternity.

For this reason love is greater than faith and hope. However, it does not follow from this that love is to be preferred to faith and hope in all respects. For as faith is the mother and efficient cause of love: so it is also both prior and superior to its effect. It is the property of faith to apprehend the promise of the Gospel; to embrace Christ most closely with all the benefits of his kingdom: to struggle against distrust: to conquer the power of sin and the terrors of death: to overcome the tyranny of Satan: and to obtain from God reconciliation and righteousness; This scripture does not attribute sacred things to love. In these, therefore, its own properties and admirable effects, faith excels. Very ineptly, therefore, do the Papists conclude, while from this saying of Paul, Love is the greatest among these, they argue that we are justified before God chiefly by love. They construct the sophism thus.

The greatest virtue justifies chiefly. Love is the greatest virtue. Therefore, it justifies chiefly.

I answer, the major premise would be true if justice were from the law. But because there is no one in the world who performs the law, therefore no virtue justifies, neither small, nor great, nor greatest. For by the works of the law, no flesh shall be justified. In the Gospel, however, God has revealed this admirable method of our justification, that freely, without our works and virtues, on account of the obedience and death of Jesus Christ his Son, he wills to receive us into grace and pronounce us just, according to the saying: Being justified freely by his grace through the redemption that is in Christ Jesus, whom he set forth as a propitiation by his blood through faith. This justification does not depend upon any virtue or work of man: but upon the sole mercy of God and the merit of Jesus Christ: Nor does faith justify us by its own dignity or by reason of a work: but only as an instrument, which God has ordained for us, so that by it we might apply to ourselves the promise of the Gospel and all the benefits of the mediator. Therefore, a greater one does not exist according to the doctrine of the Gospel. The minor premise is also to be understood concerning perpetuity, and concerning perfect and integral love, such as does not exist in this fragile and impure nature of men.

Latin:

Ex parte enim cognoscimus: & ex parte Prophetamus. Cùm autem venerit, quod perfectum est, hoc, quod ex parte est, abolebitur. Cùm puer essem, ut puer loquebar: ut puer sapiebam: ut puer ratiocinabar: cùm autem factus sum vir, abolevi puerilia.

Quomodo intelligi velit, quod supr à dixit, aboleri Prophetiam & linguas, nunc exponit, nimirum, non quòd omnium rerum cognitio sit peritura in vita aeterna: sed quod ea cessabunt, quae huius vitae infirmitati servierunt. In altera enim vita, non indigebimus huius mundi elementis. Non dicet alter alteri cognosce Dominum: Omnes enim cognoscent dominum. Non igitur hoc vult Paulus, quòd omnis cognitio & scientia sit peritura: sed quae in hoc mundo est obscura, tenuis, mixta, erroribus & dubitationibus, tumerit lucidissima, immunis ab omni errore & dubitatione: Coràm enim intuebimur Deum: & cognoscemus Deum, sicuti cogniti sumus. Imperfectio abolebitur, non res ipsa scientiae. Quae nunc est abstractiva noticia, tunc erit intuitiva.

Ex parte nunc cognoscimus. Non loquitur de doctrinae imperfectione: quasi non omnia nobis sint patefacta, quae ad nostram pertinent salutem: sed de nostra imbecillitate & imperfectione: quia nos imperfecti sumus, & fulgorem praesentiae Dei ferre non possumus: ideò nobis opus esse Prophetiis, disciplinis, linguarum cognitione, & varia scientia. Et tamen haec omnia sunt & obscura, & tenuia, & mixta cum nostris dubitationibus. Itaque haec in altera vita abolebuntur, & coràm tum sumus contemplaturi Deum patrem, filium & Spiritum sanctum: & sine omni caligine, sine omni dubitatione, sine omni errore ludicissimam sumus cognituri veritatem. In meridie & claraluce multò perfectius cognoscimus hominem, quàm si eum in crepusculo intueamur.

Cùm puer essem, ut puer loquebar: Exemplo suo ostendit, quomodo cessatura sit Prophetia & cognitio, nimirum, ut pueriles cessant in virili aetate cogitationes. Tum enim homo & propius considerat, & gravius cogitat, & plenius intelligit res: Sic in vita aeterna omnia erunt perfectiora. In hoc mundo licet renati simus, tamen veluti infantes balbutimus de Deo, de tribus personis, de duabus naturis in Christo, de futurae vitae gloria.

Cernimus enim nunc per speculum in aenigmate: tunc autem facie ad faciem: nunc enim cognosco ex parte: tunc vero cognoscam, quemadmodum & cognitus sum.

Rursus alia similitudine declarat, quòd multò illustrior, firmior & uberior noticia futura sit in vita aeterna, quàm in hac vita per ministerium verbi acquiramus. Omnia quidem patefecit nobis filius Dei per Evangelion, in quibus nostra consistit salus: & tantam licet nobis ministerio verbi comparare noticiam Dei, quae nobis sufficiat ad vitam aeternam consequendam. Neque hîc fingendum est, vel doctrinam Apostolorum obscuritatis, vel ambiguitatis condemnari, velspem & cognitionem nostram incertitudinis accusari. Doctrina enim Evangelii omnium est clarissima, apertissima & firmissima: Et ex verbo Dei spem vitae aeternae habemus certissimam. Hoc autem indicat Paulus, nos admiranda illa mysteria doctrinae Christi non penitus pervidere in hac vita. Audimus, legimus et credimus Deum esse spiritualem & aeternam essentiam, quae ubique adsit & omnia impleat. Quis verò nostrum tantum mysterium cogitatione & intellectu assequi potest? Una est essentia divina: & tres distinctae personae divinitatis: hoc omnem captum humani ingenii excedit. Testatur sacra scriptura duas naturas in Iesu Christo unitas esse: divinam, quae ab aeterno à patre est genita. & humanam, quae nostrae carni sit similis. Hoc sanè incomprehensibile & ineffabile est mysterium, ad cuius considerationem Angeli in coelo obstupesiunt. Quis nostrum intelligere potest modum, quo omnes mortui in novissimo die sint, resurrecturi? quomodo animae rediturae ad sua quaeque corpora. Articuli quidem fidei clari, perspicui & indubii sunt: sed rerum coelestium maiestas & ubertas incomprehensiblis est nobis in hac vita. Rectè igitur confert Paulus ministerium Evangelii aenigmati, Id est, senteniae involutae, quae reconditum & arcanum sensum in se contineat. Item speculo confert, in quo nobis repraesentetur noticia Dei et voluntatis ipsius, quantam haec quidem vita ferre potest, & nobis ad consequendam vitam aeternam necessaria est. Verùm ipsam Dei essentiam non licet nobis intueri in hac vita. Faciem meam videre non potes, inquit ad Mosen: non enim videbit me homo & vivet. In altera verò vita videbimus Deum facie ad faciem: Id est, coràm ipsam aeternam essentiam intuebimur, sine omini involucro, & impedimento. Sic. 2. Corinth: 5. inquit Paulus. Nos peregrinamur à domino: per fidem enim ambulamus, non per aspectum: Id est, in hac vita non licet nobis intueri coram ipsam divinam essentiam: Haec beatitudo futurae vitae reservata est, Si ergo noticia Dei, quae existit in nobis in hac vita, compares cum ea, quae in nobis fulsura est in consuetudine coelesti, verè aenigma & speculum est: multo enim tenuior, languidior & obscurior est, quàm illa futura sit: plurima nunc involuta latent, quae tum in illa admiranda luce, revelabuntur. Quod ad hanc verò vitam attinet, noticia Dei, quam ex verbo comparamus, & clarissima est & ad consequendam vitam aeternam sufficiens.

Ex parte se dicit cognoscere Paulus: Nondum enim plenam & perfectam Dei cognitionem, qualem in coelesti consuetudine adepturi sumus, obtinuit. Nondum intuitus est ipsam Dei essentiam: Raptus quidem fuit in tertium coelum, & audivit verba ineffabilia: sed qualis sit Deus secundum essentiam, non conspexit, Habitat enim Deus lucem inaccessibilem. Cùm ergò haec tam immensa gloria et beatitudo reposita sit nobis in coelo, ut coram oculis nostris ipsum Deum, sicuti est, Deum patrem, filium & Spiritum sanctum, facie ad faciem sine omni involucro & velamine conspecturi sumus, oremus dominum Iesum, ut per Spiritum suum sanctum aeternae consuetudinis cum Deo desiderium ardens in nobis accendat, & quotidie augeat:

Nunc aut manet, fides, spes, charitas: tria haec: maxima ex his charitas.

Concludit tandem Paulus suam concionem, qua dilectionem commendavit, & omnibus donis spiritualibus praetulit: & hoc inprimis urget, pleraque dona Spiritus tantum in hac vita locum habere: ut fidem & spem: dilectionem verò in omnem aeternitatem duraturam. Quòd ex hoc loco tantum tres virtutes Thelogicas comminiscuntur, ineptum est: pietas, timor Dei, invocatio, gratiarum actio, patientia, confessio nominis divini, zelus, praedicatio verbi, sunt sané Theologicae virtutes, & differunt à fide, spe & dilectione. Paulus vero primas & praecipuas spiritualis hominis virtutes, nimirum, fidem & spem, ut quae tantum in hac vita locum habent, cum dilectione confert, ut hanc à per petuitate commendet, & pios ad studium eius excitet.

Fides est motus in corde accensus à Spiritu sancto, innitens certò Dei verbo, quo certa fiducia statuimus iuxta Dei promissionem omnia peccata nobis remissa, Deum nobis reconciliatum, nos vitae aeterna haeredes constitutos esse, & nos omnia bona, quae nobis in verbo promissa sunt, impetraturos. Sic Epistola ad Hebr: Fides est firma fiducia rerum sperandarum, & demonstratio eorum, quae non videntur. Hanc fidem postulat Deus à nobis in hac vita. Et hoc veluti organo largitur nobis iustitiam, Spiritum sanctum, & vitam aeternam. Haec enim bona regni Christi offert nobis in verbo: Evangelion enim est potentia Dei ad salutem omni credenti. Verbo autem à se prolato, vult Deus haberi fidem: & in credente operatur salutem, unde Habacuk. Iustus fide sua vivet. Magna igitur virtus est fides, quia à Spiritu sancto accenditur: tribuit Deo laudem veritatis: opponit se omnibus argumentis ex necessitate naturae allatis: superat mortem & peccatum: adprebendit mediatorem cum omnibus beneficiis: impetrat iustitiam apud Deum: & conscientiae adfert pacem & laeticiam. Hae tantae res, quae nullius creaturae vi effici possent, fide obtinentur. At in altera vita mansura non est, ubi novissimus dies illuxerit, tum metam attinget fides, & finis erit certaminis fidei: Verbo enim & sacramentis non erit amplius opus: siquidem coràm intuebimur Deum, & quae hîc credidimus, tum adspiciemus, & fidei praemia amplissima obtinebimus.

Spes est motus accensus à Spiritu sancto, nitens expressò Dei verbo, quo certa fiducia expectamus mitigationem aerumnarum in hac vita, & exauditionem in omni invocatione, & tandem certam haereditatem vitae aeternae, unde Paulus Rom: 8. inquit, Spe salvi facti sumus. Victni planè motus sunt, fides & spes. Hoc autem differunt, quod fides est causa efficiens: spes effectus. Ex fide enim adprehendente promissionem Evangelii, et acquiescente in misericordia Dei, et intercessione mediatoris nascitur spes, certò expectans & liberationem ex periculis & donationem vitae aeternae. Et fides praesentia bona, ut remissionem peccatorum, reconciliationem cum Deo & donationem spiritus sancti: sed spes futura bona expectat. Est igitur spes virtus excellens, utpote accensa à Spiritu sancto, tribuens Deo laudem iustitiae, clementiae & veritatis: superans omnis generis tentationes, fortiter adprehendens verbum Dei, & sustentans animum in summis difficultatibus & periculis. Plurimùm differt haec spes nitens verbo Dei à vanis hominum spebus seu somniis, quas ipsi sibi fingunt. Humani animi spes est adfectus, quo cor expectat & sibi pollicetur optatum bonum, sed incerto argumento. Pindarus non inepté nominat: spes hominum, somnia vigilantium. Plerumque enim plenae sunt vanitatis. Sed spes Christianorum est motus à Spiritu sancto accensus, qui certo & infallibili nititur verbo. Itaque spes pii frustrari non potest. Spes, inquit Paulus, non confundit: Et Psalm 2. Beati omnes, qui sperant meo. Tantum verò in hac vita spes habet locum. Nam ut Paulus inquit, Quae quis videt, ea non sperat. Visuri autem sumus in altera vita ipsum Deum qualis est, & omnia bona regni Christi possessuri. Spe igitur, ubi ad istam metam ventum fuerit, non erit opus.

Dilectio est ardens motus in Deo accensus à Spiritu sancto, & ortas ex fide acquiescente in mediatore, quo verè diligimus Deum super omnia, & proximum sicuti nosmetipsos. De dilectione enim loquimur, qualem lex divina flagitat, quae sit perfecta & omnibus numeris absoluta. Nostra quidem natura adeò corrupta & labefactata est peccato, ut non solum non praestemus integram dilectionem, sed nec quid propriè sit dilectio, satis intelligimus. Dilectio enim motum significat ardentissimum, quo homo laetatur in Deo, delectatur eo tanquam summo bono, antefert eum omnibus creaturis, & promptissimo animo praestat et obedientiam iuxta omnia praecepta, proximum etiam diligit sicut seipsum propter Deum. Huius modi dilectio omnis generis virtutes, in sese complectitur, & est legis impletio. Etsi autem à nemine in hac vita integrè praestari possit talis dilectio, tamen meta haec, quam lex nobis praefigit, intuenda, & totius vitae cursus eò dirigendus est, quantum auxiliante Deo fieri potest. Nascitur autem haec dilectio ex vera in Deum fidu tia, operante eam Spiritu sancto. Post quam enim deprehendit homo, quàm ingentia beneficia, impetret à Deo gratis sine omni merito, accendit Spiritus sanctus in corde ipsius mirificum amorem, quo homo delectatur tam clementi & benefico Deo.

Quòd ergò hïc Paulus adserit dilectionem maiorem esse fide & spe: id sanè verissimum est. Siquidem Paulus praecipue respicit, quod dilectio suis officiis latissimè sese extendat: & quod duret in omni aeternitate. Fides & spes tantum cum Deo agunt, & nostrae serviunt saluti: at Dilectio Deum intuetur perpetuò in omnibus officiis, deinde universae servit Ecclesiae, nec solum in hac vita usum habet, sed ad omnem perpetuitatem sese extendit.

Hac ratione dilectio maior est fide & spe. Non autem hinc sequitur dilectionem in omnibus praeferendam esse fidei & spei. Fides enim ut est mater & causa efficiens dilectionis: ita etiam & prior & potior est suo effectu. Proprium fidei est adprehendere promissionem Evangelii; Christum cum omnibus beneficiis regni sui arctissimè complecti: luctari adversus diffidentiam: vincere peccati vim & terrores mortis: superare tyrannidem Satanae: & impetrare à Deo reconciliationem & iustitiam; Haec scriptura sacra non tribuit dilectioni. In his igitur proprietatibus suis, et admirandis effectibus excellit fides. Valde igitur ineptè colligunt Pontificii, dum ex hoc Pauli dicto, Dilectio est maxima in his, argumentantur nos dilectione potissimùm coram Deo iustos esse. Sophisma sic contexunt.

Maxima virtus potissimùm iustificat.Dilectio est maxima virtus.Ergò potissimùm iustificat.

Respondeo, maior vera esset, si ex lege esset iustitia. Quia verò nemo est in mundo, qui praestat legem, ideò nulla virtus iustificat, nec parva, nec magna, nec maxima. Ex operibus enim legis, non iustificabitur ulla caro. In Evangelio autem admirandam hanc iustificationis nostrae rationem patefecit Deus, quòd gratis sine nostris operibus et virtutibus, propter obedientiam & mortem Iesu Christi filii sui, velit nos recipere in gratiam et iustos pronunciare, iuxta dictum: Iustificati gratis gratia ipsius per redemptionem, quae est in Christo Ie su, quem proposuit propiciatorium in sanguine ipsius per fidem. Haec iustificatio non pendet ab ulla virtute vel opere hominis: sed à sola Dei misericordia & merito Iesu Christi: Nec fides nos iustificat sua dignitate vel ratione operis: sed tantum veluti organum, quod nobis ordinavit Deus, ut eo promissionem Evangelii & universa beneficia mediatoris nobis adplicaremus. Maior ergò iuxta Evangelii doctrinam non consistit. Minor etiam intelligenda est de perpetuitate, ac de dilectione perfecta & integra, qualis in hac fragili & impura hominum natura non existit.

## 13:12 Places of Doctrine
Places of Doctrine.

1. The principal place of this chapter is concerning love. For the whole chapter is a notable commendation of love from its properties and comparison with other spiritual gifts.

2. Doctrine concerning the necessity of good works in the justified. Paul testifies that faith, even if it should move mountains, if it is devoid of love, is nothing. Therefore, love necessarily follows faith in the reborn.

3. Concerning true patience, which is the constant companion of true love, and is necessary in the whole conversation of men and in individual actions.

4. Concerning beneficence, which is the proper effect of love.

5. Concerning the avoiding of emulation and envy.

6. On avoiding petulance and insolence.

7. On avoiding pride, and arrogance, and indecorous behavior.

8. On avoiding pleonexia or avarice.

9. On avoiding irascibility and hot-temperedness.

10. On avoiding suspicions which rely on no certain argument.

11. On avoiding ἐπιχαιρεκακίᾳ.

12. On avoiding obstinacy: and that truth should always be preferred to our own reputation and advantage.

13. On showing candor, by which we interpret ambiguous things in a better light.

14. On gentleness, by which the amendment of those who have fallen through human infirmity is to be hoped for.

15. That the preaching of the Gospel and the whole ministry of the word will have an end after this life; for it serves only the infirmity of this life.

16. On the admirable light and glory which will shine in the saints in the blessed life, because we are to behold God face to face without a veil, as He is.

17. On faith: which, as it is especially necessary in this life, so, with the ministry abolished, it will have no place in the other life.

18. Concerning hope, the use of which is likewise only in this life.

Latin:

Loci Doctrinae.

1. Praecipuus huius capitis locus est de dilectione. Totum enim caput est insignis commendatio dilectionis à proprietatibus & collatione cum aliis donis spiritualibus.

2. Doctrina de necessitate bonorum operum in iustificatis. Testatur Paulus fidem, etiam si montes transferat, si sit expers dilectionis, nihil esse. Necessario igitur fidem sequitur dilectio in renatis.

3. De vera patientia, quae est comes adsidua verae dilectionis, & in universa hominum conversatione & singulis actionibus necessaria est.

4. De beneficentia, quae est effectus proprius dilectionis.

5. De vitanda aemulatione & livore.

6. De vitanda petulantia & insolentia.

7. De vitanda superbia, & arrogantia, & indecoro gestu.

8. De vitanda pleonexia seu avaritiae.

9. De vitanda iracundia & excandescentia.

10. De vitandis suspicionibus, quae nullo certo nituntur argumento.

11. De vitanda ἐπιχαιρεκακίᾳ.

12. De vitanda pertinacia: & quod veritas nostrae existimationi & commodo semper sit praeferenda.

13. De candore praestando, quo ambigua in meliorem partem interpretemur.

14. De lenitate, qua speranda est emendatio eorum, qui ex infirmitate humana lapsi sunt.

15. Quod praedicatio Evangelii & totum ministerium verbi, finem sit habiturum post hanc vitam; tantum enim huius vitae infirmitati servit.

16. De admiranda luce & gloria, quae in sanctis fulsura est in vita beata, quòd Deum facie ad faciem sine involucro, sicuti est, conspecturi sumus.

17. De fide: quae ut in hac vita inprimis est necessaria: ita abolito ministerio, in altera vita locum non habebit.

18. De spe, cuius usus similiter est tantum in hac vita.

## 14:1 Argument
CHAPTER XIV.

Paul continues to instruct the Corinthians concerning spiritual gifts: and he repeatedly inculcates that one must primarily strive for love, which everywhere serves all, and always promotes the edification of the Church. Then, that those gifts are especially to be sought and exercised which contribute most to the Church, such as Prophecy, that is, the faculty of explaining the holy scripture, and of instructing the people concerning God, and the benefits of the mediator. The Corinthians admired the gift of various languages greatly, and they displayed it in public assemblies: just as if the Holy Spirit had adorned the Church with the gift of tongues for this purpose, that the pious might have something by which they could be proud before the Church or the nations. Paul therefore refutes this error at length and with many arguments. He teaches that the gift of prophesying, that is, of expounding the holy scripture, and of instructing the people, is much more necessary and useful than the gift of tongues: although this also is excellent and great, if only one uses it, not for vain ostentation, but for the benefit of the Church. Then he establishes in what order prophets or teachers ought to teach in the Church. He forbids that power of preaching in public be given to women. Finally, he concludes this passage with a notable rule; that effort must be made so that all things in the Church may be done decently and in order.

Latin:

CAPUT XIIII.

Paulus adhuc erudit Corinthios de donis spiritualibus: & subinde inculcat, inprimis studendum esse dilectioni, quae passim servit omnibus, & semper promovet aedificationem Ecclesiae. Deinde illa dona praecipuè expetenda & exercenda esse, quae plurimùm conducunt Ecclesiae, ut est Prophetia, Id est, facultas explicandi sacram scripturam, & erudiendi populum de Deo, & beneficiis mediatoris. Corinthii donum variarum linguarum plurimùm admirabantur, & illud ostentabant in publicis congressibus: perinde ac si Spiritus sanctus hoc consilio Ecclesiam dono linguarum ornasset, ut pii haberent, quo coram Ecclesia vel gentibus superbire possent. Hunc igitur errorem refellit Paulus prolixè & multis argumentis. Docet donum prophetandi, hoc est, exponendi sacram scripturam, & erudiendi populum multò magis esse necessarium & conducibilius, quàm donum linguarum: quanquam & hoc excellens & magnum est, si quis modò eo, non ad inanem ostentationem, sed ad utilitatem Ecclesiae utatur. Deinde constituit, quo ordine prophetae vel doctores in Ecclesia docere debeant. Vetat ne mulieribus detur potestas concionandi in publico. Tandem insigni regula concludit hunc locum; Dandam esse operam, ut in Ecclesia omnia decenter & ordine fiant.

## 14:1
Pursue love, and zealously desire spiritual gifts, but especially that you may prophesy.

He has shown the mistress of all spiritual gifts, and the goal of all the duties of a pious man, namely, love, which he wishes to shine before every action. And this precept, which he wishes to be always in our sight, he repeats even now. But lest the Corinthians now neglect the study and exercise of gifts, he teaches which are the most excellent and most necessary gifts after love. He did not prefer love for the reason that the rest should be held in contempt: but that they might be used and exercised with greater fruit for the Church, he showed the norm which must be applied. This necessary foundation having been laid, he teaches which spiritual gifts contribute most to the Church, and proves by arguments Prophecy, That is, the gift of explaining sacred scripture, and teaching the people about religion is more profitable, and more necessary, than the gift of various languages.

Latin:

Sectemini caritatem, cum zelo expetite spiritualia, magis autem ut prophetetis.

Magistram omnium donorum spiritualium, & scopum omnium officiorum hominis pii monstravit, nimirum, dilectionem, quam omni actioni vult praelucere. Atque hoc praeceptum, quod semper nobis vult in conspectu esse, etiamnum repetit. Ne autem Corinthii iam negligant studium et exercitium donorum, docet quae sint post dilectionem praestantissima & maximè necessaria dona. Non ideò praetulit dilectionem, ut reliqua haberentur contemptui: sed ut cum maiore fructu Ecclesiae usurparentur & exercerentur, normam, quae adhibenda est, monstravit. Hoc necessario fundamento iacto, docet quae dona spiritualia plurimùm conducant Ecclesiae, & argumentis probat Prophetiam, Id est, donum explicandi sacram scricturam, & docendi populum de religione plus prodesse, & magis necessarium esse, quàm donum variarum linguarum.

## 14:2-19
For he who speaks in a tongue, speaks not to men, but to God: for no one hears: but in the Spirit he speaks mysteries: But he who prophesies speaks to men for edification, exhortation and consolation. He who speaks in a tongue, edifies himself: but he who prophesies, edifies the Church. I wish however that you all speak in tongues: but rather that you Prophesy, For greater is he who Prophesies, than he who speaks in tongues, unless he interprets, so that the Church may receive edification.

This is the first argument, by which he proves that the gift of Prophecy, That is, the faculty of explaining sacred scripture, and teaching the people about God, is a much more excellent and useful gift than the gift of various languages, taken from a comparison of the effects of both gifts. The gift which more edifies the Church, is more excellent. Prophecy more edifies the Church than the gift of tongues: Therefore it is more excellent, and more to be sought after. It has always been customary in the Church to set forth Prophetic and Apostolic writings. And indeed the pious have consulted the very fountains: the Hebrew writings of the Prophets, and the Greek writings of the Apostles. And truly there is an immense utility in this diligence and care of inquiring into and searching the fountains of Israel. For the knowledge of the Prophetic and Apostolic language brings great light to doctrines, and renders the conscience most certain. But the Corinthians were attempting to use a foreign Hebrew or Chaldean idiom in public only for the sake of ostentation. And so Paul corrects them, and teaches that there is no use of a foreign language in public: unless an interpretation is added. He who speaks in tongues: That is, he who in public uses a foreign language, speaks not to men, but to God. For the common people do not understand a foreign language. And therefore they perceive no fruit from it. He speaks mysteries in the Spirit, that is, the things which he says are indeed good: whether he says hymns, or recites prayers, or brings forth Prophetic sayings. And if he were speaking such things in the Spirit and faith to God by himself at his own home, they would have their place: but to show off the knowledge of foreign languages in public is inept, and brings no utility to the Church.

He who prophesies, speaks to men: That is, he who explains Holy Scripture in the vernacular and in a language known to all, and instructs the people concerning God and eternal life (for this is what prophesying is for Paul here), he speaks with notable fruit for the Church: he instructs many: and he serves the salvation of many. He speaks, he says, for edification, exhortation, and consolation.

The kinds of sermons of which there is need in the Church are distinct. Paul calls edification instruction in the heads of piety. When a pastor instructs the people concerning God, concerning the three persons of the divinity, concerning the two natures united in Jesus Christ by personal union, concerning the law, concerning the fall of our first parents, concerning human powers, concerning sin: concerning the Gospel, concerning the justification of man before God, concerning the office of the mediator, concerning repentance, concerning good works, concerning the Church, concerning eternal life and all the remaining articles of our faith, in which our salvation consists. For these things are necessary to be known by all Christians who hope for eternal salvation: and they are perceived only from the preaching of the Gospel. Here, therefore, not only must individual things be handed down perspicuously, clearly, simply, and in a known language and in proper words without any ambiguity: but they must also be confirmed and established by testimonies of Holy Scripture. Therefore, it is a work of great labor this duty is: but its utility is also immense. Furthermore, the Church needs exhortation: for it must be stirred up by speech to a diligent study of heavenly doctrine, to serious piety, to invocation, to thanksgiving, to a cheerful confession of the divine name, to assiduous repentance, to faith, to works of charity, to the pursuit of peace, to patience, and to virtues of every kind.

Here the divine threats are to be set forth, by which God deters us from sins: the most ample promises are to be inculcated, by which God invites men to obedience.

Consolation, moreover, is from time to time necessary for the whole Church and for individual pious people. For the Church is pressed in this life by the cross and afflictions and is exposed in the world to various dangers and injuries. Here, unless it were sustained by the consolation of the divine word, it could not stand in faith. But the word of GOD supplies the most ample and most efficacious consolations in every tribulation, as much bodily as spiritual. These, therefore, the pastor ought assiduously to set forth to his hearers and to raise up terrified minds.

He who speaks in a tongue, edifies himself: but he who prophesies, edifies the Church. It is the same as what he said above. He who with a foreign idiom uses it, he serves himself: for because he understands the language, he is able to instruct himself, to confirm himself in the faith, to console, and to exhort. But the Church perceives no fruit from it. For since the language is not understood, it can neither be instructed, nor stirred up, nor raised up to receive consolation.

I wish, however, that you all spoke in tongues: Lest the Corinthians should suspect that Paul either held the excellent gift of the Holy Spirit in contempt, or envied the Corinthians themselves, he explains his wish. He wishes that individuals in the Church were instructed in the knowledge of various languages: but yet he wishes this more, that they might excel in the gift of prophesying or teaching. For he who prophesies is greater: For there is greater necessity and utility in the Church for a prophet than for the knowledge of foreign languages, unless interpretation accompanies it.

But now brothers, if I come to you speaking in tongues, what will I profit you, unless I have spoken to you, either by revelation, or by knowledge, or by prophecy, or by doctrine.

The second argument from the example of Paul. If I, Paul says, were to wish to show off among you the gift of various languages, if I were to preach to you in Greek or in Hebrew, or in Latin, or in Spanish, you would perceive no utility from it, unless I were to explain the individual things to you at the same time. You understand, therefore, that the ostentation of a foreign language in the Church, without interpretation, is without any fruit.

He sets forth here four species with the fruit of speaking in the Church, through revelation, through knowledge, through prophecy, through doctrine.

Revelation is when it is explained to the Church what has been divinely revealed and made manifest to us. As Paul. Act: 22. He explains in a sermon a revelation, that the Lord Jesus appeared to him: Item, Actorum 23. he explains a revelation, that the Lord Jesus confirmed him in the barracks. The Apostle Peter, Actorum 11: He explains a revelation, which he saw in ἐκστάσει. Item, 2. Petri 1. He explains through revelation, that he saw the glory of Jesus Christ on Mount Tabor.

Knowledge or cognition is when we show to the people in obscure and dangerous matters right and salutary counsels from the word of God: When we teach men what is to be looked at in political government, how a governor can be happy: Why a spouse, the companion of life, is to be sought: how pious spouses can be happy: how the whole life is to be directed to the norm of the divine word. Through knowledge Paul speaks, 1 Cor. 7, where he supplies counsel to the doubting Church in various cases. Item: at Eph. 5 & 6, when he instructs fathers and mothers of families, children and servants, as to what the duty of each one is, through knowledge Solomon speaks to the Church in the Proverbs; through knowledge he speaks to the whole Church: for he teaches all men how each one ought to walk prudently in his own calling and in all the actions of life.

I understand prophecy here, as above, concerning the explanation of the prophetic writings. As Paul at Rom. 4, explaining the saying of Moses, Gen. 15, Abraham believed God and it was reckoned to him for righteousness, speaks to the Church through prophecy.

Doctrine is when the heads of piety are explained in order, as in the Epistle to the Romans: first he accuses the human race of sin; then he explains the highest article of faith, how a man is justified before God; he shows the effects of faith. He teaches what sin is, what grace is, what the law is; he delivers the doctrine concerning election. Item, concerning good works. Through doctrine, therefore, he spoke to the Church. The mind of Paul is that, whatever species of teaching we may use in the Church, effort is to be given that we use that language and kind of speech which can be understood by all.

Even things without life giving sound, whether pipe or harp, unless they give a distinction in the sounds, how shall it be known what is piped or harped? For if the trumpet give an uncertain sound, who shall prepare himself to the battle? So likewise ye, except ye utter by the tongue easy to be understood, how shall it be known what is spoken? for ye shall speak into the air.

This third argument is taken from musical instruments, by which he proves that the use of a foreign tongue which is not understood by the people is of no profit; the similitude is clear. When a piper or a harper produces confused sounds, it delights no one, nor can it be known what he intended to play. Thus a foreign and unknown tongue neither instructs nor affects the minds of men, but is only a sound, and indeed an ungrateful and barbarous one to the one not understanding. He made mention of the trumpet most aptly. For as the trumpet incites soldiers to battle: so the Word of God, the trumpet of the Holy Spirit, excites the minds of the pious, that they may eagerly join battle with Satan, the world, and the flesh, and fight bravely in the Spirit.

There are, for example, so many kinds of voices in the world, and none of them is without meaning: Therefore if I do not know the power of the voice, I shall be to him who speaks a barbarian: and he who speaks, a barbarian to me.

This fourth argument is taken from the example and custom of men using various languages in the world. If an Arab speaks to a Greek or Latin man, he will expose himself to laughter and will be considered a barbarian; conversely, if a Greek speaks in Greek or a Latin in Latin to an Arab, they will be received with mockery and will be barbarians to him, for the reason that they use an unknown language before a man of another language; thus also in the Church, consider the display of a foreign language without interpretation to be without any fruit. For nothing is without meaning: that is, there is no voice, of whatever language it may be, which does not have a certain signification among those who are knowledgeable of that language.

So also you, since you are followers of Spirits: seek that you may excel for the edification of the church.

From the preceding arguments he infers the conclusion: that the knowledge of a foreign language without interpretation is not to be displayed in the Church: but that all things are to be compared to the edification of the Church and that one must so strive for spiritual gifts, that we may be the better instructed for the instructing of others.

This precept is to be fixed in the deepest senses, and always to be held before the eyes. That we may direct all things, and especially the labors of the ministry, to the illustration of the glory of God and the edification of the Church. Let the pastor always take up useful and necessary subjects: Let him give effort to instruct the people in Catechism, let him faithfully deliver, assiduously repeat, and from time to time inculcate the necessary articles of faith, let him seriously exhort the hearers to repentance: let him gravely tax the sins and errors spreading in the Church: let him confirm the weak: let him console those wasting away in sorrow: let him excite the sluggish: let him refute the sophists: Let him not seek the applause of the people: let him not accommodate his sermons to the will of the powerful: let him not bring empty subtleties into the pulpit: let him not play with jokes before the Church of Jesus Christ: let him not study ambiguities: but in all things let him seek the edification of the Church.

Therefore let him who speaks in a tongue pray that he may interpret. For if I pray in a tongue, my spirit prays: but my mind is without fruit. What then? I will pray with the spirit: but I will pray also with the mind: I will sing with the spirit: but I will sing also with the mind. Otherwise if you bless with the spirit: how shall he who fills the place of the unlearned say, Amen, to your thanksgiving: since he does not know what you are saying. You indeed give thanks well: but the other is not edified.

This is the fifth argument taken from the use of public prayers: which unless it is done in the vernacular language known to all, they do not aid the edification of the Church. If anyone, he says, is instructed with the gift of tongues: let him pray to the Lord, that he may also receive the gift of interpretation: Unless he has obtained this from God, let him not display the gift of a foreign tongue in the Church. For neither do public prayers, which are made in a foreign tongue, have a place in the Church. If I pray, he says, in a foreign tongue: my spirit prays: That is, in the spirit indeed and true motion of the heart I call upon God: because I understand the words which I speak: and by consideration of the Prophetic scripture from which I recite the prayer, my faith, invocation, and joy in God are kindled.

But my mind is without fruit: This is, while I do not bring forth through a known language the sentiment and doctrine, which is contained in a foreign tongue, and the consolation, which I have conceived in my mind from the prayer, the fruit perishes, which others ought to have perceived from my understanding and spiritual gift. As Paul, using the prayer of Jacob in Hebrew: I am less than all thy mercies. He prays in the Spirit, and spiritual motions are kindled in him. But unless he explains it in a known speech, the fruit perishes, which others could perceive, if he were to reveal in a known tongue his pious meditations, which his mind sees. Therefore I will pray in the Spirit, he says, by myself: but I will pray with the mind also, that is, in a public assembly I will set forth my mind and sentiment, which I understand in the words of scripture, so that others also may know what I pray, and may learn from me, how and what is to be sought from God. Thus I will sing in the Spirit, namely in a foreign tongue by myself: but I will sing with the mind also: That is, I will sing in a known tongue in public, so that others may understand the thoughts of my mind. Otherwise how shall the unlearned say, Amen. The Apostle warns that even if some minister leads by praying aloud, yet individuals ought to join their own vows. for the Church is one body: Therefore individual members ought to contribute their works to the common salvation. But that cannot be done, if the prayer, or the act of thanksgiving, is recited in an unknown tongue. For the unlearned do not understand what is being said. Therefore, the vernacular language must be used in the assemblies of the Church.

The Roman Antichrist cast aside this doctrine of the Holy Spirit with horrible audacity and trampled it underfoot. For he willed that infants be baptized, Psalms be sung, prayers be recited, Gospels be read, worship be performed, and masses be celebrated only in the Latin idiom, and indeed among those peoples who were entirely ignorant of the Latin language, such as among the Germans, Gauls, Spaniards, English, Poles, Danes, etc. For the Roman pontiff, the sworn enemy of the truth, feared that if the word of God were recited in the vernacular language, the people would arrive at the true knowledge of God and the benefits of the mediator, and would detect the deceits and idolomania of the Pope. Let us therefore detest the monstrous audacity and malice of the Roman Antichrist: And according to the counsel of Paul, let us strive that the Churches of Jesus Christ everywhere in their worship may use the vernacular language, which serves for edification.

I thank my God, that I speak with tongues more than you all: but in the Church I had rather speak five words with my understanding, that I might instruct others, than ten thousand words in a tongue.

He proposes his own example again to the whole Church, that he does not desire to show off the gift of tongues in the Church, even if he were more instructed in this gift than all who were at Corinth and were boasting of the gift of tongues. To speak with the understanding is to set forth one's own mind in a known kind of speech, so that others may perceive the thoughts of our mind and be instructed: to speak with a tongue, for Paul, is to use a foreign language among the unskilled.

Latin:

Nam qui loquitur lingua, non hominibus loquitur, sed Deo: nullus enim audit: Spiritu verò loquitur mysteria: Qui verò prophetat hominibus loquitur ad aedificationem, exhortationem & consolationem. Qui loquitur lingua, seipsum aedificat: at qui prophetat, Ecclesiam aedificat. Volo autem omnes vos loqui linguis: magis tamen ut Prophetetis, Maior enim qui Prophetat, quàm qui linguis loquitur, nisi interpretetur, ut Ecclesia aedificationem accipiat.

Primum est hoc argumentum, quo probat multò praestantius & utilius donum esse, Prophetiam, Id est, facultatem explicandi sacram scripturam, & docendi populum de Deo, quam donum variarum linguarum, sumptum à collatione effectuum utriusque doni. Donum quod magis aedificat Ecclesiam, est praestantius. Prophetia magis aedificat Ecclesiam, quàm donum linguarum: Ergò est praestantius, et magis expetendum. Semper in Ecclesia usitatum fuit, proponere scripta Prophetica et Apostolica. Et quidem ipsos fontes consuluerunt pii: Hebraica scripta Prophetarum, & Graeca scripta Apostolorum. Ac immensa sanè utilitas est huius diligentiae & curae inquirendi & scrutandi fontes Israelis. Cognitio enim linguae Propheticae & Apostolicae, magnam adfert lucent doctrinis, & conscientiam reddit certissimam. At Corinthii tantum ostentationis causa in publico Hebraico vel Chaldaico idiomate uti conabantur. Itaque corrigit eos Paulus, & docet nullum esse usum peregrinae linguae in publico: nisi accedat interpretatio. Qui loquitur linguis: Id est, qui in publico utitur lingua peregrina, non loquitur hominibus, sed Deo. Plebs enim non intelligit peregrinam linguam. Ideoque nullum fructum inde percipit. Spiritu loquitur mysteria, hoc est, bona quidem sunt, quae dicit: sive hymnos dicat, sive precationes recitet, sive dicta Prophetica proferat. Et si domi suae apud se Deo tatia loqueretur in Spiritu & fide suum haberent locum: sed in publico ostentare peregrinarum linguarum congnitionem, ineptum est, & nihil utilitasis adfert Ecclesiae.

Qui Prophetat, hominibus loquitur: Hoc est, qui vernacula & omnibus nota lingua exponit sacram scripturam, & erudit populum de Deo & vita aeterna (Hoc enim Paulo hìc est Prophetare,) is cum insigni fructu Ecclesiae loquitur: multos ille erudit: & multorum servit saluti. Loquitur inquit ad aedificationem, exhortationem, & consolationem.

Distincta sunt concionum genera, quibus opus est in Ecclesia. Aedificationem nominat Paulus institutionem in capitibus pietatis. Cùm pastor erudit populum de Deo, De tribus personis divinitatis, De duabus naturis in Iesu Christo unione personali unitis, De lege, De lapsu primorum parentum, De viribus humanis, De peccato: De Evangelio, De iustificatione hominis coram Deo, De officio mediatoris, De poenitentia, De bonis operibus, De Ecclesia, De vita aeterna et reliquis omnibus fidei nostrae articulis, in quibus nostra consistit salus. Haec enim omnibus Christianis, salutem aeternam sperantibus, cognitu sunt necessaria: Et tantum ex praedicatione Evangelii percipiuntur. Hîc ergò non tantum singula perspicue, clarè, simpliciter, & nota lingua & propriis verbis sine omni ambiguitate tradenda: verumetiam testimoniis sacrae scripturae confirmanda & stabilienda sunt. Magni igitur laboris est hoc officium: sed etiam utilitas eius est immensa. Exhortatione deinde eget Ecclesia: sermone enim excitanda est ad diligens studium doctrinae coelestis, ad seriam pietatem, ad invocationem, ad gratiarum actionem, ad alacrem confessionem nominis divini, ad poenitentiam adsiduam, ad fidem, ad opera caritatis, ad studium pacis, ad patientiam, & ad omnis generis virtutes.

Hîc comminationes divinae proponendae sunt, quibus Deus deterret nos a peccatis: inculcandae sunt amplissimae promissiones, quibus Deus invitat homines ad obedientiam.

Consolatio praeterea subinde necessaria est toti Ecclesiae et singulis piis. Premitur enim Ecclesia in hac vita cruce et adflictionibus et in mundo ex posita est variis periculis & iniuriis. Hîc nisi sustentaretur consolatione verbi divini, consistere in fide non posset. Suppeditat autem DEI verbum amplissimas & efficacissimas consolationes in omni tribulatione, tam corporali quam Spirituali. Has igitur pastor suis auditoribus assiduè proponere & perterrefactas mentes erigere debet.

Qui loquitur lingua, seipsum aedificat: Qui verò Prophetat, Ecclesiam aedificat. Idem est, quod supra dixit. Is qui peregrino idiomate utitur, sibi servit: quia enim intelligit idioma, seipsum erudire, in fide confirmare, consolari, et exhortari potest. At Ecclesia nullum inde fructum percipit. Idiomate enim non intellecto nec erudiri, neque excitari, neque ad capiendam consolationem erigi potest.

Volo autem vos omnes loqui linguis: Ne Corinthii suspicarentur Paulum vel contemptui habere donum Spiritus sancti excellens, aut ipsis Corinthiis invidere, votum suum exponit. Optare se ut singuli in Ecclesia instructi essent variarum linguarum cognitione: sed tamen potius se hoc optare, ut singult dono Prophetandi seu docendi, excellerent. Maior enim est, qui prophetat: Nam Maior est necessitas & utilitas in Ecclesia Prophetae, quàm peregrinarum linguarum cognitio, nisi interpretatio ascedat.

Nunc verò fratres, si venero ad vos linguis loquens, quid vobis prodero, nisi vobis locutus fuero, aut per revelationem, aut per cognitionem, aut per Prophetiam, aut per doctrinam.

Secundum argumentum ab exemplo Pauli. Si ego, Paulus inquit, vellem apud vos ostentare donum variarum linguarum, si vobis Graecis concionarer vel Hebraice, vellatinè, vel Hispanicè, nihil utilitatis inde percepturi essetis, nisi simul explicarem vobis singula. Intelligitis igitur ostentationem linguae peregrinae in Ecclesia, sine interpretatione absque omni fructu esse.

Quatuor hîc ponit species cum fructu loquendi in Ecclesia, per revelationem, per scientiam, per Prophetiam, per doctrinam.

Revelatio est, cùm exponitur Ecclesiae, quid nobis divinitus reverlatum & patefactum est. Ut Paulus. Act: 22. Exponit in concione revelationem, quòd dominus Iesus illi adparuerit: Item, Actorum 23. exponit revelationem, quòd Dominus Iesus eum confirmarit in casiris. Apostolus Petrus, Actorum 11: Exponit revelationem, quam viderit in ἐκστάσει. Item, 2. Petri 1. Exponit per revelationem, quòd viderit Iesu Christi gloriam in monte Thabor.

Scientia sive cognitio est, cùm populo in obscuris & periculosis rebus monstramus recta & salutaria consilia ex verbo Dei: Cum docemus homines, quid sit spectandum in gubernatione politica, quomodo gubernator possit esse felix: Cur expelenda sit coniunx vitae socia: quomodo pii coniuges possint esse felices: quomodo universa vita sit dirigenda ad normam verbi divini. Per scientiam loquitur Paulus, 1. Cor: 7. Ubi Eccle: dubitanti consilia in variis casibus sup peditat. Item: ad: Eph. 5. & 6. Cùm erudit patres & matres familias, liberos & ministros, quod cuiusque sit officium, per scientiam loquitur Ecclesiae Salomon in proverbiis per scientiam loquitur toti Ecclesiae: Docet enim omnes homines, quomodo quisque in sua vocatione & omnibus actionibus vitae prudenter ambulare debeat.

Prophetiam hîc intelligo, ut suprà de explicatione Propheticorum scriptorum. Ut Paulus ad Rom: 4. ex ponens dictum Moisis. Gene: 15. Credidit Abraham Deo & imputatum est illi ad iustitiam, per Prophetiam loquitur Ecclesiae.

Doctrina est, cùm ordine capita pietatis explicantur, ut in Epistola ad Roma: primùm accusat genus humanum de peccato: deinde exponit articulum fidei summum, quomodo iustificetur homo coram Deo: ostendit fidei effectus. Docet quid sit peccatum, quid gratia, quid lex: Tradit doctrinam de electione. Item de bonis operibus. Per doctrinam igitur locutus est Ecclesiae. Mens Pauli est, quacunque specie docendi utamur in Ecclesia, operam esse dandam, ut ea lingua & genere sermonis utamur, quod ab omnibus possit intelligi.

Quin & inamina vocem reddentia, sive tibia, sive cithara, nisi distinctionem sonis dederint, quomodo cognoscetur, quod vel tibia, vel cithara canitur? Etenim si incertam vocem tuba dederit, quis praeparabitur ad bellum? Sic & vos per linguam, nisi significantem sermonem dederitis, quomodo intelligetur quod dicitur? eritis enim in aërem loquentes.

Tertiùm est hoc argumentum sumptum ab organis musicis, quo probat usum linguae peregrinae quae non intelligitur à populo, nihil prodesse; perspicua est similitudo. Cùm tibicen vel citharaedus confusos edit sonos, neminem delectat, nec sciri potest, quid canere instituerit. Itae lingua peregrina & ignota, nec erudit, nec adficit mentes hominum, sed tantum est sonus, & quidem ingratus & barbarus non intelligenti. Aptissimè tubae fecit mentionem. Ut enim tuba ad praelium incitat milites: Ita Verbum Dei tuba Spiritus sancti, excitat mentes piorum, ut alacriter cum Satana, mundo, & carne manus conserant, & Spiritu pugnent fortiter.

Tàm multa, verbi gratia, genera vocum in mundo sunt, & nihil horum mutum: Itaque si nesciero vim vocis, ero ei, qui loquitur, barbarus: & qui loquitur, apud me barbarus.

Quartum est hoc argumentum sumptum ab exemplo & consuetudine homnium variis linguis in mundo utentium. Si Arabs loquatur graeco vel latino homini: risui sese exponet, & barbarus habebitur, rursus si Graecus graecè, vel Latinus latinè loquatur Arabi ludibrio excipientur, & erunt illi barbari, eò quòd ignota lingua utantur apud hominem alterius linguae sic et in Ecclesia existimate linguae peregrimae ostentationem sine interpretatione, sine omni fructa esse. Nihil enim est mutum: ld est, nulla est vox cuiuscunque sit linguae, quae non habeat certam significationem apud eos, qui eius linguae sunt gnari.

Sic & vos, siquidem sectatores estis Spirituum: aedificationem quae rite, ut excellatis.

Ex superioribus argumentis infert conclusionem: cognitionem peregrinae linguae sine interpretatione in Ecclesia non esse ostentandam: sed omnia esse comparanda ad aedificationem Ecclesiae & ita studendum donis spiritualibus, ut instructiores simus ad erudiendos alios.

Praeceptum hoc imis sensibus infigendum, & semper antè oculos habendum est. Ut omnia & inprimis labores ministerii dirigamus ad gloriae Dei illustrationem & aedificationem Ecclesiae. Pastor sumat semper materias utiles & necessarias: Det operam ut populum erudiat in Catechesi, fideliter tradat, adsiduè repetat, subindè inculcet necessarios fidei articulos, seriò hortetur auditores ad poenitentiam: graviter taxet peccata & errores grassantes in Ecclesia: confirmet imbecilles: consoletur moerore tabescentes: excitet socordes: refellet sophistas: Non captet adplausum populi: non accommodet suas conciones ad voluntatem potentum: non adferat inanes subtilitates in suggestum: non ludat iocis coram Ecclesia Iesu Christi: non studeat ambiguitatibus: sed in omnibus quaerat aedificationem Ecclesiae.

Quapropter qui loquitur lingua oret ut interpretetur. Nam si orem lingua, Spiritus meus orat: sed mens mea fructu caret. Quid igitur? orabo Spiritu: orabo autem & mente: canam Spiritu: sed canam & mente. Alioquin si benedixeris Spiritu: is qui locum implet idiotae, quomodo dicturus est, Amen, ad tuam gratiarum actionem: quandoquidem quid dicas nescit. Tu quidem bene gratias agis: sed alius non aedificatur.

Quintum hoc est argumentum sumptum ab usu publicarum precationum: quae nisi fiat vernacula lingua nota omnibus nihil iuvant Ecclesiae aedificationem. Si quis, inquit, instructus est dono linguarum: precetur dominum, ut & donum interpretationis accipiat: Hoc nisi impetraverit à Deo, non ostentet donum peregrinae linguae Ecclesia. Nam nec publicae preces, quae peregrina lingua fiunt locum habent in Ecclesia. Si orem, inquit, lingua peregrina: Spiritus meus orat: ld est, in Spiritu quidem & vero motu cortu cordis invoco Deum: quia intelligo verba, quae loquor: & consideratione Propheticae scripturae ex qua precationem recito, accenditur mea fides, invocatio, & laeticia in Deo.

Sed mens mea fructu caret: Hoc est, dum sententiam & doctrinam, quae peregrina lingua continetur, & consolationem, quam ego mente ex precatione concepi, non profero per notam linguam, perit fructus, quem alii ex meo intellectu & dono spirituali percipere debebant. Ut Paulus Hebraicè usurpans precationem Iacobi: Minor sum cunctis miserationibus tuis. Spiritu orat, & accenduntur in eo motus spirituales. Sed nisi explicuerit noto sermone, perit fructus, quem alii percipere possent, si pias suas meditationes, quas mens eius videt, lingua nota patefaceret. Itaque orabo Spiritu, inquit, apud me: sed & mente orabo, id est, in publico congressu mentem & sententiam meam, quam ego intelligo in verbis scripturae, exponam, ut & alii sciant quid ego orem, & a me discant, quomodo & quid sit à Deo petendum. Sic canam Spiritu, nimirum lingua peregrina apud me: sed & mente canam: ld est, canam lingua nota in publico, ut alii mentis meae cogitationes intelligant. Aloqui quomodo idiota dicet, Amen. Monet Apostolus etiamsi minister aliquis praeeat voce imprecando, tamen singulos debere sua coniungere vota: Ecclesia enim unum est corpus: Itaque singulà membra ad communem satutem operas suas conferre debent. Id autem fieri nequit, si lingua ignota recitetur precatio, vel gratiarum actio. Indocti enim non intelligunt quid dicatur. Vernaculaigitur lingua in congressibus Ecclesiae est utendum.

Hanc Spiritus sancti doctrinam Romanus Antichristus horribili audacia proiecit & pedibus conculcavit. Voluit enim tantum latino idiomate baptizari infantes, cani Psalmos, recitari precationes, tegi Evangelia, peragi cultus, & celebrari missas, & quidem apud eos populos, qui prorsus erant ignari latinae linguae ut apud Germanos, Gallos, Hispanos, Anglos, Polonos, Danos, etc. Metuit enim iuratus hostis veritatis Romanus pontifex, ne si verbum Dei vernacula lingua recitaretur, populus ad veram Dei et beneficiorum mediatoris noticiam perveniret, & dolos et idolomaniam Papae deprehenderet. Detestemur igitur immanem Antichristi Romani audaciam & maliciam: Et iuxta consilium Pauli demus operam, ut Ecclesiae Iesu Christi passim in cultibus vernacula lingua, quae aedificationi serviat utantur.

Gratias ago Deo meo, quod magis, quàm vos omnes linguis loquor: sed in Ecclesia volo quinque verba mente mea loqui, ut alios instituam, potius quàm decem milia verborum lingua.

Svum rursus exemplum proponit toti Ecclesiae quòd non cupiat ostentare donum linguarum in Ecclesia, etiamsi magis instructus sit hoc dono, quàm omnes, qui Corinthi erant, & donum linguarum iactitabant. Verba loquimente, est mentem suam exponere noto sermonis genere, ita ut alii mentis nostrae cogitata percipiant, & erudiantur: lingua loqui, Paulo est peregrina lingua uti apud imperitos.

## 14:20
Brethren, do not be children in understanding: but in malice be children: but in understanding be perfect.

He intersperses an admonition concerning the use of gifts: which are not to be shown off childishly or ineptly, but are to be used wisely. Do not be children in this sense: as if he were saying, do not be so delirious, do not be so childish as to admit thoughts into your mind, so that you might think that religion and the happiness of Christians consists in this, if only it is permitted for you to display the gifts of the Spirit without any fruit. Even common sense understands that it is inept to display a foreign language among those who are ignorant of it. You, therefore, illuminated by the Holy Spirit, ought to have been wiser than other men who are outside the Church. Be children in malice: That is, in evil and prohibited things, be simple and ignorant: do not affect sharpness or cleverness in evil arts or deceits, but in your senses be perfect. This is, always progress in wisdom and the knowledge of the will of God: acquire for yourselves true, spiritual, and perfect wisdom, as far as it can be done. Perfect here does not signify absolute in all numbers, but that which is sincere, upright, and solid: and it is opposed to that which is corrupt, feigned, falsified, and mutilated: the wisdom of the flesh is imperfect and adulterated with folly and error: but the wisdom of the Spirit is perfect, although it grows from time to time in the pious. The mind of Paul, therefore, is that spiritual gifts must be used wisely: not for vain ostentation, not so that we may capture the applause of the people, just as foolish nations are accustomed to play the fool: but for the illustration of the glory of God: and the edification of the Church. For thus is solid [wisdom] acquired. glory, not only in the world, but in all eternity to endure, when we refer all things to the glory of God. For most true and most ample is the promise: Those who glorify me, I will glorify.

In the law it is written, by men of other tongues, and other lips I will speak unto this people: and yet for all that they will not hear me, saith the Lord. Wherefore tongues are for a sign, not to them that believe, but to them that believe not: but prophecy serveth not for them that believe not, but for them which believe.

This is the sixth argument taken from the final cause, and the effects of the gifts, both of tongues and of prophecy. Those things which are ordained by God for the faithful are more excellent than those which are given as a sign and a wonder to the unfaithful. But foreign tongues were given as a sign not to the faithful, but to the unfaithful. Therefore, the gift of prophecy, which edifies the faithful, is a more excellent gift than the gift of foreign tongues: therefore, one should rather strive for prophecy.

That foreign tongues were given as a sign to the unfaithful, Paul proves by the testimony of Isaiah The Prophets, from Chapter 28. Where the Prophet first gravely accuses the blindness, errors, and stupor of the Jewish people: They have staggered in wine, they have wandered in strong drink: the Priest and the Prophet have wandered: all tables are full of vomit: That is, the people have plainly fallen away from the truth of God: they are full, and plainly drunk with errors and superstitions, now bumping into this, now into that idolatry after the manner of drunkards: The Prophets and Priests, like the Pharisees and Sadducees, fill the tables, which they ought to furnish with the best dishes of the divine word and sermons, concerning the benefits of the mediator, by which the consciences of the miserable could be refreshed, with vomit, with impious dogmas, with human traditions, with superstitions, with idol-manias, and with the butcheries of consciences. Whom therefore shall he teach knowledge? them that are weaned from the milk, and drawn from the breasts, as if he were saying, Since the Jews with their Pharisees and scribes disdain the doctrine of the Gospel, for the reason that they are drunk with errors and the traditions of men: and wish to hear neither Christ nor the Apostles: whither therefore shall God turn himself? Is it necessary that there be some Church, and that Christ have disciples? whom therefore shall Christ and the Apostles teach? Those weaned from the milk and drawn from the breasts, That is, the exiled Jews, whom God has chastised with exiles, and for a long time has drawn away from the breasts of Prophetic doctrine:

item, the nations, which God has weaned from the milk of the Gospel, and torn away from the breasts of the ministry: just as was done on the day of Pentecost: where God taught knowledge to the Jews, proselytes, and Gentiles, who had come to Jerusalem from all nations. For those who have been chastised by various hardships, and thirst for truth and justice, these are fit to receive doctrine.

He then adds another reason why God is about to strike the Jews with blindness, and to reveal the Gospel to the Gentiles, namely, because they are not only drunk with errors, but also receive with disdain the truth of the most high God, and the most wholesome sermons of Christ and the Apostles. Precept upon precept: expectation upon expectation: a little here, a little there, he recites by mimesis the words of the impious Jews, Pharisees, and scribes, as if they were saying: the Prophets bring nothing, except one precept after another: they constantly inculcate the same precepts: they always command us to wait: and they entice men with empty hope. That the promise of the Messiah is about to come at any moment: but they wish to say that these are mere deceptions. Therefore it is better that we eat and drink: and care nothing for the sermons of the Prophets: thus the Jews mocked Christ: when they said. Who can listen to him: he is insane: he has a demon: Therefore God threatens the impious and

with the blaspheming Jews mocking the word of God, here with the words which Paul cites. Certainly with stammering lips and another tongue will the Lord speak to this people. This is, the Lord will in turn mock those blasphemers, He will cause that the Apostles through the Holy Spirit use foreign and various tongues in Jerusalem, and preach the great benefits and works of God, by which stupendous miracle the impious Jews will be more blinded, and the Pharisees will be driven into a fury: but to the Gentiles and converted Jews, and proselytes, the mysteries of the kingdom of Jesus Christ will be revealed. From this threat of the Prophet, therefore, it is manifest that the gift of various tongues was given as a sign not to the faithful, but to the incredulous, the mockers, the hypocrites, and the blasphemers.

When therefore God shows His wrath, when He speaks to us in a foreign tongue and one unknown to us: it is very inept and foolish to wish to be proud in the Church by that very thing, as if by an excellent gift, by which God punishes and blinds the incredulous and blasphemers. Therefore if anyone displays in the Church the knowledge of a foreign tongue, which he does not interpret, he demonstrates that he envies the Church the light of truth, and that he rejoices in the ignorance of the pious. And here the reasons are to be considered, why God gave the gift of tongues to the Church.

1. First, that it might be a testimony of the presence of God and the Holy Spirit in the Church: for it is a distinguished and admirable benefit and gift of God to instruct men in the knowledge of various languages in one moment.

2. Second, that God might avenge with this prodigy the malice, pride, and sarcasms with which the Jewish people mocked the doctrine of Christ and the Apostles: for the Lord struck them more with blindness and madness of heart after the Apostles used foreign languages.

3. Third, that the doctrine of the Gospel might be propagated so much the more quickly among various nations, which use most diverse languages.

4. Fourth, that it might be a testimony that the doctrine of the Gospel concerning the benefits of the mediator pertains not only to the people of Israel, but also to other nations: In this place Paul especially urges the second cause, which exists in the sermon of the Prophet Isaiah. Prophecy is not for unbelievers, but for believers: That is, the gift of explaining sacred scripture pertains only to the Church, and serves for edification.

Therefore if the whole Church has come together in one place and all speak in tongues:

But if the unlearned or unbelievers enter, will they not say that you are mad? But if all prophesy, and an unbeliever or unlearned person enters, he is convicted by all, he is judged by all: And thus the secrets of his heart are made manifest: and so falling on his face, he will worship God, proclaiming that God is truly among you.

The seventh argument is from the testimony and judgment of unbelievers; if you all use a foreign language in the Church, unbelievers will say that you are mad; for to what purpose does it pertain to beat the air in vain, and to utter sounds in public which no one understands. Reason also mocks this madness. Why therefore do you Corinthians, who are illuminated by the Spirit of God, not see and point out this folly?

But if you all prophesy: That is, if each of you be instructed with the gift of explaining the holy scripture, and of handing down doctrine concerning God and eternal life, then the unbeliever will be convicted and judged by all. This is, he will be convinced in his heart that he is in error; but in the Church great light is to shine. If any unbeliever approaches the assemblies and gatherings of the pious, and hears a hymn or prayer in a foreign tongue, he is not converted from it, nor is he edified, but rather mocks the barbaric sound. But if he hears many in the assemblies explaining the doctrine concerning God, concerning the law, concerning the fall of the human race, concerning the cause of death and calamities, concerning the benefits of the mediator, concerning good works, concerning the Church, concerning eternal life: if he hears idols refuted gravely and from the foundations, lusts and crimes censured, men called to repentance, threats and examples of divine wrath proposed, the most ample promises explained, he is convinced and reproved in his heart that the doctrine in the Church is sounder than among the Heathens, who pollute themselves with foul lusts and crimes, devise hideous idols, are involved in the horrendous darkness of errors and blasphemies, and at length, destitute of all consolation, rush despairing into destruction.

And if God converts the unbeliever by His Spirit in the assembly, so that the word of God does not depart without fruit, then he will spontaneously reveal the hidden thoughts of his heart, he will confess that he is convinced by the evidence of the matter. He will detest the idols which he has hitherto worshipped, he will marvel at the darkness in which he previously lived with other Heathens; he will cast away the crimes by which he previously was polluting himself.
