For because he mentions the universal resurrection, which is to be in the coming of Christ from the clouds, departing a little from the scope of the disputation, he teaches that this form of the kingdom of Christ, which consists in the word and faith, will not always remain. The Son of God, raised from death, indeed sits at the right hand of the eternal Father, and through the word and the Holy Spirit, he teaches, defends, and governs the entire Church: he has indeed broken the power of Satan and of death: but yet Satan still tempts us: and death devours all men: the faithful do not yet enjoy that eternal beatitude which has been promised to them in the word. For another state remains, which the coming of Jesus Christ will initiate. Therefore he says. Afterwards the end, when he shall have delivered up the kingdom to God and the Father, as if he were to say, This entire form of the kingdom of Jesus Christ, in which we war against Satan, sin, the world, the flesh, death, and enemies of every kind, will have an end in the coming of Christ in the clouds. Christ will deliver up the kingdom, that is, he will bring the Church gathered by the Gospel from the whole human race into the sight of God and the Father: so that the Church may behold face to face the Father, in whom it has believed, and now joyfully triumph over all enemies conquered through Christ, and enjoy the sweetest fellowship of God in all eternity. Then God will no longer deal with us through the word, through the Sacraments: then there will be no need to believe, which we do not see; but we shall immediately behold the divinity, immediately God will suffuse us with his light, wisdom, justice, life, and joy: We shall see God as he is, face to face without any covering: then we shall experience and in reality possess those things which we believe here according to the word of God. This is to deliver the kingdom to God and the Father, namely to establish the triumphant Church over all its enemies in the sight of the Father.

After he has abolished every principality: He teaches that then at the coming of the Son of God the mediator there will be an end to all our warfare. Here we must endure hatreds, exiles, miseries, diseases, punishments, terrors: here we must fight constantly against the flesh, the world, Satan, death, and sin: But then Christ will abolish every principality: He speaks not only of the end of the wicked, but also of the tyranny of Satan, and of all our enemies: Indeed, even of the abolition of ministries and offices in the Church. For he will abolish every principality: first he will abolish the empires and principalities of the world: No Caesar, no King, no Prince or consul will be then: then he will abolish the ministries and offices in the Church: no Apostle, no Bishop, no Pastor, no governor will be then. Furthermore also the principalities and ministries of the Angels he will abolish: for he will not guard or defend the Church through Angels. Fourthly, he will utterly destroy the tyranny of the Devils also, and will thrust them down to the lowest hells. Lastly of all, he will thoroughly abolish death itself. Thus at length the Church will triumph and will enjoy eternal victory in the sight of the eternal God.

For he must reign, until he hath put all enemies under his feet. That is, In the meantime this form of the kingdom of Christ remains until the coming of CHRIST and the universal resurrection of the dead. Christ sits at the right hand of the eternal Father, he is the high priest, king and mediator of the Church, he rules his Church by the word, he calls men to repentance, he regenerates them by the Sacraments, he consoles them in afflictions, he exposes them to various dangers, he defends them against the furies of the world and of Satan, he sanctifies them through the holy Spirit, he gradually increases in them the knowledge of God, he sustains them in faith: he allows them to be submerged into death, and reserves them for the future resurrection. This kingdom Christ must exercise, until he has gathered the whole Church, which the Father chose from eternity in the Son, and has conquered all enemies in the whole world. For this kingdom the Father commanded to the Son: I will put, he says, enmities between thee and the woman: between thy seed and her seed: It shall crush thy head yours: Gen: 3. & Psalm 110. The Lord shall send the rod of your strength out of Zion: rule in the midst of your enemies.

The last enemy that shall be destroyed is death: For he has put all things under his feet, from Psalm. 8. & 110. Paul proves that Christ must be the victor over all enemies: It is not enough, therefore, that Christ should deliver us in this life from the tyrants & terrors of death: but it is necessary that he also abolish death, & every principality, so that he alone may be sublime. Paul excepts the Father, for he is the author & founder of the kingdom of Christ: He shall not, therefore, be subjected to Christ: but then his divine majesty shall be most clearly seen by all, & the immense wisdom & power by which he established the kingdom of Christ. This opinion does not conflict with the fact that Christ shall deliver the kingdom to God & the Father: since there are so many promises of holy scripture concerning the eternity of the kingdom of Christ; as Isa: 9. And of his kingdom there shall be no end. For Christ shall not cease to be king & mediator & head of the Church: only that form of the kingdom shall be changed, the ministry of the word & Sacraments, faith & hope shall cease: And we shall behold the divinity itself face to face: And because the divine essence of the Father, Son, & Holy Spirit is one, since the father possesses the kingdom in all eternity, it is necessary for the son to retain the kingdom.

Then also the son shall be subjected to the father: Christ, God and man, when he shall have brought the Church into the sight of the father, then he is to show that he received the kingdom from the eternal father, and that he honors him with ineffable reverence and obedience, that all things have proceeded from him, that he has performed all things by his command, that he has referred all things to his glory. This subjection of the son, however, does not take away the equality of the essence of the father and the son: For the very appellation of son both teaches that he is of the same essence with the father, and that he is most tightly bound by reverence toward the father.

That God may be all in all: This is, that the divine majesty itself may shine in the son, and in the whole Church: Then God will no longer rule the Church through the ministry of the Gospel, and the Sacraments, but the divinity will immediately communicate heavenly goods, will fill us with perfect light, will adorn us with complete justice, will suffuse us with solid joy, will kindle in us eternal life: no infirmity will hinder us, we will need no instruments, nothing will be denied to our desire: To see God will be both the highest sweetness, and the greatest happiness, and it will be eternal joy: we will learn the wisdom of God without weariness: we will perform justice without trouble: we will enjoy joy without perturbation. The glory of the blessed will indeed be diverse: but there will be no envy there, no there will be room for emulation. For the Lord will satisfy the desires of all: and God himself will be all in all, no one will seek anything more, while it is permitted to him to enjoy the sight of God. O Lord Jesus, when we have happily completed our course, which you have commanded to us, with the help of your Spirit, lead us to this highest and unique happiness, and eternal joy: so that the fruit of your passion may shine in us also: and that we may love the eternal Father, you, and the Holy Spirit, without end, and celebrate without weariness, Amen.

Latin:

Postea finis quando tradiderit regnum Deo & patri, quando aboleverit omnem principatum & omnem potestatem & virtutem. Oportet enim ipsum regnare, donec posuerit omnes inimicos sub pedes suos. Novissimus hostis, qui destruetur mors est. Omnia enim subiecit sub pedes eius. Cùm verò dixerit, quòd omnia subiecta sint, clarum est, quod ille excipiatur, qui illi subiecit omnia. Cùm verò omnia illi subiecta fuerint, tunc & ipse filius subiicietur ei, qui subiecit illi omnia, ut sit Deus omnia in omnibus.

Quintum est hoc membrum huius capitis, in quo confert formam regni Christi, quod in hac vita gerit cum forma regni, quod in altera vita, post quam omnes hostes eius devicti fuerint, habiturus est. Quia enim universalis resurrectionis, quae in adventu Christi ex nubibus futurae est, meminit, paululum digrediens à scopo disputationis, docet non semper mansuram hanc regni Christi formam, quae consistit in verbo & fide. Sedet quidem filius Dei resuscitatus ex morte ad dexteram aeterni patris, & per verbum & Spiritum sanctum, docet, defendit & gubernat universam Ecclesiam: fregit quidem potentiam Satanae & mortis: sed tamen Satan adhuc tentat nos: & mors devorat omnes homines: fideles nondum fruuntur illa beatitudine aeterna, quae ipsis in verbo promissa est. Restat enim alius status, quem adventus Iesu Christi inchoabit. Ideò inquit. Postea finis, quando tradiderit regnum Deo & patri, quasi dicat, Universa haec forma regni Iesu Christi, in quae militamus contra Satanam, peccatum, mundum, carnem, mortem, & omnis generis hostes, finem habebit in adventu Christi in nubibus. Tradet Christus regnum, id est, Ecclesiam collectam Evangelio ex toto genere humano adducet in conspectum Dei & patris: ut Ecclesia coràm intueatur patrem, in quem credidit, & iam laeta triumphet de omnibus hostibus per Christum devictis, & dulcissima consuetudine Dei in omni aeternitate fruatur. Tum non amplius aget Deus nobiscum per verbum, per Sacramenta: tum non opus erit credere, quae non videmus; sed immediate intuebimur divinitatem, immediatè Deus perfundet nos sua luce, sapientia, iustitia, vita & Laeticia: Videbimus Deum sicuti est, facie ad faciem sine omni involucro: tum experiemur & reipsa possidebimus, quae hîc secundum Dei verbum credimus. Hoc est regnum Deo & patri tradere, nimirum triumphantem Ecclesiam de omnibus hostibus suis statuere in conspectum patris.

Postquam abolevit omnem principatum: Docet tum in adventu filii Dei mediatoris finem fore universae militiae nostrae. Hîc nobis sustinenda sunt odia, exilia, miseriae, morbi, supplicia, terrores: hîc nobis adsiduè praeliandum contra carnem, mundum, Satanam, mortem & peccatum: At tum abolebit Christus omnem principatum: Non solum de fine impiorum loquitur, sed etiam de tyrannide Satanae, & omnium hostium nostrorum: Imo etiam de abolitione ministeriorum & officiorum in Ecclesia. Omnem enim principatum abolebit: primùm abolebit imperia & principatus mundi: Nullus Caesar, nullus Rex, nullus Princeps vel consul tum futurus est: deinde abolebit ministeria & officia in Ecclesia: nullus tum Apostolus, nullus Episcopus, nullus Pastor, nullus gubernator tum futurus est. Adhaec & Angelorum principatus & ministeria abolebit: non enim per Angelos custodiet aut defendet Ecclesiam. Quartò Diabolorum quoque tyrannidem prorsus destruet, & eos ad ima tartara detrudet. Postremò omnium & ipsam mortem penitus abolebit. Ita tandem trumphabit Ecclesia & aeterna fruetur victoriam conspectu aeterni Dei.

Oportet autem ipsum regnare, donec posuerit inimicos sub pedes suos. Id est, Interea manet haec forma regni Christi usque ad adventum CHRISTI & universalem resurrectionem mortuorum. Sedet Christus ad dexteram aeterni patris, est summus sacerdos, rex & mediator Ecclesiae, regit Ecclesiam suam verbo, vocat homines ad poenitentiam, regenerat eos Sacramentis, consolatur eos in adflictionibus, obiicit illos variis periculis, defendit illos contra furores mundi et Satanae, sanctificat eos per Spiritum sanctum, subinde auget in illis noticiam Dei, sustentat illos in fide: sinit illos mergi in mortem, & reservat eos futurae resurrectioni. Hoc regnum oportet Christum exercere, donec totam collegerit Ecclesiam, quam pater ab aeterno in Filio elegit, & omnes devicerit hostes in toto orbe. Hoc enim regnum pater mandavit filio: Ponam inquit inimicitias inter te & mulierem: inter semen tuum & semen illius: Ipsum conteret caput tuum: Gen: 3. & Psalm 110. Sceptrum regni tui emittet dominus ex Zion: dominare in medio inimicorum tuorum

Ultimus hostis, qui aboletur est mors: Nam omnia subiecit sub pedes eius, ex Psalm. 8. & 110. probat Paulus Christum oportere omnium hostium fore victorem: Non ergo satis est, ut in hac vita Christus nos liberet a tyrannis & terroribus mortis: sed necesse est eum etiam abolere mortem, & omnem principatum, ut ille solus sit sublimis. Patrem excipit Paulus, nam hic est author & conditor regni Christi: Non igitur subiicietur Christo: sed tum omnium clarissimè conspicietur eius divina maiestas, & immensa sapientia & potentia, qua regnum Christi constituit. Non pugnat haec sententia, quòd Christus tradet regnum Deo & patri: cum tot promissionibus sacrae scripturae de aeternitate regni Christi; ut Ies: 9. Et regni eius non erit finis. Non enim desinet Christus esse rex & mediator & caput Ecclesiae: tantum forma illa regni mutabitur, desinet ministerium verbi & Sacramentorum, fides & spes: Et coràm intuebimur ipsam divinitatem: Et quia una est essentia divina Patris, Filii, & Spiritus sancti, cùm pater obtineat regnum in omni aeternitate, necesse est filium retinere regnum.

Tum & filius subiieietur patri: Christus Deus & homo, ubi adduxerit Ecclesiam in conspectum patris, tum ostensurus est, quòd regnum acceperit à patre aeterno, quòdque eum ineffabili reverentia & obedientia colat, quòd omnia ab ipso profecta sint, quòd omnia eius mandato peregerit, quòd omnia ad ipsius gloriam retulerit. Haec autem subiectio filii non tollit aequalitatem essentiae patris & filii: Ipsa enim adpellatio filii & docet eum eiusdem esse cum patre essentiae, & eum reverentia erga patrem arctissimè devinctum esse.

Ut Deus sit omnia in omnibus: Hoc est, ut ipsa divina maiestas luceat in filio, & in tota Ecclesia: Tum non reget Deus amplius Ecclesiam per ministerium Evangelii, & Sacramenta, sed divinitas immediatè communicabit coelestia bona, implebit nos persecta luce, ornabit nos integra iustitia, perfundet nos solido gaudio, accendet in nobis aeternam vitam: nulla nos impediet infirmitas, nullis indigebimus organis, nihil nostro negabitur desiderio: Deum videre & summs suavitas, & maxima felicitas, & aeterna erit laeticia: sapientiam Dei discemus sine fastidio: iustitiam praestabimus sine molestia: laeticia fruemur sine perturbatione. Diversa quidem erit gloria beatorum: sed nullus isthic invidiae, nullus aemulationi erit locus. Omnium enim desideriae explebit dominus: & omnia erit ipse Deus in omnibus, nemo quidquam expetet amplius, dum licet ei conspectu Dei frui. O domine Iesu, ubi cursum nostrum, quem tu nobis mandasti, feliciter tui Spiritus auxilio absolverimus, perducito nos ad hanc summam & unicam felicitatem, & aeternum gaudium: ut tuae passionis fructus in nobis quoque luceat: utque patrem aeternum te & Spiritum sanctum, sine fine diligamus, & sine taedio celebremus, Amen.

## 15:29-33
Otherwise what shall they do, who are baptized for the dead? If the dead do not rise at all, why are they baptized for the dead? Why do we also stand in jeopardy every hour? I die daily by our boasting, which I have in Christ Jesus our Lord. If according to man I have fought with beasts at Ephesus, what does it profit me, if the dead do not rise? Let us eat and drink: for tomorrow we shall die: Do not err: Evil communications, corrupt good manners.

The brief digression returns to the proof of the article concerning the resurrection of the dead, and employs an argument from the testimony and authority of the Church. In certain Churches there was a custom that Catechumens were baptized at the tombs of the dead, so that there they might first utter a confession concerning the resurrection of the dead, and in this way testify to their sincere faith in Jesus Christ. For they judged this to be the end and scope of the entire Christian religion: If anyone affirmed that he believed in Christ the resurrection of the bodies of the dead, which lay in the tombs, they considered his faith to be sincere and correct: If anyone doubted concerning the resurrection of the dead, this person clearly showed that he did not understand the kingdom of Christ, nor believe his promises. Since, therefore, by this public custom the Church testifies that it certainly believes the resurrection of the dead, it is manifest that the False Apostles, who deny the resurrection of the dead, contradict the Holy Spirit to his face. Concerning the phrase ὑπέρ τῶν νεκρῶν, for the dead, not only recent, but also ancient writers have disputed various things. Those who explained it as for the dead, that is, in the place and stead of the dead: They have completely hallucinated. For Paul would not have passed over such a vicious custom without rebuke. For it fights against the article concerning justification. The righteous (says the Prophet) shall live by his faith. Others have explained it as for the dead, that is, the dying, those about to die shortly, who were held as if dead, and yet were seeking Baptism, so that they might feel its fruit not in this, but also in the other life. But this explanation seems more forced. Therefore, the simplest of all is this. They are baptized with a confession having been made for the dead: testifying that the dead were certainly going to rise again.

Why do we also stand in jeopardy every hour? Another argument from the testimony and authority of the Apostles and of all the martyrs. If there were no resurrection of the dead, then the Apostles and martyrs would be the most foolish of all men: since without cause they expose themselves every hour to the danger of death by the confession of the truth, of which constancy and will they would receive no fruit after this life, except that they cut off this life so much the sooner. Moreover, it would be extreme madness to condemn the Apostles and martyrs, in whom such great wisdom and light of the Holy Spirit shines, of folly or stupidity.

Therefore, in truth there is a resurrection of the dead, looking upon which the Apostles and martyrs endure every kind of punishment and torture: and with a constant will they despise the threats of all tyrants and all the goods of this life: for they establish with certain confidence that they will rise again from death with glorious bodies, and will enjoy a copious reward for their labors. By swearing an oath he testifies that he dies daily: he signifies that he is exercised by continuous calamities, dangers, and terrors on account of the ministry of the Gospel. Outside, he says, are fightings, within are fears. For not only did tyrants, and heretics, and false brothers afflict Paul: but also evil spirits vexed him with terrors, and the angel of Satan struck him with blows. Therefore, he was admonished daily of imminent death, and that is rather dying than living: but he patiently sustains these constant torments by the hope of the resurrection of the dead, which will free him from all miseries and terrors. Therefore, from the testimony of Paul, which shines forth from his patience in such great miseries and terrors, which he experiences on account of the doctrine of the Gospel, they could gather and establish that the dead will altogether rise again, and by this hope all martyrs undergo all kinds of punishments constantly.

If according to man I fought with beasts, what does it profit me? The same argument from the testimony of Paul, which he shows in the fight with beasts at Ephesus. Paul preferred to fight with beasts with the gravest danger to his life, than to omit the confession of the truth: By this constancy, therefore, Paul demonstrated that he believed in the resurrection of the dead, for the joyful hope of which he set aside this life and its advantages for the confession of the truth. He understands his boasting as confidence, joy, and hope, which he has in the Lord Jesus: and it is just as if he had sworn by his entire salvation. This attestation is therefore grave.

Let us eat, let us drink, for tomorrow we shall die. By mimesis he recites the profane and impious voices of the Sadducees and Epicureans: For this being granted, as the false apostles wished, that there is no resurrection of the dead, it is necessary for men to rush into profane security, and to cast off all fear of God: So that they serve only the belly, and seek the pleasures of this life. And thus Christ, the Prophets, the Fathers, the Apostles, the Martyrs, and all the saints will be condemned for extreme folly, because they voluntarily exposed themselves to the various dangers of life, and to horrendous punishments, of which will and constancy they would have hoped for no fruit. Paul therefore refutes such profane and impious voices, and does not wish them to be used by the pious even in jest. For impure and impious speech is also accustomed to corrupt morals: Which is so manifest, that the Heathen poet Menander learned it by experience, and expressed it in a verse.

Latin:

Quid alioquin facient, qui pro mortuis Baptizantur? Si omninò mortui non resurgunt, cur Baptizantur pro mortuis? Quid & nos periclitamur singulis horis? Quotidie morior per nostram gloriationem, quam habeo in Christo Iesu domino nostro. Si secundum hominem pugnavi cum bestiis Ephesi, quid mihi prodest, si mortui non resurgunt? Edamus & bibamus: cras enim moriemur: Ne erretis: Prava colloquia, corrumpunt bonos mores.

Absoluta digressiuncula redit ad probationem articuli de resurrectione mortuorum, & usurpat argumentum à testimonio & authoritate Ecclesiae. In quibusdam Ecclesiis consuetudo erat, Catechumenos Baptizari ad sepulchra mortuorum, ut isthic prius ederent confessionem de resurrectione mortuorum, & hoc modo synceram suam fidem in Iesum Christum testarentur. Iudicarunt enim hunc esse finem & scopum universae religionis Christianae: Si quis adfirmabat se credere in Christo mortuorum corporum, quae in sepulchris iacebant, resurrectionem, huius fidem arbitrantur synceram & rectam esse: Si quis dubitaret de resurrectione mortuorum, hic clarè ostendebat se non intelligere regnum Christi, nec credere promissionibus eius. Cûm ergò hac publica consuetudine Ecclesia testetur se certò credere resurrectionem mortuorum, manifestum est Pseudoapostolos, qui negant resurrectionem mortuorum, Spiritui sancto in os contradicere. De Phrasi ὑπέρ τῶν νεκρῶν, pro mortuis, non solum recentes, sed & veteres varia disputarunt. Qui exposuerunt pro mortuis, id est, vice & loco mortuorum: Prorsus hallucinati sunt. Huiusmodi enim viciosam consuetudinem Paulus non transiisset sine reprehensione. Pugnat enim cum articulo de iustificatione. Iustus (inquit Propheta) fide sua vivet. Alii exposuerunt pro mortuis, hoc est, moribundi, brevi morituri, qui tanquam mortui habebantur, & tamen Baptismum expetebant, ut eius fructum non in hac, sed etiam in altera sentirent vita. Verúm haec expositio coactior videtur. Omnium igitur simplicissima est. Baptizantur edita confessione promortuis: testificantes, quòd mortui certò resurrecturi essent.

Quid & nos periclitamur omni hora: Aliud argumentum à testimonio & authoritate Apostolorum & omnium martyrum. Si nullae esset mortuorum resurrectio, tum Apostoli & martyres omnium hominum essent stolidissimi: siquidem sine causa singulis horis exponunt se periculo mortis confessione veritatis, cuius constantiae & voluntatis nullum sint post hanc vitam percepturi fructum, nisi quòd tantò celerius hanc vitam abrumpunt. Extrema autem dementia esset Apostolos & martyres, in quibus tanta sapientia & lux Spiritus sancti fulget, stutitiae vel stoliditatis condemnare.

Ergò revera est resurrectio mortuorum, quam intuentes Apostoli & martyres nulla non sustinent supplicia et cruciatus: & constanti voluntate contemnunt omnium tyrannorum minas, & universa huius vitae bona: certa enim siducia statuunt, se cum gloriosis corporibus resurrecturos ex morte, & copiosa mercede laborum fruituros. Quòd iureiurando testatur, se quotidie mori: significat, se continuis exerceri calamitatibus, periculis, terroribus propter ministerium Evangelii. Foris inquit pugnae intus pavores. Non solùm enim tyranni, & haeretici, & falsi fratres adfligebant Paulum: sed etiam mali Spiritus vexabant eum terreribus, & Angelus Satanae caedebat eum colaphis. Quotidie igitur de morte imminente admonitus fuit, atque id mori est potius, quàm vivere: Hos verò cruciatus adsiduos patienter sustinet spe resurrectionis mortuorum, quae ipsum ab omnibus aerumnis & terroribus liberabit. Ex Pauli ergò testimonio, quod lucet ex patientia ipsius in tantis aerumnis & terroribus, quos experitur propter doctrinam Evangelii, colligere & statuere poterant, omninò resurrecturos esse mortuos, & hac speomnes martyres omnis generis supplicia constanter subire.

Si secundum hominem pugnavi ad bestias, quid mihi prodest? Idem argumentum à testimonio Pauli, quòd ostendit in pugna ad bestias Ephesi. Maluit Paulus ad bestias pugnare cum gravissimo periculo vitae, quàm omittere veritatis confessionem: Hac ergò constantia demonstravit Paulus se credere resurrectionem mortuorum, cuius laeta spe hanc vitam & eius commoda, post posuit confessioni veritatis. Gloriationem suam intelligit, fiduciam, laeticiam & spem, quam habet in domino Iesu: ac perinde est, ac si per universam suam salutem iurasset Gravis igitur est haec attestatio.

Edamus, bibamus, cras enim moriemur. Mimesi recitat prophanas & impias voces Sadduceorum & Epicureorum: Hoc enim concesso, ut Pseudoapostoli volebant, quòd nulla sit resurrectio mortuorum, necesse est homines ruere in prophanam securitatem, & omnem exuere timorem Dei: Ita ut tantum serviant ventri, & quaerant huius vitae voluptates. Atque itae Christus, Prophetae, Patres, Apostoli, Martyres, & omnes sancti extremae stulritiae condemnabuntur, quòd sponte se exposuerunt variis vitae periculis, & horrendis suppliciis, cuius voluntatis & constantiae nullum fructum speraverint. Redarguit igitur Paulus tam prophanas & impias voces, & ne per iocum quidem vult usurpari eas à piis. Impurus enim & impius sermo etiam mores corrumpere solet: Quod adeò manifestum est, ut Poëta Ethnicus Menander experientia id didicerit, & versu expresserit.

## 15:34
Awake to righteousness, and do not sin; for some have the ignorance of GOD: I say this to bring shame upon you.

He intersperses a sharp rebuke, so that he may shake off the torpor from the sleepy and secure Corinthians, and rouse them to a diligent inquiry of the truth, and its constant defense. And that he may impel them to true fear, serious repentance, and the exercises of sincere piety. It is easily gathered that there was a great and detestable security among the Corinthians, since they lent such easy ears to a profane and impious error, which with one stroke deletes the entire religion. Therefore he rouses them as if from the sleep of security: And he exhorts them, that they should beware for themselves, lest they fall into sins. For the gifts of the Holy Spirit gradually decrease and are extinguished, unless they are roused by assiduous repentance, study, meditation, prayer, and the struggle against the assaults and snares of Satan. The Christian soldier always either progresses or regresses. But if he gives himself to leisure and security, he is exposed to the various snares of Satan, who is intent on this, that he may either seduce Christians into error, or precipitate them into sins, and thus overwhelm and extinguish the faith in them.

To some he objects ignorance of God: The Corinthians were wonderfully pleased with themselves on account of their wisdom and erudition, but Paul argues against them, because they did not yet know God, as they ought: For he who allows himself to be persuaded that the dead do not rise again, he in truth neither knows God, nor believes the Gospel, nor is he worthy of the Christian name. Therefore the Corinthians are deservedly suffused with shame, because when they arrogated to themselves a great knowledge of religion, they were overturning the chief weight of the Christian name, and the sole goal of our entire hope.

Latin:

Evigilate iustè, & ne peccetis Ignorantiam enim DEI quidam habent: Hoc ad pudorem vobis(incutiendum) dico.

Acrem reprehensionem interspergit, ut somnolentis & securis Corinthiis torporem excutiat, & excitet eos ad diligentem veritatis inquisitionem, eiusque constantem defensionem. Utque impellat eos ad verum timorem, seriam poenitentiam, et syncerae pietatis exercitia. Facilè colligitur magnam & detestandam securitatem fuisse apud Corinthios, cùm tam faciles aures praebuerunt errori prophano & impio, qui una litura universam delet religionem. Itaque excitat eos tanquam è somno securitatis: Et hortatur, ut caveant sibi, ne in peccata prolabantur. Paulatim enim decrescunt, & extinguuntur dona Spiritus sancti, nisi excitentur adsidua poenitentia, studio, meditatione, precatione, & luctà contra insultus & insidias Satanae. Semper aut proficit aut deficit miles Christianus. Quòd si dederit se ocio & securitati, variis insidiis Satanae est expositus, qui in hoc est intentus, ut vel in errorem seducat, vel in peccata praecipitet Christianos, atque ita fidem in ipsis obruat & extinguat.

Quibusdam obiicit ignorationem Dei: Mirè sibi placebant Corinthii ob sapientiam & eruditionem, sed Paulus arguit eos, quòd nondum noverunt Deum, sicuti debebant: Qui enim patitur sibi persuaderi mortuos non resurgere, is reverae nec Deum novit, nec credit Evangelio, neque dignus est nomine Christiano. Pudore itaque meritò suffunduntur Corinthii, quòd cùm magnam sibi religionis scientiam arrogarent, praecipuum pondus Christiani nominis, & unicum scopum universae spei nostrae evertebant.

## 15:35-38
But someone will say: How are the dead raised? With what body will they come? You fool, what you sow is not made alive, unless it has died. And what you sow, you do not sow the body that will be born: But a bare grain, for example, of wheat or of any other kind. But GOD gives it a body, just as He wills, and to each of the seeds its own body.

This is the sixth member of this chapter, in which he describes the manner of the future resurrection. And he refutes the blasphemies of those who agitated against the doctrine of the resurrection of the dead as absurd fables and a thing altogether impossible. Just as the Sadducees also gathered many absurdities from the resurrection of the dead. A certain woman, they say, married seven brothers in order: whose wife therefore will she be in the resurrection of the dead? The Epicureans objected similar things: We see bodies reduced to dust and dissipated: how therefore can it be that bodies rise again? And what is the future form and condition of bodies in the other life? Will they need food and drink, rest and sleep? Will they perform labors? Will they be subject to diseases and pains? Reason pleases itself wonderfully in inventing cavils of this kind. But Paul, with an Apostolic Spirit, condemns such impious arguments and cavils of human reason against the express Word of God as extreme foolishness: and he shows that God places before our eyes every year in nature an image of the resurrection: And thus, by the very food by which we are nourished, the madness of those who cavil that it is impossible for bodies resolved into dust to rise again is refuted. We scatter seeds into the earth, and we see them rot and die in the earth: yet we do not doubt that we, after some months, will receive them back with greater fruit and abundance: Why therefore do you doubt that bodies, which have once rotted and been dissipated, can rise again? He who vivifies dead seeds, and produces from them a great quantity of grain: The same is able also to vivify the dead bodies of men, and to produce them from the earth. It is indeed a miraculous thing, the very generation of grains: For if anyone keeps it, it remains alone without fruit: If anyone casts it into the earth, and allows it to die there, it produces fruit, it bears a stalk, an ear, many grains: Thus the bodies of the saints will rise from the earth with great interest and glory.

And this which you sow, is not this body, which is born: But you cast a naked grain into the earth: Then indeed God for His admirable Wisdom produces first the herb, then the stalk, then the ear, then many grains in the ear, fortified on all sides with spikes: And to individual species of grain God gives their own bodies. Such will be also the resurrection of the dead: They will not rise with that foulness and weakness, with which they are committed to the earth. But God will produce from the earth bodies entirely new and glorious. Not that different bodies are to rise again: but these same, which we now carry, will rise again: I shall be surrounded again (says Job) with my skin, and in this my flesh I shall see God.

But the condition of the bodies will be far different than it is now. Now they are in need of food, drink, sleep, rest, excretion, clothes: they are subject to diseases and infirmities: And they have various impediments: But then the bodies will be glorious, living perpetually without food and drink, just as the Spirit: subject to no evils, full of splendor. Foolish, therefore, are the thoughts which human reason fashions to mock the doctrine concerning the resurrection of the dead.

Latin:

At dicet aliquis: Quomodo resurgent mortui? Quali corpore venient? Stulte tu, quod seminas, non vivificatur, nisi mortuum fuerit. Et quod seminas, non corpus, quod nascetur, seminas: Sed nudum granum, exempli causa, tritici aut alterius cuiusvis generis. DEUS autem dat illi corpus, quemadmodum vult, & unicuique seminum suum corpus.

Sextum est hoc membrum huius capitis, quo describit modum futurae resurrectionis. & refutat blasphemias eorum, qui doctrinam de resurrectione mortuorum, tanquam absurdas fabulas & rem prorsus impossibilem exagitabant. Quemadmodum & Sadducaei, multa absurda collige bant ex resurrectione mortuorum. Foemina quaedam, inquiunt, nupsit ordine septem fratribus: cuius ergò uxor erit in resurrectione mortuorum? Similia Epicurei obiiciebant: Videmus corpora redigi in pulverem & dissipari: quomodo igitur fieri potest, ut resurgant corpora? Et quaenam futura est corporum forma & ratio in altera vita? Indigebunt ne cibo & potu, quiete & somno? exercebunt ne labores? obnoxia ne erunt morbis & doloribus? Mirè placet sibi ratio in fingendis huiuscemodi cavillationibus. At Paulus Apostolico Spiritu extremae stultitiae condemnat eiusmodi impias humanae rationis argumentationes & cavillationes contra expressum Dei Verbum: & ostendit Deum nobis quotannis ob oculos ponere in natura imaginem resurrectionis: Atque adeò cibo ipso, quo nutrimur refutari illorum dementiam, qui cavillantur, fieri non posse ut corpora in pulverem resoluta, resurgant. Semina spargimus in terram, & videmus computrescere, et mori in terra: nec tamen dubitamus nos post aliquot menses, cum maiore fructuet copia recepturos: Cur ergo dubitatis corpora, quae semel computruerunt & dissipata sunt, posse resurgere? Qui mortua semina vivificat, & producit ex eis magnam vim frumenti: Idem potest & mortua corpora hominum vivisicare, & ex terra producere. Est sanè miraculosa res, ipsa frumentorum generatio: Si quis enim adseruet, solum manet absque fructu: Si quis abiiciat in terram, & sinat ibi emori, fructum producit, fert culmum, aristam, multa grana: Ita corpora sanctorum resurgent ex terra cum magno faenore & gloria.

Et hoc quod seminas, non est hoc corpus, quod nascitur: Sed nudum granum proiicis in terram: Inde vero Deus pro sua admiranda Sapientia producit primùm herbam, deinde culmum, deinde aristam, deinde grana multa in arista, munitae undique spicis: Et singulis frument: speciebus dat Deus sua corpora. Talis erit & resurrectio mortuorum: Non resurgent corpora ea foeditate & imbecillitate, qua mandantur terrae Sed nova prorsus & gloriosa corpora producet DEUS ex terra. Non quòd diversa corpora sintr esurrectura: sed haec eadem, quae nunc gestamus, resurgent: Circum dabor rursus (inquit lob) pelle mea, & in hac carne mea videbo Deum.

At longè alia ratio corporum futura est, quàm nunc sit. Nunc indigent cibo, potu, somno, quiete, egestione, vestibus: sunt obnoxia morbis & aegritudinibus: Et varia habent impedimenta: At tum corpora erunt gloriosa, sine cibo & potu perpetuò viventia, sicuti Spiritus: nullis malis obnoxia, plena splendore. Fatuae igitur sunt cogitationes, quas ratio humana fingit ad irridendam doctrinam de resurrectione mortuorum.

## 15:39
Not all flesh is the same flesh: But there is one flesh of men, another indeed the flesh of beasts, another of birds, another of fishes.

This is the second similitude, by which he teaches that there is nothing absurd in the fact that we believe more excellent bodies will rise again than those we now carry about. Since indeed we see now in this life, that not all flesh is of one kind or quality. Since indeed God forms one flesh for man, another for the beast, another for the bird, another for the fish, indeed one flesh for the wolf, another for the salmon, another for the smallpox, another for other species. Why could God not be able to give another and more excellent flesh to man in the resurrection of the dead, than we now have. Thus he compares the present state of bodies with the future, and demonstrates that it is not difficult for God to raise up more glorious bodies than those we now bear.

Latin:

Non omnis caro eadem caro: Sed alia caro hominum, alia verò caro pecudum, alia volucrum, alia piscium.

Secunda haec est similitudo, qua docet nihil esse absurdi, quòd credimus praestantiora corpora resurrectura, quàm nunc circumgestamus. Siquidem nunc videmus in hac vita, non omnem carnem unius esse generis aut qualitatis. Siquidem aliam carnem format Deus homini, aliam pecudi, aliam volucri, aliam pisci imò aliam carnem lupo, aliam salmoni, aliam variolo, aliam aliis speciebus. Cur non posset Deus aliam & praestantiorem carnem dare homini in resurrectione mortuorum, quàm nunc habeamus. Ita praestentem statum corporum, confert cum futuro, & demonstrat Deo non esse difficile magis gloriosa corpora resuscitare quàm nunc geramus.

## 15:40-41
There are also celestial bodies: There are also terrestrial: And the glory of the celestial is one, and the glory of the terrestrial is another: There is one glory of the sun: Another glory of the moon: Another glory of the stars: And star differs from star in glory.

The third similitude, by which he proves that it is not difficult for God to resurrect our bodies adorned with other qualities, and more glorious than they now are. The matter of the celestial bodies is the same: And yet God has adorned those celestial lights with great distinction. And the light of the sun is greater and more splendid than that of the moon or of other planets: Lucifer is much more splendid than one of the fixed stars. If, therefore, we see before our eyes one star adorned by God with greater splendor, another with lesser, when all are of the same matter and substance: why do we doubt that God cannot perform this in our bodies? That He may adorn them with more light, strength, glory, and life than in this life? Thus he also makes mention of terrestrial things: The substance of gold is one, that of silver another, that of copper another, that of tin another, that of lead another: The wood of the oak is one thing, that of the beech another, that of the alder another, that of the fir another, that of the linden another: Which God, who produces such various species of metals and trees, with such great distinction of qualities from the earth: He will also be able to adorn our bodies resurrected from death with more excellent qualities than those with which they are now endowed.

Although Paul brings forward these comparisons in such a way that he may teach by them that the condition and glory of our bodies in the resurrection of the dead will be different than it is now: Nevertheless, it is also rightly gathered from this that there will be degrees of the saints in the other life: And that in some there will be a greater splendor of glory, in others a lesser: Yet so that each one will be content with his own measure, without any envy and emulation. Thus Daniel says that those who instruct many unto righteousness will shine like the stars in the heaven.

Latin:

Sunt & corpora coelestia: Sunt & terrestria: Et alia est gloria coelestium, alia terrestrium: Alia gloria solis: Alia gloria Lunae: Alia gloria stellarum: Et stella à stella differt in gloria.

Tertia similitudo, qua probat Deo non esse difficile resuscitare corpora nostra aliis ornata qualitatibus, & magis gloriosa, quàm nunc sint. Eadem est materia corporum coelestium: Et tamen Deus magno discrimine coelestia illa lumina exornavit. Et maius & splendidius lumen est solis, quam Lunae vel aliarum Planetarum: Multò splendidior est Lucifer, quàm una ex stellis fixis. Si ergò coràm videmus aliam stellam maiore, aliam minore splendore à Deo exornari, cùm omnes sint eiusdem materiae & substantiae: cur dubitamus Deum id praestare non posse in nostris corporibus? Ut ea magis ornet luce, robore, gloria, vita, quàm in hac vita? Sic & terrestrium meminit: Alia est substantia auri, alia argenti, alia cupri, alia stanni, alia plumbi: Aliud lignum quercus, aliud fagi, aliud alni, aliud abietis, aliud tiliae: Qui Deus tam varias species metallorum & arborum, tanto discrimine qualitatum producit à terra: Is etiam corpora nostra ex morte resuscitata exornare poterit praestantioribus qualitatibus, quàm nunc sunt praeditae.

Etsi autem Paulus ita adducit has similitudines, ut iis doceat, aliam fore conditionem & gloriam nostrorum corporum in resurrectione mortuorum, quàm nunc sit: Tamen rectè etiam hinc colligitur gradus fore sanctorum in altera vita: Et in aliis maiorem fore gloriae splendorem, in aliis minorem: Ita tamen ut quisque sua mensura futurus sit contentus, absque omni invidia & emulatione. Sic Daniel dicit eos, qui erudiunt multos ad iustitiam, fulsuros, tanquam stellas in coelo.

## 15:42-45
So also the resurrection of the dead: It is sown in corruption, it rises in incorruption: It is sown in dishonor, it rises in glory: It is sown in weakness, it rises in power. It is sown a natural body, it rises a spiritual body: There is a natural body: And there is a spiritual body: As it is written: And the first man Adam was made into a living soul: The last Adam into a life-giving Spirit: But not first that which is spiritual: But that which is natural: Afterwards, that which is spiritual. The first man is from the earth, earthly: The second man is the Lord from heaven. As is the earthly, such also are the earthly: And as is the heavenly, such also are the heavenly. And as we have borne the image of the earthly: We shall also bear the image of the heavenly.

He adapts the comparisons to the doctrine concerning the resurrection of the dead: And he demonstrates that our bodies will be far more excellent and more splendid in the resurrection of the dead than they are in this life. That our bodies are committed to the earth, he compares to seed. For the heavenly Father is the husbandman: And we are his husbandry and wheat. Our bodies are sown in corruption: That is, they are subject to corruption: As long as we dwell in this life: Until we are plunged into death. But in the resurrection, the bodies will be subject to no corruption, nor to any change: But they will be immortal. It is sown in dishonor: It rises in glory. The dishonor of bodies is that they are polluted with many sins: And they lack the purity with which they were adorned in the first creation, and because of sin they are subject to the wrath of God and to death: And they must be returned to the dust. When someone is led to punishment because of a crime, he sustains a grave ignominy. Thus our bodies sustain a grave ignominy: Because on account of sin they are plunged into death. But they will rise again in glory: They will be adorned with their pristine purity, no filth of sins will be seen in them: They will shine with brightness and integrity: They will be clothed with beauty and glory. It is sown in weakness: For our bodies in this life are subject to various diseases and accidents: We are in need of food and drink, evacuation, clothing, shelters. And we protect ourselves with difficulty against cold, storms, heat, wild beasts: We are frequently exposed to a thousand dangers, even a grape seed or a fly or a crumb of bread can kill a man. Therefore there is a huge weakness of bodies in this life: And they must eventually rot. But they will rise again in power, then he says they will be endowed with complete strength: They will not be fatigued by labor, they will not be vexed by diseases, they will not be exposed to dangers, they will not feel impediments.

It is sown an animal body, and it rises a spiritual one. He calls it an animal body, which is endowed with animal life, and has the actions of all Of the powers of the soul: The soul in this life provides life to the body, stirs up all actions, and gives vegetation, lest it be a corpse. Therefore, it is called animal from the soul, by which it is vegetated. And indeed, this animal life is in need of food, drink, sleep, and clothing. But the spiritual body is that which is vivified by the Spirit, and lives spiritually. Paul does not mean by this that the substance of the body is to be changed into the substance of the Spirit: for this would be to deny the resurrection of bodies. Therefore, the same substance of the bodies remains: but the qualities and conditions are changed. The body, which previously was vivified by the soul and was in need of food, drink, and sleep: when it rises, it will be vivified by the Spirit, which needs neither food nor drink, and it will live in a spiritual manner, just as the angels of God. It will assume spiritual conditions and qualities. Not only does the same individual remain, but also the same species: but the qualities and conditions are changed: for that which was mortal will become immortal, with the Spirit vivifying the body in all eternity. Then the rising man will put off every sin and every infirmity: He will retain nothing from the oldness of Adam: But in body and soul he will be entirely spirit and a new man, in whom the Holy Spirit, and the whole trinity, will shine. This, therefore, is to have a spiritual body, also to live spiritually in the body, to enjoy spiritual life and glory.

As it is written. The first man Adam was made into a living soul. He proves the designation of an animal body by the testimony of Holy Scripture, Gen: 2. And God breathed into his face the breath of life, and man was made into a living soul. Moses embraces both here, both that God implanted and breathed a rational soul into man, and that by the conjunction of the soul with the body He gave him an animal life, which stands in need of food, drink, sleep, and clothing. And Paul teaches that, even if Adam had not sinned, but had persisted in that integrity and justice in which he was created, he would nevertheless have lived an animal life, which stands in need of nourishment, until God had translated him to a heavenly and spiritual life. There is no doubt that Adam, created in the image of God, was a host of the Holy Spirit, for he was created in true justice and holiness. Justice and holiness, however, do not exist without the Holy Spirit. And therefore Adam had the motions of the Holy Spirit: but he did not live a purely spiritual, or heavenly, life, but an animal one, which stood in need of food and drink. Therefore, by the testimony of Scripture, Paul teaches that the first man was created for an animal life, from which the animal life of all men exists.

The last Adam into a life-giving Spirit.

He compares here again Adam and Christ, as the authors of both the present and the future life: And he shows what kind of difference there is between this present and the future life. The animal life, which needs food and drink, began in Adam, and is propagated into all descendants. For even after man fell, God granted him animal life at least for a time, so that the human race might be propagated, and man might be converted by the ministry of the word. But Christ, the other and last Adam, as the new root of the elect Church, has been made for us into a life-giving Spirit, that is, he is for us the author of spiritual and heavenly life, which needs no food or drink: And it will endure for all eternity. Christ himself, having been raised from the dead, began this spiritual life, and made a way for us to that life. He himself will raise us from the dead, and will make our humble body conformable to his glorious body, he will pour his holy Spirit into us, he will fill us with light, life, joy, and righteousness, and in all eternity he will most closely unite us with God. Christ therefore is for us a life-giving Spirit, that is, the author of a new and spiritual life through the holy Spirit, whom he received from the Father and imparts to us. Paul warns here that no man becomes a participant of spiritual life, except through our Lord Jesus Christ, who is the last Adam.

But the spiritual was not first: He warns that God observed this order, that He placed the animal life first: But let the spiritual life follow. Therefore, the glory of the future life is to be expected according to the order established by God.

Latin:

Sic & resurrectio mortuorum: Seminatur in corruptione, resurgit in incorruptione: Seminatur in ignominia, resurgit in gloria: Seminatur in infirmitate, resurgit in potentia. Seminatur corpus animale, resurgit corpus spirituale: Est corpus animale: Et est corpus spirituale: Quemadmodum scriptum est: Et factus est primus homo Adam in animam viventem: Postremus Adam in Spiritum vivificantem: Sed non primùm quòd spirituale est: Sed quòd animale: Deinde, quòd spirituale est. Primus homo ex terra, terrenus: Secundus homo Dominus è coelo. Qualis terrenus, tales & terreni: Et qualis coelestis, tales & coelestes. Et quemadmodum portavimus imaginem terreni: Portabimus & imaginem coelestis.

Accommodat similitudines ad doctrinam de resurrectione mortuorum: Et demonstrat longè praestantiora & splendidiora corpora nostra fore in resurrectione mortuorum, quàm sint in hac vita. Quòd corpora nostra mandantur terrae, sementi confert. Agricola est enim Pater coelestis: Et nos sumus ipsius agricultura & triticum. Corpora nostra seminantur in corruptione: Hoc est, obnoxia sunt corruptioni: Quàm diu in hac vita versamur: Donec in mortem mergamur. At in resurrectione corpora nulli corruptioni, nec mutationi erunt obnoxia: Sed immortalia erunt. Seminatur in ignominia: Resurgit in gloria. Ignominia corporum est, quòd sunt polluta multis peccatis: Et carent puritate, qua ornata, fuerunt in prima creations, quòdque propter peccatum obnoxia sunt irae Dei & morti: Et necesse habent recondi in pulverem. Cùm quis ad supplicium ducitur propter scelus, ignomiam gravem sustinet. Sic corpora nostra ignominiam sustinent gravem: Quia propter peccatum merguntur in mortem. At resurgent in gloria: Ornabuntur pristina puritate, nullae peccatorum sordes in eis conspicientur: Fulgebunt claritate & integritate: Induentur decore & gloria. Seminatur in infirmitate: Corpora enim nostra in hac vita obnoxia sunt variis morbis, & casibus: Indigemus cibo & potu, egestione, vestibus, tuguriis. Et difficulter nos munimus contra frigus, tempestates, aestum, feras: Subinde expositi sumus mille periculis, vel acinus uvae vel musca, vel mica panis hominem interficere potest. Ingens ergò infirmitas corporum est in hac vita: Et ea tandem putrescere necesse est. At resurgent in potentia, tum inquit praedita erunt integro robore: Non fatigabuntur labore, non vexabuntur morbis, non exponentur periculis, non sentient impedimenta.

Seminatur corpus animale, & resurgit sprituale. Animale corpus vocat, quod animali vita est praeditum, & actiones habet omnium potentiarum animae: Anima in hac vita, corpori praebet vitam, ciet omnes actiones, & vegetat, ne sit cadaver. Ab anima igitur, à qua vegetatur animale dicitur. Et quidem cibo, potu, somno, vestitu, indiget haec animalis vita. At spirituale corpus est, quod à Spiritu vivificatur, & spiritualiter vivit. Non hoc vult Paulus substantiam corporis mutatum iri in substantiam Spiritus: Hoc enim esset negare corporum resurrectionem. Manet ergò eadem corporum substantia: qualitates verò & conditiones mutantur. Corpus, quod antea ab anima vivificabatur & cibo, potu, somno indigebat: Cùm resurget vivificabitur à Spiritu, qui nec cibo nec potu eget, & vivet spirituali modo, sicuti angeli Dei. Adsumet conditiones et qualitates spirituales. Non solum idem individuum manet, sed etiam eadem species: Qualitates verò & conditiones mutantur: nam quod fuit mortale, fiet immortale, Spiritu vivificante corpus in omni aeternitate. Exuet tum homo resurgens omne peccatum & omnem infirmitatem: Nihil retinebit ex vetustate Adae: Sed corpore & anima totus erit spiritus & novus homo, in quo lucebit Spiritus sanctus, & tota trinitas. Hoc est ergò habere corpus spirituale, etiam corpore spiritualiter vivere, spirituali vita & gloria frui.

Quemadmodum scriptum est. Primul homo Adam factus est in animam viventem. Appellationem animalis corporis probat testimonio sacrae scripturae, Gen: 2. Et inspiravit Deus in faciem eius spiraculum vitae, & factus est homo in animam viventem. Utrumque complectitur hîc Moises, & quòd animam rationalem indiderit atque inspiraverit Deus homini, & quòd coniunctione animae cum corpore dederit ei vitam animalem, quae cibo, potu, somno, vestibus indiget. Ac docet Paulus, etiamsi Adam non peccasset, sed in illae integritate & iustitia perstitisset in qua fuit conditus, tamen vixisset vitam animalem, quae alimentis indiget, donec eum Deus ad vitam coelestem & spiritualem transtulisset. Non est dubium, quin Adam conditus ad imaginem Dei fuerit hospitium Spiritus sancti, fuit enim conditus in iustitia & sanctitate vera. Iustitia autem & sanctitas non existunt absque Spiritu sancto. Atque ideò Adam habuit motus Spiritus sancti: Sed non vixit vitam planè spiritualem, seu coelestem, sed animalem, quae cibo & potu indigebat. Scripturae ergò testimonio docet Paulus, quòd primus homo ad vitam animalem fuerit conditus, unde vita animalis omnium hominum existit.

Postremus Adam in Spiritum vivificantem.

Confert hîc rursus Adamum & Christum, ut authores utriusque vitae praesentis & futurae: Et ostendit quale sit discrimen inter hanc praesentem & futuram vitam. Animalis vita, quae cibo & potu eget, caepit in Adam, & propagatur in omnes posteros. Nam etiam post quam lapsus est homo, Deus concessit illi vitam animalem saltem ad tempus, ut genus humanum propagari, & homo ministerio verbi converti posset. At Christus alter & postremus Adam, tanquam nova radix Ecclesiae electae, factus est nobis in Spiritum vivificantem, hoc est, ille nobis author est vitae Spiritualis & coelestis, quae nullo eget cibo velpotu: Et durabit in omnem aeternitatem. Ipse Christus resuscitatus à mortuis, exorsus est hanc vitam spiritualem, & ad eam vitam nobis viam fecit. Ipse resuscitabit nos ex mortuis, & humile nostrum corpus faciet conforme glorioso suo corpori, ille Spiritum suum sanctum in nos effundet, replebit nos luce, vita, laeticia, & iustitia, & in omni aeternitate arctissimè nos copulabit cum Deo. Christus ergò nobis est Spiritus vivificans, hoc est, author novae & spiritualis vitae per Spiritum sanctum, quem ille accepit à patre & nobis impertit. Monet hîc Paulus nullum hominem fieri participem vitae spiritualis, nisi per dominum nostrum Iesum Christum, qui est postremus Adam.

Sed non fuit primùm, spirituale: Monet Deum hunc ordinem servasse, ut praemiserit vitam animalem: Subsequatur verò vita spiritualis. Expectanda est igitur futurae vitae gloria iuxta ordinem à Deo constitutum.

## 15:47
The first man is of the earth, earthly: The second man is the Lord from heaven: In order to show the notable difference between the future and the present life, he again compares with one another the roots, in a certain way, both of the human race and of the Church, Adam and Christ. From Adam, animal life is propagated: from Christ, spiritual life is given to us: how much they differ from one another, it is permitted to see in their persons: Adam was made from the slime of the earth, and was earthly, a creature of God. But the second man Christ is the Lord from heaven: This is, he is not only true man clothed in our flesh, which he assumed from the Virgin Mary: but at the same time he is himself the Lord Iehova, the eternal and omnipotent God, who descended from heaven and was made man. Therefore, the author of the future life, the second Adam, is infinitely more excellent and more powerful than the first Adam, in whom animal life began. It is not, therefore, a wonder if a more excellent life proceeds from Christ God than from Adam. Let the reader observe here a notable testimony concerning both natures of Jesus Christ. He names the second man Jesus Christ: For He truly took on human flesh from the virgin Mary: then he affirms this Jesus to be the Lord from heaven. Therefore he testifies that Christ is Jehovah the eternal and omnipotent God, who descended from heaven for our salvation: Yet there are not two Christs: But one and the same man is the Lord from heaven. The Valentinians and Anabaptists do violence to this passage, who attempt to build from this that the flesh of Christ was brought from heaven, and was not of the same kind as ours. For Paul does not say this: but he means this, that Christ is not only a man, as Adam was a mere man: But that He is at the same time the Lord Jehovah the eternal God from heaven. The divinity of Christ is from heaven: since indeed the Son was born from the essence of the Father from eternity. His humanity is from the womb of the virgin Mary. But because the two natures are united by a personal union, Paul rightly said the second man is the Lord from heaven, just as it is also rightly said that the man Christ is from eternity: Although the humanity of Christ is not from eternity: But through the communication of idioms, that which is proper to one nature is attributed to the whole person in the concrete on account of the hypostatic union. For that person, who is man, is the Lord from heaven: And that person is from eternity, namely, according to the divine nature.

Latin:

Primus homo de terra terrenus: Sccundus homo Dominus ex coelo: Ut diffirentiam insignem ostendat inter futuram & praesentem vitam, rursus inter se confert primas quodammodo radices, cùm generis humani tum Ecclesiae, Adamum & Christum. Ab Adamo propagatur vita animalis: à Christo donatur nobis vita spiritualis: quantum inter se differant, in personis licet videre: Adam de limo terrae est factus, & tenerenus fuit, creatura Dei. At secundus homo Christus est dominus è coelo: Hoc est, non est tantum verus homo carne nostra, quam ex Maria virgine adsumpsit, indutus: sed simul est ipse Dominus Iehova, Deus aeternus & omnipotens, qui de coelo descendit & homo factus est. In infinitum igitur praestantior & potentior est futurae vitae author secundus Adam, quàm primus Adam, in quo caepit vita animalis. Non igitur mirum, si à Christo Deo vita praestantior proficiscitur, quàm ab Adam. Observet hîc lector insigne testimonium de utraque natura Iesu Christi. Hominem secundum nominat Iesum Christum: Veram enim carnem humanam ex virgine Maria suscepit: deinde adfirmat hunc Iesum esse Dominum ex coelo. Testatur ergò Christum esse Iehova Deum aeternum & omnipotentem, qui de coelo descendit propter nostram salutem: Non tamen sunt duo Christi: Sed unus, & idem homo est dominus ex coelo. Vim faciunt huic loco, Valentiniani & Anabaptistae, qui hinc extruere conantur, carnem Christi de coelo fuisse allatam, & non fuisse eiusdem generis cum nostra. Non enim hoc dicit Paulus: sed hoc vult, Christum non esse tantum hominem, ut Adam purus fuit homo: Sed simul esse dominum Iehova Deum aeternum ex coelo. Divinitas Christi ex coelo est: siquidem filius de essentia patris ab aeterno natus est. Humanitas eius est ex utero Mariae virginis. Quia verò duae naturae personali unione unitae sunt, rectè Paulus dixit hominem secundum esse Dominum ex coelo, ut rectè etiam dicitur, hominem Christum esse ab aeterno: Licet humanitas Christi non sit ab aeterno: Sed per communicationem idiomatum, id quod uni naturae est proprium, tribuitur toti personae in concreto propter unionem hypostaticam. Illa enim persona, quae est homo, est Dominus ex coelo: Et illa persona est ab aeterno, scilicet, secundum divinam naturam.

## 15:48
As is the earthly, such are they also that are earthly: As is the heavenly, such are they also that are heavenly: Paul shows the diversity of animal and spiritual life, to be seen especially in the authors, in Adam and in Christ. From Adam we have animal life, which needs food and drink: Through Christ we are to have spiritual life, which will need neither food nor drink, and yet is to endure for all eternity.

Before he spoke of the animal life of Adam, which was kindled in him before the fall, so that he might show the source of animal life: but now he descends to Adam corrupted by the fall: For undoubtedly when he names the earthly Adam, he looks to the testimony: Earth thou art and unto earth shalt thou return; because thou wast taken from the earth: which saying testifies that our bodies are subject to corruption. Therefore, such as the earthly Adam was: such also are we earthly, namely, subject to corruption. But such as the heavenly Jesus Christ is, raised from the dead, and now living a spiritual and heavenly life: such also will the heavenly be, that is, the faithful, who believe in Christ: for these shall be raised from death, and with Christ shall live a spiritual life in all eternity. As we have borne the image of the earthly, let us also bear the image of the heavenly: Here he shows still more clearly that concerning the corrupted Adam he speaks: nor is there any doubt that he took these words from the fifth chapter of Genesis: where Adam is said to have begotten Seth in his own image. For Adam did not propagate the image of God into his descendants, to which he was created: but he had horribly deformed it by sin, and had lost its most important part, namely, righteousness and spiritual life. Therefore, to bear the image of the earthly is to consist indeed of body and soul, to live an animal life, to be endowed with human reason: but at the same time to be destitute of the glory of God and the integrity of nature, to be polluted by sin, subject to death and corruption: Therefore we have all borne the image of the earthly: that is, both in animal life, and in that we are subject to corruption, in this we represent our parent Adam. And indeed, the Holy Scripture signifies the saddest thing of all, when it names the image of the earthly man. For it teaches that the image of God, to which man was first created, does not shine in us by nature as it shone in Adam before the fall. But that we are clearly infected, deformed, and corrupted by sin, we now lack by nature the knowledge of God, true righteousness, freedom of will, and spiritual life: by nature we are children of wrath and enemies of God: and we are in need of renewal and regeneration through the Holy Spirit. The ancients, both Ambrose and , wished to say the same thing. The moderns, when they called man, corrupted by sin and turned away from God, an image or rather a mask of Satan: for by lie and by sin in reality, the corrupted man represents the unclean Spirit, the father of lies and the first author of sin. But this image or mask of Satan in man is not substantial, as Illyricus raves with the Manichaeans: but it is accidental, for the corrupted man has the substance of body and soul from God, not from Satan. It is blasphemy against God that Illyricus asserts that the impious are essentially generated by Satan. It is blasphemy that he says that corrupted man is the work and creature of Satan. It is blasphemy that he says that Satan has transformed man essentially into his own image. These portents of errors were entirely unknown to the orthodox and to Luther. But Luther understood an accidental mask or image of Satan, namely that man represents the unclean and most foul Satan by foul qualities, depravity, lying, deformity, and impurity. And therefore Paul says that the earthly image must be put off: so that we may bear the heavenly: For Christ wipes away the poison of sin in our nature so that righteousness and life, kindled by the Holy Spirit, may shine in it. Whence also Luther says, for sin and death are separable evils: if anyone Therefore, let him use these phrases soberly and according to the analogy of faith, that a corrupt man bears the image or mask of Satan, and let him understand it concerning an accidental mask, that is, concerning corruption, impurity, falsehood, and the filth of sin; I do not disapprove of them, even if the phrases themselves do not exist in Holy Scripture. But I execrate and detest Illyricus's monstrous figment concerning the substantial image of Satan in man, for the reason that it savors of Manichaeism: and it either makes God the author of sin, or establishes Satan as the creator. The modesty of the Apostle Paul, who borrowed his sentences from the fountains of Israel, is worthy of praise and is salutary for the Church. Those who understand these words of Paul (let us bear the image of the heavenly) as an exhortation to the pursuit of a new and heavenly life do not indeed err: but yet they expound this passage in a forced manner. Paul's intention is that, as we have represented our archetype Adam by an animal life and by sins: so we ought to seek the resurrection of the dead, that we may represent the new archetype JESUS CHRIST, raised from the dead, in complete righteousness and spiritual life.

Latin:

Qualis est terrenus, tales sunt & terreni: Qualis est coelestis, tales sunt & coelestes: Ostendit Paulus diversitatem vitae animalis & spiritualis, potissimùm conspici in authoribus, in Adam & in Christo. Ab Adam vitam habemus animalem, quae cibo & potu eget: Per Christum habituri sumus vitam spiritualem, quae nec cibo, nec potu egebit, & tamen in omnem aeternitatem est duratura.

Antea dixit de vita animali Adae, quae in ipso ante lapsum accensa fuit, ut fontem animalis vitae monstraret: nunc verò descendit ad Adamum corruptum lapsu: Haud dubiè enim cùm nominat Adamum terrenum, testimonium intuetur: Terraes & in terram reverteris; quia de terra sumptus es: quod dictum testatur corpora nostra corruptioni esse obnoxia. Qualis ergò fuit Adam terrenus: tales & nos terreni sumus, nimirum, corruptioniobnoxii. Qualis verò coelestis est Iesus Christus resuscitatus à mortuis, & nunc spiritualem & coelestem vitam vivens: tales & coelestes erunt, hoc est, fideles, qui in Christum credunt: nam hi resuscitabuntur ex morte, & cum Christo spiritualem vitam vivent in omni aeternitate. Quemadmodum portavimus imaginem terreni, portemus & imaginem coelestis: Hîc dilucidius adhuc ostendit, quod de corrupto Adamo loquatur: nec dubium est, quin haec verba sumpserit ex quinto capite Genes: ubi Adam dicitur genuisse Seth ad imaginem suam. Adam enim non propagavit imaginem Dei in posteros, ad quam conditus fuit: sed eam horribiliter deformaverat peccato, et partem eius potissimam, nimirum, iustitiam & vitam spiritualem amiserat. Imaginem igitur terreni gestare, est corpore quidem et anima constare, vivere vitam animalem, praeditum esse ratione humana: at simul destitui gloria Dei & naturae integritate, esse pollutum peccato, obnoxium morti & corruptioni: Portavimus ergò omnes imaginem terreni: hoc est & vita animali, & quod corruptioniobnoxii sumus, in eo repraesentamus parentem nostrum Adamum. Ac sanè rem omnium tristissimam significat sacra scriptura, quum nominat imaginem terreni hominis. Docet enim imaginem Dei, ad quam primum fuit conditus homo, non ita lucere in nobis à natura, ut fulsit in Adam ante lapsum. Sed nos peccato planè infectos, deformatos & corruptos esse, caremus nunc natura noticia Dei, vera iustitia, libertate arbitrii, & vita spirituali: natura sumus filii irae & inimici Dei: & indigemus renovatione & regeneratione per Spiritum sanctum. Idem voluerunt dicere, cùm veteres ut Ambrosius, tum recentes, quum vocarunt hominem peccato corruptaem & à Deo aversum, imaginem vel potius larvam Satanae: mendacio enim & peccato re, praesentat corruptus homo immundum Spiritum, patrem mendacii & primùm authorem peccati. Haec verò imago vel larva Satanae in homine non est substantialis, ut Illyricus cum Manichaeis delirat: sed est accidentalis, substantiam enim corporis & animae etiam corruptus homo habet à Deo non à Satana. Blasphemia in Deum est, quod Illyricus adserit impios essentialiter à Satanageneratos esse. Blasphemia est quod dicit hominem corruptum esse opus & creaturam Satanae. Blasphemia est quod dicit Satanam transformasse hominem essentialiter in suam imaginem. Haec errorum portenta orthodoxis & Luthero prorsus ignota fuerunt. Accidentalem verò larvam seu imaginem Satanae intellexit Lutherus, nimirum hominem foedis qualitatibus, pravitate, mendacio, deformitate, impuritate repraesentare immundum & foedissimum Satanam. Atque ideò Paulus dicit deponendam esse imaginem terrem: ut portemus coelestem: Nam Christus exterget peccati venenum in nostra natura ut in ea luceat iustitia & vita accensa per Spiritum sanctum. Unde & Lutherus dicit, sunt enim peccatum & mors separabilia mala: si quis ergò sobriè & iuxta fidei analogiam usurpet has phrases, hominem corruptum gestare imaginem vel larvam Satanae & de accidentali larva hoc est de corruptione, impuritate, mendacio, & sordibus peccati intelligat, non improbo eas, etiamsi phrases ipsae non extent in sacra scriptura. At Illyrici portentosum figmentum, de substantiali imagine Satanae in homine, execror & detestor, eò quod Manicheismum sapit: & vel Deum facit authorem peccati, vel Satanam constituit conditorem. Verecundia Apostoli Pauli, qui ex fontibus Israel mutuatus est suas sententias laude digna, & Ecclesiae salutaris est. Qui haec verba Pauli (portemus imaginem coelestis) intelligunt tanquam exhortationem ad studium novae & coelestis vitae, non quidem errant: Sed tamen coacte hunc locum exponunt. Pauli mens est, ut vita animali & peccatis repraesentavimus archetypum nostrum Adamum: Ita expetere debemus resurrectionem mortuorum, ut integra iustitia & vita spirituali novum archetypum IESUM CHRISTUM ex morte resuscitatum repraesentemus.

## 15:50
Now this I say (brethren) that flesh and blood cannot inherit the kingdom of God they cannot possess: nor shall corruption possess incorruption.

By exegesis Paul declares why the image of the heavenly man must be sought by us, namely because this nature infected and corrupted by sin is not suitable for the heavenly and eternal kingdom, for there is no place for sin and death, or corruption, in the sight of God and in the spiritual and eternal kingdom. It is necessary, therefore, to put off the image of the earthly Adam: it is necessary that our flesh be purged, illuminated, and restored, it is necessary that sin and death be wiped away from our nature: and that righteousness and spiritual life be kindled in it, therefore Paul says. Flesh and blood cannot possess the kingdom of God by inheritance, namely without change. Unless the flesh has been cleansed from sin, and adorned with new qualities, it cannot enter into the kingdom of heaven. And therefore the Son of God renews our flesh and blood, body and soul, through the Holy Spirit so that it may be suitable for the kingdom of heaven.

The ancient Manichaeans and Marcionites wickedly and impudently abused this passage of Paul. For by this sentence of Paul they wished to establish that there would be no resurrection of our bodies. But what pious person would not detest such a profligate impudence of heretics. Since with this noble sermon Paul most gravely refutes the monstrous error which denies the resurrection of bodies, and demonstrates with most evident arguments that our bodies are also going to rise again: nevertheless the impudent Manichaeans dared to seek from this the colors of their fiction. Antiquity, however, gravely refuted them: Irenaeus and others teach that Paul did not deny salvation to the flesh, but demanded a change of qualities. Flesh and blood without change cannot possess the kingdom of God. But when flesh and blood have been raised from death and vivified by the Spirit, then certainly they will possess the kingdom of God by inheritance. For in my flesh I shall see God, says Job. And Christ Jesus will make our miserable body conformable to his glorious body.

Matthias Flacius Illyricus follows the Manichaeans rather than the orthodox Church while he depraves this passage, and contends that flesh signifies sin of origin itself, and corruption itself: and that the flesh itself must in some way be abolished, and transformed into a new species, namely into essential righteousness. These Manichaean portents are alien to the mind of Paul. Paul does not say that flesh and blood are sin of origin, but he says this, that flesh and blood are corrupted: inasmuch as they cannot possess the kingdom of God. But the meanings are most diverse, to be corrupt, and to be original sin itself. The soul of man is corrupt, but it is not original sin itself. Nor does Paul say that the essence of flesh and blood is to be abolished: but that its conditions and qualities are to be changed, namely mortality, and uncleanness, and depravity. Illyricus overturns the foundation of our salvation when he contends that the essence of flesh, which is original sin, must be abolished: Jesus Christ did not come to destroy human flesh: but to destroy sin and death in the flesh: and to save the flesh: Isaiah says, God has swallowed up death in victory, and has wiped away every tear from the face of all men. Christ did not swallow up the flesh, but the death which was raging in the flesh. In that Illyricus pretends that for Paul flesh and corruption signify the same thing, and that flesh is original sin itself, in that he affects the creator of human flesh with atrocious insult. For Satan alone is the author of original sin: God is not the author of any sin, neither original nor actual; but of flesh and blood, even when corrupt, the eternal and omnipotent God is the creator, preserver, and restorer. Therefore, although the flesh is corrupt, it is not original sin itself, but it is the subject in which the foulest stain of original sin adheres. Nor does the Apostle say this That flesh and corruption are one and the same: this is a fabrication of Illyricus. For flesh signifies the corrupted subject, and that in which corruption is: But corruption signifies the evil, which is in the subject: and Paul: by that exegesis: (corruption cannot inherit incorruption) wished to declare himself, that in the preceding sentence, he had not spoken of the abolition of the substance of the flesh, but of the change of qualities. As long as flesh is subject to corruption, it is not capable of the kingdom of God. But when the flesh shall have been freed from all corruption, then it will entirely possess the kingdom of God: For evident is the testimony Job: 19. I shall be surrounded again by my skin: and I shall behold God in my flesh. I myself shall see him, and my eyes and not another. It is a lie, therefore, that the new Manichaeans imagine original sin to be the flesh and blood itself: it is a lie, that they imagine original sin to be a corrupted nature: it is a lie that flesh and corruption are one and the same without any distinction: it is a lie that the substance of our flesh is to be in some way abolished and transformed into a new substantial form. That is truer, which Augustine says, that we are thus made fit for the heavenly gift to inhabit heaven, not with nature lost, but with quality changed: thus also Luther and Philippus explaining this place of Paul they clearly affirm that the substance of flesh and blood remains: but that the condition of mortality and infirm qualities are changed and abolished: and not only recent theologians, but also the ancient orthodox have expounded the words of Paul in this sense. Therefore, the καινολογία: of Illyricus is worthy of grave reprimand, by which he attaches new and foreign and prodigious opinions to Paul, so that he may gather colors from everywhere for his fiction concerning the substantial sin of origin. Let the reader consider the series of the Pauline disputation, and he will not obscurely detect the meaning. Let us bear, he says, the image of the heavenly: For flesh and blood cannot possess the kingdom of God: therefore the mind of Paul is that flesh and blood stand in need of renewal through the Spirit, and of resuscitation from the dead, so that it may reflect Christ in life and Spirit. Therefore the substance of flesh will remain, and the whole species of man, as much the matter as the substantial form: but the qualities will be changed, mortality will be abolished, and corruption being removed, flesh and blood will be clothed with immortality and heavenly glory.

Latin:

Hoc autem dico (fratres) quod caro & sanguis regnum Dei haereditate possidere non possunt: neque corruptio incorruptionem possidebit.

Exegesi declarat Paulus, cur nobis imago coelestis hominis sit expetenda, nimirum quia haec peccato infecta & corrupta natura non sit idonea ad regnum coeleste & aeternum, peccato enim & morti, seu corruptioni locus non est in conspectu Dei et regno spirituali atque aeterno. Necesse est igitur exui imaginem terreni Adae: necesse est purgari, illustrari, & restitui nostram carnem, necesse est peccatum & mortem extergi ex nostra natura: & in ea accendi iustitiam & vitam spiritualem, Ideò Paulus dicit. Caro & sanguis non possunt haereditate possidere regnum Dei, scilicet sine mutatione. Nisi caro fuerit mundata à peccato, et ornata novis qualitatibus non potest ingredi in regnum coelorum. Atque ideò filius Dei renovat nostram carnem & sanguinem corpus & animam, per Spiritum sanctum ut sit idonea ad regnum coelorum.

Veteres Manichaei & Marcionitae scelerate & impudenter abusi sunt hoc loco Pauli. Hac enim sententia Pauli astruere voluerunt, nullam fore corporum nostrorum resurrectionem. Quis verò pius non detestetur tàm profligatam haereticorum impudentiam. Cùm hac nobili concione Paulus gravissime refellat prodigiosum errorem, qui negat corporum resurrectionem, & evidentissimis argumentis demonstret, corpora nostra etiam resurrectura esse: tamen impudentes Manichaei, hinc sui commenti colores petere ausi sunt. Antiquitas autem graviter eos refutavit: Ireneus et alii docent Paulum non denegasse carni salutem: sed qualitatum mutationem postulasse. Caro & sanguis sine mutatione regnum Dei possidere non possunt. Ubi verò caro & sanguis resuscitata fuerint ex morte & vivificata Spiritu, tunc certe haereditate possidebunt regnum Dei. In carne enim mea videbo Deum inquit Iob. Et Christus Iesus corpus nostrum miserum, conforme faciet glorioso suo corpori.

Matthias Flacius Illyricus Manichaeos potius quam orthodoxam sequitur Ecclesiam dum hunc locum depravat, & contendit carnem significare ipsum peccatum originis, & ipsam corruptionem: Et ipsam carnem quodammodo abolendam, & in novam speciem nimirum in essentialem iustitiam, transformandam esse. Haec Manichaea portenta aliena sunt à mente Pauli.
