Non dicit Paulus carnem & sanguinem esse peccatum originis, sed hoc dicit, carnem & sanguinem corrupta esse: siquidem regnum Dei possidere non possunt. Diversissimae autem sunt sententiae, esse corruptum, & esse ipsum peccatum originis. Anima hominis corrupta est, sed non est ipsum peccatum originis. Nec dicit Paulus abolendam esse essentiam carnis & sanguinis: sed immutandas eius conditiones & qualitates, nimirum mortalitatem, & immundicem, & pravitatem. Evertit Illyricus fundamentum salutis nostrae cum contendit, essentiam carnis, quae sit peccatum originis esse abolendam: Iesus Christus non venit ad destruendam carnem humanam: sed ad destruendum peccatum & mortem in carne: & ad salvandum carnem: Iesaias inquit, Absorpsit Deus mortem cum victoria, & abtersit omnem lachrymam à facie omnium hominum. Non absorpsit Christus carnem, sed mortem quae grassabatur in carne. Quod fingit Illyricus Paulo idem significare carnem & corruptionem, et carnem esse ipsum peccatum originis, in eo conditorem carnis humanae adficit atroci contumelia. Solus enim Satanas est author peccati originis: Deus non est author peccati ullius, neque originalis neque actualis; Carnis verò & sanguinis etiam corrupti, conditor, conservator & reparator est aeternus & omnipotens Deus. Itaque caro licet corrupta, non est ipsum peccatum originis, sed est subiectum, in quo haeret foedissima labes peccati originis. Neque hoc dicit Apostolus quod caro & corruptio sint unum & idem: figmentum est hoc Illyrici. Caro enim significat subiectum corruptum, & in quo est corruptio: At corruptio significat malum, quod est in subiecto: et Paul: illa exegesi: (corruptio non potest haereditate possidere incorruptionem) sese declarare voluit, quod in praecedente sententia, non de abolitione substantiae carnis, sea de mutatione qualitatum dixisset. Caro quamdiu corruptioni obnoxia est, non est capax regni Dei. Ubi verò caro ab omni corruptione liberata fuerit, tum omninò possidebit regnum Dei: Evidens enim est testimonium Iob: 19. Circumdabor rursus cute mea: & spectabo Deum in carne mea. Ego ipse videbo eum, & oculi mei & non alius. Mendacium est igitur, quòd novi Manichaei fingunt peccatum originis esse ipsam carnem & sanguinem: mendacium est, quòd fingunt peccatum originis esse corruptam naturam: mendacium est carnem & corruptionem esse unum & idem sine omni discrimine: mendacium est substantiam carnis nostrae quodammodo abolendam & in novam formam substantialem transformandam. Illud verius est, quod Augustinus dicit, sic nos fieri idoneos coelesti dono ad incolendum coelum, non amissa natura, sed mutata qualitate: sic et Lutherus & Philippus enarrantes hunc Pauli locum disertè adfirmant substantiam carnis & sanguinis manere: sed conditionem mortalitatis & qualitates infirmas mutari & aboleri: nec tantum recentes Theologi, sed & veteres orthodoxi in hanc sententiam Pauli verba exposuerunt. Gravi igitur repraehensione digna est illyrici καινολογία: qua novas & peregrinas, & prodigiosas sententias adfingit Paulo, ut suo commento de substantiali peccato originis colores undique colligat. Consideret lector seriem disputationis paulinae, & non obscurè depraehendet sententiam. Portemus inquit imaginem coelestis: Nam caro & sanguis regnum Dei possidere non possunt: mens ergò Pauli est, carnem & sanguinem indigere renovatione per Spiritum, & resuscitatione ex mortuis, ut Christum vita & Spiritu referat. Manebit ergò substantia carnis, & tota hominis species, tam materia, quàm forma substantialis: sed mutabuntur qualitates, abolebitur mortalitas, & corruptione sublata, caro & sanguis induentur immortalitate & gloria coelesti.

## 15:51
Behold a mystery I tell you: we shall not all indeed sleep, but yet we shall all be changed: in a point of time,

Latin:

Ecce mysterium vobis dico: non omnes quidem dormiemus, sed tamen omnes immutabimur: in puncto temporis,

## 15:52-56
in the twinkling of an eye, at the last trumpet: for the trumpet shall sound: and the dead shall rise incorruptible, and we shall be changed. For this corruptible must put on incorruption: and this mortal must put on immortality.

After Paul refuted the absurdities by which the Sadducees and Epicureans were agitating the doctrine concerning the resurrection of the dead, and showed the distinction between the animal life and the spiritual life, he reveals a mystery to the world, as an Apostle by divine manifestation, and describes how the dead are to rise. For although it was fitting for us to assent simply to the divine promise, without any inquiry into either causes or circumstances: yet such is the goodness of God, that He often reveals to us both the manner and the causes of His counsel, so that we may be all the more prompt to believe His word, and every handle for doubting may be cut off from us. This manifestation, however, he calls a mystery: because the doctrine concerning the resurrection of the dead is unknown to all human reason, and has been revealed only by God.

We shall not all indeed sleep: That is, not all are to die: But some will be survivors on the last day: We shall all, however, be changed: Those whom the last day will overtake will not be transferred into eternal life with this kind of animal life and corruptible flesh. But they will be changed suddenly by divine power: from mortal they will become immortal: they will put off all the infirmity of this life: they will put on new light, eternal life, and immortality. For corrupt flesh cannot possess the kingdom of God. When Paul says, we shall all be changed, he expressly signifies that the substance of our flesh and blood is not to be abolished, but that its qualities and the conditions of mortality are to be changed. Luther understands the change both as a translation into another place, from earth into heaven, and as a change of quality, by which our bodies will be suffused with light.

In a moment of time, in the twinkling of an eye, at the last trumpet sounding: With incredible speed God will show the coming of his son from the clouds: the angels will gather all the saints from the four corners of the world: the son of God will most swiftly carry out his judgment: and will transfer his own into the heavenly and eternal kingdom. Paul also mentions the last trumpet in 1 Thess. 4 For the Lord himself will descend from heaven with a shout, and with the voice of the archangel, and with the trumpet of God: And Christ says John 5 All who are in the graves will hear the voice of the son of God. Therefore, by these so illustrious testimonies, in which both the circumstances of the resurrection of the dead are described, let us confirm our faith, and let us prepare ourselves for this joyful day of the coming of Christ from the clouds with serious repentance.

For the trumpet shall sound, and the dead shall rise incorruptible, and we shall be changed: Paul speaks of the faithful, whom he intends both to instruct and to console: Therefore he says that the dead shall rise incorruptible.

For this corruptible must put on incorruption: and this mortal must put on immortality: He repeats and explains what he said above concerning the change. As long as this flesh is subject to corruption, diseases, and death, it is not fit for receiving the heavenly kingdom: we shall therefore be changed, and indeed in this way: the substance of the body and soul is to remain: but it shall put off all infirmity, mortality, and corruption: for Christ shall wipe away sin and death from our nature: since they are separable evils. But the substance of our body and soul shall put on heavenly light, perfect righteousness, and immortal life. The resurrection of the dead, therefore, is not to be understood only concerning the renewal in this life, and the beginning of new obedience, but also concerning the resuscitation of bodies from the dead, and the change, clarification, and translation of our whole nature to the heavenly life.

When this corruptible shall have put on incorruption, and this mortal shall have put on immortality, then shall come to pass the saying that is written, Death is swallowed up in victory: O death, where is thy sting? And where, O hell, is thy victory? Now the sting of death is sin: and the strength of sin is the law.

This is the seventh member of this chapter, in which he first proves by two illustrious testimonies of holy scripture that God had long ago predicted through the Prophets such an abolition of human death, and a glorious victory, which will restore the whole Church now subject to death to immortal life. Then, however, he shows the cause of human death, and the use and office of the divine law.

When this corruptible shall put on incorruption, that is, when our mortal bodies shall have been resurrected from death and adorned with immortality, then will truly be fulfilled what Isaiah and Hosea predicted by the divine Spirit concerning the abolition of human death. As long as the bodies of the saints are still detained in the sepulchers, the prophecies of the Prophets concerning the abolition of death are not yet fulfilled.

Paul took the first testimony from 25. Cap: Iesa: The Lord will also take away on this mountain the face of the covering, which covers all peoples, and the veil, which covers all nations. For He has swallowed up death in victory, and the Lord God has wiped away the tear from all faces, etc. It is manifest that the whole discourse of the Prophet speaks of this immense benefit of the Mediator Jesus Christ, that He is about to blot out sin and death, and to destroy the works of Satan, and to bring back righteousness and eternal life. On this mountain, that is, in this kingdom, in this Church, which is gathered by the Gospel, God takes away the face of the covering, and the veil. Thus he calls death: for dead corpses are accustomed to be wrapped in linens, and thus to be hidden in the earth: and all nations are subject to this miserable condition. Therefore, by metonymy, he names death a covering, which covers all nations: as he soon explains himself in proper words. For He has swallowed up death in victory, the Son of God Jesus Christ undergoing death for us, and rising again on the third day, broke the universal power of death, blotted out its tyranny, and opened the way for us to eternal life: He who believes in me, he says, shall not come into condemnation: but has passed from death into life: and I will raise him up on the last day. And concerning the universal resurrection of the dead That the Prophet spoke is manifest because he adds, & the Lord God wiped away the tear from all faces.

Some wonder why Paul preferred to translate it passively: κατεπόθη ὁ θάνατος ἐις νῖκος: death is swallowed up in victory, which in the Hebrew is read actively. But I truly think that Paul was moved by a serious cause. The Apostle noticed that the pious had read the short saying of Isaiah with an ambiguous meaning. For the LXX interpreters read κατέπιεν ὁ θάνατος ἰσχύσας. Death has devoured, prevailing: which sentiment contains no consolation: but was also known to the Heathens, as:

Dark death calls all things under its laws.

But those who looked more closely at the mind of the prophet, read: The Lord has swallowed up death, prevailing, or with victory, gloriously overcoming death. And Isaiah wished to propose to us this sum of all consolation concerning the victory of Christ against death. Therefore, so that Paul might remove this ambiguity and show us undoubted consolation against the tyranny of death, he translated it passively, by the Apostolic Spirit, illuminating the prophecy of the Prophet. Death will no longer be the devourer of the human race, but death has now been devoured, through the victor and triumpher our Lord Jesus Christ, who gloriously defeated our enemies. This immense consolation will be demonstrated by the very resurrection of the dead. By this illustrious example, the Apostle Paul teaches us how Holy Scripture is to be expounded and treated: the Holy Spirit does not move λογομαχίας, in vain, but wills that the sense of Scripture be explained as plainly, simply, and clearly as possible, and that every ambiguity be removed: Paul did not change the opinion of Isaiah, but illustrated it remarkably. The other testimony is taken from the Prophet Osee Cap: 13. And the sense of both testimonies is the same, namely that through our Lord Jesus Christ, crucified, dead, and resurrected on the third day, the power of death has been destroyed, hell has been vanquished, and the way to heavenly and eternal life has been made for us. Because of the fall of Adam and the sin of the human race, death ruled over all men, it spared no one: no man, however endowed with nobility of birth, or wisdom, or virtue, was safe against the tyranny of death: all were equally compelled to obey this master: and it would have held us bound for all eternity, had not a liberator come to us. But there has been given to us the Son of GOD JESUS CHRIST our Lord, who undergoing death and

Rising by divine power, He broke the empire of death, destroyed, blotted out, and utterly swallowed up death: so that it can neither exercise its force upon the pious, nor detain our bodies in the sepulchers: For Christ is the leader and author of life and He will resurrect our bodies: and eternal life will suffuse us. Rightly, therefore, do the pious with the Prophet and Paul in the Spirit insult the most cruel and most savage tyrant, now disarmed, defeated, and led as a spectacle in triumph through Christ. Where now is your sting, O death? Where now is your victory, O Hell? Before, you used to insult us and laugh at our strengths and plans, which we agitated to drive away death: for you knew that we were wasting our labor: because you prevailed over us all. But now there is a change: We insult you and laugh at your threats and specters: for we know that you have been disarmed, and all your power has been broken through Jesus Christ. Dare now, if you can, to harm anything? Nay, you are compelled to serve our advantage: And Jesus Christ is our resurrection, through whom we mock you, and in the Spirit trample you underfoot. O Hell, before you used to open your horrendous jaws, and swallow everyone with an insatiable gullet. Where now is that vast abyss of yours? Where now is your immense tyranny and victory? By which you used to prevail even over all the most powerful Monarchs? Truly the Son of God Jesus Christ has torn your jaws, and led captivity captive: So that you are forced to dismiss the pious who believe in Christ with ignominy. For Christ leads our souls back from the underworld, and raises our bodies from the sepulchers, and transfers us into eternal life and the heavenly kingdom. Repentance (says the Lord) is hidden from my eyes: I shall never be led to repentance regarding this matter; I shall never change this will and promise of mine. As this is a most plain sentence of the Prophet, so it has been aptly and most conveniently adduced by Paul discussing the resurrection of the dead.

But that this passage of the Prophet is accustomed to be translated in two ways by interpreters, there is no reason why it should disturb or delay anyone. For the same meaning arises in both cases. And both interpretations provide the same consolation. And therefore Paul retained the customary reading. For that mockery of death absorbed by Christ and insult against the underworld conquered by Christ proceeded from the Spirit of God, and is full of consolation. Otherwise, in the sources it is held thus. I will redeem them from the hand of the underworld: and I will free them from death. I will be your plagues, O death: I will be your destruction, O underworld. These are the words of Jesus Christ, promising liberation from death and resurrection into eternal life to those who believe in him. The Son of God calls himself the plague of death: That is, a powerful enemy, and the victor of death, who is about to devour death, just as death previously devoured us. Since this consolation is most certain, we rightly mock death in the Spirit: and we say, Where now is your plague or sting, O death? Christ has killed you, and has been a plague to you: you are disarmed, we fear you no longer. Thus I will be your pestilence, O hell; that is, just as a savage pestilence instantly kills the most powerful tyrant, so I, the Son of God, the Messiah, will suddenly kill you, O hell, so that henceforth you shall not have tyranny over my own. Deservedly, therefore, we insult this defeated and oppressed tyrant with these words: Where now, O hell, is your victory? You boasted before that you conquered everyone with your strength, and that no one could be exempted from your tyranny. But now you are prostrate and defeated, victory has been snatched from you through Christ. Thus, the meaning and consolation are entirely the same, whether you follow the words of the Prophet, or the interpretation of the LXX and Paul. The words of the Prophet, adorned with distinguished metaphors, show the victor of death and hell more clearly. The interpretation of the LXX and Paul, with the distinguished σχήματι of speech, illustrates the fruit and immense consolation of victory. Therefore, effort must always be made so that we may properly grasp and follow the spiritual sense of scripture and the breadth of its consolation.

Paul attaches to the testimony of the Prophet an illustrious declaration of the doctrine concerning the cause of human death, and the office of the divine law. The sting of death is sin: the Holy Spirit compares death to a cruel tyrant, who is so armed with a horrible and very sharp weapon, by which he has finished off the whole human race: This weapon, because Christ, who was the plague of death, extorted it from death: therefore the pious insult death: Where now is thy sting, O death? But Paul now adds that this sting of death is sin. For on account of sin the human race was cast into death according to the threat. On whatever day you shall eat of that tree, you shall die the death. And Paul says Rom; 6. Death is the wages of sin. And Moses says: Psalm 90. For we have failed in thy wrath, and in thy indignation we have been troubled: thou hast set our iniquities before thy sight, our secrets in the light of thy countenance. Therefore the first man was not subject to death before the fall; Nor does the human race die rashly, nor by chance. Nor is the perpetual flux of matter rushing into other forms, or the Aristotelian figment concerning privation the cause of the death of men: but sin, which entered into the world through Adam, and clings to all men: since indeed the stain of original sin, most foul, and the most bitter root of all sins, is transferred by carnal propagation into all the descendants of Adam: it is the cause of death, and as it were the weapon by which death destroys us. But Christ wrenched this weapon from death: For He blotted out our handwriting, He expiated our sins, and as a sacrifice for sin He condemned sin: He cast all our sins into the sea. And thus He disarmed death, our most bitter enemy. Here Paul teaches and warns us that consolation and victory against death cannot be obtained, unless by faith we obtain the remission of sins through Christ.

The power of sin, however, is the law: Reason by itself does not see that sin clinging to human nature is such a savage and powerful weapon: for it does not understand the sublime judgment of God: nor does it see the magnitude and baseness of sin: In particular, it does not see the evil of origin. Without the law, therefore, sin sleeps in man, and lies at the door. But the divine law, which reveals the wrath of God from heaven, excites sin, and makes sin exceeding sinful. For it shows the most ardent wrath of God, which cannot be appeased by the service of any creature. It reveals the magnitude and foulness of sin, by which we offend the most holy God: it denounces present and eternal punishments, which we have deserved by our sins. There then ineffable terrors are kindled in the conscience: so that at the sight of our sins there is nothing more terrible to us. Truly, therefore, the power of sin is the law: for the law awakens sleeping sin: it brings knowledge and consideration of sin: and it works wrath; therefore, righteousness and life are not through the law, but rather the law is the ministry of death. For the law is the power of sin: sin is the sting of death. Thus the law convinces us that we are stripped of all righteousness, and full of sin: and it delivers us to the executioner, namely, death.

Latin:

in nictu oculi, cum postrema tuba: tuba enim canet: & mortui resurgent incorruptibiles, & nos immutabimur. Oportet enim corruptibile hoc induere incorruptionem: & mortale hoc induere immortalitatem.

Postquam Paulus absurda refutavit, quibus Sadducaei & Epicurei exaguabant doctrinam de resurrectione mortuorum. & discrimen monstravit inter vitam animalem, & vitam spiritualem, mysterium revelat mundo, tanquam Apostolus ex patefactione divina, & deseribit quomodo mortui sint resurrecturi. Etsi enim decebat nos simpliciter adsentiri promissioni divinae, sine omni inquisitione vel causarum, vel circumstantiarum: tamen tanta est Dei bonitas, ut nobis saepè & modum & causas sui consilii patefaciat, ut tantò promptiores simus ad credendum eius verbo, & omnis nobis ansa dubitandi praescindatur. Hanc verò patefactionem nominat mysterium: quia universae rationi humanae ignota est doctrina de resurrectione mortuorum, & tantum divinitus est revelata.

Non omnes quidem dormiemus: Id est, non omnes morituri sunt: Sed aliqui erunt superstites die novissimo: Omnes tamen immutabimur: Illi, quos comprehendet dies novissimus, non transferentur in vitam aeternam cum huiusmodi animali vita, & corruptibili carne. Sed subitò divina virtute immutabuntur: ex mortalibus fient immortales: exuent omnem infirmitatem huius vitae: induent novam lucem, vitam aeternam, & immortalitatem. Nam caro corrupta regnum Dei possidere non potest. Cùm Paulus dicit, omnes immutabimur, disertè significat non esse abolendam carnis & sanguinis nostri substantiam, sed mutatum iri eius qualitates & mortalitatis conditiones. Lutherus mutationem intelligit, & de translatione in alium locum, ex terra in coelum, & de mutatione qualitatis, qua corpora nostra luce perfundentur.

In puncto temporis in nictu oculi, postrema canente tuba: Incredibili celeritate Deus ostendet è nubibus filii sui adventum: angeli colligent omnes sanctos è quatuor plagis mundi: filius Dei celerrimè suum peraget iudicium: & suos transferet in regnum coeleste & aeternum. Ultimae tubae meminit Paulus etiam 1. ad Thessalo: 4.Quoniam ipse Dominus cum clamore, & voce archangeli, & cum tuba Dei descendet de coelo: Et Christus Ioan: 5.inquit. Omnes, qui sunt in monumentis, audient vocem filii Dei. His ergò tam illustribus testimoniis, in quibus & circumstantiae resurrectionis mortuorum describuntur, fidem nostram confirmemus, & ad laetum hunc diem adventus Christi è nubibus seria nos praeparemus poenitentia.

Tuba enim canet, & mortui resurgent incorruptibiles, & nos immutabimur: De fidelibus loquitur Paulus, quos & erudire & consolari instituit: Ideò dicit incorruptibiles resurrecturos mortuos.

Oportet enim corruptibile hoc induere incorruptionem: & mortale hoc induere immortalitatem: Repetit & exponit, quod suprà dixit de mutatione. Quandiu haec caro obnoxia est corruptioni, morbis, & morti, non est idonea ad regnum coeleste percipiendum: mutabimur igitur, & quidem ita: substantia corporis & animae mansura est: sed haec exuet omnem infirmitatem, mortalitatem, & corruptionem: Christus enim exterget ex nostra natura peccatum & mortem: siquidem sunt separabila mala. Induet autem substantia corporis & animae nostrae lucem coelestem, iusticiam perfectam, et immortalem vitam. Resurrectio igitur mortuorum, non tantum de renovatione in hac vita, & inchoatione novae obedientiae, intelligenda est, sed etiam de corporum resuscitatione ex mortuis, & totius naturae nostrae mutatione, clarificatione & ad coelestem vitam translatione.

Quando verò corruptibile hoc induerit incorruptionem, & mortale hoc induerit immortalitatem, tunc fiet sermo, qui scriptus est, absorpta est mors cum victoria: Ubi est mors aculeus tuus: Et ubi est infernè victoria tua? Aculeus autem mortis peccatum est: virtus autem peccati lex est.

Septimum est hoc membrum huius capitis, in quo primùm duobus illustribus testimoniis sacrae scripturae probat, Deum per Prophetas dudum praedixisse talem abolitionem mortis humanae, & victoriam gloriosam, quae universam Ecclesiam nunc morti obnoxiam vitae immortali restituet. Deinde verò monstrat causam mortis humanae, & usum atque officium legis divinae.

Cùm corruptibile hoc induet incorruptionem, hoc est, ubi corpora nostra mortalia resuscitata fuerint ex morte & ornata immortalitate, tum verè erit impletum, quod Iesaias & Osee de abolitione mortis humanae divino Spiritu praedixerunt. Quandiu corpora sanctorum detinentur adhuc in sepulchris, nondum sunt impleta Prophetarum vaticinia de abolitione mortis.

Primum testimonium desumpsit Paulus ex 25. Cap: Iesa: Tollet quoque Dominus in monte isto faciem involucri, quòd involvit omnes populos, & operimentum, quod operit omnes gentes. Absorpsit enim mortem cum victoria, & abster sit Dominus Deus lachrymam ab omnibus faciebus, &c. Manifestum est totam Prophetae concionem loqui de immenso hoc beneficio Mediatoris Iesu Christi, quod deleturus sit peccatum & mortem, & destructurus opera Satanae, & reducturus iustitiam & vitam aeternam. In hoc monte, id est, in hoc regno, in hac Ecclesia, quae Evangelio colligitur praecipit abit Deus faciem involucri, & operimentum. Sic appellat mortem: linteis enim involvi solent mortua cadavera, & sic in terram recondi: & huic miserae conditioni omnes gentes sunt obnoxiae. Per metonymiam igitur mortem nominat tegumentum, quod omnes gentes tegat: ut mox propriis verbis sese exponit. Absorpsit enim mortem cum victoria, filius Dei Iesus Christus subiens mortem pro nobis, & resurgens tertia die, fregit universam potentiam mortis, delevit eius tyrannidem, & viam nobis patefecit ad vitam aeternam: Qui credit in me inquit, in condemnationem non veniet: sed de morte in vitam transivit: & ego resuscitabo eum in novissimo die. Ac de universali mortuorum resurrectionem locutum esse Prophetam manifestum est quia addit, & abstersit dominus Deus lachrymam abomnium faciebus.

Mirantur aliqui, cur Paulus maluerit passivè transferre: κατεπόθη ὁ θάνατος ἐις νῖκος: absorpta est mors cum victoria, quod in Hebraeo legit activè. Ego verò existimo Paulum gravi causa motum esse. Animadvertit Apostolus pios ambiguo sensu legisse breve dictum lesaiae. Nam LXX. interpretes legerunt κατέπιεν ὁ θάνατος ἰσχύσας. Devoravit mors praevalescens: quae sententia nullam continet consolationem: sed etiam Ethnicis nota fuit, ut:

Omnia sub leges mors vocat atra suas.

Qui verò propius mentem propheta adspexerunt, legerunt. Dominus absorpsit mortem praevale scens, velcum victoria, gloriosè superans mortem. Atque hanc omnium summam consolationem de victoria Christi contra mortem nobis proponere voluit Iesaias. Ut igitur Paulus tolleret hanc ambiguitatem & monstraret nobis indubitatam consolationem contra tyrannidem mortis passivè transtulit, Apostolico Spiritu, illustrans vaticinium Prophetae. Non amplius mors erit devorator generis humani, sed mors iam devorata est, per victorem & triumphatorem dominum nostrum Iesum Christum, qui hostes nostros gloriosè devicit. Haec immensae consolatio demonstrabitur, ipsa resurrectione mortuorum. Hoc illustri exemplo docet nos Apostolus Paulus, quomodo sit exponenda & tractandae sacra scriptura: Spiritus sanctus non movet inanes λογομαχίας, sed vult ut quàm planissimè, simplicissimè & clarissimè sensus scripturae explicetur, & omnis tollatur ambiguitas: non mutavit sententiam Iesaiae Paulus, sed eam insigniter illustravit. Alterum testimonium sumptum est ex Propheta Osee Cap: 13. Estque utriusque testimonii idem sensus, nimirum per dominum nostrum Iesum Christum crucifixum, mortuum & resuscitatum tertia die destructam esse potentiam mortis, debellatum esse infernum, & viam nobis factam esse ad vitam coelestem & aeternam. Propter lapsum Adae, & peccatum generis humani, mors dominabatur in omnes homines, nemini parcebat: nemo hominum quantavis vel nobilitate generis, velsapientia, vel virtute praeditus esset, tutus erat contra mortis tyrannidem: omnes pariter huic domino parere cogebantur: & in omnem aeternitatem tenuisset nos devinctos, nisi contigisset nobis liberator. Datus autem nobis est filius DEI IESUS CHRITUS dominus noster, qui subiens mortem &

resurgens divina virtute, fregit mortis imperium, destruxit, delevit, & prorsus absorpsit mortem: ita ut nec in pios vim suam exercere, nec corpora nostra in sepulchris detinere possit: Nam Christus dux & author vitae & resuscitabit nostra corpora: & vita aeterna nos perfundet. Rectè ergò pii cum Propheta & Paulo in Spiritu insultant tyranno crudelissimo & savissimo per Christum nunc exarmato, devicto, & prospectaculo in triumpho ducto. Ubi nunc est aculeus tuus ô mors? Ubi nunc est victoria tua ô Inferne? Antea nobis insultabas & ridebas nostras vires & consilia, quae agitabamus, ad pellendam mortem: sciebas enim nos ludere operam: quia praevalebas nobis omnibus. At nunc vicissitudo est: Insultamus tibi & ridemus tuas minas & spectra: scimus enim te exarmatum esse, & totam tuam potentiam fractam esse per Iesum Christum. Aude nunc, si potes nocere quidquam? Imò nostro commodo servire cogeris: Et Iesus Christus nostra est resurrectio, per quem tibi illudimus, & Spiritute conculcamus. O inferne ante à horrendas tuas fauces pandebas, & omnes absorbebas inexplebili gula. Ubi nunc est vastus ille tuus gurges? Ubi nunc est immanis tua tyrannis et victoria? Qua omnibus etiam potentissimis Monarchis praevale scebas? Nimirum filius Dei Iesus Christus fauces tuas dilaniavit, & captivam duxit captivitatem: Ita ut pios in Christum credentes cum ignominia dimittere cogaris. Christus enim ex inferis reducit anima nostras, & ex sepulchris resuscitat corpora nostra, & transfert nos in vitam aeternam & regnum coeleste. Poenitentia (inquit Dominus) abs condita est ab oculis meis: nunquam ducar ego poenitentia super hac re;nunquam mutabo meam hanc voluntatem & promissionem. Haec ut est planissima sententia Prophetae, ita à Paulo disserente de resurrectione mortuorum concinnè & commodissimè adducta est.

Quòd verò hic Prophetae locus bifariam transferri solet ab interpretibus, non est, quod quenquam turbet aut remoretur. Eadem enim sententia surgit utrobique. Et utraque interpretatio eandem suppeditat consolationem. Ideoque Paul: usitatam lectionem retinuit. Illa enim irrisio mortis per Christum absorptae & insultatio contra infernum per Christum debellatum à Spiritu Dei profecta est, & plena est consolationis. Alioquin in fontibus sic habetur. De manu inferorum redimam eos: & de morte liberabo eos. Ero pestes tuae mors: ero lues tua inferne. Verba sunt Iesu Christi, promittentis liberationem ex morte & resurrectionem in vitam aeternam iis, qui credunt in ipsum. Filius Dei nominat se pestem mortis: Hoc est, potentem hostem, & victorem mortis, qui devoraturus sit mortem, quemadmodum mors antea nos devoravit. Haec consolatio cùm sit certissima, rectè illudimus Spiritu morti: & dicimus, Ubi nunc est pestis vel stimulus tuus ò mors? Christus te interfecit, & tibi fuit pestis: exarmata es, nihil te iam metuimus. Sic ero lues tua inferne; hoc est, sicuti saeva lues è vestigio enecat potentissimum tyrannum, ita ego filius Dei Messias subitò interficiam te infernum, ut deinceps tyrannidem in meos non sis habiturus. Meritò igitur insultamus huic devicto & oppresso tyranno his verbis: Ubi nunc est inferne victoria tua? Gloriabaris antea te omnes vincere robore tuo, & neminem tuae tyrannidi eximi posse. At nunc prostratus & devictus es, erepta est tibi victoria per Christum. Ita prorsus eadem est sententia & consolatio, sive Prophetae verba, sive LXX & Pauli interpretationem sequaris Prophetae verba insignibus metaphoris ornata, victorem mortis & inferni clarius monstrant. LXX & Pauli interpretatio insigni σχήματι orationis victoriae fructum & consolationem immensam illustrat. Semper ergò danda est opera, ut spiritualem scripturae sensum & amplitudinem consolationis probè teneamus et sequamur.

Testimonio Prophetae attexit Paulus illustrem declarationem doctrinae de cause mortis humanae, & officio legis divinae. Aculeus mortis peccatum est: Spiritus sanctus confert mortem truci tyranno, qui horribili & praeacuto telo sic armatus, quo confecerit totum genus humanum: Hoc telum, quia extorsit morti Christus, qui fuit pestis mortis: idcircò insultant pii morti: Ubi nunc est mors telum tuum? Paulus verò nunc addit hoc telum mortis esse peccatum. Nam propter peccatum genus humanum coniectum est in mortem iuxta comminationem. Quacunque die comederis de arbore ista, morte morieris. Et Paulus Rom; 6inquit. Mors est stipendium peccati. Et Moses inquit: Psalm 90. Quoniam desecimus in ira tua, & in indignatione tua turbati sumus: posuisti iniquitates nostras in conspectu tuo, occulta nostra in lumine vultus tui. Non ergò morti obnoxius fuit primus homo ante lapsum; Nec temerè, nec casu moritur genus humanum. Nec perpetuus fluxus materiae ruentis ad alias formas, vel Aristotelicum figmentum de privatione est causa mortis hominum: sed peccatum, quod per Adam intravit in mundum, & in omnibus haeret hominibus: siquidem peccatum originis labes foedissima, & radix amarissima omnium peccatorum carnali propagatione transfertur in omnes posteros Adae: causa est mortis, & velutitelum, quo nos conficit mors. Christus verò extorsit hoc telum morti: Nam delevit Chirographum nostrum, expiavit peccata nostra, & hostia pro peccato damnavit peccatum: proiecit omnia peccata nostra in mare. Atque ita mortem hostem nostrum acerbissimum exarmavit. Hîc docet & monet nos Paulus, consolationem & victoriam contra mortem obtineri non posse, nisi fide remissionem peccatorum per Christum impetremus.

Potentia autem peccati lex est: Ratio per se non videt peccatum haerens in humana natura, tam saevum & potens telum esse: non enim intelligit sublime Dei iudicium: nec videt magnitudinem & turpitudinem peccati: Inprimis malum originis non videt. Sine lege igitur peccatum dormit in homine, & cubat prae foribus. At lex divina quae de coelo revelat iram Dei, excitat peccatum, & facit supra modum peccans peccatum. Ostendit enim ardentissimam Dei iram, quae nullius creaturae officio placari possit. Patefacit magnitudinem & foeditatem peccati, quo sanctissimum Deum offendimus: denunciat praesentes & aeternas poenas, quas nostris peccatis meriti sumus. Ibi tum terrores in conscientia ineffabiles accenduntur: ita ut conspectu peccatorum nostrorum nobis nihil sit terribilius. Verè igitur potentia peccati lex est: Lex enim excitat dormiens peccatum: adfert cognitionem & considerationem peccati: & operatur iram; Non ergò per legem est iustitia & vita, sed potius lex est ministerium mortis. Nam lex est potentia peccati: peccatum est stimulus mortis. Ita lex convincit nos exutos esse omniiustitia, & plenos peccato: & tradit nos carnifici, nimirum, morti.

## 15:57
But thanks be to God, who has given us the victory through our Lord Jesus Christ.

He concludes the whole sermon and disputation concerning the resurrection of the dead with a notable act of thanksgiving, in which he repeats and inculcates the chief consolation concerning the abolition of death and sin through Jesus Christ. It is indeed true (he says) that sin is the sting and cause of death: and that sin becomes sin exceeding sinful through the law: but praise be to the eternal and omnipotent God, who has given us the victory through our Lord Jesus Christ: for he has abrogated the law and redeemed us from the curse of the law, having been made a curse for us. He has taken away the sins of the world:

and destroyed death and hell and all the works of the Devil. This is our illustrious victory: for which I desire with my whole heart to give thanks to you, eternal God the Father, and to you, Son of God Jesus Christ, and to you, Holy Spirit, in all eternity.

Latin:

At Deo gratia, qui dedit nobis victoriam per dominum nostrum Iesum Christum.

Totam concionem & disputationem de resurrectione mortuorum concludit insigni gratiarum actione, in qua repetit & inculcat praecipuam consolationem de abolitione mortis & peccati per Iesum Christum. Verùm quidem est (inquit) peccatum esse stimulum & causam mortis: & peccatum fieri supra modum peccans peccatum per legem: sed laus Deo aeterno & omnipotenti, qui nobis dedit victoriam per dominum nostrum Iesum Christum: hic enim abrogavit legem & redemit nos à maledictione legis, factus pro nobis maledictum. Hic sustulit peccata mundi:

& destruxit mortem & infernum & omnio opera Diaboli. Haec illustris nostra est victoria: pro qua tibi aeterno Deo patri, & tibi filio Dei Iesu Christo, & tibi Spiritui sancto in omni aeternitate cupio toto pectore gratias agere.

## 15:58
Therefore my beloved brethren, be steadfast, immovable, always abounding in every work of the Lord: knowing this, that your labor will not be in vain in the Lord.

The eighth and last is this member of this chapter. With the disputation completed and the foundations of the doctrine concerning the resurrection of the dead demonstrated, he adds a serious exhortation, that the Corinthians and all the pious should diligently apply themselves to knowing the immovable foundations of Christian doctrine: and that they should constantly persist in the acknowledged truth: and not suffer themselves to be disturbed by fanatical opinions, nor allow themselves to be led into any errors. For he who will have persevered unto the end, this one will be saved. Paul warns by this exhortation that a sincere faith cannot be retained without struggle and conflict: for Satan stirs up various sects, and moves every stone, so that he may turn us from the simple truth. Therefore, the doctrine of piety is not to be known carelessly, nor is one to live securely, but the Holy Scripture is to be searched with great zeal, the solid foundations of the articles of faith are to be inquired into, fanatical opinions are to be prudently avoided, and the Son of God, Jesus Christ, is to be assiduously invoked, so that by his Holy Spirit he may lead us into all truth.

Abounding in the work of the Lord: After he confirmed them by the resurrection of the dead, he exhorts them to proceed strenuously in the ministry of the word, in confession, in love of neighbor, in patience, and in every work of the Lord to gather the Church and to illustrate the glory of God: and he attaches a most sweet and very noble promise. Your labor will not be in vain in the Lord: The blasphemous dogma, which denies the resurrection of the dead, as it takes away all consolation, so it extinguishes all zeal, effort, and will to labor in the Church and to do good works. For all our duties, all our struggles, all our labors lack fruit if there is no resurrection of the dead. Therefore, Satan could not devise any more pernicious dogma. But because Paul proved the resurrection of the dead with most evident demonstrations, he restored all consolations, and he wishes these to be perpetually in our sight. Although Paul especially considers the most grievous labors, dangers, and struggles of those who are in the ministry: yet he does not speak only of these, but extends the consolation to the universal labors and all the duties of all the faithful and saints. No one's labors or duties, or struggles, shall be without fruit: for a copious reward is laid up for the pious in heaven. He adds significantly, In the Lord; hinting that all the labors, contentions, pursuits, struggles, duties, noble deeds, miseries, and punishments of those who are strangers to the faith of Jesus Christ perish eternally and are without fruit. Hercules sustained great labors, but in vain: for he perished eternally with his labors. Hector fell for his fatherland: Miltiades exposed himself to dangers: Scipio, after noble deeds, bore the ingratitude of his fatherland with a great spirit: Camillus brought aid to an ungrateful fatherland: Regulus preferred to undergo atrocious punishments rather than break his word. All these labors are void and empty, because they were not undertaken in the faith of Jesus Christ. Therefore, it is not the voice of Cicero, but of all the impious who are in the world, that is most true and most sad; O the deceptive hope of men, and fragile fortune, and our empty contentions, which are broken and collapse in the middle of the space: he ought to have added and are entirely lacking in all fruit. But the labors of Moses, David, Jehoshaphat, Hezekiah, The struggles of Jeremiah, the contests of Paul: the exiles of Athanasius: the punishments of Ignatius, Polycarp, Vincent, Blandina, the dangers of Luther & the duties, studies, and efforts of all the saints, whatever they perform diligently, and whatever they endure patiently, by no means departs without fruit; but it will be compensated by eternal and immortal glory. Those who instruct many unto justice shall shine like the stars in the firmament of heaven. Dan: 12.

Latin:

Quamobrem fratres mei dilecti, firmi sitis, immobiles, abundantes, in omni opere domini semper: hoc scientes, quòd labor vester non erit inanis in domino.

Octavum & ultimum est hoc membrum huius capitis. Absoluta disputatione & monstratis fundamentis doctrinae de resurrectione mortuorum subiungit seriam adhortationem, ut Corinthii & omnes pii sedulò dent operam, ad cognoscenda immota fundamenta doctrinae Christianae: utque in agnita veritate constanter persistant: non patiantur se perturbari fanticis opinionibus, non sinant se duci in quosvis errores. Qui enim perseveraverit usque ad finem, hic salvus erit. Monet Paulus hac exhortatione fidem synecram sine certamine & lucta retineri non posse: Satan enim varias suscitat sectas, & omnem movet lapidem, ut nos à simplici veritate abducat. Non igitur oscitanter cognoscenda est doctrina pietatis: nec securè vivendum: sed magno studio scrutanda sacra scripsura: inquirenda solida fundamenta articulorum fidei: prudenter cavendae fanaticae opiniones: & adsiduè invocandus filius Dei Iesus Christus, ut suo spiritu sancto ducat nos in omnem veritatem.

Abundantes in opere domini: Posteaquam confirmavit eos resurrectione mortuorum, hortatur, ut strenuè pergant ministerio verbi, confessione, dilectione proximi, patientia et omni opere domini colligere Ecclesiam, & illustrare Dei gloriam: & attexit dulcissimam & valdè nobilem promissionem. Non erit labor vester inanis in domino: Blasphemum dogma, quod negat resurrectionem mortuorum, ut omnem aufert consolationem, ita extinguit omne studium conatum & voluntatem laborandi in Ecclesia & bene operandi. Omnia enim officia nostra, omnia certamina, omnes labores carent fructu, si nulla est resurrectio mortuorum. Itaque nullum perniciosius dogma excogitare posset Satan. Quia verò Paulus evidentissimis demonstrationibus probavit mortuorum resurrectionem, restituit omnes consolationes, & has vult nobis percetuo in conspectu esse. Etsi Paulus praecipuè intuetur gravissimos labores, pericula & certamina eorum, qui sunt in ministerio: tamen non tantum de his loquitur, sed extendit consolationem ad universos labores & omnia officia omnium fidelium & sanctorum. Nullius labores vel officia, vel certamina, erunt absque spuctu: copiosa enim piis reposita est merces in caelis. Significanter autem addit. In domino; innuensomnes labores, contentiones, studia, certamina, officia, praeclara facta, aerumnas, & supplicia eorum, qui alieni sunt à fide Iesu Christi, perire in aeternum & esse absque fructu. Magnos labores sustinuit Hercules, sed frustrà: Periit enim in aeternum cum suis laboribus. Hector occubuit pro patria: Miltiades exposuit se periculis: Scipio post praeclara facta magno animo tulit ingratitudinem patriae: Camillus ingratae patriae opem tulit: Regulus supplicia atrocia subire maluit, quàm fidem fallere. Omnes hi labores irriti & inanes sunt, propterea, quod in fide Iesu Christi non sunt suscepti. Non ergò Ciceronis, sed omnium impiorum, qui in mundo sunt, verissima & tristissima vox est; O fallacem hominum spem, fragilemque fortunam, & inanes nostras contentiones, quae in medio spacio franguntur & corruunt: addere debuisset & omni prorsus fructu carent. At labores Mosis, Davidis, Iosaphath; Hiskiae, Ieremiae, certamina Pauli: exilia Athanasii: supplicia Ignatii, Polycarpi, Vincentii, Blandinae, pericula Lutheri & omnium sanctorum officia, studia, conatus, quidquid praestant sedulo, & quidquid sustinent patienter, nequaquam abit sine fructu; sed aeterna & immortali gloria compensabitur. Qui erudiunt multos ad iustitiam, quasi stellae lucebunt in firmamento coeli. Dan: 12.

## 15:58 Places of Doctrine
Places of Doctrine.

1. The first and principal place in this chapter is the doctrine concerning the resurrection of the dead: And this chapter is the seat of this article: since the solid foundations of this article are shown here: and how the resurrection of the dead will be, is explained here.

2. Concerning the efficacy of the Evangelical ministry; that the preaching of the Gospel is not an empty sound; but that through it God works salvation in the hearts of men, converts wills, and illuminates minds.

3. The sum of all holy scripture, that Jesus Christ died for our sins: and rose again on the third day.

4. The histories of the appearances of Christ raised from death, by which his resurrection is demonstrated.

5. An illustrious example of the immense mercy of God: since he not only received Paul, the cruel persecutor of the Church, into favor, but also appointed him a distinguished Apostle.

6. A testimony of the grace of God, against the proud patrons of free will: Whatever good we perform is not from us, but from the grace of God, which is in us.

7. Concerning the cause of human death: which does not arise from a concurrence of atoms, nor from a privation of matter: but from sin, by which the human race offended the wrath of God. Through one man, he says, death came: namely, through the fall of Adam: Item, The sting of death is sin.

8. Doctrine concerning Original sin: that in Adam the entire nature of men is corrupted, and infected with sin, and made subject to death and corruption.

9. That Jesus Christ is the second Adam, to whom God entrusted and committed the entire life, justice, and salvation of the world a second time; who also restores and recovers for us those things which we lost in Adam, namely justice, light, life, joy, and eternal salvation.

10. Concerning the diverse forms of the kingdom of Christ in this and the future life. In this life Christ reigns sitting at the right hand of the eternal Father invisibly through the word and Sacraments, in faith and hope. But after this life He will bring the whole Church into the sight of the eternal Father: and then without word and Sacraments He will impart to us life, righteousness, and heavenly joy.

11. Testimony concerning the divine nature of Jesus Christ: for Paul confesses that all things are subject to Him, and testifies that He is the Son of God.

12. Concerning the glorious kingdom of Jesus Christ, that He will be the victor over all His enemies: tyrants, heretics, the world, sin, Satan, death, and hell.

13. Concerning the destruction and abolition of all kingdoms and empires in the world.

14. Concerning the various calamities and miseries to which the Apostles and all the pious are exposed in this life; that at every hour they are exposed to most atrocious dangers, and are cruelly treated in the world.

15. That evil communications corrupt good manners.

16. That there will be distinct degrees of glory for the saints in eternal life.

17. That our bodies will rise again, and will live spiritually, adorned with admirable light, strength, and immortality.

18. Concerning the distinction between the animal life, which began in Adam; and the spiritual life, which the Son of God has merited for us and supplies.

19. Concerning the two natures in Jesus Christ: that he is true man, and the Lord from heaven.

20. Concerning the double image which is borne by the pious: of the earthly man, and of the heavenly man. We bear the image of the earthly, while by sin, weakness, mortality, and animal life we represent Adam the first man: we shall bear the image of the heavenly, when we shall not only have been renewed in this life by the Holy Spirit, into the same image of God from glory to glory: but also when we have been resurrected from death through Christ, and clothed with new light, righteousness, life, and heavenly glory.

21. That flesh and blood on account of sin and corruption cannot inherit the kingdom of God without change. Whence it is manifest that human nature is totally corrupted by sin and horribly deformed: and is in need of reparation and transformation through Jesus Christ and the Holy Spirit.

22. Concerning the use and office of the divine law: that God did not promulgate his law to this end, that we might be justified through it and obtain salvation: but rather to this end, that it might stir up sleeping sin, show us the uncleanness of our nature, denounce the wrath of God, and strike the conscience with terrors. For thus the law is the power of sin, while it makes sin sinning above measure, and through sin works death.

23. That the immense benefit of God, which through his son our Lord Jesus Christ gave us victory against Satan, sin, and death, and transferred us into the kingdom of light, is to be celebrated with true thanksgiving.

24. That the solid foundations of our faith are to be sought, and we must constantly persist in the acknowledged truth, and all kinds of corruptions and deceits of errors are to be avoided with great diligence.

25. That the labor of the saints is not in vain in the Lord.

Latin:

Loci Doctrinae.

1. Primus ac principalis locus est in hoc capite doctrina de resurrectione mortuorum: Estque hoc caput sedes huius articuli: siquidem solida fundamenta huius articuli hîc monstrantur: & quomodo futura sit resurrectio mortuorum, hîc explicatur.

2. De efficacia ministerii Evangelici; quòd praedicatio Evangelii non sit inanis sonitus; sed quòd per eam operetur Deus salutem in cordibus hominum, convertat voluntates, & illuminet mentes.

3. Summa totius sacrae scripturae, quò Iesus Christus mortuus est pro peccatis nostris: & resurrexit tertia die.

4. Historiae adparitionum Christi à morte resuscitati, quibus demonstratur ipsius re surrectio.

5. Exemplum illustre immensae misericordiae Dei: siquidem Paulum persecutorem Ecclesiae saevum, non tantum recepit in gratiam, sed etiam insignem constituit Apostolum.

6. Testimonium gratiae Dei, contra superbos liberi arbitrii patronos: Quidquid praestamus boni, non est à nobis, sed à gratia Dei, quae in nobis est.

7. De causa mortis humanae: quae non oritur ex concursu atomorum, neque ex privatione materiae: sed ex peccato, quo genus humanum offendit iram Dei. Per unum hominem inquit, venit mors: nimirum, per lapsum Adae: Item, Aculeus mortis peccatum est.

8. Doctrina de peccato Originis: quòd in Adam universa hominum natura sit corrupta, et peccato infecta, & morti atque corruptioni facta obnoxia.

9. Quòd Iesus Christus sit secundus Adam, cui Deus universam mundi vitam, iustitiam, & salutem secundo credidit & commisit; qui & restituat & recuperet nobis ea, quae in Adam amisimus, nimirum iustitiam, lucem, vitam, laeticiam & sempiternam salutem.

10. De diversis formis regni Christi in hac & futura vita. In hac vitaregit Christus sedens ad dexteram patris aeterni invisibiliter per verbum & Sacramenta, in fide & spe. At post hanc vitam adducet totam Ecclesiam in conspectum aeterni patris: & tum sine verbo & Sacramentis impertiet nobis vitam, iustitiam & laeticiam caelestem.

11. Testimonium de divina natura Iesu Christi: Paulus enim fatetur omnia illi subiecta esse, & testatur eum esse filium Dei.

12. De glorioso regno Iesu Christi, quod futurus sit victor omnium hostium suorum: tyrannorum, haereticorum, mundi, peccati, Satanae, mortis & inferni.

13. De interitu & abolitione omnium regnorum & imperiorum in mundo.

14. De variis calamitatibus & miseriis, quibus Apostoli & omnes pii expositi sunt in hac vita; quòd singulis horis expositi sint periculis atrocissimis, & crudeliter tractentur in mundo.

15. Quòd prava colloquia corrumpant bonos mores.

16. Quòd distincti gradus gloriae sanctorum futuri sint in vita aeterna.

17. Quòd corpora nostra resurrectura, & spiritualiter victura sint, ornata admiranda luce, robore, & immortalitate.

18. De discrimine inter vitam animalem, quae in Adam incaepit; & vitam spiritualem, quam filius Dei nobis promeruit & suppeditat.

19. De duabus naturis in Iesu Christo: quòd sit verus homo, & dominus ex coelo.

20. De duplici imagine, quae à piis gestatur: hominis terreni, & hominis coelestis. Imaginem terreni gestamus, dum peccato, imbecillitate, mortalitate, vita animali repraesentamus Adamum primum hominem: Imaginem coelestis portabimus, cùm non solum in hac vita renovati erimus per Spiritum sanctum, in eandem Dei imaginem à claritate in claritatem: sed etiam per Christum resuscitati à morte, & induti nova luce, iustitia, vita & gloria coelesti.

21. Quòd caro & sanguis propter peccatum & corruptionem sine mutatione regnum Dei haereditate capescere non possit. Unde manifestum est humanam naturam peccato toiam corruptam & horribiliter deformatam esse: & egere reparatione & transformatione per Iesum Christum & Spiritum sanctum.

22. De usu & officio legis divinae: quòd non hoc fine Deus promulgaverit legem suam, ut per eam iustificaremur & salutem consequeremur: sed potius hoc fine, ut ea excitaret dormiens peccatum, ostenderet nobis immundiciem nostrae naturae, denunciaret iram Dei, & terrores conscientiae incuteret. Sic enim lex est potentia peccati, dum facit peccatum supra modum peccans peccatum, & per peccatum mortem operatur.

23. Vera gratiarum actione celebrandum esse immensum Dei beneficium, quod per filium suum dominum nostrum Iesum Christum victoriam nobis dedit contra Satanam, peccatum & mortem, & transtulit nos in regnum lucis.

24. Solida esse inquirenda fundamenta nostrae fidei, & constanter in agnita veritate persistendum, & omnis generis corruptelas & errorum praestigias magna diligentia cavendas esse.

25. Quod labor sanctorum non sit inanis in domino.

## 16:1 Argument
CHAPTER XVI.

In this last chapter he treats of three things. First, he exhorts the Corinthians to contribute alms, by which the poverty of the Jerusalem Church might be relieved. And he explains his plan concerning his departure to the Corinthians: And he warns them to receive Timothy humanely, and not to hold him in contempt. He excuses Apollos, because he did not come to them. Secondly he repeats a grave and highly necessary admonition: That they should not be secure, that they should not learn the doctrine of the Church sluggishly, but should always be vigilant, persist constantly in the faith, bravely endure dangers and miseries, and show themselves to be men against the insults of Satan and of impostors. The last part is consumed with greetings.

Now concerning the collection, which is made for the saints, as I have ordered to the Churches of Galatia, so also do you: On the first day of the week, let each one of you lay by him in store, what he has prospered: that when I come, collections may not be made then for the first time. And when I am present, whomsoever you shall approve by letters, them will I send, to carry your bounty to Jerusalem. But if it be worth the while that I also go, they shall go with me.

Several places of scripture testify that the Jerusalem Church labored under great poverty. For in the Epistle to the Galatians the Apostles ask Paul to exhort the Gentiles to help the Church collected from the Jews, Gal: 2. And at Rom: 15. Paul commends the pious in Macedonia and Achaia, because they relieved the poverty of the saints in Jerusalem. And he adds that the Gentiles owe this duty to the Jews: since the Gentiles received the Gospel from the Jews. The heavy persecutions, without a doubt, which arose in Jerusalem after Christ was raised, and the famine which pressed the world under Claudius, which the prophet Agabus Act: 11. had predicted, had reduced the saints in Judea to such great destitution. Therefore, Paul everywhere diligently exhorts the Gentiles to come to the aid of the poverty and necessity of the saints in Jerusalem.

And by his own example he teaches that it is the duty of pious pastors to take care of the poor, and to diligently exhort the hearers of the word to come to the aid of the poverty of the miserable. But most worthy of all of the help and aid of the wealthy are those who are pressed by poverty and exile on account of the profession of the Gospel. And liberality toward the needy, as it is a necessary virtue in the Church, which is for the most part exercised by exile and poverty, so it is also proper to the pious: For those who are alien to piety seek only the things that are their own, and for the most part labor under greed.

But in those in whom sincere faith shines, and who are led by the Holy Spirit, these are moved by mercy, and strive to imitate the Father, who is in heaven, from whom they receive innumerable benefits. Therefore let the pious always be mindful of the most ample promise of Christ: Amen, Amen I say to you, If anyone shall have given a drink of cold water to one of these least ones, he shall not lose his reward.

Λογίας, Paul calls alms collected from the contribution of the saints. On the first of the Sabbaths, he calls the Lord's day, on which the pious were accustomed to assemble. For to refute the superstition of the Jews, the Sabbath having been abrogated, the Apostles instituted the Lord's day as distinguished by the resurrection of Jesus Christ, so that on it every week the Church might assemble to hear the word of God and to distribute the Sacraments.

But I will come to you, when I shall have passed through Macedonia: for I am to pass through Macedonia. But with you perhaps I shall remain, or even winter: that you may conduct me whithersoever I shall go. For I do not wish to see you now in passing: but I hope that I shall remain with you for some time, if the Lord shall permit. But I am to remain in Ephesus until Pentecost. For a great and effective door has been opened to me, and there are many adversaries.

He promises that he will come to Corinth, so that he may confirm them in person. And he sets forth the plans of his journey, so that he may signify his zeal in propagating the Gospel of Jesus Christ: and that he may shine forth to others by his example. He also commemorates the happy success with which the Lord adorns his preaching: so that he may teach that the Church is not gathered, and the Gospel widely spread, by human diligence, or prudence, or industry: but divinely. As in all other business, so especially in the ministry of the Gospel, it is true what Nazianzen says.

Θεοῦ διδόντος μηδὲν ἰσχύει φθόνος. Καὶ μή διδόντος οὐδέν ἰσχύει πόνος.

Paul therefore rejoices that a door has been divinely opened to him for widely spreading the light of the Gospel, and that God is effective through his voice. Meanwhile, adversaries, who either attempt to turn the minds of the simpler ones away from the purity of the doctrine of Christ by deceptions, or attempt to extinguish the light of the divine word and oppress the faithful ministers by tyranny, are not lacking. For it is Christ's to rule in the midst of His enemies.

Latin:

CAPUT XVI.

In hoc ultimo capite tria agit. Primum hortatur Corinthios ad conferendam Eleemosynam, qua possit sublevari inopia Ecclesiae Hierosolymitanae. Et consilium suum de profectione sua exponit Corinthiis: Et monet ut Timotheum excipiant humaniter, & non contemptim habeant. Excusat Apollo, quòd non venerit ad ipsos. Secundò gravem & summè necessariam commonefactionem repetit: Ne sint securi, ne oscitanter discant Ecclesiae doctrinam, sed semper vigilent, constanter in fide persistant, fortiter sustineant pericula & aerumnas, & viros se praebeant contra insultus Satanae & praestigiatorum. Ultimae pars salutationibus consumitur.

Caeterùm de collecta, quae fit in sanctos, quemadmodum ordinavi Ecclesiis Galatiae, sic & vos facite: In una Sabbathorum, quisque vestrum apud se ponat thesaurizans, quod prosperè obtigerit: ne cum venero tum primum collectae fiant. Ubi autem adfuero, quos probaveritis per Epistolas, eos mittam, ut perferant beneficium vestrum in Hierusalem. Quod si operae precium fuerit me quoque proficisci, mecum proficiscentur.

Hierosolymitanam Ecclesiam inopia magnae laborasse aliquot loci scripturae testantur. Nam in Epistola ad Galatas Apostoli rogant Paulum, ut gentes hortetur ad iuvandam Ecclesiam ex Iudaeis collectam, Gal: 2. Et ad Rom: 15. Paul: commendat pios in Macedonia & Achia, quòd inopiam sanctorum in Hierusalem sublevarint. Et subiungit gentes hoc officium debere ludaeis: siquidem gentes à Iudaeis Evangelion acceperunt. Graves haud dubiè persecutiones, quae exortae sunt Hierosolymis post resuscitatum Christum, & fames, quae sub Claudio pressit orbem, quam Agabus Propheta Act: 11. praedixerat, ad tantam egestatem sanctos in Iudaea redegerat. Passim igitur Paulus diligenter hortatur gentes, ut inopiae & necessitati sanctorum in Hierusalem subveniant.

Ac suo exemplo docet piorum pastorum officium esse curam agere pauperum, & diligenter hortari auditores verbi, ut inopiae miserorum subveniant. Omnium autem dignissimi sunt auxilio & ope ditiorum, qui propter Evangelii professionem premuntur paupertate & exilio. Ac liberalitas in egenos, ut virtus est necessaria in Ecclesia, quae plerunque exilio & paupertate exercetur, ita & propria piorum: Qui enim à pietate alieni sunt, tantum quarunt, quae sua sunt, & plerunque laborant pleonexia.

In quibus verò lucet fides syncera, & ducuntur Spiritu sancto, hi misericordia moventur, & patrem, qui in coelis est, a quo innumera beneficia accipiunt, imitari student. Sint ergò pii semper memores amplissimae promissionis Christi: Amen, Amen dico vobis, Si quis potum aquae frigidae dederit uni ex minimis hisce, non perdet mercedem suam.

Λογίας, vocat Paulus eleemosynas ex contributione sanctorum collectas. Unam Sabbathorum, vocat diem dominicum, quo pii convenire solebant. Ad refutandam enim Iudaeorum superstitionem, Sabbatho abrogato, diem dominicum ut insignem resurrectione Iesu Christi, instituerunt Apostoli ut eo singulis septimanis Ecclesia ad audiendum Dei verbum & distribuenda Sacramenta conveniret.

Veniam autem ad vos, cùm Macedoniam transiero: Macedoniam enim transiturus sum. Apud vos verò fortè permanebo, aut etiam hybernabo: ut vos me deducatis quocunque proficiscar. Nolo enim nunc vos in transcursu videre: sed spero me ad aliquod tempus mansurum apud vos, si dominus permiserit. Mansurus autem sum in Epheso usque ad Pentecosten. Ianua enim mihi aperta est magna, & efficax & adversarii multi.

Promittit se Corinthum venturum, ut coràm eos confirmet. Et consilia profectionis suae exponit, ut significet suum studium in propagando Evangelio Iesu Christi: & aliis suo perluceat exemplo. Commemorat & felicem successum, quo dominus praedicationem eius ornet: ut doceat non humana diligentia, aut prudentia, aut industria colligi Ecclesiam, & latè diffundi Evangelion: sed divinitùs. Cùm in omnibus aliis negociis, tum in primis verum est in ministerio Evangelii, quod Nazanzenus dicit.

Θεοῦ διδόντος μηδὲν ἰσχύει φθόνος. Καὶ μή διδόντος οὐδέν ἰσχύει πόνος.

Laetatur igitur Paulus ostium sibi divinitùs esse apertum ad latè spargendam lucem Evangelii, & Deum per vocem eius efficacem esse. Interea adversarii, qui vel praestigiis simpliciorum mentes avertere conantur à puritate doctrinae Christi, vel tyrannide lucem verbi divini extinguere & fideles ministros opprimere conantur, non de sunt. Christi enim est dominari in medio inimicorum suorum.

## 16:10-12
If Timothy comes, see that he may be without fear among you, for he works the work of the Lord, just as I do. Let no one therefore despise him, but send him on with peace, that he may come to me: for I expect him with the brothers. Moreover, concerning brother Apollo, I strongly urged him to come to you with the brothers, and it was not his will at all to go now: but he will come when it is convenient for him.

He urges the Corinthians to receive Timothy, a fellow worker of Paul, kindly: and to hold him in reverence because of the work of the Lord, that is, because of the preaching of the Gospel. And he forbids them either to disdain him because of his age, or to terrify him with arrogance. For just as the preaching of the Gospel is a most difficult work: so those who serve in it are to be strengthened with consolation rather than terrified with pride and harshness; lest the holy zeal and pious effort of propagating the Gospel be extinguished in them. One must not look to the person, nor to the age: but to the work which they exercise, which is not their own, but of the highest and omnipotent God, whose ambassadors they are to us, procuring our salvation. Then Apollo excuses himself, because he did not come to Corinth.

Latin:

Quòd si venerit Timotheus, videte ut absque metu sit apud vos, opus enim domini operatur, quemadmodum & ego. Nequis igitur eum spernat, sed prosequamini eum cum pace, ut veniat ad me: Expecto enim eum cum fratribus. Porrò de Apollo fratre, multum hortatus sum eum, ut veniret ad vos cum fratribus, & omninò non fuit voluntas nunc eundi: Veniet autem quum oportunum ei fuerit.

Hortatur Corinthios ut humaniter excipiant Timotheum Synergum Pauli: & reverenter eum habeant propter opus domini, hoc est, propter praedicationem Evangelii. Et vetat ne eum vel fastidiant propter aetatem, vel arrogantia terrefaciant. Ut enim praedicatio Evangelii opus est difficilimum: ita qui in ea serviunt consolatione potius confirmandi, quam fastu & duritie terrendi sunt; ne sanctum studiùm & pius conatus propogandi Evangelion in ipsis extinguatur. Non ad personam, neque ad aetatem est respiciendum: sed ad opus quod exercent, quod non est ipsorum, sed altissimi & omnipotentis Dei, cuius sunt legati ad nos nostram procurantes salutem. Apollo deinde excusat, quod non venerit Corinthum.

## 16:13
Watch, stand fast in the faith, act like men, be strong, let all your things be done in charity.

This is the second member of this chapter, in which he repeats and inculcates a most necessary exhortation. Satan incessantly lays snares for us, so that he may precipitate the secure and the incautious into either errors or crimes. Therefore, one must watch with zeal and prayer: sacred scripture must be turned over in the hands assiduously: the foundations of our religion must be inquired into: and the oracles of the Holy Spirit must be weighed. Jugglers must be prudently avoided: and God must be assiduously prayed to, that He may direct us by His Holy Spirit in the truth. Constancy also must be shown in the acknowledged truth, lest by levity of mind or ambition we either devise new dogmas, or approve those devised by others. Virile fortitude and the strength of the Spirit must be shown in sustaining the labors, dangers, insults, miseries, and temptations which are accustomed to happen to the pious. For in this contest no one is crowned, unless he has fought bravely and constantly and has obtained the palm.

He also repeats the commandment concerning the exercising of charity in every kind of duty: For this ought to be the moderator of all our actions and counsels. And indeed above he inculcated this commandment with many words: Here, however, at the end of the Epistle he repeats it, so that it may remain fixed in the memory.

Latin:

Vigilate, state in fide, viriliter agite, robusti estote, omnia vestra in charitate fiant.

Secundum est hoc membrum huius capitis, in quo repetit & inculcat maximè necessariam adhortationem. Indesinenter struit nobis insidias Satanas, ut securos & incautos vel in errores vel scelera praecipitet. Vigilandum est igitur studio & precatione: adsiduè voluendum est manibus sacra scriptura: inquirenda fundamenta nostrae religionis: & ponderanda oracula Spiritus sancti. Prudenter cavendi sunt praestigiatores: Et adsiduè orandus Deus, ut dirigat nos Spiritu suo sancto in veritate. Constantia etiam in agnita veritate praestanda est, ne ingenii levitate vel ambitione nova dogmata vel excogitemus, vel excogitata ab aliis adprobemus. Fortitudo virilis, & robur Spiritus praestandum est in sustinendis laboribus, periculis, conviciis, miseriis, & tentationibus, quae piis evenire solent. In hoc enim certamine nemo coronatur, nisi qui fortiter & constanter pugnaverit & palmam consecutus fuerit.

Repetit etiam praeceptum de exercenda charitate in omni genere officiorum: Haec enim esse debet moderatrix omnium actionum & consiliorum nostrorum. Ac suprà quidem multis verbis inculcavit hoc praeceptum: Hic verò in fine Epistolae repetit illud, ut haereat infixum memoriae.

## 16:15-22
I beseech you brethren, you know the house of Stephanas, that it is the firstfruits of Achaia: and that they have ordained themselves to the ministry of the saints: that you also may be subject to such, and to everyone that helpeth and laboureth. I rejoice, moreover, at the presence of Stephanas, and Fortunatus, and Achaicus: Because they have supplied your want. For they have refreshed my spirit and yours. Know them therefore that are such. The churches of Asia salute you. Aquila and Priscilla salute you much in the Lord, with the church that is in their house. All the brethren salute you: Salute one another with a holy kiss. The salutation of me Paul with my own hand. If any man love not our Lord Jesus Christ, let him be anathema, Maran atha. The grace of our Lord

Latin:

Hortor autem vos fratres, nostis domum Stephanae primitias esse Achaiae: & quòd se in ministerium sanctorum ordinaverint: ut etiam vos subiecti sitis talibus, & omnibus qui cooperantur & laborant. Gaudeo autem de praesentia Stephanae, & Fortunati, & Achaici: Quia defectum vestrum ipsi impleverunt. Refocillarunt enim Spiritum meum & vestrum. Agnoscite ergò tales. Salutant vos Ecclesiae Asiae. Salutant vos multum in Domino Aquilas & Priscilla, cum domestica ipsorum Ecclesia. Salutant vos fratres omnes: Salutate vos invicem osculo sancto. Salutatio mea manu Pauli. Si quis non amat dominum Iesum, sit anathema, Maran atha. Gratia domini

## 16:23-24
Jesus Christ be with you. My love be with you all in Christ Jesus, Amen.

The First to the Corinthians was written from Philippi by Stephanas, and Fortunatus, and Achaicus, and Timothy.

The final part of this chapter contains commendations of the saints, greetings, a warning, and a prayer. The commendations testify that the piety of those who perform duties for the ministers of the Gospel and for the saints is most pleasing to God: And that the Church owes gratitude to such people. Christ says: He who receives a Prophet in the name of a Prophet, shall receive a Prophet's reward. The greetings indeed teach that Churches everywhere ought to be concerned also about other gatherings of the pious, so that as members of the whole body they may protect the common salvation. The imprecation warns that hypocrites will not bear it with impunity, because under the pretext and appearance of piety, they seek what is their own: they study ambition, they accumulate wealth, they indulge in pleasures, they burn with contentions. But they are entirely alien to the true love of Christ. For they do not aid the edification of the Church, they do not illustrate the glory of CHRIST, but rather they excite schisms, promote false dogmas, afflict pious teachers, and deform the Church with scandals; against such he denounces anathema, that is, excommunication, a curse, and eternal damnation. For anathema has no part in the kingdom of Christ: but is pressed down by the curse of God. And here the Apostle Paul teaches that not only those are anathema before God who are excommunicated by public judgment and the voice of the Church: but those also who cover their impiety with an external appearance of religion: and with great art simulate a zeal for piety: when they are full of hatred for Christ and the truth: or are in such a place and rank in the Church that the thunderbolt of excommunication cannot be hurled at them. Although these may sell themselves or even be held as pillars of the Church: yet because they lack sincere love for Christ, by the sentence of the Apostle they are anathema, that is, a thing condemned by God and destined for eternal torments, unless they have been converted to God. Interpreters dispute variously concerning the added word Maran atha and most follow the interpretation of Ambrose, which says that Maran atha, in the Syriac language, signifies Our Lord comes. But to me this opinion seems to agree little with the preceding word: what need was there also for Paul to speak Syriac among the Corinthians? Therefore, the interpretation of Bibliander, Capito, and Burgensis pleases me more, who read Mecherem atha, and affirm that this word is the same as the Hebrew Cherem, that is, anathema. Therefore Paul repeated the same thing, anathema: Maran atha, or Maranatha. Anathema, you are excommunicated and cursed, you, namely, whoever you are, who do not love Christ Jesus the savior of the world. It is no wonder that the voice of a foreign language was either written differently by the Apostle or corrupted by the scribes. But just as he threatens hypocrites and the impious, so he prays well again for the pious. The grace of Jesus Christ be with you. Grace signifies the mercy of God and all the benefits of the mediator. He also testifies that he, as an Apostle, embraces with ardent love all who are in Christ Jesus, on account of Jesus Christ. But you, Lord Jesus, eternal God and redeemer of the world, kindle our breasts with your holy Spirit, so that we may love you with sincere faith, lest we become anathemas: but that, joined to you by the closest bond of the Spirit, we may see your heavenly glory, live with you, and celebrate you in all eternity, Amen.

Latin:

nostri Iesu Christi sit vobiscum. Dilectio mea cum vobis omnibus in Christo Iesu, Amen.

Ad Corinthios Prior Scripta Est Philippis Per Stephanam, & Fortunatum, & Achaicum, & Timotheum.

Postrema pars huius capitis, continet commendationes sanctorum, salutationes, comminationem, & precationem. Commendationes testantur pietatem eorum, qui officia praestant ministris Evangelii & sanctis Deo esse gratissimam: Et Ecclesiam debere gratitudinem talibus. Christus inquit: Qui Prophetam suscipit in nomine Prophetae, Prophetae mercedem accipiet. Salutationes verò docent Ecclesias passim de aliis quoque piorum caetibus debere esse sollicitas, ut membra totius corporis communem salutem tuentur. Imprecatio monet non impurè laturos hypocritas, quod sub praetextu & specie pietatis, quae suae sunt, quaerunt: student ambitioni, cumulant opes, indulgent voluptatibus, fervent contentionibus. A vera autem Christi dilectione toti sunt alieni. Non enim iuvant aedificationem Ecclesiae, non illustrant gloriam CHRISTI, sed potius excitant schismata, promovent falsa dogmata, adfligunt pios doctores, scandalis deformant Ecclesiam; talibus denunciat anathema, hoc est, excomminationem, maledictionem, & perpetuam damnationem. Anathema enim partem in regno Christi non habet: Sed premitur maledictione Dei. Atque hic docet Apostolus Paulus non tantum eos esse anathemata coram Deo, qui publico iudicio & voce Ecclesiae excommunicantur: sed illos quoque, qui externa specie religionis tegunt suam impietatem: & magna arte simulant zelum pietatis: cùm pleni sint odio Christi & veritatis: aut eo loco & gradu sunt in Ecclesia, ut fulmen excommunicationis in eos torqueri non possit. Hi licet se venditent vel etiam habeantur pro columnis Ecclesiae: tamen quia carent syncera dilectione Christi, sententia Apostoli sunt anathema, hoc est, res damnata à Deo & destinata ad cruciatus aeternos, nisi conversi ad Deum fuerint. Interpretes de voce adiecta Maran atha variè disputant et plerique sequuntur Ambro: interpretationem, quae dicit, Maran atha, in lingua Syriaca significare Dominus noster venit. Mihi verò videtur haec sententia parum convenire praecedenti voci: quid etiam opus erat Paulo Syriace loqui apud Corinthios? Magis igitur placet Bibliandri, Capitonis, & Burgensis interpretatio, qui legunt Mecherem atha, & adfirmant hanc vocem idem esse, quod Hebraeis Cherem, id est, anathema. Idem ergòrepetiit Paulus, anathema: Maran atha, vel Mecherem atha. Anathema tu excommunicatus & maledictus, tu scilicet quisquis es, qui Christum Iesum mundi salvatorem non diligis. Peregrinae linguae vocem vel aliter ab Apostolo scriptam vel à liberariis corruptam esse nihil est mirum. Ut verò hypocritis et impiis minatur, ita rursus bene precatur piis. Gratia Iesu Christi sit vobiscum. Gratia significat misericordiam Dei & omnia beneficia mediatoris. Testatur etiam se ut Apostolum omnes, qui sunt in Christo Iesu, propter Iesum Christum ardenti dilectione complecti. Tu verò domine Iesu aeterne Deus & redemptor mundi, accende pectora nostra tuo sancto Spiritu, ut te fide syncera diligamus, ne fiamus anathemata: sed ut tibi arctissimo nexu Spiritus copulati, tuam coelestem videamus gloriam, tecum vivamus, & te in omni aeternitate celebremus, Amen.

## 16:24 Places of Doctrine
Places of Doctrine.

1. It pertains to the office of pastors that they have regard for the poor in the Church, and often exhort the pious to contribute alms.

2. God requires this duty from the pious in the Church, that according to the measure of their means they relieve the need of those who, on account of the profession of the Gospel, endure exiles and are oppressed by poverty.

3. That those who handle the work of the Lord, and serve faithfully in the preaching of the Gospel, are to be received humanely and held in reverence: not to be terrified by arrogance or austerity.

4. That one must watch, indeed with eager zeal, to inquire into the solid foundations of truth: and with unceasing prayer, that we may be guarded by the Holy Spirit in the purity of heavenly doctrine. That one must persist constantly in the faith, and resist bravely both sectarians and the various deceptions of Satan.

5. Those who do not love the Lord Jesus Christ, even if they are not condemned by the public judgment of the Church, are nevertheless anathemas before God.

Θεῷ δόξα .

Latin:

Loci Doctrinae.

1. Ad pastorum pertinere officium, ut rationem habeant pauperum in Ecclesia, & saepè hortentur pios ad conserendas Eleemosynas.

2. Deum requirere hoc officium à piis in Ecclesia, ut pro modo suarum facultatum sublevent inopiam eorum, qui propter Evangelii professionem sustinent exilia & paupertate premuntur.

3. Eos qui opus domini tractant, & in praedicatione Evangelii fideliter serviant, humaniter excipiendos & reverenter habendos esse: non arrogantia vel austeritate terrendos.

4. Vigilandum esse nimirum studio alacri inquirendi solida fundamenta veritatis: & indesinenti precatione, ut Spiritu sancto custodiamur in puritate doctrinae coelestis. Constanter in fide persistendum esse, & sortiter resistendum cùm sectariis tum variis satanae praestigiis.

5. Qui dominum Iesum Christum non diligunt, etiamsi publico iudicio Ecclesiae non damnentur, tamen coram Deo sunt anathemata.

Θεῷ δόξα.
